steps.overview: This step builds the Linux and networking base that every later tool depends on: Docker, Kubernetes, Terraform runners and CI agents all run on Linux. The CKA and CKAD exams are done entirely in a terminal, so you must be fast with files, permissions, systemd, logs, Bash and network checks. By the end you should be able to debug a service that will not start, using only the shell.
objectives: Manage files, ownership and permissions with chmod, chown, users and groups
Inspect and control processes with ps, top, kill and signals, and manage services with systemctl and journalctl
Write safe Bash scripts using variables, loops, functions, exit codes and set -euo pipefail
Diagnose network problems with ip, ss, dig, curl and SSH key authentication
Debug a failing systemd service end to end from the terminal

concepts.explanation: Every file has an owner, a group and permission bits for user, group and others: r=4, w=2, x=1. chmod 750 gives the owner rwx, the group r-x and others nothing. On a directory, x means you can enter it and r means you can list it. umask removes bits from new files; the common 022 gives 644 files and 755 directories.

Users and groups are stored in /etc/passwd and /etc/group, and password hashes in /etc/shadow. Use useradd -m, usermod -aG docker alice (always keep -a, or other groups are removed) and id to check membership. A new group membership applies only after the user logs in again or runs newgrp.

Every process has a PID and a parent PID; view them with ps aux, ps -ef, top or pgrep. SIGTERM (15) asks a process to stop cleanly, and SIGKILL (9) forces it and cannot be caught. SIGHUP (1) often makes a daemon reload its config, and SIGINT (2) is Ctrl+C. Kubernetes sends SIGTERM first, waits for the grace period, then sends SIGKILL.

systemd is PID 1 and manages units. Service files live in /etc/systemd/system (admin overrides) and /usr/lib/systemd/system (package defaults). Key commands are systemctl start, stop, restart, status, enable --now and daemon-reload. Run daemon-reload after you edit a unit file, or systemd keeps using the old version.

journalctl reads the systemd journal. journalctl -u nginx -n 50 --no-pager shows the last 50 lines for one unit. -f follows new lines live, -b limits output to the current boot, -p err filters by priority, and --since '10 min ago' limits by time. It is your first stop when a service fails.

set -e exits when a command fails, -u treats unset variables as errors, and -o pipefail makes a pipeline fail if any part of it fails, not only the last command. Always quote variables ("$var") so values with spaces do not split. $? holds the last exit code: 0 means success and any non-zero value means failure.

Scripts tell callers about success through exit codes, and CI systems, systemd and Kubernetes probes all read these codes. Use if cmd; then ...; fi, [[ ]] for tests, and || and && for short-circuit logic. Exit code 127 means command not found, and 128+N means the process was killed by signal N (for example, 137 = SIGKILL).

A service listens on an IP and port, for example 0.0.0.0:80 for all interfaces or 127.0.0.1:8080 for local only. ss -tulpn lists TCP and UDP listening sockets along with the owning process. 'Address already in use' means another process holds the port. A service bound to 127.0.0.1 cannot be reached from other hosts.

dig example.com +short returns the A record; dig @8.8.8.8 queries a specific resolver. The resolver settings are in /etc/resolv.conf, and /etc/hosts overrides DNS. curl -v shows the connection, TLS and headers, curl -I fetches headers only, and curl -sf exits non-zero on HTTP errors, which makes it ideal in scripts.

Create a key pair with ssh-keygen -t ed25519 and copy the public key with ssh-copy-id user@host, which appends it to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys. Permissions matter: ~/.ssh must be 700 and authorized_keys 600, or sshd may refuse the key. Keep the private key secret, and use ssh -v to debug login failures.

keyFacts: Octal permissions: r=4, w=2, x=1; 755 = rwxr-xr-x, 644 = rw-r--r--, 600 = rw-------.
Special bits: setuid=4000, setgid=2000, sticky=1000 (the sticky bit on /tmp stops users deleting each other's files).
SIGTERM=15 can be caught; SIGKILL=9 and SIGSTOP=19 cannot be caught or ignored.
Exit code 0 = success; 1 = general error; 126 = not executable; 127 = command not found; 130 = Ctrl+C; 137 = killed by SIGKILL (common for OOMKilled containers).
After editing a unit file, run systemctl daemon-reload; 'enable' starts the unit at boot, 'start' starts it now, and 'enable --now' does both.
Well-known ports: 22 SSH, 53 DNS, 80 HTTP, 443 HTTPS; Kubernetes API server 6443, etcd 2379-2380, kubelet 10250.
ss -tulpn: t=TCP, u=UDP, l=listening, p=process, n=numeric (no name lookups).
Name resolution order is controlled by /etc/nsswitch.conf; /etc/hosts usually wins over DNS.

example.caption: health-check.sh: checks disk, memory and a service, and exits non-zero on any failure
example.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

SERVICE="${1:-nginx}"
DISK_MAX="${DISK_MAX:-90}"     # percent used on /
MEM_MIN_MB="${MEM_MIN_MB:-200}" # available memory in MB
fail=0

log() { echo "[$(date +%H:%M:%S)] $*"; }

disk_used=$(df --output=pcent / | tail -1 | tr -dc '0-9')
if (( disk_used > DISK_MAX )); then
  log "FAIL disk: ${disk_used}% used (max ${DISK_MAX}%)"; fail=1
else
  log "OK   disk: ${disk_used}% used"
fi

mem_avail=$(free -m | awk '/^Mem:/ {print $7}')
if (( mem_avail < MEM_MIN_MB )); then
  log "FAIL memory: ${mem_avail}MB available"; fail=1
else
  log "OK   memory: ${mem_avail}MB available"
fi

if systemctl is-active --quiet "$SERVICE"; then
  log "OK   service: $SERVICE is active"
else
  log "FAIL service: $SERVICE is not active"; fail=1
  journalctl -u "$SERVICE" -n 5 --no-pager || true
fi

exit "$fail"

pitfalls: Running usermod -G without -a replaces all of the user's supplementary groups instead of adding one.
Editing a unit file and then running only systemctl restart: without daemon-reload, systemd keeps using the old unit definition.
Using kill -9 first: the process gets no chance to clean up, so locks and temp files are left behind. Send SIGTERM first.
Relying on set -e inside if conditions, || chains or command substitutions, where it does not trigger as you expect. Check critical commands explicitly.
Leaving variables unquoted, such as rm -rf $DIR/*. With set -u off and DIR empty, this becomes rm -rf /*.
Assuming 'connection refused' is a DNS problem. 'Refused' means the host was reached but nothing listens on that port, while 'could not resolve host' points to DNS.

workflow.title: Debugging a service that will not start

steps.label: Check status
steps.detail: Run systemctl status myapp to see its state, exit code, main PID and the last log lines.

steps.label: Read the logs
steps.detail: Run journalctl -u myapp -b -n 100 --no-pager to find the real error message.

steps.label: Inspect the unit file
steps.detail: Run systemctl cat myapp to check ExecStart, User, WorkingDirectory and EnvironmentFile paths.

steps.label: Verify files and permissions
steps.detail: Use ls -l and namei -l to confirm the binary is executable and the service user can read its config.

steps.label: Check port conflicts
steps.detail: Run ss -tulpn | grep :PORT to see whether another process already holds the port.

steps.label: Run the command manually
steps.detail: Run ExecStart as the service user (sudo -u appuser ...) to reproduce the error directly.

steps.label: Fix, reload, restart
steps.detail: Apply the fix, run systemctl daemon-reload and restart, then confirm with status and curl.

project.title: linux-healthcheck
project.summary: A Bash health-check script checks disk, memory, a systemd service, its TCP port, DNS and HTTP, and exits non-zero on any failure. A systemd timer runs it every minute against a small demo web service. install.sh shows users, groups and octal permissions. The unit files show systemd services, timers and logging to journald. The README walks through a 'service will not start' debugging drill done only in the terminal.
project.run:
sudo apt-get install -y curl dnsutils python3   # Debian/Ubuntu; on RHEL use: sudo dnf install -y curl bind-utils python3
chmod +x install.sh scripts/healthcheck.sh
sudo ./install.sh
/usr/local/bin/healthcheck.sh; echo "exit code: $?"
systemctl list-timers healthcheck.timer
journalctl -u healthcheck.service -n 30 --no-pager

files.code:
# linux-healthcheck

Step 1 project: Linux, the shell and networking.

## What is inside
- `scripts/healthcheck.sh`: strict-mode Bash. It checks disk, memory, a service, its port (ss), DNS (dig) and HTTP (curl).
- `config/healthcheck.env`: thresholds and targets in KEY=value format. systemd and Bash both read it.
- `systemd/demo-web.service`: a tiny Python web server. It runs as the unprivileged user `demoweb`.
- `systemd/healthcheck.service` + `.timer`: run the script every minute. Output goes to the journal.
- `install.sh`: creates the user, sets owners and octal modes, then enables the units.

## Exit codes
`0` = all checks pass. `1` = one or more checks failed. `2` = a required tool is missing.

## Debugging drill (the checkpoint)
Break the service, then fix it using only the terminal.

1. Break it: `sudo chmod 000 /srv/demo-web && sudo systemctl restart demo-web`
2. Run the health check: `healthcheck.sh; echo $?`. The HTTP check fails and the exit code is 1.
3. Investigate step by step:
   - `systemctl status demo-web`: is it active, failed or restarting?
   - `journalctl -u demo-web -b --no-pager -n 50`: read the real error.
   - `ss -ltnp 'sport = :8080'`: is anything listening? Which PID?
   - `namei -l /srv/demo-web`: check the permissions on every part of the path.
   - `sudo -u demoweb ls /srv/demo-web`: test the access as the service user.
4. Fix it: `sudo chmod 0750 /srv/demo-web`. Then run `healthcheck.sh` again. The exit code should be 0.

Try these too:
- Port clash: start `python3 -m http.server 8080 --bind 127.0.0.1` first. Then restart demo-web and read the journal.
- Signals: `sudo systemctl kill -s SIGKILL demo-web`. `Restart=on-failure` brings the service back. A plain `systemctl stop` sends SIGTERM and does not trigger a restart.

## SSH to a lab VM
Create a key pair: `ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C you@laptop`.
Copy it to the VM: `ssh-copy-id user@vm`.
Copy the project: `scp -r linux-healthcheck user@vm:`.
The private key must be mode 600. `~/.ssh` must be mode 700.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Checks disk, memory, a systemd service, its port, DNS and HTTP.
# Exit codes: 0 = healthy, 1 = a check failed, 2 = setup error.
set -euo pipefail  # -e: stop on error; -u: unset variable is an error; pipefail: a pipe fails if any command in it fails

CONFIG_FILE="${CONFIG_FILE:-/etc/healthcheck/healthcheck.env}"
# shellcheck source=/dev/null
[[ -r "$CONFIG_FILE" ]] && source "$CONFIG_FILE"

# Defaults: ${VAR:-default} stays safe under set -u
SERVICE_NAME="${SERVICE_NAME:-demo-web}"
PORT="${PORT:-8080}"
HEALTH_URL="${HEALTH_URL:-http://127.0.0.1:${PORT}/}"
DNS_NAME="${DNS_NAME:-example.com}"
DISK_PATH="${DISK_PATH:-/}"
DISK_MAX_PCT="${DISK_MAX_PCT:-90}"
MEM_MIN_MB="${MEM_MIN_MB:-200}"

for tool in df awk systemctl ss dig curl; do
  command -v "$tool" >/dev/null || { echo "FATAL: missing tool: $tool" >&2; exit 2; }
done

check_disk() {
  local used
  used=$(df --output=pcent "$DISK_PATH" | tail -n 1 | tr -dc '0-9')
  echo "disk ${DISK_PATH} used=${used}% (max ${DISK_MAX_PCT}%)"
  (( used < DISK_MAX_PCT ))          # the last command's status is the function's return code
}
check_memory() {
  local avail
  avail=$(awk '/^MemAvailable:/ {print int($2/1024)}' /proc/meminfo)
  echo "memory available=${avail}MB (min ${MEM_MIN_MB}MB)"
  (( avail >= MEM_MIN_MB ))
}
check_service() {
  echo "service ${SERVICE_NAME} state=$(systemctl is-active "$SERVICE_NAME" || true)"
  systemctl is-active --quiet "$SERVICE_NAME"   # exit 0 only when the state is active
}
check_port() {
  echo "port ${PORT}/tcp listening?"
  ss -Hltn "sport = :${PORT}" | grep -q .      # -l listening, -t TCP, -n numeric, -H no header
}
check_dns() {
  local answer
  answer=$(dig +short +time=2 +tries=1 "$DNS_NAME" || true)
  echo "dns ${DNS_NAME} -> ${answer:-<no answer>}"
  [[ -n "$answer" ]]
}
check_http() {
  local code
  code=$(curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' --max-time 5 "$HEALTH_URL" || true)
  echo "http ${HEALTH_URL} status=${code}"     # curl prints 000 when the connection fails
  [[ "$code" == 2* ]]
}

failures=0
for check in check_disk check_memory check_service check_port check_dns check_http; do
  # set -e is ignored inside an 'if' condition, so a failing check does not stop the script
  if "$check"; then echo "  OK   $check"; else echo "  FAIL $check"; failures=$((failures + 1)); fi
  # Do not use ((failures++)): it returns status 1 when failures is 0, and set -e would exit
done

if (( failures > 0 )); then
  echo "RESULT: ${failures} check(s) failed" >&2
  exit 1
fi
echo "RESULT: all checks passed"

# Read by systemd (EnvironmentFile=) and sourced by healthcheck.sh.
# Format: KEY=value only. Do not use 'export' and do not put spaces around '='.

# Service and port to check (must match systemd/demo-web.service)
SERVICE_NAME=demo-web
PORT=8080
HEALTH_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8080/

# dig asks a DNS server directly. It does not read /etc/hosts, so use a real public name.
DNS_NAME=example.com

# Resource thresholds
DISK_PATH=/
DISK_MAX_PCT=90
MEM_MIN_MB=200

# /etc/systemd/system/demo-web.service
# A tiny web server to monitor. Logs: journalctl -u demo-web
[Unit]
Description=Demo web server for the health-check lab
Wants=network-online.target
After=network-online.target

[Service]
# Run as an unprivileged system user, not as root
User=demoweb
Group=demoweb
WorkingDirectory=/srv/demo-web
# Bind to localhost only. Port 8080 matches PORT in healthcheck.env
ExecStart=/usr/bin/python3 -m http.server 8080 --bind 127.0.0.1
# Restart after a crash or SIGKILL, but not after 'systemctl stop'
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=3
# Basic hardening
NoNewPrivileges=yes
PrivateTmp=yes

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

# /etc/systemd/system/healthcheck.service
# Runs the script once. If the script exits with a non-zero code, the unit shows as 'failed'.
# See the results: systemctl status healthcheck ; journalctl -u healthcheck
[Unit]
Description=Host and service health check
Wants=network-online.target
After=network-online.target demo-web.service

[Service]
Type=oneshot
# Variables are loaded from this file before ExecStart runs
EnvironmentFile=/etc/healthcheck/healthcheck.env
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/healthcheck.sh
# Run as a temporary unprivileged user (least privilege)
DynamicUser=yes
# stdout and stderr go to journald, tagged with this identifier
SyslogIdentifier=healthcheck

# /etc/systemd/system/healthcheck.timer
# Starts healthcheck.service every minute. Check it with: systemctl list-timers
[Unit]
Description=Run the health check every minute

[Timer]
# First run 1 minute after boot
OnBootSec=1min
# Then run again 1 minute after each activation
OnUnitActiveSec=1min
Unit=healthcheck.service

[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Installs the demo service, the health-check script and the timer. Run with: sudo ./install.sh
set -euo pipefail
cd "$(dirname "$0")"   # work from the project root

# EUID 0 means root
[[ $EUID -eq 0 ]] || { echo "Please run with sudo" >&2; exit 1; }

# System user with no login shell and no home directory
if ! id demoweb &>/dev/null; then
  useradd --system --no-create-home --shell /usr/sbin/nologin demoweb
fi

# 0750 = owner rwx, group r-x, others nothing
install -d -o demoweb -g demoweb -m 0750 /srv/demo-web
echo "demo-web is up" > /srv/demo-web/index.html
chown demoweb:demoweb /srv/demo-web/index.html
# 0640 = owner rw-, group r--, others nothing
chmod 0640 /srv/demo-web/index.html

# The script must be executable by everyone (0755). The config is readable by all (0644) because it holds no secrets
install -m 0755 scripts/healthcheck.sh /usr/local/bin/healthcheck.sh
install -d -m 0755 /etc/healthcheck
install -m 0644 config/healthcheck.env /etc/healthcheck/healthcheck.env

# Unit files belong in /etc/systemd/system. Reload systemd so it sees new or changed units
install -m 0644 systemd/demo-web.service systemd/healthcheck.service systemd/healthcheck.timer /etc/systemd/system/
systemctl daemon-reload

# enable = start at boot; --now = also start immediately
systemctl enable --now demo-web.service healthcheck.timer

echo "Installed. Try: healthcheck.sh; echo \$?"

revision.examFocus: No exam on this path tests Linux alone, but CKA uses it heavily. Its Troubleshooting domain (30%) has you fix broken nodes in a live terminal: kubelet down, wrong unit config, ports not listening. CKAD, PCA, DOP-C02 and AZ-400 assume you can read exit codes, logs, ports and DNS errors, and the GitHub Actions exam assumes Bash and exit-code behaviour in run steps.

compare.difference: restart re-runs the unit definition systemd already has in memory. Only daemon-reload makes systemd re-read edited unit files and drop-ins, such as kubelet's 10-kubeadm.conf.
compare.chooseA: Pick restart when only the app's own config (for example /etc/nginx/nginx.conf) changed.
compare.chooseB: Pick daemon-reload plus restart when anything under /etc/systemd/system or /usr/lib/systemd/system changed, including drop-in .d files.

compare.difference: Refused means the host answered with a reset because no process listens on that port. A timeout means packets got no answer, usually a firewall, security group, wrong IP or routing issue.
compare.chooseA: Choose 'check the service and ss -tulpn' when the error is refused.
compare.chooseB: Choose 'check firewall, security group or NetworkPolicy, and routing' when the error is a timeout.

compare.difference: dig queries the DNS server directly and ignores /etc/hosts and nsswitch.conf. getent and curl use the system resolver, so they follow /etc/hosts first.
compare.chooseA: Use dig to prove what the DNS server returns, for example which record type or which TTL.
compare.chooseB: Use getent or curl to see what the application will actually resolve, including /etc/hosts overrides.

compare.difference: SIGTERM lets the process run cleanup handlers. SIGKILL is enforced by the kernel and gives the process no cleanup. Kubernetes sends SIGTERM, waits terminationGracePeriodSeconds, then sends SIGKILL.
compare.chooseA: Send SIGTERM first, always, for graceful shutdown.
compare.chooseB: Send SIGKILL only when the process ignores SIGTERM after a reasonable wait.

compare.b: Explicit check (if ! cmd; then ...; exit 1; fi)
compare.difference: set -e is skipped inside if/while tests, && and || chains, and some command substitutions, so it is a safety net, not a guarantee.
compare.chooseA: Use set -euo pipefail at the top of every script as a baseline.
compare.chooseB: Add explicit checks around commands whose failure must stop the script, such as health checks and deploy steps.

cues.cue: Node shows NotReady
cues.pick: SSH to the node, then run systemctl status kubelet and journalctl -u kubelet
cues.why: On kubeadm clusters kubelet is a systemd service, and it is the most common cause of NotReady.

cues.cue: Container exit code 137 or OOMKilled
cues.pick: Memory limit exceeded or SIGKILL; raise the limit or fix the leak
cues.why: 137 = 128 + 9, so something sent SIGKILL, usually the kernel OOM killer.

cues.cue: Exit code 143
cues.pick: Process received SIGTERM (128 + 15), a normal graceful stop
cues.why: Any exit code above 128 means 128 plus the signal number.

cues.cue: Exit code 127 in a CI step or container command
cues.pick: Binary missing from PATH or image; install it or fix the path
cues.why: 127 means the shell could not find the command at all.

cues.cue: 'Could not resolve host'
cues.pick: DNS: check /etc/resolv.conf, nsswitch.conf and dig against the nameserver
cues.why: Name lookup failed before any connection was attempted.

cues.cue: SSH 'Permission denied (publickey)' with the right key
cues.pick: Fix permissions: ~/.ssh 700, private key and authorized_keys 600, correct owner
cues.why: sshd's StrictModes rejects keys in files or directories that others can write to.

cues.cue: Service works now but is gone after reboot
cues.pick: systemctl enable (or enable --now)
cues.why: start does not persist; only enable creates the boot-time symlink.

cues.cue: Pipeline in script hides a failure (e.g. curl | jq)
cues.pick: set -o pipefail
cues.why: Without it, a pipeline's exit code is only that of its last command.

scenario.situation: In a CKA-style task, node worker-1 is NotReady. You SSH in and systemctl status kubelet shows 'activated (auto-restart)' with exit code 1. A colleague had edited /etc/systemd/system/kubelet.service.d/10-kubeadm.conf yesterday and then ran systemctl restart kubelet. What is the fastest correct path to bring the node back to Ready?
reasoning: Do not reboot or rejoin the node. That wastes exam time and does not find the cause.
Read the error first: run journalctl -u kubelet --no-pager | tail -50 (or -xe). Look for a bad flag, a wrong config path or a missing certificate file.
The edited drop-in is the prime suspect. Fix the typo or path in 10-kubeadm.conf or /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml.
A drop-in file changed, so a plain restart is not enough. Run systemctl daemon-reload, then systemctl restart kubelet, and make sure it is enabled.
Verify with systemctl is-active kubelet on the node, then kubectl get nodes from the control plane.
scenario.answer: Read journalctl -u kubelet to find the bad setting, fix the drop-in or config file, then run systemctl daemon-reload, systemctl restart kubelet and systemctl enable kubelet. The previous restart had no effect on the unit change because daemon-reload was skipped.

memoryAids: Exit codes above 128 = 128 + signal: 130 = INT(2), 137 = KILL(9), 143 = TERM(15). Learn three signals and you can decode any of these.
Debug order 'S-J-P-C' = Status (systemctl status), Journal (journalctl -u), Port (ss -tulpn), Connect (curl/dig). Never skip the journal.
umask subtracts: files start at 666 and directories at 777. umask 022 gives 644/755; umask 077 gives 600/700.
cheatSheet: Unit file or drop-in edited: daemon-reload, then restart. Persist across reboot: enable.
journalctl -u <unit> -f follows live logs; -b shows this boot; --since '10 min ago' narrows the window; -p err shows errors only.
systemctl is-active and is-enabled return exit codes, so you can use them directly in Bash if-tests.
Refused = nothing listening (fix the service). Timeout = blocked path (fix firewall or routing). Cannot resolve = DNS.
dig bypasses /etc/hosts; getent hosts and curl respect it.
ss -tulpn needs sudo to show processes owned by other users; check that the listen address is 0.0.0.0 and not 127.0.0.1.
Bind address 127.0.0.1 means reachable only locally, which is a classic 'works on the box, refused from outside' cause.
Always quote variables: "$VAR". Use ${VAR:?} to abort if empty before any rm.
Add usermod -aG group user; the user must log in again (or run newgrp) for the new group to apply.
SSH key setup: ssh-keygen -t ed25519, ssh-copy-id user@host, private key mode 600.
kill -0 PID checks that a process exists without sending a real signal.
Script health checks: test, print a clear message to stderr, exit 1. Exit 0 only when everything passes.
selfCheck: I can find why a systemd service fails to start using only systemctl status and journalctl, and fix it, including the daemon-reload step.
I can decode any exit code from 126 upward and name the likely cause in a container or CI job.
I can tell DNS, firewall and 'service not listening' failures apart from the exact curl or ssh error text.
I can write a strict-mode Bash health-check script that checks disk, memory and a service, quotes every variable and exits non-zero on failure.
I can set file permissions and ownership in octal for SSH keys, scripts and shared directories without looking them up.
I can confirm which process owns a port with ss -tulpn and check whether it listens on localhost or on all interfaces.

objective.question: A config file must be readable and writable by its owner, readable by its group, and give no access to anyone else. Which command sets this?
options: chmod 750 app.conf
chmod 460 app.conf
chmod 604 app.conf
chmod 640 app.conf
objective.explanation: 640 is owner rw- (4+2), group r-- (4) and others --- (0). 604 gives read access to others instead of the group, 750 adds execute bits, and 460 gives the owner read only and the group read-write.

objective.question: A user's shell has umask 027. They run 'touch report.txt' and 'mkdir logs'. What permissions do the new file and directory get?
options: File 750, directory 750
File 600, directory 700
File 644, directory 755
File 640, directory 750
objective.explanation: Files start from 666 and directories from 777, and the umask bits are removed: 666 minus 027 gives 640, and 777 minus 027 gives 750. 644/755 comes from umask 022, and 600/700 comes from umask 077.

objective.question: You run 'systemctl stop myapp'. The application has a SIGTERM handler that flushes data, but it often takes several minutes to finish. What does systemd do by default?
options: Sends SIGKILL immediately because it cannot be caught
Sends SIGHUP and waits forever for the process to exit
Sends SIGSTOP and waits for the process to exit on its own
Sends SIGTERM, waits up to TimeoutStopSec, then sends SIGKILL
objective.explanation: systemd sends KillSignal (SIGTERM by default), waits for TimeoutStopSec, and then escalates to SIGKILL. SIGKILL is the fallback, not the first step. SIGSTOP only pauses a process, and systemd does not wait forever.

objective.question: You edited /etc/systemd/system/api.service to change ExecStart. You ran 'systemctl restart api', but the old command still runs and systemctl prints a warning that the unit file changed on disk. What did you miss?
options: systemctl reset-failed api
journalctl --rotate
systemctl enable api
systemctl daemon-reload
objective.explanation: systemd caches unit definitions. After you edit a unit file, 'systemctl daemon-reload' makes systemd re-read it. 'enable' only controls start at boot, 'reset-failed' clears the failed state, and rotating the journal does nothing to the unit.

objective.question: A service failed during the current boot. You want only its error-level and more severe messages from this boot. Which command fits best?
options: journalctl --disk-usage -u payments.service
systemctl list-units --failed payments.service
journalctl -f payments.service
journalctl -u payments.service -b -p err
objective.explanation: -u filters by unit, -b limits output to the current boot, and -p err shows priority err and above. -f only follows new lines and does not take a unit name like that, --disk-usage reports journal size, and list-units shows state but not logs.

objective.question: A script starts with 'set -euo pipefail'. Its next lines are: count=$(grep ERROR app.log | wc -l) and then echo "errors: $count". app.log has no lines containing ERROR. What happens?
options: It prints 'errors: 0' because wc succeeded
It prints 'errors: ' with an empty value because of -u
It loops forever because grep waits for input
The script exits with status 1 and never prints the echo line
objective.explanation: grep exits 1 when it finds no match. With pipefail the pipeline takes that non-zero status even though wc succeeded, and -e then stops the script at that assignment. Without pipefail the line would succeed, and -u only matters for unset variables.

objective.question: A container keeps restarting. 'kubectl describe pod' shows the last state as Terminated with exit code 137. What is the most likely meaning?
options: The container command was not found in the image
The entrypoint file is not executable
The application exited normally after finishing its work
The process was killed with SIGKILL, often by the OOM killer after exceeding its memory limit
objective.explanation: 137 = 128 + 9, which means the process was terminated by SIGKILL. This is the usual result of OOMKilled. Command not found is 127, not executable is 126, and a normal exit is 0.

objective.question: Nginx fails to start with 'bind() to 0.0.0.0:80 failed (Address already in use)'. Which command most directly shows which process owns port 80?
options: dig localhost 80
curl -I http://localhost
ss -tun
sudo ss -tlpn | grep ':80 '
objective.explanation: -t limits output to TCP, -l to listening sockets, -n keeps ports numeric, and -p shows the owning process. sudo is needed to see processes owned by other users. ss -tun shows no process information, dig does DNS lookups only, and curl only shows that something answers.

objective.question: 'dig api.internal +short' returns 10.0.5.20, the correct new IP. However, 'curl http://api.internal' on the same server still reaches the old server at 10.0.1.7. What is the most likely cause?
options: curl always caches DNS results for 24 hours
The DNS TTL on the record is too low
dig uses a different DNS port than curl
A stale entry in /etc/hosts, which the system resolver checks before DNS as set in /etc/nsswitch.conf
objective.explanation: dig queries DNS servers directly and ignores /etc/hosts. curl uses the system resolver, which follows /etc/nsswitch.conf and usually reads /etc/hosts first. 'getent hosts api.internal' would show the stale entry. Both tools use port 53 for DNS, curl has no 24-hour cache, and a low TTL would not cause this.

objective.question: You added your public key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on a server, but SSH still says 'Permission denied (publickey)'. The server log shows 'bad ownership or modes'. The file is mode 664. What fixes it?
options: chmod 777 ~/.ssh so sshd can read it
Set PasswordAuthentication yes in sshd_config
Copy the private key into authorized_keys instead
chmod 700 ~/.ssh && chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
objective.explanation: With StrictModes (the default), sshd refuses key files that other users can write to. Use 700 on ~/.ssh and 600 on authorized_keys. 777 makes the problem worse, private keys must never be copied to the server, and enabling passwords works around the problem without fixing it.

objective.question: After a bad deployment, a service crashed repeatedly. Now 'systemctl start worker' fails at once and the journal shows 'Start request repeated too quickly'. You have fixed the bug. What must you do before the service will start again?

code.code:
[Unit]
Description=Queue worker
StartLimitIntervalSec=60
StartLimitBurst=3

[Service]
ExecStart=/opt/worker/bin/worker
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=2

options: Run 'systemctl daemon-reexec' to restart PID 1
Reboot the server, because the start limit can only be cleared at boot
Change Restart=on-failure to Restart=always, because only that bypasses the limit
Run 'systemctl reset-failed worker', then start it
objective.explanation: The unit hit its start rate limit (3 starts in 60 seconds) and entered a failed state. 'systemctl reset-failed' clears the counter and the failed state, so a new start is allowed. A reboot also clears it but is not required. Re-executing systemd is not the intended fix, and Restart=always is still subject to the start limit.

objective.question: An API runs on a VM. 'curl http://localhost:8080/health' works on the VM, but other machines get 'Connection refused'. The output below is from the VM. What is the most likely cause?

code.code:
$ sudo ss -tlnp | grep 8080
LISTEN 0  511  127.0.0.1:8080  0.0.0.0:*  users:(("node",pid=2231,fd=19))

options: The application is bound only to the loopback interface, so it does not accept connections on external interfaces
The listen backlog of 511 is full
DNS for the VM resolves to the wrong IP address
A host firewall is dropping packets on port 8080
objective.explanation: The local address 127.0.0.1:8080 means the socket only accepts loopback traffic. The app must bind to 0.0.0.0 or to the VM's interface IP. A firewall DROP rule usually causes a timeout rather than an immediate refusal. A wrong DNS answer would not explain this socket output.

objective.question: This script runs on a host where /etc/app.conf does not exist. What is the script's exit status?

code.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
echo "checking config"
[[ -f /etc/app.conf ]] && echo "config present"

options: 1, because the test fails and it is the last command, so its status becomes the script's exit status
The script aborts at the test because of set -e, and 'checking config' is never printed
2, because [[ ]] returns 2 when the file is missing
0, because set -e ignores failures inside && lists
objective.explanation: set -e does not exit on a failing command that is part of an && list, unless it is the last command in the list. So the script is not aborted early. However, a script's exit status is the status of the last command it ran, and that is the failed test (1). This is a common reason for false CI failures. Use an if statement or add '|| true' when the check is optional.

objective.question: A health-check script runs: code=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' --max-time 5 http://10.0.2.15:9000/ready). The variable code contains '000'. What does this indicate?
options: curl received no HTTP response at all, for example because the connection was refused, timed out or DNS failed
The endpoint redirected, and curl did not follow the redirect
The server returned a status code that curl does not recognise
The server returned an empty response body with status 200
objective.explanation: %{http_code} prints 000 when no HTTP response was received. Check curl's own exit code to tell the causes apart, for example 7 for a failed connection and 28 for a timeout. A redirect would show 301 or 302. An empty body still reports the real status code.

objective.question: 'ps -eo pid,ppid,stat,cmd' shows hundreds of processes in state Z, all with the same parent PID 4120. 'kill -9' on these PIDs has no effect. What is the correct fix?
options: Free up memory, because zombies are processes stuck waiting for RAM
Remount /proc to remove the stale process entries
Fix or restart the parent process 4120 so the zombies are reaped, either by the parent or by PID 1 after the parent exits
Run 'kill -9 -1' to signal every process
objective.explanation: A zombie has already exited. It is only a process-table entry that waits for its parent to call wait(). It cannot be killed, so signals sent to it have no effect. Once the parent is fixed or exits, its children are re-parented to init (or a subreaper), which reaps them. The other options do not remove zombies, and 'kill -9 -1' is destructive.

objective.question: This line is added to /etc/sudoers.d/deploy using visudo. Which statement is correct?

code.code: deploy ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/systemctl restart myapp

options: deploy can run 'systemctl restart myapp' only on the host named ALL
deploy must still type the root password for this command
deploy can run only 'systemctl restart myapp' as root without a password; other arguments, such as 'systemctl stop myapp', are denied
deploy can run any systemctl command as root without a password
objective.explanation: When a sudoers rule lists a command with arguments, only that exact command line matches. 'ALL' here is the host field, and it matches any host. NOPASSWD removes the password prompt. This is a good least-privilege pattern for deploy users.

objective.question: User alice is currently in the groups alice (primary), sudo and developers. An admin runs the command below to give her Docker access. What is the result?

code.code: sudo usermod -G docker alice

options: alice's supplementary groups become only docker, so she loses sudo and developers
alice's primary group changes from alice to docker
The command fails because -a is mandatory with -G
alice is added to docker and keeps sudo and developers
objective.explanation: Without -a, usermod -G replaces the whole supplementary group list with the groups given. The correct command is 'usermod -aG docker alice'. -G never touches the primary group (that is -g), and the command does not fail without -a.

objective.question: In this script, the cp command fails because app.tar is missing. What does the script print, and what is its exit status?
options: The cp error, then 'deployed', then 'OK', and exits 0
An 'unbound variable' error from set -u
The cp error, then 'deployed', then exits 1 because the if sees the failure
The cp error only; the script stops at once with a non-zero status
objective.explanation: set -e is ignored for every command inside a function called as an if condition. cp fails, echo still runs, and the function returns echo's status 0, so the if takes the 'OK' branch. Check critical commands explicitly, for example 'cp ... || return 1'.

objective.question: A cleanup script must delete the contents of $DIR. DIR may be unset or empty because of a bug upstream. Which line is safest?
options: rm -rf "$DIR"/*
rm -rf "${DIR:?DIR is not set}"/*
rm -rf "${DIR:-/tmp}"/*
rm -rf $DIR/*
objective.explanation: ${DIR:?msg} makes the shell print the message and abort if DIR is unset or empty, so rm never runs. Quoting alone still expands to /* when DIR is empty. A default value such as /tmp silently deletes the wrong directory's contents.

objective.question: A worker process is hung and is not managed by systemd. Which order of steps stops it most safely?
options: Find the PID with pgrep, send SIGTERM, wait and check whether it exited, send SIGKILL only if it is still alive, then remove any stale lock or temp files
Delete the lock file first, then send SIGTERM, then SIGKILL immediately
Send SIGSTOP, then SIGTERM, then reboot the host if it is still running
kill -9 the PID, delete its lock file, then check with ps
objective.explanation: SIGTERM lets the process flush data and release locks. SIGKILL is the last resort because it cannot be caught, so cleanup may then be needed by hand. Deleting a lock while the process is still running can let a second instance corrupt data.

objective.question: After a reboot, this service fails with 'could not resolve db.internal: Name or service not known'. A manual 'systemctl restart report' a minute later works fine. What is the correct fix?

code.code:
[Unit]
Description=Report service
After=network.target

[Service]
ExecStart=/opt/report/bin/report
User=report

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

options: Add Wants=network-online.target and After=network-online.target
Change WantedBy=multi-user.target to WantedBy=network.target
Increase TimeoutStartSec to 300
Replace After=network.target with Requires=network.target
objective.explanation: network.target only means the network stack is being set up. It does not mean interfaces have addresses or that DNS works. network-online.target, pulled in with Wants= and ordered with After=, waits until the network is actually up. A longer start timeout does not delay the first connection attempt.

objective.question: You run 'curl -v --connect-timeout 10 http://10.0.3.4:5432' from an app server. Which result most strongly suggests that a firewall or security group is silently dropping packets?
options: curl: (7) Failed to connect ... Connection refused
curl: (28) Connection timed out after 10001 milliseconds
curl: (60) SSL certificate problem
curl: (6) Could not resolve host
objective.explanation: A silent drop means no reply ever arrives, so curl waits until the timeout. 'Refused' means the host answered but nothing listens on that port, or a firewall actively rejected the connection. Error 6 is DNS, and error 60 means the TCP connection worked and TLS failed.

objective.question: You run 'sudo usermod -aG app bob'. In bob's existing SSH session, 'id' does not list the app group, and he still gets 'Permission denied' on /srv/app. What is the cause?
options: Group membership is read at login, so bob must log out and back in, or run 'newgrp app'
-aG only works for system groups, so bob needs 'gpasswd' instead
The /srv/app directory must be re-created after a group change
The command needs a reboot to take effect
objective.explanation: A process gets its group list when the session starts. Changes to /etc/group only apply to new logins, or to a new shell started with newgrp. No reboot is needed, and usermod -aG works for any group.

objective.question: 'systemctl start server' hangs for about 90 seconds, then fails with 'start operation timed out'. While it hangs, the application logs show it is serving requests normally. What is wrong?

code.code:
[Service]
Type=forking
ExecStart=/opt/app/server --foreground
User=app

options: The ExecStart path must be inside /usr/bin
The unit needs Restart=always to report success
Type=forking makes systemd wait for the started process to exit, but the server stays in the foreground, so use Type=simple or Type=exec
The User= directive needs a matching Group= line
objective.explanation: With Type=forking, systemd treats the service as started only when the parent process exits after forking a daemon. A foreground process never exits, so the start job times out and the process is killed. Group= and Restart= do not affect start-up readiness.

objective.question: pg_dump fails because the database is unreachable. What does this nightly backup script do?

code.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -e
pg_dump mydb | gzip > /backups/mydb.sql.gz
echo "Backup done"

options: It prints 'Backup done', exits 0 and leaves a tiny, useless .gz file
set -e makes bash retry pg_dump once before failing
gzip fails too because it gets no input, so the script exits 1
It exits non-zero at the pipeline and never prints 'Backup done'
objective.explanation: Without pipefail, a pipeline's exit status is that of its last command. gzip succeeds on empty input, so set -e never triggers. Adding 'set -o pipefail' makes the pipeline fail when pg_dump fails.

objective.question: User bob (not root, not in group root) runs 'cat /srv/reports/report.csv' and gets 'Permission denied'. The output is shown below. Why?

code.code:
$ ls -ld /srv/reports
drwxr--r-- 2 root root 4096 Mar 3 10:00 /srv/reports
$ sudo ls -l /srv/reports/report.csv
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root 2048 Mar 3 10:00 /srv/reports/report.csv

options: Bob lacks execute (search) permission on the directory, so he cannot get to any file inside it
Bob needs write permission on the directory to read files
The sticky bit is missing on /srv/reports
The file needs execute permission to be read
objective.explanation: On a directory, r lets you list names and x lets you enter it and reach the files inside. Without o+x, bob cannot open report.csv even though the file itself is world-readable. Running 'chmod 755 /srv/reports' fixes it. Files never need x to be read.

objective.question: Running 'ssh -i deploy_key ubuntu@10.0.1.5' prints 'WARNING: UNPROTECTED PRIVATE KEY FILE! Permissions 0644 for deploy_key are too open' and the key is ignored. What fixes this?
options: Generate a new key pair with ssh-keygen
chmod 600 deploy_key on the client
chmod 700 ~/.ssh on the server only
chmod 644 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the server
objective.explanation: The SSH client refuses to use a private key that other users can read, so it must be readable only by its owner (600, or 400). The error comes from the client's local key file, so changing modes on the server or regenerating the key does not fix it.

subjective.question: A systemd service will not start after a deployment. Walk through how you would debug it using only the terminal.
subjective.answer: First I run 'systemctl status app' to see the state, the main PID, the exit code and the last few log lines. Then I read the full logs with 'journalctl -u app -b --no-pager', or follow them with -f while I retry. Next, I check the unit itself with 'systemctl cat app'. I confirm the ExecStart path exists and is executable; a 203/EXEC result often means a wrong path or a missing x bit. I also check User=, WorkingDirectory= and EnvironmentFile=. If I changed the unit, I run daemon-reload. Then I run ExecStart by hand as the service user, using 'sudo -u appuser'. This usually shows the real error, such as a permission denied on a config or log file, a bad config value, or a missing dependency. If the error mentions a port, 'ss -tlpn' shows a conflict. Finally I check disk space with df -h and memory with free -m, then restart and confirm the fix with curl or ss.
keyPoints: systemctl status and journalctl -u <unit> -b first
Inspect the unit with systemctl cat; check the ExecStart path, User and environment
Run the command manually as the service user to reproduce the error
Check ports (ss), permissions, disk and memory; daemon-reload after edits
Verify the fix with a health check

subjective.question: Explain what 'set -euo pipefail' does and describe one pitfall of each option.
subjective.answer: -e makes the script exit when a command returns non-zero, so errors do not pass silently. Pitfall: -e is ignored for commands inside if, while, && or || tests. Commands that return non-zero normally, like grep with no match, can also kill the script unless you write 'grep ... || true'. -u treats an unset variable as an error. This prevents disasters like 'rm -rf $DIR/' when DIR is empty. Pitfall: optional variables need defaults such as ${VAR:-}, and positional arguments like $1 fail if they are missing. -o pipefail makes a pipeline return the status of the last command that failed, not just the status of the last command. Without it, 'curl url | jq .' succeeds even when curl fails. Pitfall: commands like 'head' can make the earlier command die with SIGPIPE, which then counts as a failure. Together these options make scripts fail fast and visibly, which is what you want in CI.
keyPoints: -e exits on a non-zero command, but not inside conditionals
-u fails on unset variables; use ${VAR:-default}
pipefail returns the failing status from anywhere in a pipeline
Handle expected non-zero results explicitly with || true or an if test

subjective.question: Compare SIGTERM, SIGKILL and SIGSTOP. Why does graceful shutdown matter in container platforms?
subjective.answer: SIGTERM (15) is a polite request to stop. A process can catch it to finish in-flight requests, close connections and flush data. SIGKILL (9) is handled by the kernel. It cannot be caught, blocked or ignored, so the process gets no chance to clean up. SIGSTOP (19 on Linux x86) pauses a process and also cannot be caught; SIGCONT resumes it. Ctrl+C sends SIGINT, which gives exit code 130. Graceful shutdown matters because orchestrators follow the same pattern as systemd. Kubernetes sends SIGTERM, waits terminationGracePeriodSeconds (30 seconds by default), and then sends SIGKILL. If the app ignores SIGTERM, or a shell wrapper runs as PID 1 and does not forward signals, users see dropped requests or half-written data. The pod also shows exit code 137. So apps should handle SIGTERM, and entrypoints should use exec so the app receives signals directly.
keyPoints: SIGTERM 15 can be caught; SIGKILL 9 and SIGSTOP cannot
systemd and Kubernetes both send SIGTERM, wait for a grace period, then send SIGKILL
Exit code 137 means the process was SIGKILLed
Use exec in entrypoints so PID 1 receives the signals

subjective.question: What are the setuid, setgid and sticky bits? Give a real example of each.
subjective.answer: These are special permission bits. In octal they are written before the normal three digits. setuid (4000) on an executable makes it run with the file owner's privileges. /usr/bin/passwd is setuid root so that normal users can update /etc/shadow. ls shows it as 's' in the owner execute position. setgid (2000) on an executable makes it run with the group's privileges. On a directory, new files inherit the directory's group, which is useful for shared team folders like chmod 2775 /srv/project. The sticky bit (1000) on a directory means only the file's owner, the directory owner or root can delete or rename files in it. /tmp is 1777, so everyone can write there but nobody can delete other users' files. It shows as 't'. From a security view, setuid binaries are a privilege-escalation risk, so audit them with 'find / -perm -4000'.
keyPoints: setuid 4000: runs as the owner, e.g. passwd
setgid 2000: group inheritance on directories
sticky 1000 on /tmp (1777) prevents deleting other users' files
Audit setuid files for security

subjective.question: List the common shell exit codes and explain how a script should use them.
subjective.answer: 0 means success, and anything else is failure. 1 is a general error. 2 often means misuse of a command or bad arguments. 126 means the file was found but is not executable, for example a missing x bit. 127 means command not found, usually a typo or a wrong PATH. 130 means the script was stopped with Ctrl+C (128 + SIGINT 2). 137 means it was killed by SIGKILL (128 + 9), often by the OOM killer. In general, 128 + N means the process was ended by signal N. In scripts, $? holds the last exit status. A cleaner style is 'if ! systemctl is-active --quiet nginx; then ...; fi'. Scripts should exit with a meaningful non-zero code on failure, because CI pipelines, cron jobs, systemd and Kubernetes probes all decide success purely from the exit code. Printing 'ERROR' while still exiting 0 hides the failure.
keyPoints: 0 is success; non-zero is failure
126 not executable, 127 not found, 130 Ctrl+C, 137 SIGKILL
128+N means the process was killed by signal N
Test commands directly in if; always exit non-zero on failure

subjective.question: Describe how you would write a Bash health-check script for disk, memory and a service that exits non-zero on failure.
subjective.answer: I start with '#!/usr/bin/env bash' and 'set -euo pipefail'. I define thresholds as variables with defaults, such as DISK_MAX=${DISK_MAX:-85}. For disk, I read the use percentage with 'df --output=pcent / | tail -1 | tr -dc 0-9' and compare it with -gt. For memory, I read MemAvailable from /proc/meminfo, or use 'free -m' with awk, and fail below a minimum. For the service, 'systemctl is-active --quiet nginx' gives a clean exit code. I can add 'curl -fsS --max-time 5 http://localhost/health' to check that the app really responds, not just that the process exists. I collect failures in a counter instead of exiting on the first one, so a single run reports every problem. Each check prints OK or FAIL to stderr. At the end, 'exit 1' runs if any check failed, otherwise 'exit 0'. Then it works in cron, CI or monitoring. I lint it with shellcheck.
keyPoints: Strict mode and configurable thresholds
df for disk, /proc/meminfo or free for memory
systemctl is-active --quiet plus curl -f for the service
Collect failures and exit non-zero if any check failed
Clear output; lint with shellcheck

subjective.question: An app runs but you cannot reach it from another machine. How do you check whether it is listening and reachable?
subjective.answer: On the server, I run 'sudo ss -tlpn' to confirm the process is listening on the expected port. I check the local address carefully. 127.0.0.1:8080 means it only accepts local connections, while 0.0.0.0:8080 or [::]:8080 means it accepts connections on all interfaces. Binding only to localhost is a very common cause. Next, 'curl -v http://127.0.0.1:8080' tests the app locally. If that works, I curl the server's real IP from the server itself, then from the client machine. A 'connection refused' error usually means nothing is listening on that address. A timeout usually points to a firewall, a security group or a routing problem. I then check the host firewall with nft, iptables, ufw or firewalld, and any cloud security groups. I also make sure the client is resolving the right IP, using dig or getent.
keyPoints: ss -tlpn shows the port, bind address and process
Test with curl -v locally, then remotely
Refused = nothing listening; timeout = firewall or network

subjective.question: How does name resolution work on Linux, and how do you troubleshoot a DNS problem?
subjective.answer: Applications use the system resolver, which follows /etc/nsswitch.conf. The 'hosts:' line usually reads 'files dns', so /etc/hosts is checked before DNS. The DNS servers come from /etc/resolv.conf, which on many systems points to the systemd-resolved stub at 127.0.0.53. To troubleshoot, I first run 'getent hosts name', which uses the same path as applications. Then 'dig name' queries DNS directly and shows the status (NOERROR, NXDOMAIN or SERVFAIL), the answer and the TTL. 'dig @8.8.8.8 name' or a query to the authoritative server shows whether the problem is my local resolver. 'dig +trace' walks the delegation from the root. If getent and dig disagree, check /etc/hosts or local caching. Remember that DNS itself uses port 53, over UDP and TCP. In Kubernetes, search domains and ndots in resolv.conf also affect lookups.
keyPoints: nsswitch.conf sets the order; /etc/hosts usually wins
resolv.conf lists the nameservers
getent follows the app's path; dig queries DNS directly
Use dig @server and +trace to isolate the problem; DNS uses port 53

subjective.question: How do you set up SSH key authentication securely for a server?
subjective.answer: On my machine, I generate a key pair with 'ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "me@laptop"' and protect the private key with a passphrase. I copy only the public key to the server, using 'ssh-copy-id user@host' or by appending it to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys. Permissions matter. ~/.ssh should be 700, authorized_keys 600, and the private key 600, otherwise sshd or ssh will refuse to use them. After I confirm key login works in a second session, I harden /etc/ssh/sshd_config. I set PasswordAuthentication no and PermitRootLogin no, or prohibit-password. I validate the config with 'sshd -t' and then reload the service. I keep the private key off servers and repositories. I use ssh-agent for convenience and ~/.ssh/config for host aliases. In CI, I use deploy keys scoped to one repo and stored as secrets.
keyPoints: Generate ed25519 keys with a passphrase
Only the public key goes to authorized_keys
Permissions: 700 for .ssh, 600 for keys
Disable password and root login; test with sshd -t before reloading

subjective.question: Explain users, groups and sudo, and how you apply least privilege on a shared server.
subjective.answer: Every process runs as a user ID and has one primary group plus supplementary groups. Files are checked against the owner, group and others permissions. Accounts live in /etc/passwd, password hashes in /etc/shadow, and groups in /etc/group. I create accounts with useradd or adduser. 'usermod -aG docker alice' adds a group; the -a matters because without it you replace all supplementary groups. The user must log in again before a new group takes effect. sudo lets chosen users run commands as root, and every use is logged. I edit the rules only with visudo, or with files in /etc/sudoers.d, so syntax errors are caught. For least privilege, I run services as dedicated non-login system users. I grant sudo only for the specific commands people need, for example restarting one service. I avoid shared root passwords, and I use groups to give a team access to shared directories. Membership of the docker group is effectively root, so I grant it carefully.
keyPoints: Owner, group and others checks; passwd, shadow and group files
usermod -aG; group changes need a new login
Edit sudo rules with visudo or sudoers.d; sudo use is logged
Dedicated service users and command-limited sudo; the docker group equals root

subjective.question: An application starts fine when you run its command manually in your shell, but it fails when it is started as a systemd service. What differences between the two environments would you investigate?
subjective.answer: First I read 'systemctl status' and 'journalctl -u app -b' to get the real error. Then I compare the two environments. systemd does not load my shell profile, so PATH and environment variables like DATABASE_URL may be missing. I set them with Environment= or EnvironmentFile=. The service may run as a different User=, which cannot read the config files or write to the log directory. The working directory is / by default unless WorkingDirectory= is set, so relative paths break. Ordering matters too: if the app needs the network or a database at startup, I add After= and Wants=network-online.target. Hardening options like ProtectSystem=, PrivateTmp= or NoNewPrivileges= can block writes. SELinux or AppArmor may deny access, so I check the audit log. Finally, I reproduce the failure as the service user with 'sudo -u appuser env -i' plus the same command, which shows the missing piece quickly.
keyPoints: No login shell, so PATH and environment variables differ; fix with Environment= or EnvironmentFile=
User= and file permissions, plus the default working directory
Ordering dependencies such as network-online.target
Sandboxing options and SELinux/AppArmor denials
Reproduce the failure as the service user with a clean environment

subjective.question: Explain what this script does, why the trap is useful, and what would go wrong without it.

code.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
tmpdir=$(mktemp -d)
cleanup() {
  rc=$?
  rm -rf "$tmpdir"
  exit "$rc"
}
trap cleanup EXIT
curl -fsSL https://example.com/release.tar.gz -o "$tmpdir/r.tgz"
tar -xzf "$tmpdir/r.tgz" -C "$tmpdir"
cp "$tmpdir/bin/tool" /usr/local/bin/

subjective.answer: The script creates a private, uniquely named temporary directory with mktemp -d. This avoids name clashes and symlink attacks in /tmp. It then downloads a release, extracts it and installs one binary. 'trap cleanup EXIT' registers a function that runs whenever the shell exits, whether it succeeds, fails under set -e, or calls exit itself. Inside cleanup, rc=$? captures the original exit status before rm runs. 'exit "$rc"' then preserves that status, so CI still sees the failure. curl -f makes HTTP errors such as 404 return non-zero, so set -e stops the script instead of extracting an HTML error page. Without the trap, any failure would leave the temp directory behind. On a busy build agent these leftovers fill the disk over time. Note that EXIT traps do not run on SIGKILL. Traps on INT and TERM are also handled through EXIT in Bash when the shell is terminated by those signals.
keyPoints: mktemp -d gives a safe, unique working directory
The EXIT trap runs cleanup on success, on failure and on explicit exit
Capturing $? first preserves the real exit code
curl -f turns HTTP errors into failures that set -e catches
Without the trap, temporary files leak and fill the disk; SIGKILL cannot be trapped

subjective.question: df -h shows / is 100% full, but 'du -sh /*' adds up to far less than the disk size. Applications fail to write. How do you find and fix the problem?
subjective.answer: The gap between df and du usually means deleted files that are still held open. A common case is a log file removed with rm while the application keeps writing to it. The space is only freed when the last file descriptor closes. I find these files with 'sudo lsof +L1' or 'lsof | grep deleted', which shows the PID and the size. The clean fix is to restart or reload that process, or to signal it to reopen its logs. In an emergency I can truncate the file through /proc/PID/fd/N with ': > /proc/PID/fd/N'. I also run 'df -i', because inode exhaustion from millions of small files gives 'No space left on device' even when blocks are free. Files hidden under a mount point can also be missed by du. To prevent a repeat, I use logrotate with copytruncate or postrotate reload, set journald size limits, and add alerts on disk usage.
keyPoints: Deleted but still-open files explain the df vs du gap
Find them with lsof +L1, then restart the process or truncate via /proc/PID/fd
Check inode usage with df -i
Files can hide under mount points
Prevent it with logrotate, journald limits and disk alerts

subjective.question: Write, or describe, a production-ready systemd unit for a web application that runs as a non-root user, loads secrets from a file, restarts on crashes and starts after the network is ready. Explain each key directive.
subjective.answer: In [Unit], I set Description=, then After=network-online.target and Wants=network-online.target, so the app starts only once networking is up. In [Service], I use User=webapp and Group=webapp for least privilege, and WorkingDirectory=/opt/webapp. I set EnvironmentFile=/etc/webapp/env, with the file owned by root and mode 600, so secrets stay out of the unit file. I give ExecStart= with an absolute path. Restart=on-failure with RestartSec=5 handles crashes without fast restart loops. TimeoutStopSec= and KillSignal=SIGTERM give the app time for a graceful shutdown. I add basic hardening: NoNewPrivileges=true, ProtectSystem=strict with ReadWritePaths= for the data directory, and PrivateTmp=true. LimitNOFILE= raises the file descriptor limit if needed. In [Install], WantedBy=multi-user.target lets 'systemctl enable' start it at boot. After creating the unit I run 'systemctl daemon-reload' and 'systemctl enable --now webapp', then check the journal.
keyPoints: After= plus Wants=network-online.target for ordering
Non-root User= and EnvironmentFile= with tight permissions
Restart=on-failure with RestartSec= and graceful stop settings
Hardening directives such as NoNewPrivileges= and ProtectSystem=
WantedBy=multi-user.target, daemon-reload and enable --now

subjective.question: 'curl https://payments.example.com/api' fails from a server. Describe a layer-by-layer approach to find out where it breaks.
subjective.answer: I go bottom-up and test one layer at a time. First DNS: 'dig payments.example.com +short' and 'getent hosts payments.example.com'. These show what the system resolver actually returns, including entries from /etc/hosts. Next TCP: 'nc -vz host 443', or curl -v, shows whether the connection succeeds, is refused, or times out. A refusal points to nothing listening on the port. A timeout points to a firewall, security group or routing problem. I also check whether a proxy is required through the HTTPS_PROXY variable. Then TLS: 'openssl s_client -connect host:443 -servername host' shows the certificate chain, its expiry, hostname mismatches and missing CA bundles. Finally HTTP: 'curl -v' shows the status code, headers and redirects. A 401 or 403 points to authentication, and a 5xx is a server-side problem. The exit codes of curl help too, for example 6 (could not resolve host), 7 (failed to connect), 28 (timeout) and 60 (certificate problem). Comparing results from another host isolates whether the problem is local.
keyPoints: DNS: dig and getent, including /etc/hosts
TCP: refused vs timeout, firewall and proxy checks
TLS: openssl s_client with SNI, cert chain and expiry
HTTP: curl -v status codes and redirects
Use curl exit codes and compare from another host

subjective.question: Engineers must reach private servers through a bastion host using SSH keys. How would you configure this securely, and why is ProxyJump preferred over agent forwarding?

code.code:
Host bastion
  HostName bastion.example.com
  User alice
  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

Host 10.0.*
  User alice
  ProxyJump bastion
  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

subjective.answer: This ~/.ssh/config sends any connection to a 10.0.x.x host through the bastion using ProxyJump. The client opens a TCP tunnel through the bastion and authenticates to the private host end to end, so the private key never leaves the laptop. With agent forwarding (ssh -A), the bastion gets access to your agent socket. Anyone with root on the bastion could use your keys to log in elsewhere while you are connected. That is why ProxyJump is safer. On the server side, I use ed25519 keys protected by a passphrase, and I disable PasswordAuthentication and root login in sshd_config. I restrict the bastion users with AllowUsers or AllowGroups, and I set AllowAgentForwarding no there. Security groups should allow port 22 on private hosts only from the bastion. I would also log sessions and consider short-lived SSH certificates or a managed option like AWS Systems Manager Session Manager.
keyPoints: ProxyJump tunnels through the bastion; the private key stays on the client
Agent forwarding exposes your agent to anyone with root on the bastion
Harden sshd: no passwords, no root login, AllowUsers or AllowGroups
Network rules allow SSH to private hosts only from the bastion
Consider SSH certificates or session-manager tools for auditing

subjective.question: Review this health-check script, which runs from a monitoring job. Spot the mistakes and explain how you would fix each one.

code.code:
#!/bin/bash
THRESHOLD=90
usage=$(df / | tail -1 | awk '{print $5}' | tr -d %)
if [ $usage -gt $THRESHOLD ]; then
  echo "disk high"
fi
if ! systemctl is-active nginx; then
  echo "nginx down"
  pkill -9 nginx
  systemctl start nginx
fi
echo "all good"
exit 0

subjective.answer: The biggest bug is that the script always prints 'all good' and exits 0, so monitoring never sees a failure. I would keep a status variable, set it to 1 on each failed check, and finish with 'exit "$status"'. There is no strict mode, so I would add 'set -euo pipefail'. $usage is unquoted. If df fails, the test breaks with a syntax error, so I would quote it and validate that it is a number. 'df -P --output=pcent /' is more stable than parsing column 5. 'systemctl is-active' prints its state, so I would use --quiet. Error messages should go to stderr with >&2. Finally, a health check should detect problems, not fix them. 'pkill -9' skips graceful shutdown and can drop in-flight requests. Restarts belong to Restart=on-failure in the unit or to an alerting runbook, and they should use 'systemctl restart', which sends SIGTERM first.
keyPoints: Always exiting 0 hides failures; track a status and exit non-zero
Add strict mode and quote variables used in tests
Use systemctl is-active --quiet, and send errors to stderr
Do not remediate with kill -9 inside a check; let systemd handle restarts gracefully

subjective.question: You need to run a database backup every night at 02:00 on a Linux server. Compare a cron job with a systemd timer and say which you would choose and why.
subjective.answer: Cron is simple and works everywhere: one line in a crontab. But it gives you little control. Output goes to local mail or is lost. It runs with a minimal environment and PATH. A missed run while the server is down never happens. It also has no built-in protection against overlapping runs. A systemd timer needs two files, a .timer and a .service, but it gives more. Logs go to the journal, so 'journalctl -u backup.service' shows every run and its exit status. 'systemctl list-timers' shows the last and next run times. Persistent=true runs a missed job after boot. Only one instance of the service runs at a time. You also get the service's User=, resource limits, sandboxing options and OnFailure= hooks for alerting. RandomizedDelaySec spreads load across a fleet. For a production backup I would choose the systemd timer, because the logs and failure handling matter more than the extra file.
keyPoints: Cron: simple and portable, but weak logging and a minimal environment
Timer: journal logs, list-timers, Persistent= catches missed runs
Systemd prevents overlapping runs and supports OnFailure alerting
Choose timers for production jobs where failures must be visible

subjective.question: An 8-core server shows a load average of 40 and users report slowness. Put your investigation steps in order and explain what each one tells you.
subjective.answer: First, 'uptime' shows the 1, 5 and 15-minute averages, so I can see whether load is rising or falling. Second, 'top' (or htop) shows the CPU breakdown. High us or sy means CPU-bound work. High wa means processes are waiting on disk. Third, because Linux load counts both runnable tasks (R) and uninterruptible tasks (D), I run 'ps -eo pid,stat,wchan,cmd | awk '$2 ~ /D/'' to find tasks blocked on I/O or NFS. Fourth, if I/O is the issue, 'iostat -x 1' or iotop shows which device is saturated and which process is causing it. 'free -m' and 'vmstat 1' show whether swapping is involved. Fifth, I identify the owner with 'ps -o ppid' or 'systemctl status <pid>', and check 'journalctl -p err -b' and dmesg for disk or OOM errors. Only then do I act: renice the process, stop it gracefully with SIGTERM or systemctl stop, or fix the storage. I record what I found before I change anything.
keyPoints: Check the load trend first, then the CPU breakdown (us/sy/wa)
Load includes D-state tasks, so high load is not always a CPU problem
Use iostat, vmstat and free to confirm I/O or memory pressure
Identify the owner and check logs before acting gracefully

subjective.question: Case study: a team needs /srv/project on a shared server. Requirements: (1) only members of group devs can access it, (2) new files and folders belong to devs automatically, (3) every member can edit files others create, (4) members cannot delete files owned by other members. How do you set this up?
subjective.answer: First, 'groupadd devs' and add each member with 'usermod -aG devs <user>'. Remember -a, and the members must log in again. Then 'chgrp devs /srv/project' and 'chmod 3770 /srv/project'. 770 gives the owner and group full access and others nothing, which covers requirement 1. The setgid bit (2000) makes new files and subdirectories inherit the devs group, which covers requirement 2. The sticky bit (1000) means only a file's owner, the directory owner or root can delete or rename it, which covers requirement 4. For requirement 3, files must be group-writable when they are created, but most umasks (022) remove group write. Rather than relying on every user's umask, I would set a default ACL: 'setfacl -d -m g:devs:rwX /srv/project' plus 'setfacl -m g:devs:rwX /srv/project'. Finally, I would test as two different users: create, edit, and try to delete each other's files.
keyPoints: Use chgrp devs and mode 770 to block others
Setgid on the directory makes new files inherit the group
The sticky bit stops members deleting others' files
Use a default ACL (or umask 002) so new files are group-writable; then test as two users

subjective.question: A server rebooted unexpectedly overnight. You run 'journalctl -b -1' to see what happened before the reboot, but it reports that no such boot exists. What is the cause and how do you fix it for next time?
subjective.answer: The journal is probably stored only in memory under /run/log/journal, so it is lost at every reboot. This happens when journald's Storage= is 'volatile', or when it is 'auto' (the default) and /var/log/journal does not exist. I would confirm with 'journalctl --list-boots', which shows only the current boot, and by checking whether /var/log/journal exists. To fix it, I would set Storage=persistent in /etc/systemd/journald.conf or a drop-in under journald.conf.d. Creating /var/log/journal also works when Storage=auto. Then I run 'systemctl restart systemd-journald'. I would also cap disk use with SystemMaxUse= so logs cannot fill the disk. For tonight's incident, I would look elsewhere for clues: /var/log/syslog or messages if rsyslog is installed, cloud provider console logs, 'last -x reboot', and hardware or BMC logs. Once the journal is persistent, 'journalctl -b -1 -p warning' will show the end of the previous boot.
keyPoints: The volatile journal lives in /run and is lost on reboot
Set Storage=persistent or create /var/log/journal, then restart journald
Limit size with SystemMaxUse
Use other sources (syslog, last -x, cloud console) for the current incident

subjective.question: Spot the mistakes in this unit file and rewrite the key lines correctly.

code.code:
[Unit]
Description=Report API

[Service]
ExecStart=cd /opt/report && source .env && python3 app.py
Restart=always
Environment=DB_PASSWORD=Sup3rS3cret

[Install]
WantedBy=default.target

subjective.answer: First, ExecStart does not run through a shell. 'cd', 'source' and '&&' are not interpreted, and systemd needs an absolute executable path. I would use 'WorkingDirectory=/opt/report', 'EnvironmentFile=/opt/report/.env' and 'ExecStart=/usr/bin/python3 /opt/report/app.py'. Second, the password sits in the unit file. Unit files are normally world-readable, and the value shows up in 'systemctl show', so I would move it into the EnvironmentFile (owned by root, mode 600) or use LoadCredential=. Third, there is no User=, so the API runs as root. I would add a dedicated User=report and Group=report. Fourth, it does not wait for the network. I would add Wants= and After=network-online.target. Fifth, for a system service WantedBy should be multi-user.target. Restart=on-failure with RestartSec=5 is usually better than always. After editing, I run 'systemctl daemon-reload', then 'systemctl enable --now report'.
keyPoints: ExecStart has no shell: use WorkingDirectory, EnvironmentFile and absolute paths
Never put secrets in the unit file; use a 600 file or LoadCredential
Add a non-root User=
Add network-online ordering and WantedBy=multi-user.target, then daemon-reload

subjective.question: You run 'kill 2311' on a misbehaving app. Within seconds the app is running again under a new PID. What is happening, and what is the right way to stop or restart it?
subjective.answer: Something is supervising the process and restarting it. On most servers this is systemd with Restart=always or on-failure. It could also be supervisord, a container runtime, or a cron watchdog. I would confirm with 'systemctl status 2311', which shows the unit the PID belongs to, or with 'ps -o ppid= -p <pid>' to see the parent. For a systemd unit, killing the PID by hand fights the supervisor. To restart it, I run 'systemctl restart app'. To stop it, I run 'systemctl stop app', which sends SIGTERM to the whole cgroup and waits for TimeoutStopSec. To send a specific signal, such as SIGHUP for a reload, I use 'systemctl kill --signal=HUP app'. To stop it starting at boot I disable it, and to prevent any start at all, even as a dependency, I use 'systemctl mask app'. I always work through the supervisor so its state stays correct.
keyPoints: A supervisor (often systemd Restart=) restarts the process
Find the owner with systemctl status <pid> or the parent PID
Use systemctl stop, restart or kill instead of killing PIDs directly
Use disable or mask to prevent the service from starting again

subjective.question: A teammate committed deploy.sh from a Windows laptop. On the Linux server, './deploy.sh' first says 'Permission denied'. After a chmod it fails with the error below, yet 'cat deploy.sh' looks fine. Explain both problems and how to prevent them.

code.code: -bash: ./deploy.sh: /bin/bash^M: bad interpreter: No such file or directory

subjective.answer: There are two separate problems. 'Permission denied' means the file has no execute bit. Git stores an executable flag, and files created on Windows usually do not have it. I would fix it on the server with 'chmod +x deploy.sh', and permanently in the repository with 'git update-index --chmod=+x deploy.sh' and a commit. The second error comes from Windows CRLF line endings. The ^M is a carriage return at the end of the shebang line, so the kernel looks for an interpreter literally named '/bin/bash\r', which does not exist. cat does not show the \r, but 'cat -A' or 'file deploy.sh' reveals it. I would fix it with 'dos2unix deploy.sh' or "sed -i 's/\r$//' deploy.sh". To prevent it, I would add a .gitattributes rule such as '*.sh text eol=lf' and run shellcheck in CI.
keyPoints: Permission denied: missing execute bit; fix in Git with update-index --chmod=+x
^M means CRLF endings break the shebang
Detect with cat -A or file; fix with dos2unix or sed
Prevent with .gitattributes eol=lf and CI checks

subjective.question: SSH logins to one server pause for 20–30 seconds before the prompt appears. Once logged in, everything is fast. How do you find and fix the cause?
subjective.answer: First, I would find where the pause happens. Running 'ssh -vvv user@host' shows timestamps for each stage. If it stalls before authentication, I would suspect network or server-side DNS lookups. If it stalls after 'Authentication succeeded', the problem is in session setup. On the server, I would watch 'journalctl -u ssh -f' (the unit is sshd on RHEL-family systems) while logging in. Common causes are: sshd doing a reverse DNS lookup of the client (UseDNS yes) against a slow or unreachable nameserver; GSSAPIAuthentication being tried and timing out; a dead nameserver in /etc/resolv.conf, which delays every lookup by its timeout; and slow PAM modules or login scripts such as dynamic MOTD, or a profile script calling a remote service. The fixes are to set 'UseDNS no' and 'GSSAPIAuthentication no' where they are not needed, correct the resolver configuration, or remove the slow login script. I would validate with 'sshd -t', reload, and time a fresh login.
keyPoints: Use ssh -vvv timestamps to locate the stall
Reverse DNS (UseDNS) or a dead resolver causes timeout-length delays
GSSAPI attempts, PAM modules and login scripts are other causes
Fix the config, validate with sshd -t, reload and re-test

subjective.question: For deployments, one design copies new files over /opt/app in place. Another unpacks each version into /opt/app/releases/<version> and points a symlink /opt/app/current at it. Which is better and why? How do you switch the symlink atomically?
subjective.answer: The release-directory design is better. Copying in place leaves a window where the app has a mix of old and new files. A failed copy leaves a broken install, and rollback means redeploying the old version. With separate release directories, each version is complete before it goes live. Switching is just repointing a symlink, and rollback is repointing it back. Running processes keep the files they already opened, because an open file stays alive through its inode. Hard links cannot be used here, because they cannot point to directories or cross filesystems. Note that 'ln -sfn new current' is not strictly atomic: it removes the old link and then creates a new one, so a request could briefly find no link. The atomic way is 'ln -s /opt/app/releases/v42 /opt/app/current.tmp && mv -T /opt/app/current.tmp /opt/app/current', because rename() is atomic. Then I restart or reload the service and keep the last few releases for fast rollback.
keyPoints: In-place copies create mixed states and make rollback hard
Release directories plus a symlink give instant switching and rollback
Use symlinks, not hard links (no links to directories, no cross-filesystem links)
For an atomic switch, create a temporary link then mv -T (rename)

subjective.question: You must disable SSH password login on a remote production server that you can only reach over SSH. List the steps in order so that you cannot lock yourself out.
subjective.answer: Step one: confirm that key login works for your sudo user from a new terminal, and confirm that sudo works there. Step two: keep an existing root or sudo session open for the whole change, and know your fallback, such as the cloud provider's serial console. Step three: make the change. Set 'PasswordAuthentication no', 'KbdInteractiveAuthentication no' and 'PermitRootLogin no' (or prohibit-password) in sshd_config or a drop-in under sshd_config.d. Remember that for most options the first value read wins, and some cloud images ship a drop-in that sets PasswordAuthentication yes. Step four: check the effective settings with 'sshd -t' and 'sshd -T | grep -i passwordauth'. Step five: run 'systemctl reload ssh' (sshd on RHEL-family systems); existing sessions stay up.
