Step six: from a new terminal, confirm that key login works and that 'ssh -o PubkeyAuthentication=no user@host' is refused. Only then close the old session.
keyPoints: Prove key login and sudo work before changing anything
Keep an existing session open and have console access as a fallback
Watch for first-match-wins and conflicting drop-in files
Validate with sshd -t and -T, reload, then test key and password logins in a new session

steps.overview: This step covers how teams use Git to collaborate safely: commits, branches, merge vs rebase, conflict resolution, branching strategies, pull requests with branch protection, and release versioning with tags. These ideas sit under every later CI/CD topic. The GitHub Actions and AZ-400 exams test branch protection, triggers on branches and tags, and branching strategy choices directly.
objectives: Create, branch, merge and rebase commits, and resolve merge conflicts from the command line
Compare trunk-based development and GitFlow, and choose one for a given team and release cadence
Configure a protected main branch with required pull request reviews and required status checks
Apply semantic versioning with annotated tags and keep a changelog tied to releases
Explain how pull requests, code owners and CI checks together gate changes to main

concepts.explanation: A commit is an immutable snapshot identified by a SHA, pointing to its parent commits. A branch is just a movable pointer to a commit, and HEAD points to the branch you are on. Creating a branch is cheap because Git only writes a small reference.

Merge joins two histories. When the branches have diverged, it creates a merge commit, which keeps the true history. Rebase replays your commits on top of another base and gives a linear history, but it rewrites the commit SHAs. Never rebase commits that others have already pulled. Rebase local feature branches only.

A fast-forward merge just moves the branch pointer when there is no divergence, so no merge commit is made. A squash merge combines all PR commits into a single commit on main, which keeps the main history clean. GitHub offers merge commit, squash and rebase merge, and you can disable any of them per repository.

A conflict happens when both sides change the same lines, or one side edits a file the other deletes. Git marks the conflict regions with <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>>. You edit the file, then git add it, then run git commit or git rebase --continue. Use git merge --abort or git rebase --abort to back out.

Developers integrate small, short-lived branches (hours to a day or two) into main frequently. Unfinished work is hidden behind feature flags. This approach suits continuous delivery, and DORA research links it to high performance.

GitFlow uses long-lived main and develop branches plus feature/*, release/* and hotfix/* branches. It suits scheduled, versioned releases or supporting several versions at once. It adds merge overhead, and its own author now recommends simpler flows for continuously delivered software.

These are GitHub rules on a branch pattern. They can require a pull request, a number of approving reviews, review from Code Owners, required status checks, up-to-date branches, linear history and signed commits. They can also block force pushes and deletions. Rulesets are the newer, layered way to apply the same controls, including to tags and across an organisation.

A CODEOWNERS file in .github/, the repo root or docs/ maps path patterns to users or teams. Those owners are auto-requested as reviewers. If branch protection requires Code Owner review, an owner must approve.

The format is MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. Increase MAJOR for breaking changes, MINOR for backward-compatible features and PATCH for backward-compatible fixes. Pre-release labels look like 1.4.0-rc.1. Version 0.y.z means the public API is not yet stable.

An annotated tag (git tag -a) stores the tagger, date and a message, and is the right choice for releases. A lightweight tag is just a pointer. A changelog (for example in Keep a Changelog format) lists Added, Changed, Fixed and Removed per version. Conventional Commits can automate both the changelog and the version bump.

keyFacts: git push does not push tags by default. Use git push origin v1.2.0 or git push --follow-tags.
git pull is fetch plus merge by default. git pull --rebase uses rebase instead.
Use git push --force-with-lease rather than --force, so you do not overwrite a teammate's work.
Branch protection status checks only appear in the list after the check has run at least once in the repo, and they match the job or check name.
'Require branches to be up to date before merging' forces a rebase or merge with main so that checks run against the latest main.
In Conventional Commits, feat → MINOR, fix → PATCH, and 'BREAKING CHANGE:' or '!' → MAJOR.
GitHub Actions can trigger on tags with on: push: tags: ['v*'] and on PRs with on: pull_request: branches: [main].
By default, administrators can bypass branch protection unless the setting that applies rules to admins is enabled. In rulesets, use the bypass list carefully.
Use git revert for shared history, because it adds an undo commit. git reset rewrites history and is for local work only.

example.caption: Protect main with GitHub CLI and a workflow whose job name is the required check
example.code:
# .github/workflows/ci.yml must contain a job named 'build' triggered on pull_request to main
gh api -X PUT repos/OWNER/REPO/branches/main/protection \
  -H 'Accept: application/vnd.github+json' --input - <<'EOF'
{
  "required_status_checks": {"strict": true, "contexts": ["build"]},
  "enforce_admins": true,
  "required_pull_request_reviews": {
    "required_approving_review_count": 1,
    "require_code_owner_reviews": true,
    "dismiss_stale_reviews": true
  },
  "restrictions": null,
  "required_linear_history": true,
  "allow_force_pushes": false,
  "allow_deletions": false
}
EOF
# Release after merge
git switch main && git pull --ff-only
git tag -a v1.3.0 -m "feat: add health endpoint"
git push origin v1.3.0

pitfalls: Rebasing or force-pushing a shared branch rewrites history and breaks teammates' clones.
Adding a required status check name that never runs (for example, a workflow not triggered on pull_request) blocks every PR forever.
Leaving admins able to bypass protection means the checkpoint 'nothing reaches main without review' is not really true.
Choosing GitFlow on an exam question about continuous deployment or small, frequent releases is usually the wrong answer. Trunk-based development is expected there.
Forgetting to push tags, or using lightweight tags, so tag-triggered release pipelines never fire or lack metadata.
Not dismissing stale approvals, so new commits pushed after approval merge without a fresh review.

workflow.title: Change flow from branch to protected main to release

steps.label: Branch from latest main
steps.detail: Run git switch -c feat/x after git pull --ff-only, so you start from current main.

steps.label: Commit small, conventional changes
steps.detail: Write focused commits with messages like 'feat:' or 'fix:' so versioning can be automated.

steps.label: Rebase and push
steps.detail: Rebase your local branch on origin/main, resolve any conflicts, then push with --force-with-lease if needed.

steps.label: Open pull request
steps.detail: The PR auto-requests CODEOWNERS as reviewers and triggers the CI workflow on pull_request.

steps.label: Pass review and checks
steps.detail: Branch protection blocks merging until the required approvals exist and the status checks are green on an up-to-date branch.

steps.label: Squash merge to main
steps.detail: Merge using the allowed method, which keeps main linear and deployable.

steps.label: Tag and publish release
steps.detail: Create an annotated SemVer tag and update the changelog, which triggers the release pipeline.

project.title: protected-main-demo
project.summary: A tiny Node.js semver library inside a GitHub repository whose main branch is locked down by a Terraform-managed ruleset, so nothing merges without a code-owner review and a green CI check. infra/main.tf creates the repo and ruleset, ci.yml is the required status check, release.yml turns semver tags into releases with changelogs, CODEOWNERS routes reviews, and src/ plus test/ are the code the pipeline protects.
project.run:
export GITHUB_TOKEN=<fine-grained PAT with Administration + Contents read/write>
cd infra && terraform init
terraform apply -var owner=<your-user> -target=github_repository.demo

files.code:
name: ci

# Runs on every PR to main and on pushes to main
on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
  push:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  contents: read # least privilege for the GITHUB_TOKEN

jobs:
  test:
    name: test # this check name is required by the ruleset
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 22

      # Built-in Node test runner, no dependencies needed
      - name: Run unit tests
        run: node --test "test/**/*.test.js"

      # Fail fast if a merge conflict marker was committed by mistake
      - name: Check for conflict markers
        run: |
          if grep -rnE '^(<<<<<<<|>>>>>>>)( |$)' src test; then
            echo "Conflict markers found"; exit 1
          fi

name: release

# Triggered when a maintainer pushes a semver tag, e.g. v1.2.0
on:
  push:
    tags:
      - "v[0-9]+.[0-9]+.[0-9]+"

permissions:
  contents: write # needed to create the GitHub Release

jobs:
  release:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 22

      # Never release code that fails tests
      - run: node --test "test/**/*.test.js"

      # Changelog is generated from merged PR titles since the last tag
      - name: Create release with generated notes
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
        run: |
          gh release create "$GITHUB_REF_NAME" \
            --title "$GITHUB_REF_NAME" \
            --generate-notes \
            --verify-tag

# Later rules override earlier ones. The last matching pattern wins.
# Replace the handles with real users or teams that have write access.

# Default owner for everything
*                       @your-github-user

# Pipeline and protection changes need the platform owner
/.github/               @your-github-user
/infra/                 @your-github-user

# Library code
/src/                   @your-github-user

# Note: GitHub never lets you approve your own PR.
# Add a second collaborator here to complete the review loop.

# protected-main-demo

Goal: nothing reaches `main` without a review and a green pipeline.

## What each file does
- `infra/main.tf` - creates the repo and a branch ruleset on main: PR required, 1 code-owner approval, `test` check green and up to date, linear history, no force push or delete.
- `.github/workflows/ci.yml` - job `test`, the required status check.
- `.github/CODEOWNERS` - who must review which paths.
- `.github/workflows/release.yml` - tag `vX.Y.Z` -> GitHub Release with generated changelog.
- `src/semver.js`, `test/` - the code being protected.

## Why two Terraform applies
The ruleset requires check `test`. That check only exists once `ci.yml` is on main, so push the code first, then apply the ruleset.

## Trunk-based flow (try it)
```
git switch -c feat/prerelease-bump
# edit src/semver.js, commit: "feat: support prerelease bump"
git push -u origin feat/prerelease-bump
gh pr create --fill
```
- Direct `git push origin main` is now rejected.
- Merge stays blocked until `test` is green and a code owner approves.
- Use Squash merge (one commit) or Rebase merge. Merge commits are disabled.

## Conflict practice
Edit the same line on two branches. Merge one PR. The other is now behind main (strict checks), so update it:
```
git fetch origin && git rebase origin/main
# fix the file, remove <<<<<<< ======= >>>>>>> markers
git add src/semver.js && git rebase --continue
git push --force-with-lease   # allowed on your branch, never on main
```

## Release
```
git switch main && git pull
git tag -a v1.1.0 -m "v1.1.0" && git push origin v1.1.0
```
feat -> MINOR, fix -> PATCH, `!` or BREAKING CHANGE -> MAJOR.

## Checkpoint
Try to push to main, merge without approval and merge with a red test. All three must fail.

revision.examFocus: This step maps to the AZ-400 domain on designing and implementing a source control strategy: branching strategies, pull request workflows, branch policies and repository management. It also maps to the GitHub Actions exam objectives on workflow triggers, events and filters. Questions are scenario-based. You read a team's release cadence or governance need and pick the branching model, merge strategy, protection setting or trigger that meets it with the least risk.

compare.difference: Trunk-based uses short-lived branches (hours to a day or two) merged into main often, and hides unfinished work behind feature flags. GitFlow uses long-lived develop and release branches plus hotfix branches, built for planned, versioned releases.
compare.chooseA: Pick it when the question says continuous delivery or deployment, several releases a day, small batches, or reducing merge pain.
compare.chooseB: Pick it when the question describes scheduled releases, several supported versions in production at once, or strict release stabilisation phases.

compare.difference: A merge commit keeps the true history and never rewrites existing commits. Rebase and squash produce a linear history, but they create new commit IDs.
compare.chooseA: Pick merge when the branch is shared, when auditors need the exact history, or when the question warns against rewriting history.
compare.chooseB: Pick rebase or squash when the requirement is a linear or clean history, one commit per feature on main, or 'Require linear history' is enabled.

compare.difference: Revert adds a new commit that undoes an earlier one, so history stays intact for everyone. Reset moves the branch pointer and discards or unstages commits, which rewrites history.
compare.chooseA: Pick revert to undo something already pushed to main or to any shared branch.
compare.chooseB: Pick reset only to clean up local commits that nobody else has pulled.

compare.difference: Only one classic rule applies to a given branch. Rulesets can stack, can target tags as well as branches, can be set at organisation level, and have an explicit bypass list.
compare.chooseA: Pick classic rules for a simple single-repo setup where one rule per branch pattern is enough.
compare.chooseB: Pick rulesets for central governance across many repos, for protecting tags such as v*, or for layering several rule sets on the same branch.

compare.difference: An annotated tag is a full Git object with tagger, date and message, and it can be signed. A lightweight tag is only a named pointer to a commit.
compare.chooseA: Pick annotated tags for releases. git describe and git push --follow-tags work with annotated tags by default.
compare.chooseB: Pick lightweight tags only for private or temporary local bookmarks.

cues.cue: deploy to production many times a day / small frequent releases
cues.pick: Trunk-based development with feature flags
cues.why: Long-lived branches delay integration and conflict with continuous deployment.

cues.cue: undo a bad commit that is already on main
cues.pick: git revert, delivered through a PR
cues.why: It undoes the change without rewriting shared history, and it still passes review and checks.

cues.cue: a specific team must approve changes to a folder (e.g. /infra or /.github/workflows)
cues.pick: CODEOWNERS plus 'Require review from Code Owners'
cues.why: CODEOWNERS alone only requests reviewers; the protection setting is what makes their approval mandatory.

cues.cue: PR stuck on 'Expected — Waiting for status to be reported'
cues.pick: Required check name does not match, or the workflow is not triggered on pull_request
cues.why: The required check must run on the PR under exactly the same job or check name.

cues.cue: Azure Repos: block completion of a PR unless the build passes
cues.pick: Branch policy with build validation, plus minimum reviewers
cues.why: Build validation is Azure DevOps' version of a required status check.

cues.cue: release pipeline should run only when a version is published
cues.pick: on: push: tags: ['v*'] with an annotated tag that is explicitly pushed
cues.why: Tags are not pushed by default, and a tag-based trigger keeps release builds separate from PR builds.

cues.cue: many PRs merging at once keep breaking main despite green checks
cues.pick: Merge queue (with workflows also triggered on merge_group)
cues.why: The queue tests each PR against the latest main plus the PRs ahead of it, so checks reflect what will actually land.

cues.cue: no exceptions, even for administrators
cues.pick: Enforce the rule for admins / keep the ruleset bypass list empty
cues.why: Admin bypass quietly breaks the 'nothing reaches main without review' guarantee.

scenario.situation: A fintech team has protected main with one required approval. Auditors found three changes on main with no valid review. Two were pushed directly by a repository admin. One was approved, then had new commits added before it was merged. The team also wants every merge to pass the 'ci / build-and-test' job. Which configuration closes all the gaps?
reasoning: Name each gap first: admin bypass, stale approval, and no required check. A correct answer must fix all three.
Eliminate answers that only add more reviewers. A higher approval count does nothing about admin pushes or commits added after approval.
Eliminate answers that rely on CODEOWNERS or team policy documents alone. They request reviews but do not enforce anything on admins.

Keep the option that enforces rules for admins (or empties the ruleset bypass list), turns on 'Dismiss stale pull request approvals when new commits are pushed', and adds 'ci / build-and-test' as a required status check.
Confirm that the required check is triggered on pull_request targeting main and has already run once, so it can be selected and will not block PRs forever.
scenario.answer: Use a ruleset or branch protection rule on main that requires one approval, dismisses stale approvals, requires the 'ci / build-and-test' status check, and applies to administrators with no bypass. Only this combination makes 'nothing reaches main without review and a green pipeline' actually true.

memoryAids: SemVer from Conventional Commits: 'Fix Patches, Features Minor, Breaks Major' (fix → PATCH, feat → MINOR, BREAKING CHANGE or ! → MAJOR).
Golden rule: 'Rebase what is mine, merge what is ours.' Shared history gets revert, never reset or force-push.
Checkpoint locks, R-S-S-A: Reviews required, Stale approvals dismissed, Status checks required, Admins not exempt.
cheatSheet: Continuous deployment or frequent releases → trunk-based development. Multiple supported versions or scheduled releases → GitFlow or release branches.
Feature flags let you merge unfinished work to trunk safely. They are the standard partner of trunk-based development.
Squash merge gives one commit per PR on main. Rebase merge keeps each commit but makes them linear. Merge commit keeps the full branching history.
Never rebase or force-push a shared branch. If you must force-push your own branch, use --force-with-lease.
To resolve a conflict: edit the files, remove the markers, git add them, then run git merge --continue or git rebase --continue. Run git merge --abort or git rebase --abort to back out.
In GitHub Actions, on: pull_request: branches: [main] filters on the PR's target (base) branch, not the source branch.
A required status check must run on every PR under exactly the same name. Otherwise the PR waits forever.
'Require branches to be up to date' and merge queues both make checks run against the latest main.
CODEOWNERS works only together with 'Require review from Code Owners'. The last matching pattern in the file wins.
In Azure Repos, branch policies are the equivalent: minimum reviewers, build validation, linked work items, comment resolution, and limits on merge types.
SemVer is MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. A pre-release such as 1.2.0-rc.1 ranks below 1.2.0. Versions 0.y.z are unstable initial development.
Release tags should be annotated and pushed explicitly. Rulesets can protect v* tags from being deleted or moved.
selfCheck: I can choose trunk-based development or GitFlow from a scenario's release cadence, and explain why the other option is wrong.
I can decide between merge, squash, rebase, revert and reset for a given situation without rewriting shared history.
I can configure GitHub branch protection or a ruleset so that admins, stale approvals and missing checks cannot bypass review, and I can map those settings to Azure Repos branch policies.
I can diagnose a PR stuck waiting on a required check, and fix the workflow trigger or the job name.
I can derive the next semantic version from a list of Conventional Commits, and publish an annotated tag that triggers a release workflow.
I can explain in an interview why CODEOWNERS, merge queues and 'require up to date' each exist, and what failure each one prevents.

objective.question: You created a tag locally with git tag -a v1.2.0 -m "Release 1.2.0" and then ran git push origin main. Your GitHub Actions release workflow uses on: push: tags: ['v*'], but it never started. What is the most likely cause?
options: Annotated tags cannot trigger GitHub Actions workflows; only lightweight tags can
The pattern 'v*' only matches branches, not tags
Tag-triggered workflows only run when the tag is created in the GitHub web UI
git push does not push tags by default, so the tag never reached GitHub
objective.explanation: A plain git push sends branch commits but not tags. You must run git push origin v1.2.0 or git push --follow-tags. Both annotated and lightweight tags can trigger workflows, and the tags filter matches tag names.

objective.question: You rebased your feature branch on the latest main and now need to update the remote copy of that branch. A teammate may have pushed a small fix to the same branch in the last hour. Which command is safest?
options: git push --tags
git push --no-verify
git push --force-with-lease
git push --force
objective.explanation: --force-with-lease refuses to overwrite the remote branch if it has moved since your last fetch, so it protects your teammate's commit. --force overwrites without checking. --tags and --no-verify do not solve a rewritten-history push.

objective.question: A commit that broke the login page was merged to main two days ago. Ten other developers have since pulled main and built on top of it. What is the correct way to undo the change?
options: git revert <commit> and push the new commit through a pull request
Delete main and recreate it from the commit before the bad one
git rebase -i on main and drop the commit, then force-push
git reset --hard <commit>^ on main, then force-push
objective.explanation: git revert adds a new commit that undoes the change without rewriting shared history, so nobody's clone breaks. Reset, interactive rebase and recreating the branch all rewrite history that others already have.

objective.question: You are adding a required status check to main's branch protection. Your new workflow has a job named 'unit-tests', but it does not appear in the list of checks you can select. The workflow file was merged only a few minutes ago and has never run. What should you do?
options: Run the workflow at least once in the repository, then select 'unit-tests' from the list
Add the check name to the CODEOWNERS file
Enable 'Require linear history' first, which unlocks the status check list
Rename the job to 'status-check' because GitHub only recognises that name
objective.explanation: A status check appears in the selection list only after it has run at least once in the repo, and it is matched by job or check name. There is no special required name, and CODEOWNERS or linear history have nothing to do with it.

objective.question: Your project uses Conventional Commits and is at version 1.4.2. Since the last release, these commits were merged: 'fix: handle empty cart', 'feat: add coupon field', 'feat(api)!: remove v1 orders endpoint'. What should the next version be?
objective.explanation: The '!' marks a breaking change, which requires a MAJOR bump, and the highest bump wins. So 1.4.2 becomes 2.0.0 and MINOR and PATCH reset to zero. Without the '!' the result would have been 1.5.0.

objective.question: PR A and PR B both passed CI against main and were approved. PR A was merged first. Then PR B was merged, and main's build immediately failed because the two changes conflict logically, even though Git reported no textual conflict. Which branch protection setting would most directly have prevented this?
options: Require branches to be up to date before merging
Require conversation resolution before merging
Require signed commits
Require a pull request before merging
objective.explanation: 'Require branches to be up to date before merging' forces PR B to be merged or rebased with the latest main. Its checks then rerun against code that includes PR A. The other settings do not make CI test the combined code.

objective.question: Your audit found that a repository administrator merged a PR into main with no approval and with failing checks, even though branch protection requires both. What is the correct fix?
options: Add the administrator to CODEOWNERS
Switch the repository from public to private
Enable the branch protection option that applies the rules to administrators (do not allow bypassing), or remove admins from the ruleset bypass list
Remove the administrator's write access permanently
objective.explanation: By default, administrators can bypass classic branch protection. In rulesets, anyone on the bypass list can do the same. Enforcing the rules for admins, or tightening the bypass list, closes the gap. The other options either do not address bypass or are far too broad.

objective.question: Your team wants main to have a linear history with exactly one commit per pull request. Developers want to keep their messy 'wip' commits on feature branches. Which merge method should you allow on the repository?
options: Squash and merge
Rebase and merge
Fast-forward only with no squashing
Create a merge commit
objective.explanation: Squash and merge combines all PR commits into a single commit on main, so history stays linear and one commit maps to one PR. A merge commit makes history non-linear. Rebase-and-merge and plain fast-forward keep every 'wip' commit.

objective.question: A team deploys to production many times a day. They hide unfinished work behind feature flags and want to avoid long-lived branches and big merge conflicts. Which branching model fits best?
options: Trunk-based development with short-lived branches merged to main frequently
One long-lived branch per developer, merged at the end of each sprint
A separate release branch per environment that is promoted by merging
GitFlow with develop, release and hotfix branches
objective.explanation: Trunk-based development uses small, short-lived branches that are integrated into main often, and it relies on feature flags and strong CI. That suits continuous deployment. GitFlow and long-lived branches add ceremony and cause large merge conflicts.

objective.question: Branch protection on main has 'Require review from Code Owners' enabled. The .github/CODEOWNERS file contains two lines, in this order: '* @acme/platform' and '/docs/ @acme/tech-writers'. A PR changes only docs/install.md. Whose approval is required?
options: Only @acme/platform, because '*' matches everything
Only @acme/tech-writers, because the last matching pattern takes precedence
Nobody, because CODEOWNERS does not apply to Markdown files
Both @acme/platform and @acme/tech-writers
objective.explanation: In CODEOWNERS, the last matching pattern for a file wins. '/docs/' comes after '*', so @acme/tech-writers owns docs/install.md. Owners are not combined across matching lines, and file type does not matter.

objective.question: A developer runs these commands to land a finished feature locally. Since the feature branch was created, two other commits have been pushed to main and pulled into local main. What happens?

code.code:
git checkout main
git pull origin main
git merge --ff-only feature/cart-discount

options: Git rebases feature/cart-discount onto main automatically and then fast-forwards
Git fast-forwards main and silently drops the two new commits from main
Git refuses the merge with an error, because main has diverged and a fast-forward is not possible
Git creates a merge commit, because --ff-only is only a preference
objective.explanation: --ff-only allows the merge only if main can simply move its pointer forward. Because main has commits the feature branch lacks, Git aborts with 'Not possible to fast-forward'. Git never creates a merge commit, rebases or drops commits in this mode.

objective.question: You are on feature/login and run 'git rebase main'. Git stops with a conflict in config.yaml. You want to keep the version from your own feature-branch commit and throw away main's version for this file. Which command does that before you run 'git add config.yaml' and 'git rebase --continue'?

code.code:
git rebase main
# CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in config.yaml

options: git checkout --theirs config.yaml
git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD
git merge -X ours main
git checkout --ours config.yaml
objective.explanation: During a rebase Git replays your commits on top of main, so 'ours' is the base being built (main) and 'theirs' is the commit being replayed (your feature work). '--ours' would keep main's version. 'reset --hard ORIG_HEAD' throws the rebase away, and 'merge -X ours' is a different operation.

objective.question: A developer opens a PR, gets the one required approval, then pushes a new commit with an untested database change and merges straight away. Branch protection on main requires one approval and passing checks, and the checks passed. Which setting most directly stops this?
options: Require conversation resolution before merging
Require signed commits
Dismiss stale pull request approvals when new commits are pushed
Require linear history
objective.explanation: Dismissing stale approvals removes the existing approval when new commits arrive, so the new change must be reviewed again. Linear history controls the shape of the commit graph. Conversation resolution only applies to open review threads. Signed commits prove who made the commit, not that it was reviewed.

objective.question: According to Semantic Versioning 2.0.0, which list is in correct order from lowest to highest precedence?
objective.explanation: A pre-release version ranks lower than the normal version it comes before. Pre-release identifiers are compared field by field: 'alpha' < 'beta' < 'rc' in ASCII order. When the shared fields are equal, the version with more fields ranks higher, so alpha < alpha.1.

objective.question: A team uses GitFlow. A critical bug is found in production version 3.2.0 while develop already holds unreleased features for 3.3.0. What is the correct GitFlow procedure?
options: Create hotfix/3.2.1 from develop, fix the bug and merge it only into main
Commit the fix directly on main and tag v3.2.1. develop will pick it up at the next release
Create hotfix/3.2.1 from main, fix the bug, merge it into main and tag v3.2.1, then merge it into develop as well
Fix the bug on develop, then create release/3.3.0 early and ship it
objective.explanation: In GitFlow, hotfix branches start from main because main matches production. They merge back into main, where the release is tagged, and also into develop so the fix is not lost. Branching from develop would ship unreleased features. Skipping the merge into develop brings the bug back in the next release.

objective.question: Your build script stamps the version using git describe. On a CI runner it prints the output below. What does it mean?

code.code:
$ git describe
v1.4.0-7-g3f2a9c1

options: The repository has 7 tags, and v1.4.0 is the newest
HEAD is 7 commits behind v1.4.0 on the remote
HEAD is 7 commits after the nearest annotated tag v1.4.0, and HEAD's abbreviated commit hash is 3f2a9c1
The commit is tagged v1.4.0-7, and 3f2a9c1 is the tag object's hash
objective.explanation: git describe finds the nearest reachable annotated tag by default. It then appends the number of commits since that tag and 'g' followed by the abbreviated commit hash. It says nothing about the total number of tags or the remote's position.

objective.question: Branch protection on main requires review from Code Owners. The .github/CODEOWNERS file is shown below. A PR changes only docs/api/v2/auth.md. Whose approval is required?

code.code:
* @acme/platform
/docs/* @acme/tech-writers

options: @acme/platform, because /docs/* matches only files directly inside docs/, not nested folders
Both teams, because every matching line adds its owners
Nobody, because no pattern matches a file three levels deep
@acme/tech-writers, because the /docs/* line comes last and matches every file under docs
objective.explanation: In CODEOWNERS, a pattern like /docs/* matches files directly in docs/ but not files in subfolders such as docs/api/v2/. So only the catch-all * line matches, and @acme/platform owns the file. Use /docs/ to cover the whole tree. Owners are never combined across lines; the last matching pattern wins.

objective.question: You enabled a merge queue on main. 'ci' is the required status check. PRs pass CI and join the queue, but they never merge and are eventually removed from the queue. The workflow is shown below. What is the cause?

code.code:
name: CI
on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
jobs:
  ci:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: make test

options: The workflow has no merge_group trigger, so the required check never runs on the queue's temporary branch
The job must be renamed so its name matches the workflow name
Merge queues need at least two required approvals before they process PRs
The workflow needs a push trigger on main so the check runs after the merge
objective.explanation: A merge queue tests each PR on a temporary merge_group branch and waits for the required checks to report there. If the workflow is not triggered on merge_group, 'ci' never reports and the queue entry fails. A push trigger on main runs too late, and approvals or job names are not the cause.

objective.question: Your team releases from main and squash-merges every PR. A tag push triggers the release workflow. Which order of steps is correct for cutting v1.5.0?
options: 1) Create an annotated tag on the release PR branch; 2) push the tag; 3) open the release PR; 4) squash-merge it
1) Push the tag v1.5.0; 2) let the workflow publish; 3) update CHANGELOG.md afterwards in a follow-up PR
1) Create a lightweight tag on main; 2) update CHANGELOG.md directly on main; 3) git push --tags; 4) open a PR for review
1) Open a release PR that bumps the version and updates CHANGELOG.md; 2) merge it after review and green CI; 3) create an annotated tag v1.5.0 on the merged commit on main; 4) git push origin v1.5.0
objective.explanation: The version bump and changelog should be reviewed and pass CI like any other change. The tag goes on the commit that actually lands on main. Tagging the PR branch is wrong because a squash merge creates a new commit with a different SHA. Pushing directly to main or tagging before review breaks the checkpoint.

objective.question: You run the commands below and Git prints the error shown. What is the cause?

code.code:
$ git switch main
$ git merge --ff-only feature/search
fatal: Not possible to fast-forward, aborting.

options: main has commits that feature/search does not contain, so the histories have diverged
--ff-only works only with remote-tracking branches such as origin/feature/search
There is a textual merge conflict between the two branches
feature/search has not been pushed to the remote yet
objective.explanation: A fast-forward is only possible when main is a direct ancestor of the feature branch. If main moved on after the branch was created, the histories have diverged. You can rebase the feature branch onto main and retry, or allow a real merge commit. Push state, remote-tracking branches and conflicts are not the cause of this error.

objective.question: To build a hotfix, you ran git checkout v2.3.0 and made two commits. Then you ran git switch main. The two commits do not appear on any branch. How do you recover them?
options: Run git checkout v2.3.0 again; the commits are attached to the tag
Run git stash pop, because Git stashed them automatically when you switched
Find the last commit's SHA with git reflog, then run git branch hotfix/2.3.1 <sha>
They are lost for good, because commits made in detached HEAD are never stored
objective.explanation: Checking out a tag puts you in detached HEAD. The commits exist but no branch points to them. The reflog records where HEAD has been, so you can create a branch at that SHA before garbage collection removes the commits. Tags do not move, and Git does not stash commits.

objective.question: Five developers push daily to a shared branch, feature/checkout-v2. It is three weeks behind main and needs main's latest fixes. Which approach is best?
options: Rebase feature/checkout-v2 onto main and push with --force-with-lease
Rebase feature/checkout-v2 onto main and push with --force
Delete the branch and have each developer cherry-pick their own commits onto a new branch
Merge main into feature/checkout-v2 and push normally
objective.explanation: Merging keeps the existing commits unchanged, so teammates' clones stay valid. Rebasing a shared branch rewrites history and breaks everyone else's copy, even with --force-with-lease. Recreating the branch with cherry-picks is slow and easy to get wrong.

objective.question: In CI, the version step fails with the output below. A release tag was created earlier with git tag v3.0.0. What is the cause and the right fix?

code.code:
$ git describe
fatal: No annotated tags can describe '4f1c2a9e...'.
However, there were unannotated tags: try --tags.

options: git describe needs a signed tag; add -s when you create it
The runner's Git version is too old and cannot read tags
v3.0.0 is a lightweight tag; recreate it as an annotated tag with git tag -a, or use git describe --tags
The tag was never pushed; run git push origin main
objective.explanation: By default, git describe uses only annotated tags. A lightweight tag is just a name for a commit, with no tagger, date or message. Annotated tags carry that metadata and are the right choice for releases. The error message itself shows that the tag is present, so pushing is not the problem, and signing is not required.

objective.question: v1.4.0 was published and downstream teams consumed it. A bug was then found. A developer deleted the tag, fixed the bug, and re-pushed v1.4.0 on a new commit. What is wrong with this?
options: It is acceptable if the changelog entry for 1.4.0 is updated
Semantic Versioning forbids changing a released version; the fix should be released as v1.4.1, and moved tags confuse caches and consumers
It is wrong only because the developer should have used git push --force for the tag
Nothing; tags can move freely as long as the tag is annotated
objective.explanation: SemVer 2.0.0 says the contents of a released version must not be modified; any change must be a new version. Consumers, package caches and pipelines may already hold the old v1.4.0, so the same name now means two different builds. A patch release, v1.4.1, is the correct fix.

objective.question: You created an organisation ruleset for main that requires a pull request with one approval and the 'ci' status check. Developers can still push directly to main without any error. The ruleset export is shown below. What is the most likely cause?
options: Enforcement is set to evaluate, which only reports what would be blocked; set it to active
Organisation rulesets apply only to new repositories
Rulesets cannot combine pull_request and required_status_checks rules
~DEFAULT_BRANCH is not valid; you must write refs/heads/main
objective.explanation: Ruleset enforcement can be Active, Evaluate or Disabled. Evaluate mode, available on GitHub Enterprise, only records rule results in insights and blocks nothing. ~DEFAULT_BRANCH is a valid target, and the rules can be combined.

objective.question: feature-b was branched from feature-a. feature-a was then squash-merged into main. The feature-b PR now shows feature-a's old commits and conflicts. Your local feature-a branch still points to its pre-squash tip. Which command moves only feature-b's own commits onto main?
options: git merge main into feature-b, then git revert the old feature-a commits
git rebase main feature-a
git rebase feature-a feature-b
git rebase --onto main feature-a feature-b
objective.explanation: git rebase --onto main feature-a feature-b takes the commits in feature-b that are not in feature-a, and replays them onto main. A plain rebase onto main would try to reapply feature-a's original commits, which conflict with their squashed copy. Reverting adds noise, and rebasing feature-a is pointless.

objective.question: A repository's default branch is main. It has a classic branch protection rule with the branch name pattern 'master'. It requires reviews and status checks. Developers report they can push directly to main. Why?
options: Required reviews only apply to forks
Protection takes 24 hours to apply after it is created
The rule's pattern 'master' does not match the branch 'main', so main is unprotected
Classic branch protection does not block direct pushes
objective.explanation: Branch protection applies only to branches whose names match the rule's pattern. This rule protects a branch called master, which no longer exists. Change the pattern to main, or use a ruleset that targets the default branch. Classic protection does block direct pushes when it matches, and it applies immediately.

subjective.question: Explain the difference between git merge and git rebase. When would you use each, and what is the golden rule of rebasing?
subjective.answer: Both commands integrate changes from one branch into another. git merge keeps history exactly as it happened. If the branches have diverged, it creates a merge commit with two parents, so you can always see where a branch joined. git rebase replays your commits on top of the target branch and creates new commits with new hashes. The result is a linear history that is easier to read and bisect. I rebase my own feature branch on the latest main before opening or updating a PR, often with git pull --rebase. I use merge, or the platform's merge button, to bring a reviewed PR into main. The golden rule is simple: never rebase commits that others have already based work on. Rebasing a shared branch rewrites its history, and teammates then hit duplicate commits or confusing conflicts. If I must update a rebased branch on the remote, I use --force-with-lease.
keyPoints: Merge preserves history and may add a merge commit with two parents
Rebase rewrites commits with new hashes and gives a linear history
Rebase local or own feature branches; merge PRs into main
Never rebase shared or public history; use --force-with-lease if you must push

subjective.question: Walk me through how you resolve a merge conflict that appears while rebasing your feature branch onto main.
subjective.answer: First I run git fetch and then git rebase origin/main. If Git stops with a conflict, I run git status to see which files are unmerged. In each file, Git shows conflict markers. The section between <<<<<<< and ======= is one side, and the section between ======= and >>>>>>> is the other. During a rebase, the 'ours' side is the branch I am rebasing onto, and 'theirs' is my commit being replayed. This trips many people up. I edit the file to the correct combined result, not just one side, remove the markers, and run the tests. Then I run git add on the file and git rebase --continue. If the rebase goes badly, git rebase --abort returns me to where I started. When it finishes, I push with --force-with-lease and let CI run again. If conflicts keep recurring, that tells me branches live too long and we should merge smaller and more often.
keyPoints: Identify conflicted files with git status and read the conflict markers
During a rebase, 'ours' and 'theirs' are swapped compared with a merge
Edit to the correct result, run tests, then git add and git rebase --continue
git rebase --abort is the safe exit; push with --force-with-lease
Frequent conflicts point to long-lived branches

subjective.question: Compare trunk-based development and GitFlow. Which would you recommend for a team moving to continuous delivery, and why?
subjective.answer: GitFlow uses long-lived main and develop branches, plus feature, release and hotfix branches. It suits products with scheduled releases and several supported versions, such as packaged software or mobile apps with store review. The cost is overhead. Branches live longer, merges get bigger, and integration problems show up late. Trunk-based development keeps one main branch, the trunk. Developers merge small, short-lived branches into it at least daily. Incomplete features stay hidden behind feature flags, and strong CI keeps main always releasable. For a team moving to continuous delivery, I recommend trunk-based development. It gives fast feedback, small reviewable PRs, fewer conflicts, and a main branch you can deploy at any time. To make it work, you need branch protection with required checks, good automated tests, and feature flags. If you still need to patch old versions, you can cut short release branches from trunk without adopting full GitFlow.
keyPoints: GitFlow: develop, feature, release and hotfix branches; suits versioned, scheduled releases
Trunk-based: short-lived branches merged to main frequently
Trunk-based relies on feature flags and strong CI
Recommend trunk-based for CD because of small batches and fast feedback
Release branches can still be cut from trunk when needed

subjective.question: Your manager says: 'Nothing reaches main without a review and a green pipeline.' Describe exactly how you would configure a GitHub repository to enforce this.
subjective.answer: First, I add a CI workflow triggered by on: pull_request: branches: [main] and on: push: branches: [main], and I let it run once so its job names, such as build and test, become selectable. Then I create a branch ruleset, or classic branch protection, targeting main. I turn on 'Require a pull request before merging' with at least one approval, and I enable dismissal of stale approvals when new commits are pushed. I enable 'Require review from Code Owners' and add a CODEOWNERS file for critical paths. I turn on 'Require status checks to pass' and select the exact check names, plus 'Require branches to be up to date' so checks run against the latest main. I block force pushes and deletions. Finally, I make sure administrators cannot bypass the rules, and I keep the ruleset bypass list empty or limited to a break-glass role. Then I test it by trying a direct push to main, which should be rejected.
keyPoints: CI workflow on pull_request to main, run once so checks appear by name
Require PR with approvals, dismiss stale approvals, code owner review
Required status checks plus 'up to date before merging'
Block force pushes and deletion; enforce for admins and limit the bypass list
Verify by attempting a direct push

subjective.question: What are GitHub rulesets, and how do they differ from classic branch protection rules? What risk does the bypass list introduce?
subjective.answer: Rulesets are the newer way to protect branches and tags in GitHub. A ruleset is a named set of rules, such as requiring PRs, required status checks, blocking force pushes, or requiring linear history. It targets branches or tags by name pattern. Compared with classic branch protection, several rulesets can apply to the same branch at once and their rules are layered together. Rulesets have an enforcement status, so you can disable one without deleting it. They can also protect tags, and anyone with read access can see which rules apply. At organisation level they can cover many repositories, depending on the plan. The bypass list names the roles, teams or apps allowed to skip the rules. That is the risk. If you add a broad role or a deploy bot casually, those identities can push straight to main and skip reviews and CI. I keep the list minimal, document every entry, and review it regularly in audits.
keyPoints: Rulesets are named, layered rules targeting branches or tags by pattern
Multiple rulesets can apply; enforcement can be switched off without deleting
Can protect tags and be visible to readers; org-level options exist
Bypass list lets listed actors skip all rules, so keep it minimal and audited

subjective.question: Explain semantic versioning and how Conventional Commits can automate version bumps and changelogs.
subjective.answer: Semantic versioning uses the format MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. You bump MAJOR for incompatible API changes, MINOR for backward-compatible new features, and PATCH for backward-compatible bug fixes. When you bump a higher number, the lower ones reset, so 1.4.2 with a new feature becomes 1.5.0. Pre-release labels such as 2.0.0-rc.1 rank lower than 2.0.0. Before 1.0.0, the API is treated as unstable. Conventional Commits gives commit messages a structure that tools can read. A 'fix:' commit maps to PATCH and a 'feat:' commit maps to MINOR. A 'BREAKING CHANGE:' footer, or a '!' after the type as in 'feat!:', maps to MAJOR. Other types, such as docs or chore, usually do not bump the version on their own. A release tool reads the commits since the last tag, works out the highest bump, creates the new tag, and generates a changelog grouped into features, fixes and breaking changes. To make this reliable, I enforce the message format in CI, or on the squash-merge PR title.
keyPoints: MAJOR = breaking, MINOR = compatible feature, PATCH = compatible fix; lower parts reset
Pre-release versions rank lower than the release
feat → MINOR, fix → PATCH, BREAKING CHANGE or '!' → MAJOR
Tools compute the highest bump since the last tag and generate the changelog
Enforce the commit or PR title format in CI

subjective.question: Describe a tag-driven release process using Git and GitHub Actions. Include annotated versus lightweight tags and how the tag reaches the remote.
subjective.answer: Once main is green, I create an annotated tag on the release commit: git tag -a v1.3.0 -m 'Release 1.3.0'. An annotated tag is a full Git object with the tagger's name, a date and a message, and it can be signed. That makes it the right choice for releases. A lightweight tag is only a name pointing to a commit, which is fine for private bookmarks. A normal git push does not send tags, so I run git push origin v1.3.0, or git push --follow-tags, which pushes annotated tags reachable from the pushed commits. The release workflow uses on: push: tags: ['v*']. It builds the artefact, tags the container image with the version, publishes a GitHub Release with the generated changelog, and deploys. I also protect v* tags with a ruleset, so only the release process can create them and nobody can move or delete a published tag.
keyPoints: Annotated tags store tagger, date and message and can be signed; use them for releases
Lightweight tags are bare pointers
git push does not push tags; use git push origin <tag> or --follow-tags
Workflow triggers with on: push: tags: ['v*']
Protect release tags from being moved or deleted

subjective.question: When do you use git revert versus git reset? How would you undo a bad merge commit that is already on main?
subjective.answer: git reset moves the current branch pointer to another commit. With --soft it keeps changes staged, with --mixed (the default) it keeps them in the working tree, and with --hard it discards them. Because reset rewrites history, I use it only on local commits that nobody else has. git revert creates a new commit that applies the inverse of an earlier commit. History only moves forward, so it is safe on shared branches such as main, and the undo itself is visible and reviewable. To undo a merge commit, I run git revert -m 1 <merge-sha>. The -m 1 option tells Git to keep the first parent, which is main's side, as the baseline. I raise this as a PR so it still gets a review and a green pipeline. One catch: if the feature is fixed later, merging the same branch again will not bring back the reverted changes. You must first revert the revert, or create fresh commits.
keyPoints: reset moves the branch pointer and rewrites history; local only
Know the --soft, --mixed and --hard differences
revert adds an inverse commit; safe for shared history
Merge commits need git revert -m 1
Re-merging after a revert requires reverting the revert

subjective.question: What makes a good pull request and a good code review? How do CODEOWNERS fit in?
subjective.answer: A good PR is small and focused on one change, ideally a few hundred lines at most. It has a clear title, a description of what changed and why, a link to the issue, and notes on how it was tested. Screenshots help for UI work. The author reviews their own diff first and makes sure CI is green before asking for review. A good reviewer checks correctness, design, tests, security and readability. They leave specific, kind comments, separate blocking issues from nitpicks, and respond quickly so PRs do not go stale. Formatting and linting belong in automated checks, not human review. CODEOWNERS is a file in .github/, the repository root, or docs/. It maps path patterns to users or teams, and the last matching pattern wins. Those owners are requested automatically for review. With 'Require review from Code Owners' turned on, a change to a critical path, such as Terraform modules or CI workflows, cannot merge without approval from the team that owns it.
keyPoints: Small, focused PRs with clear context and evidence of testing
Reviewers check correctness, tests, security and design, and respond quickly
Automate style checks in CI rather than in human review
CODEOWNERS maps paths to owners; the last match wins
Combine with 'Require review from Code Owners' to protect critical paths

subjective.question: A developer ran git push --force on a shared feature branch and wiped out two of a teammate's commits. How do you recover, and what do you change so it does not happen again?
subjective.answer: First, I stop further pushes to the branch. To recover, the teammate who lost the commits still has them locally. They can find them with git reflog or in their own branch history, then restore the branch, for example by resetting a local branch to the right SHA and pushing it back carefully after agreeing with everyone. If no local copy exists, the GitHub PR timeline or activity log may show the old head SHA, which may still be fetchable. Next, I teach the habits. Use git pull --rebase, or plain git pull, which is fetch plus merge, before pushing. When a rewrite is truly needed, use git push --force-with-lease, which refuses to push if the remote has moved since your last fetch. Finally, I add guard rails. Branch protection or a ruleset blocks force pushes on main and on shared release branches. Personal feature branches should have one owner, and others should contribute through PRs to that branch.
keyPoints: Recover from the teammate's local clone or git reflog using the lost SHA
Coordinate before restoring the branch
Use --force-with-lease instead of --force
git pull is fetch plus merge; --rebase replays local commits
Block force pushes on shared branches with protection or rulesets

subjective.question: Your PR has six commits, including 'fix typo' and 'address review'. Reviewers want a clean history before the merge, and the repository allows rebase merging. Explain what these commands do and when it is safe to use them.

code.code:
git commit --fixup=a1b2c3d
git rebase -i --autosquash origin/main
git push --force-with-lease

subjective.answer: 'git commit --fixup=a1b2c3d' records a new commit named 'fixup! <original subject>' that is meant to be folded into commit a1b2c3d. 'git rebase -i --autosquash origin/main' opens the todo list with each fixup commit already moved under its target and marked 'fixup'. Saving the list squashes them in, so each logical change becomes one commit, and the branch is replayed on the latest main. Because the commit hashes change, the remote branch must be force-pushed. '--force-with-lease' refuses to overwrite the remote if someone else pushed in the meantime. This is safe only on a branch you own or have agreed with collaborators. Never rewrite main or shared release branches. After the push, CI runs again on the new commits. If 'dismiss stale approvals' is enabled, reviewers must approve again.
keyPoints: --fixup creates 'fixup!' commits that point at a target commit
--autosquash reorders the list and marks those commits as fixups automatically
Rewritten hashes need --force-with-lease, not a plain --force
Only rewrite branches you own; never main or shared branches
CI and possibly approvals must run again after the rewrite

subjective.question: Branch protection on main requires review from Code Owners, but PRs that touch /payments/ are not asking the payments team for review, and nothing blocks the merge. How do you troubleshoot this?
subjective.answer: First, check where the file lives. GitHub reads CODEOWNERS from .github/, the repository root or docs/, and it must be on the PR's base branch, which is main here. A file that exists only on a feature branch has no effect. Second, open the file on GitHub. GitHub flags lines with invalid syntax or owners that cannot be resolved, and those lines are skipped. Check the path pattern: '/payments/' matches that directory from the root. Remember that the last matching line wins, so a later broad line such as '*' can override it. Third, check the owner. A team must be written as @org/team-name, must be visible, and must have write access to the repository. An owner without write access is ignored. Finally, confirm that the protection rule or ruleset actually targets main and that 'Require review from Code Owners' is enabled. Then open a test PR and confirm the team is requested automatically.
keyPoints: CODEOWNERS must be in .github/, the root or docs/ on the base branch
Invalid lines are flagged and skipped; the last matching pattern wins
Owner teams need the @org/team format, visibility and write access
The rule must target main and have 'Require review from Code Owners' enabled

subjective.question: 'backend-tests' is a required status check on main. PRs that change only README.md now stay blocked forever with 'Expected — Waiting for status to be reported'. Explain why, and how you would fix it.

code.code:
on:
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - 'src/**'
jobs:
  backend-tests:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: make test

subjective.answer: The paths filter stops the whole workflow from running when no file under src/ changed. The workflow never starts, so the 'backend-tests' check is never reported, and branch protection waits for it forever. A workflow skipped by path filtering does not count as passing. To fix it, remove the workflow-level paths filter so the workflow always runs. Inside it, add a small job that detects which files changed, for example with a paths-filter step or a git diff. Put a condition on 'backend-tests', such as 'if: needs.changes.outputs.src == true'. GitHub treats a job skipped by an 'if' condition as successful for required checks, so README-only PRs can merge. PRs that touch code still run the real tests. Another option is a single aggregator job that always runs and is the only required check. Never weaken protection by removing the required check.
keyPoints: A workflow skipped by the paths filter never reports its check, so the check stays Pending
A job skipped by an if: condition is treated as passing
Move change detection inside the workflow as a job, with conditional jobs after it
An always-running aggregator job as the single required check is a clean pattern

subjective.question: Your team squash-merges PRs. A developer squash-merged feature/search, kept working on the same branch, and opened a second PR. That PR now shows the old commits again and has conflicts with main. Why does this happen, and what should the developer and the team do?
subjective.answer: A squash merge creates one brand-new commit on main that holds the combined changes. The original branch commits are never added to main's history. Git therefore sees them as unmerged, and the second PR shows them again. Their changes overlap with the squash commit, which causes conflicts. To recover, the developer should create a new branch from the latest main and cherry-pick only the new commits. Another option is 'git rebase --onto origin/main <last-old-commit> feature/search'. The team should treat a branch as finished once it is squash-merged. Turning on 'Automatically delete head branches' enforces this. For stacked PRs, retarget the child PR to main after the parent merges, then rebase it onto main. Note that 'git branch --merged' also does not list squash-merged branches, so clean them up by PR status instead.
keyPoints: A squash merge creates a new commit; the branch commits never become ancestors of main
Reusing the branch brings old commits back and causes conflicts
Recover with a fresh branch plus cherry-pick, or rebase --onto
Auto-delete head branches, and rebase stacked PRs after the parent merges

subjective.question: You use trunk-based development and tag releases from main. Production runs v2.3.0, but main has moved on with unreleased work behind feature flags and some risky refactoring. A security fix must ship today without that refactoring. How do you release it?
subjective.answer: First, fix the bug on main through a normal PR, so main never loses the fix. Then create a short-lived release branch from the production tag: 'git switch -c release/2.3 v2.3.0'. Cherry-pick the fix with 'git cherry-pick -x <sha>'. The -x flag records the original commit in the message so you can trace it. Open a PR into release/2.3 so branch protection still requires a review and green CI. Protect release/* branches with a ruleset as well. After the merge, create an annotated tag v2.3.1 on that commit and push it with 'git push origin v2.3.1'. That push triggers the tag-driven release pipeline. It is a PATCH bump because the fix is backwards-compatible. Add a changelog entry under 2.3.1. Delete the release branch once it is no longer supported. Fixing main first avoids a regression in 2.4.0.
keyPoints: Fix on main first so the fix is not lost in later releases
Branch from the v2.3.0 tag and cherry-pick -x only the fix
Keep review and CI rules on release branches
Annotated tag v2.3.1, pushed explicitly, plus a changelog entry

subjective.question: Anyone with write access can push a v* tag and start your production release workflow. How would you use GitHub rulesets so that only your release automation can create, move or delete release tags?
subjective.answer: Create a repository ruleset or an organisation ruleset with the target set to tags, not branches. Use the pattern 'v*' as the target. Turn on 'Restrict creations', 'Restrict updates' and 'Restrict deletions'. Updates covers moving an existing tag, and deletions covers removing a published version. Set enforcement to Active, after testing in Evaluate mode if your plan supports it. In the bypass list, add only the identity that makes releases. This is ideally a dedicated GitHub App, or the repository role that your release workflow uses. Do not add broad roles such as all admins. Every bypass entry is a way around the control, and it should be audited. Then check that the release workflow creates tags only after main is green. Releases are then tied to reviewed, tested commits, and published versions stay immutable. Watch the ruleset insights for blocked attempts.
keyPoints: Rulesets can target tags with patterns such as v*
Restrict creations, updates and deletions to make published tags immutable
Keep the bypass list minimal, e.g. one release GitHub App
Test with Evaluate mode, then enforce and review insights

subjective.question: Case study: a fintech team has 40 engineers and one monorepo. They deploy to production several times a day. Auditors need proof that every change was reviewed and tested. The security team must approve anything under /infra/. Production hotfixes must be possible within an hour. Design the branching model and the repository protections.
subjective.answer: I would use trunk-based development. Developers work on short-lived branches and hide unfinished work behind feature flags. I would protect main with a ruleset that targets the default branch, with enforcement set to Active. The ruleset would require a pull request with one approval, review from Code Owners, dismissal of stale approvals, and the required checks. I would block force pushes and deletion. The bypass list would be empty, so admins cannot skip the rules. CODEOWNERS would map /infra/ to the security team. A merge queue would test PRs against the latest main, and the workflows would trigger on both pull_request and merge_group. Releases would be annotated tags on main. For a hotfix, I would branch from the release tag, cherry-pick the fix with -x, and tag a patch version. The hotfix still goes through review and CI, and a fast pipeline keeps it inside the hour. The audit evidence is the PR history, the review records and the check results.
keyPoints: Trunk-based development with feature flags fits several deploys a day
Active ruleset with required review, Code Owners, stale-approval dismissal and required checks
Empty bypass list, so the review claim is actually true
Merge queue, with workflows triggered on merge_group
Hotfix from the release tag, still reviewed, so speed comes from fast CI

subjective.question: Spot the mistakes. 'test' is the required status check on main. Every PR stays blocked with 'Expected — Waiting for status to be reported'. Find the problems in this workflow and fix them.

code.code:
name: CI
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      matrix:
        node: [18, 20]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: ${{ matrix.node }}
      - run: npm ci && npm test

subjective.answer: There are two mistakes. First, the workflow runs only on push to main, so it never runs for pull requests, and no check is ever reported on a PR. I would add a pull_request trigger for main, and a merge_group trigger if we use a merge queue. Second, a matrix job reports one check per combination, named 'test (18)' and 'test (20)'. No check named exactly 'test' will ever appear. There are two fixes. One is to require the two matrix check names. That breaks every time the matrix changes. The better fix is an aggregate job, for example 'ci-ok'. It uses needs: test and if: always(), and fails unless every matrix leg succeeded. I would make 'ci-ok' the only required check. After that, I would open a test PR to confirm the check reports and turns green.
keyPoints: A push-only trigger means no check ever reports on PRs
Matrix jobs report names like 'test (18)', not 'test'
Add pull_request and merge_group triggers
An aggregate job with needs and if: always() gives a stable required check name
Verify with a real PR before relying on it

subjective.question: Troubleshooting: your tag-triggered release workflow runs, but the changelog step produces either an empty changelog or every commit since the project began. git describe also fails in the job. It works on developers' laptops. What is the likely cause, and how do you fix it?

code.code:
on:
  push:
    tags: ['v*']
jobs:
  release:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npx conventional-changelog -r 1
      - run: git describe

subjective.answer: The cause is a shallow clone. By default, actions/checkout fetches only one commit and does not fetch the full history or the other tags. The changelog tool cannot find the previous release tag or the commits since that tag, so the output is empty or wrong. git describe has no tagged ancestor to walk back to. Laptops have the full history, so it works there. The fix is to set fetch-depth: 0 on the checkout step. This fetches all history and tags. Newer versions of the action also support fetch-tags, but changelog tools usually need the commits as well as the tags. I would also check that the release tags are annotated, because git describe ignores lightweight tags by default. After the change, I would rerun the job on a test tag and confirm the changelog covers only the commits since the last tag.
keyPoints: actions/checkout makes a shallow clone by default
Without the history and tags, the tools cannot find the previous release
Set fetch-depth: 0
git describe ignores lightweight tags by default
Laptops work because they have full clones

subjective.question: Comparison: a regulated team must trace every change to a ticket. It uses git bisect to find regressions and wants a readable main. Compare merge commits, squash merging and rebase merging for this team, and recommend one.
subjective.answer: A merge commit keeps every feature-branch commit plus a merge commit that records the PR. Traceability is very good, but the history is non-linear and noisy. git bisect can also land on half-finished 'wip' commits that do not build. Squash merging creates one commit per PR on main. The commit message can carry the PR number and the ticket ID. Every commit on main passed CI as a whole, so bisect lands on a whole PR and builds reliably. The cost is that the fine-grained commits are lost from main, although the PR still keeps them. Rebase merging gives a linear history but keeps each individual commit. That is only good if developers curate their commits so that each one builds. For this team I would recommend squash merging, with linear history required and a commit message template that includes the ticket. It is simple to audit and reliable to bisect.
keyPoints: Merge commits: full detail, but noisy, non-linear history and unbuildable bisect points
Squash: one tested commit per PR, easy to link to a ticket
Rebase merge: linear, but only clean if every commit builds
Recommend squash plus required linear history for audit and bisect

subjective.question: Put the steps in order: your team is moving from GitFlow to trunk-based development without disrupting releases. List the steps in the order you would do them, and explain why the order matters.
subjective.answer: First, make CI fast and reliable on PRs to main, because trunk-based development depends on a trustworthy pipeline. Second, add a feature-flag mechanism, so unfinished work can merge safely. Third, finish the current release from the release branch the GitFlow way and merge it back, so nothing is stranded. Fourth, merge develop into main, so main holds all the work in progress. Fifth, protect main with required review, required checks, stale-approval dismissal and no bypass. Sixth, change the default branch and PR target to main, and set a short branch-lifetime guideline, such as a day or two. Seventh, release by tagging main, and patch old releases from their tags. Last, lock develop as read-only and then delete it. The order matters because a flag system and fast CI must exist before people merge small changes to main daily. If you delete develop before draining it, work is lost.
keyPoints: Fast CI and feature flags come first
Drain the in-flight release and develop into main before switching
Protect main before making it the PR target
Tag releases from main; retire develop last

subjective.question: Spot the mistakes in this CODEOWNERS file. The goals are: payments owns /payments/, infra owns all Terraform and /infra/, writers own everything under docs, and platform owns everything else.

code.code:
# .github/CODEOWNERS
/payments/ @acme/payments
/infra/ @bob
*.tf @acme/infra
/docs/* @acme/writers
* @acme/platform

subjective.answer: The biggest bug is the catch-all '* @acme/platform' on the last line. In CODEOWNERS the last matching pattern wins, so platform now owns every file and the other lines do nothing. The catch-all must be the first line. Second, '/docs/*' matches only files directly in docs/, not nested folders. It should be '/docs/'. Third, '/infra/ @bob': if bob does not have write access to the repository, GitHub ignores him as an owner, and individuals are a single point of failure. Use @acme/infra instead. Also, '*.tf' comes after '/infra/', so Terraform files inside infra get only the '*.tf' owners. That matches the goal here, but the order needs care. Teams used as owners must also have write access. Finally, I would check GitHub's CODEOWNERS error view and test with a PR that touches each path.
keyPoints: Last matching pattern wins, so the catch-all must come first
/docs/* is not recursive; use /docs/
Owners need write access; prefer teams over individuals
Line order decides which owner wins for overlapping paths
Validate with GitHub's error view and test PRs

subjective.question: Put the steps in order: a test that passed at v2.4.0 fails on main today, and there are 300 commits in between. Describe how you use git bisect to find the commit that broke it, and how you would automate this.

code.code:
git bisect start
git bisect bad main
git bisect good v2.4.0
git bisect run ./scripts/check-login.sh
git bisect reset

subjective.answer: git bisect does a binary search through history. I run git bisect start, mark the current main as bad, and mark v2.4.0 as good. Git checks out a commit halfway between them. I test it and mark it good or bad, and Git halves the range again. With 300 commits this takes about nine steps. To automate it, I use git bisect run with a script. The script exits 0 for good, a value from 1 to 127 (except 125) for bad, and 125 to skip a commit that cannot be tested. Git then finds the first bad commit on its own. When it is done, I run git bisect reset to return to my branch. This works best when every commit on main builds, which is one reason squash merging and required CI help. Once I find the commit, I fix it forward or use git revert. I do not rewrite main.
keyPoints: Mark one bad and one good commit; Git binary-searches between them
git bisect run uses exit codes: 0 good, 1-127 bad, 125 skip
Finish with git bisect reset
Works best when every commit on main builds
Undo the bad commit with revert or a fix-forward, not a rewrite

subjective.question: Case study: a developer pushed a commit containing a live AWS access key to a feature branch and opened a PR. The PR was not merged, and secret scanning raised an alert. List what you do, in priority order.
subjective.answer: First, revoke or rotate the key immediately. Once it is pushed, assume it is compromised, because the remote, forks, clones and CI logs may already hold it. Second, check CloudTrail for any use of the key and contain any damage. Third, remove the secret from the code and load it from a secret store or OIDC-based credentials instead. Fourth, rewrite the branch history so the secret is gone from all commits. Use an interactive rebase for a few commits, or a tool like git filter-repo for more. Then force-push with --force-with-lease, after telling anyone using that branch. Fifth, ask GitHub support to purge cached views if needed, because the PR may still reference the old commits. Finally, prevent a repeat. Enable push protection for secret scanning, add a pre-commit hook, and move to short-lived credentials. Rewriting history alone is never enough. Rotation comes first.
keyPoints: Rotate or revoke the key first; rewriting history does not make it safe
Check logs for use of the key and contain damage
Move the secret to a secret store or OIDC credentials
Rewrite the branch history and coordinate the force-push
Enable push protection and pre-commit scanning

subjective.question: Case study: you use a release bot, such as release-please, that must update CHANGELOG.md and the version file on main. main requires a PR, one approval and green checks, and the bypass list is empty. How do you let the bot work without weakening the checkpoint?
subjective.answer: The cleanest way is to keep the bot inside the normal flow. The bot opens a release PR with the version bump and changelog, and a human reviews and merges it like any other PR. Required checks run on it, so the checkpoint still holds. The bot should use a GitHub App token, not the default GITHUB_TOKEN. Events created with GITHUB_TOKEN do not trigger new workflow runs, so required checks would never report on its PR. After the merge, the bot creates the annotated tag on the merged commit, and the tag push triggers the release pipeline. If the bot must create tags under a tag ruleset, I would add only that GitHub App to the bypass list of the tag ruleset, not the branch ruleset. I would avoid putting the bot on main's bypass list, because then something reaches main without review.
keyPoints: The bot opens a release PR, and a human reviews and merges it
Use a GitHub App token, because GITHUB_TOKEN events do not trigger workflows
Tag after the merge, on the merged commit
Narrow bypass only on the tag ruleset, never on main

subjective.question: Spot the mistakes in this release script that a team runs by hand.

code.code:
#!/bin/bash
git checkout develop
git pull
VERSION=$(cat VERSION)
git tag v$VERSION
git push --force origin develop
git push origin --tags

subjective.answer: There are several problems. There is no 'set -euo pipefail', so a failed pull or checkout does not stop the script. It tags develop, which is unreleased integration work. It should tag the reviewed commit on main, or the release branch in GitFlow. 'git tag v$VERSION' creates a lightweight tag with no tagger, date or message. Use 'git tag -a v$VERSION -m ...', and sign it if you can. 'git push --force origin develop' rewrites a shared branch and can wipe out teammates' commits, and a release has no reason to push the branch at all. 'git push origin --tags' pushes every local tag, including stray or experimental ones. Push only the one tag with 'git push origin v$VERSION'. The script also does not check that CI is green on that commit or that the tag does not already exist. Better still, move this into a reviewed workflow, and protect v* tags with a ruleset.
keyPoints: Add set -euo pipefail so failures stop the script
Tag the reviewed commit on main, not develop
Use annotated tags, not lightweight tags
Never force-push a shared branch; push only the single release tag
Check that CI passed and the tag is new; protect tags with a ruleset

subjective.question: Troubleshooting: a developer rebased feature/cart onto main. The push was rejected, so they ran git pull and then git push. The PR now shows every commit twice and a strange merge commit. What happened, and how do you fix it?
subjective.answer: After the rebase, the local branch held new copies of the commits, with new SHAs. The remote still had the old copies.
