The final stage copies only package.json, the production node_modules and dist, each with --chown or kept root-owned and read-only. If the image is still over budget, I switch the final base to an Alpine or distroless Node image, pinned by digest. Then I check with docker history which layers remain large. A .dockerignore also keeps .git and local node_modules out of the context.
keyPoints: Copying the full /app brings devDependencies and source along
A separate production-dependencies stage with npm ci --omit=dev
Copy only dist, production node_modules and package.json
Smaller pinned final base if still over budget; verify with docker history

subjective.question: For the Postgres data in your Compose stack, should you use a named volume or a bind mount? Compare them and give your choice.
subjective.answer: A named volume is managed by Docker and lives in Docker's storage area. Docker creates it automatically, so it works on a fresh machine without any folders existing first. On Docker Desktop for macOS and Windows it lives inside the Linux VM, which is much faster than going through the host file-sharing layer. The Postgres image can also set the right ownership on first start. A bind mount maps a host path into the container. It is great for source code during development, because you can edit files and see changes live. For a database, though, it brings problems: UID and permission mismatches with the postgres user, slow I/O on macOS and Windows, and host-specific paths that break the one-command checkpoint. My choice for Postgres data is a named volume, for example pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data. I use bind mounts only for code or for read-only init scripts in /docker-entrypoint-initdb.d. I also remind the team that 'docker compose down -v' deletes named volumes.
keyPoints: Named volumes are Docker-managed and portable to a fresh machine
Better I/O on Docker Desktop and fewer permission issues
Bind mounts suit live code editing and init scripts
Choose a named volume for database data; down -v deletes it

subjective.question: A critical OpenSSL CVE is announced and it affects the base image used by 20 of your services. Put the steps of your response in order, from detection to proof of fix.
subjective.answer: First, I identify the affected images. I query the stored SBOMs, or rescan the images currently deployed (by digest) with Trivy, to list which services and versions include the vulnerable package. Second, I check whether a patched base image exists. If it does, I update the pinned base digest in each Dockerfile. Renovate or Dependabot can open these PRs across all repos. Third, CI rebuilds each image, with --pull or no cache for the base layer so the new base is really used. Fourth, the scan gate reruns and must show the CVE as fixed. Fifth, CI pushes the images, regenerates the SBOMs and signs the new digests. Sixth, I roll out by digest, critical and internet-facing services first, with signature verification at deploy time. Seventh, I prove the fix by rescanning what is actually running and confirming the old digests are gone. If no patch exists yet, I record a time-limited exception and add mitigations, such as switching to a distroless base.
keyPoints: Use SBOMs or rescans to find affected deployed digests
Bump pinned base digests, automated with Renovate or Dependabot
Rebuild, rescan, regenerate SBOM, sign new digests
Roll out by digest, highest risk first, with signature verification
Verify running workloads; time-limited exception if unpatched

steps.overview: This step teaches the core Kubernetes objects an application developer uses every day. It covers workloads, configuration, health checks, batch jobs, networking and fast kubectl habits. CKAD is a hands-on exam in a live cluster, so speed with imperative commands and correct YAML matters as much as theory.
objectives: Create and update Pods, Deployments and Services quickly with imperative kubectl commands and generated YAML.
Configure applications with ConfigMaps, Secrets, liveness/readiness/startup probes, and resource requests and limits.
Build Jobs and CronJobs, expose apps through Ingress, and restrict traffic with NetworkPolicies.
Deploy your own container to a kind or minikube cluster with probes, limits and a working Ingress.
Finish a timed 15-task CKAD practice set inside two hours by managing time and contexts.

concepts.explanation: A Pod is the smallest deployable unit: one or more containers sharing a network namespace and volumes. A ReplicaSet keeps a set number of identical Pods running. A Deployment manages ReplicaSets and adds rolling updates and rollbacks, so you almost never create ReplicaSets directly.

A Service gives a stable virtual IP and DNS name to the Pods matched by its label selector. The type is ClusterIP by default (internal only). NodePort opens a port on every node, and LoadBalancer asks the cloud for an external load balancer. If the selector does not match the Pod labels, the Service has no endpoints.

Both hold key-value data that is injected as environment variables (env, envFrom) or mounted as files through a volume. Secrets are only base64-encoded by default, not encrypted. Encryption at rest and RBAC protect them. Env vars do not update when a ConfigMap changes; mounted files do update, after a delay, unless you use subPath.

A livenessProbe failure restarts the container. A readinessProbe failure removes the Pod from Service endpoints but does not restart it. A startupProbe holds back the other probes until it succeeds, which protects slow-starting apps. Probe handlers are httpGet, tcpSocket, exec and grpc.

The scheduler places Pods using requests. Limits cap usage at runtime: a container over its CPU limit is throttled, while one over its memory limit is OOMKilled. QoS class comes from these values. Guaranteed means requests equal limits for every container; Burstable means some requests or limits are set; BestEffort means none are set. LimitRange and ResourceQuota enforce defaults and totals per namespace.

A Job runs Pods until a set number complete successfully. Key fields are completions, parallelism, backoffLimit and activeDeadlineSeconds. restartPolicy must be Never or OnFailure. A CronJob creates Jobs on a five-field cron schedule, with concurrencyPolicy (Allow, Forbid, Replace) and history limits.

An Ingress defines HTTP/HTTPS routing rules (host and path) to backend Services. It does nothing without an Ingress controller such as ingress-nginx, selected via ingressClassName. pathType is Prefix, Exact or ImplementationSpecific. TLS is set with a Secret of type kubernetes.io/tls.

A NetworkPolicy selects Pods with podSelector and lists allowed ingress and/or egress traffic by podSelector, namespaceSelector or ipBlock, plus ports. Pods are open to all traffic until a policy selects them. After that, only explicitly allowed traffic passes. Enforcement needs a CNI that supports policies, such as Calico or Cilium.

Generators such as kubectl run, create deployment, create job, create cronjob, expose and create ingress produce correct objects in seconds. Adding --dry-run=client -o yaml writes a YAML skeleton you can edit for fields with no flag, such as probes. kubectl explain <resource>.spec --recursive shows field names without leaving the terminal.

keyFacts: CKAD: performance-based in a live cluster, 2 hours, pass mark 66%, one free retake. You may use the official Kubernetes documentation during the exam.

CKAD domain weights in the current curriculum: Application Design and Build 20%, Application Deployment 20%, Application Observability and Maintenance 15%, Application Environment, Configuration and Security 25%, Services and Networking 20%. Check the CNCF curriculum page before booking.
Deployment default strategy is RollingUpdate with maxSurge 25% and maxUnavailable 25%. Recreate kills all old Pods first.
Probe defaults: periodSeconds 10, timeoutSeconds 1, failureThreshold 3, successThreshold 1.
Job backoffLimit defaults to 6. A Job Pod's restartPolicy must be Never or OnFailure, never Always.
The default NodePort range is 30000–32767.
CPU over limit means throttling; memory over limit means OOMKilled (exit code 137).
Service DNS name format: <service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local.
Rollouts: kubectl rollout status, history, undo (add --to-revision=N for a specific version), restart.
kubectl run <name> --image=X --restart=Never creates a bare Pod. kubectl create deployment creates a Deployment.

example.caption: Speed workflow for the hands-on task: generate, edit, apply, expose, route and test
example.code:
alias k=kubectl
export do="--dry-run=client -o yaml"
# 1. Generate a Deployment skeleton, then add probes to it
k create deploy web --image=myapp:1.0 --replicas=3 --port=8080 $do > web.yaml
# In web.yaml under the container, add:
#   readinessProbe: {httpGet: {path: /healthz, port: 8080}, periodSeconds: 5}
#   livenessProbe:  {httpGet: {path: /healthz, port: 8080}, initialDelaySeconds: 10}
k apply -f web.yaml
k set resources deploy web --requests=cpu=100m,memory=128Mi --limits=cpu=500m,memory=256Mi
# 2. Config and secrets
k create cm app-cfg --from-literal=MODE=prod
k create secret generic db --from-literal=PASS=s3cret
k set env deploy/web --from=configmap/app-cfg
# 3. Networking
k expose deploy web --port=80 --target-port=8080
minikube addons enable ingress   # on kind, install ingress-nginx instead
k create ingress web --class=nginx --rule="web.local/*=web:80"
# 4. Batch
k create job once --image=busybox -- echo hello
k create cronjob tick --image=busybox --schedule="*/5 * * * *" -- date
# 5. Verify and roll back
k rollout status deploy/web
k run tmp --image=busybox --rm -it --restart=Never -- wget -qO- http://web
k set image deploy/web myapp=myapp:1.1 && k rollout undo deploy/web

pitfalls: Working in the wrong cluster or namespace. Every exam task tells you which context to use, so run the given kubectl config use-context command first and pass -n <namespace>, or edit the namespace in the YAML.
Labels do not match between the Service selector and the Pod template. Check with kubectl get endpoints <svc>: an empty list means a selector mismatch or failing readiness.
Using a livenessProbe where a readinessProbe is needed. Liveness restarts the container, so a slow app can end up in a CrashLoopBackOff restart loop. Use startupProbe for slow boots.

Assuming an Ingress works on its own. Without an installed controller and a matching ingressClassName, no traffic is routed. On kind you also need extraPortMappings or port-forwarding to reach it. The community ingress-nginx controller has been announced for retirement and Gateway API is the long-term successor. CKAD still tests the Ingress resource, so learn it.
Writing a NetworkPolicy that blocks DNS. If you restrict egress, also allow UDP/TCP port 53 to kube-dns, or name lookups fail.
Getting stuck on one hard task. Each task carries a weight, so flag it, move on and come back. Do not spend more than about 8 minutes on any single task.

workflow.title: Solving a CKAD task under time pressure

steps.label: Switch context and namespace
steps.detail: Run the context command given in the task and note the target namespace before typing anything else.

steps.label: Generate YAML imperatively
steps.detail: Use kubectl create or run with --dry-run=client -o yaml to get a correct skeleton in seconds.

steps.label: Edit only missing fields
steps.detail: Add probes, resources, volumes or securityContext in vim, using kubectl explain or the docs for exact field names.

steps.label: Apply the manifest
steps.detail: Run kubectl apply -f and fix any validation errors at once.

steps.label: Verify the result
steps.detail: Check with get, describe, logs, get endpoints, or a temporary busybox Pod running wget or nslookup.

steps.label: Move on or flag
steps.detail: If the task is not done within its time budget, flag it and return at the end.

project.title: hello-ckad
project.summary: A tiny Python HTTP service is built into a container, loaded into a local kind cluster and deployed with a ConfigMap, a Secret, startup/readiness/liveness probes, requests and limits, a Service, an Ingress, NetworkPolicies, a Job and a CronJob. app/server.py and the Dockerfile are the workload, kind-config.yaml is the cluster, the k8s/ folder holds the manifests, and README.md gives the run steps plus the imperative kubectl shortcuts you need for CKAD speed.
project.run:
kind create cluster --config kind-config.yaml
kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kubernetes/ingress-nginx/main/deploy/static/provider/kind/deploy.yaml
kubectl wait -n ingress-nginx --for=condition=ready pod -l app.kubernetes.io/component=controller --timeout=180s
docker build -t hello-ckad:1.0 .
kind load docker-image hello-ckad:1.0 --name ckad
kubectl apply -f k8s/app.yaml
kubectl apply -f k8s/ingress.yaml -f k8s/jobs.yaml
kubectl -n ckad-demo rollout status deploy/hello
curl -H 'Host: hello.local' http://localhost/

files.code:
# Small, non-root image for the hello-ckad app
FROM python:3.12-slim

WORKDIR /app
COPY app/server.py .

# Numeric UID so the kubelet can verify securityContext.runAsNonRoot: true
USER 10001

# PORT must match containerPort 8080 in k8s/app.yaml
ENV PORT=8080 \
    PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
EXPOSE 8080

CMD ["python", "server.py"]

# Single-node kind cluster named "ckad".
# Host ports 80/443 map into the node so ingress-nginx is reachable on localhost.
kind: Cluster
apiVersion: kind.x-k8s.io/v1alpha4
name: ckad
nodes:
  - role: control-plane
    kubeadmConfigPatches:
      - |
        kind: InitConfiguration
        nodeRegistration:
          kubeletExtraArgs:
            node-labels: "ingress-ready=true"   # the kind ingress-nginx manifest schedules onto this label
    extraPortMappings:
      - containerPort: 80
        hostPort: 80
        protocol: TCP
      - containerPort: 443
        hostPort: 443
        protocol: TCP

apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata: {name: ckad-demo}
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata: {name: hello-config, namespace: ckad-demo}
data:
  APP_MESSAGE: "Hello from CKAD week 6"
  WARMUP_SECONDS: "5"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata: {name: hello-secret, namespace: ckad-demo}
type: Opaque
stringData:                     # API server stores it base64-encoded; base64 is NOT encryption
  API_TOKEN: "change-me"
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: {name: hello, namespace: ckad-demo, labels: {app: hello}}
spec:
  replicas: 2                   # the Deployment creates a ReplicaSet that keeps 2 Pods running
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate: {maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0}   # zero-downtime rollouts
  selector:
    matchLabels: {app: hello}   # must match the template labels below
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: {app: hello}
    spec:
      securityContext: {runAsNonRoot: true}
      containers:
        - name: hello
          image: hello-ckad:1.0
          imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent         # use the image loaded with `kind load`
          ports: [{containerPort: 8080, name: http}]
          envFrom:
            - configMapRef: {name: hello-config} # every key becomes an env var
          env:
            - name: API_TOKEN
              valueFrom: {secretKeyRef: {name: hello-secret, key: API_TOKEN}}
            - name: POD_NAME
              valueFrom: {fieldRef: {fieldPath: metadata.name}}
          resources:
            requests: {cpu: 50m, memory: 64Mi}  # scheduler places the Pod using requests
            limits: {cpu: 200m, memory: 128Mi}  # CPU throttled, memory over limit = OOMKilled; requests < limits => Burstable QoS
          startupProbe:                         # liveness/readiness wait until this passes
            httpGet: {path: /healthz, port: http}
            periodSeconds: 2
            failureThreshold: 10
          readinessProbe:                       # failing => Pod removed from Service endpoints
            httpGet: {path: /ready, port: http}
            periodSeconds: 5
          livenessProbe:                        # failing => kubelet restarts the container
            httpGet: {path: /healthz, port: http}
            periodSeconds: 10
            failureThreshold: 3
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: {name: hello, namespace: ckad-demo}
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector: {app: hello}        # targets Pods with this label
  ports:
    - {name: http, port: 80, targetPort: http}  # Service port 80 -> container port 8080

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: hello
  namespace: ckad-demo
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx       # served by the ingress-nginx controller
  rules:
    - host: hello.local         # test with: curl -H 'Host: hello.local' http://localhost/
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: hello
                port: {number: 80}  # the Service port, not the container port
---
# Step 1: deny all incoming traffic to every Pod in the namespace
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: default-deny-ingress, namespace: ckad-demo}
spec:
  podSelector: {}               # empty selector = all Pods in ckad-demo
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
---
# Step 2: allow only the ingress controller and checker Pods to reach the app
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: allow-hello, namespace: ckad-demo}
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: {app: hello}
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
    - from:                     # two list items = OR
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: {kubernetes.io/metadata.name: ingress-nginx}
        - podSelector:          # same namespace only, because no namespaceSelector here
            matchLabels: {role: checker}
      ports:
        - {protocol: TCP, port: 8080}   # Pod port, because policies act after the Service

# One-off smoke test. Pod label role=checker is allowed by NetworkPolicy allow-hello.
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata: {name: hello-check, namespace: ckad-demo}
spec:
  backoffLimit: 3               # retry failed Pods up to 3 times
  activeDeadlineSeconds: 60     # fail the whole Job after 60 s
  ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 300  # garbage-collect the Job 5 minutes after it finishes
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: {role: checker}
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never      # Jobs need Never or OnFailure
      containers:
        - name: check
          image: busybox:1.36
          command: ["sh", "-c", "wget -qO- http://hello.ckad-demo.svc.cluster.local/"]
          resources:
            requests: {cpu: 10m, memory: 16Mi}
            limits: {cpu: 50m, memory: 32Mi}
---
# Same check every 5 minutes
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata: {name: hello-check-cron, namespace: ckad-demo}
spec:
  schedule: "*/5 * * * *"
  concurrencyPolicy: Forbid     # skip a run if the previous one is still going
  successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 3
  failedJobsHistoryLimit: 1
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      backoffLimit: 2
      template:
        metadata:
          labels: {role: checker}
        spec:
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
          containers:
            - name: check
              image: busybox:1.36
              command: ["sh", "-c", "wget -qO- http://hello.ckad-demo.svc.cluster.local/"]
              resources:
                requests: {cpu: 10m, memory: 16Mi}
                limits: {cpu: 50m, memory: 32Mi}

# hello-ckad: CKAD Step 5 hands-on

Deploy your container to kind with probes, limits, an Ingress and NetworkPolicies.

## Prerequisites
Docker, kind (recent release; its default CNI kindnet enforces NetworkPolicy), kubectl.
Note: the community ingress-nginx project has announced its retirement. It is still fine for local
practice. For real clusters, check your controller's support status or look at the Gateway API.

## Run
1. `kind create cluster --config kind-config.yaml`
2. Install ingress-nginx (kind manifest), then wait for the controller Pod (see the run steps).
3. `docker build -t hello-ckad:1.0 . && kind load docker-image hello-ckad:1.0 --name ckad`
4. `kubectl apply -f k8s/app.yaml`, then `kubectl apply -f k8s/ingress.yaml -f k8s/jobs.yaml`
5. `curl -H 'Host: hello.local' http://localhost/`. Repeat it and watch the `pod` field change.

## Verify what you built
- `kubectl -n ckad-demo get deploy,rs,pod,svc,ing,netpol`
- `kubectl -n ckad-demo get pod -o jsonpath='{.items[*].status.qosClass}'` should print Burstable
- `kubectl -n ckad-demo get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=hello` lists ready Pods only
- `kubectl -n ckad-demo logs job/hello-check` shows the JSON reply
- NetworkPolicy test (should time out):
  `kubectl -n ckad-demo run probe --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -- wget -T 3 -qO- http://hello`
  Add `--labels=role=checker` and it succeeds.

## Break it on purpose
- Set `readinessProbe.httpGet.path: /nope`. Pods run but stay 0/1 READY and get no traffic.
- Set `limits.memory: 8Mi`. Watch for OOMKilled in `kubectl describe pod`.
- Roll back with `kubectl -n ckad-demo rollout undo deploy/hello`.

## CKAD speed kit (imperative + dry-run)
```bash
alias k=kubectl
export do='--dry-run=client -o yaml'      # usage: k run x --image=nginx $do > x.yaml
export now='--force --grace-period=0'     # fast delete in practice clusters
k config set-context --current --namespace=ckad-demo

k create deploy hello --image=hello-ckad:1.0 --replicas=2 --port=8080 $do > deploy.yaml
k expose deploy hello --port=80 --target-port=8080 $do > svc.yaml
k create cm hello-config --from-literal=APP_MESSAGE=hi $do
k create secret generic hello-secret --from-literal=API_TOKEN=change-me $do
k set resources deploy hello --requests=cpu=50m,memory=64Mi --limits=cpu=200m,memory=128Mi
k create job hello-check --image=busybox:1.36 $do -- wget -qO- http://hello
k create cronjob hello-check-cron --image=busybox:1.36 --schedule='*/5 * * * *' $do -- wget -qO- http://hello
k create ingress hello --class=nginx --rule='hello.local/*=hello:80' $do
k explain deploy.spec.template.spec.containers.readinessProbe   # field docs without leaving the terminal
```
There is no imperative command for probes or NetworkPolicies. Generate the YAML, then edit it.

## Checkpoint
Rebuild all of this from scratch, imperative-first, in under 20 minutes.
Then do the 15-task timed practice set inside two hours.

revision.examFocus: This step maps to all five CKAD domains. The heaviest is Application Environment, Configuration and Security, which covers ConfigMaps, Secrets, resources, QoS and SecurityContext. Services and Networking, Deployment and Observability are each tested as hands-on fixes. The exam gives you about 15–20 tasks in live clusters. Each task asks you to create or repair a real object, so speed with imperative kubectl and fast reading of the docs matter as much as theory.

compare.difference: A failed liveness probe restarts the container. A failed readiness probe only removes the Pod from the Service endpoints and never restarts it.
compare.chooseA: Pick liveness when the app can hang or deadlock and only a restart will fix it.
compare.chooseB: Pick readiness when the app is alive but temporarily cannot serve traffic, for example while warming a cache or waiting on a dependency.

compare.difference: Both inject key-value data as env vars or files. A Secret is only base64-encoded, not encrypted by default, but RBAC and tooling treat it as sensitive.
compare.chooseA: Pick a ConfigMap for non-sensitive settings such as URLs, feature flags and config files.
compare.chooseB: Pick a Secret for passwords, tokens, keys and TLS certificates, created with kubectl create secret generic or tls.

compare.difference: RollingUpdate replaces Pods gradually and keeps the app serving. Recreate stops all old Pods before starting new ones, which causes downtime.
compare.chooseA: Pick RollingUpdate for zero-downtime releases, and tune maxSurge and maxUnavailable when the task gives numbers.
compare.chooseB: Pick Recreate when two versions must never run together, for example after a schema change or when a volume is single-writer.

compare.difference: Env vars are read once at container start. A mounted volume (without subPath) is refreshed automatically after the ConfigMap changes.
compare.chooseA: Pick env or envFrom when the app reads its config from the environment, and restart the Pods after any change.
compare.chooseB: Pick a volume mount when the task asks for a config file at a path, or when changes must reach Pods without a restart.

compare.difference: ClusterIP can be reached only from inside the cluster. NodePort also opens a static port on every node, in the NodePort range.
compare.chooseA: Pick ClusterIP, the default, for traffic between Pods and for backends sitting behind an Ingress.
compare.chooseB: Pick NodePort when the task says the app must be reachable on a node port, or gives a specific port such as 30080.

cues.cue: app takes a long time to start and keeps restarting
cues.pick: startupProbe with failureThreshold × periodSeconds longer than the boot time
cues.why: Liveness and readiness checks are held off until the startup probe succeeds, so slow boots are not killed.

cues.cue: Pod must not receive traffic until it is ready
cues.pick: readinessProbe
cues.why: Readiness controls whether the Pod appears in the Service endpoints, without restarting anything.

cues.cue: QoS class Guaranteed
cues.pick: Set requests equal to limits for both CPU and memory in every container
cues.why: If any container is missing a value or has requests different from limits, the Pod becomes Burstable, and with no values at all it is BestEffort.

cues.cue: run every N minutes, do not overlap runs
cues.pick: CronJob with concurrencyPolicy: Forbid
cues.why: Forbid skips a new run while the previous one is still active. Replace would kill the old run instead.

cues.cue: Job must stop if it runs longer than X seconds
cues.pick: spec.activeDeadlineSeconds on the Job
cues.why: It ends the whole Job when the deadline passes, whatever the retry count, while backoffLimit only caps retries.

cues.cue: deny all incoming traffic in the namespace
cues.pick: NetworkPolicy with podSelector: {} and policyTypes: [Ingress] and no ingress rules
cues.why: An empty podSelector selects every Pod, and an Ingress policy type with no rules allows nothing in.

cues.cue: allow only Pods with label X from namespace Y
cues.pick: A single 'from' entry that contains both namespaceSelector and podSelector
cues.why: Both selectors in one list item are combined with AND, while separate list items are combined with OR and allow far more traffic.

cues.cue: roll back to the previous image
cues.pick: kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name>, then kubectl rollout status
cues.why: It is quicker and safer than editing the YAML by hand, and status confirms the rollback has finished.

scenario.situation: In namespace shop, the Deployment api has Pods stuck in CrashLoopBackOff. kubectl logs shows the app starting normally, but kubectl describe shows 'Liveness probe failed' about 30 seconds after each start. The app needs about 90 seconds to load its data before it answers on /healthz. You must make the Deployment stable without changing the image, and still keep automatic restarts if the app later hangs. What is the best fix?
reasoning: Read the events in kubectl describe pod -n shop. The container is being killed by the liveness probe, not crashing on its own, so the code and image are fine.
Removing the livenessProbe stops the loop, but it breaks the requirement to restart the app if it later hangs, so reject that option.
Raising initialDelaySeconds on the liveness probe can work, but it is fragile: it delays hang detection on every start and fails if the boot gets slower.
Adding only a readinessProbe does not help, because readiness never stops liveness from killing the container.

Add a startupProbe on /healthz with periodSeconds 10 and failureThreshold 12, giving a 120-second window. Keep the liveness probe as it is. Apply with kubectl edit or patch the Deployment, then confirm with kubectl rollout status -n shop.
scenario.answer: Add a startupProbe whose failureThreshold × periodSeconds is longer than the 90-second boot time, and keep the existing livenessProbe. Kubernetes holds off liveness checks until the startup probe succeeds, so the app boots safely and hangs are still caught afterwards.

memoryAids: Probes 'S-R-L': Startup protects the boot, Readiness controls traffic, Liveness restarts the container. Only L kills.
NetworkPolicy selectors: 'same dash = AND, new dash = OR'. Each '-' starts a new list item, and each item adds another allowed source.
QoS 'G-B-B': Guaranteed means requests equal limits everywhere, Burstable means some values are set, BestEffort means nothing is set. They are evicted in reverse order, BestEffort first.
cheatSheet: First lines in the exam: alias k=kubectl; export do='--dry-run=client -o yaml'. Then generate YAML with k run/create ... $do > f.yaml.
Copy and run the use-context command at the top of every task before typing anything else.
k create deploy web --image=nginx --replicas=3 --port=80, then k expose deploy web --port=80 --target-port=8080.
k create cm app --from-literal=K=V and k create secret generic db --from-literal=pass=x. Inject them with envFrom or a volume.
k create job j --image=busybox -- sh -c 'echo hi' and k create cronjob c --image=busybox --schedule='*/5 * * * *' -- date.
k create ingress web --rule='host.com/path=svc:80' and set --class when the task names an ingressClass.
k set image deploy/web <container>=img:tag, then k rollout status. Use k rollout undo if it breaks.
Empty Service endpoints: compare the selector with the Pod labels (k get po --show-labels), then check readiness and targetPort.
Exit code 137 or OOMKilled means raise the memory limit. A slow but running app usually means CPU throttling, so raise the CPU limit.
k explain pod.spec.containers.securityContext --recursive gives field names faster than searching the docs.
Any egress NetworkPolicy also needs port 53 UDP/TCP to kube-dns, or DNS lookups fail.
Verify every task with k get or k describe. A wrong namespace or a typo in a name scores zero.
selfCheck: I can create a Deployment, Service, ConfigMap, Secret, Job, CronJob and Ingress imperatively, and use $do to get YAML I then edit, each in under 3 minutes.
I can choose correctly between startup, readiness and liveness probes for a described app behaviour, and write each one without copying from the docs.
I can set requests and limits to reach a named QoS class, and explain from Pod status whether a failure is OOMKilled or CPU throttling.
I can write a default-deny NetworkPolicy plus an allow rule that combines a namespaceSelector and podSelector with AND, and keep DNS working.
I can find and fix a Service with no endpoints, and roll a Deployment back to a specific revision.
I can finish a 15-task timed practice set inside two hours, flagging and skipping any task that runs past about 8 minutes.

objective.question: A Deployment has 4 replicas and uses the default RollingUpdate strategy with no strategy fields set. During a rollout, what is the maximum total number of Pods and the minimum number of available Pods?
options: Maximum 8 Pods, minimum 0 available
Maximum 4 Pods, minimum 4 available
Maximum 6 Pods, minimum 2 available
Maximum 5 Pods, minimum 3 available
objective.explanation: The defaults are maxSurge 25% and maxUnavailable 25%. For 4 replicas each works out to 1 Pod, so the rollout allows at most 5 Pods and keeps at least 3 available. The other options use the wrong percentages or describe Recreate-like behaviour.

objective.question: A container in your Pod keeps restarting. kubectl describe pod shows Last State: Terminated, Reason: OOMKilled, Exit Code: 137. What is the most likely cause?
options: The container used more memory than its memory limit
The image could not be pulled from the registry
The container used more CPU than its CPU limit
The liveness probe timed out
objective.explanation: Going over the memory limit makes the kernel kill the container, which shows as OOMKilled with exit code 137. Going over the CPU limit only causes throttling. A probe failure or an image pull error shows different reasons.

objective.question: You apply a Job manifest and the API server rejects it. The Pod template sets restartPolicy: Always. Which change fixes the manifest?
options: Set restartPolicy to Never or OnFailure
Add activeDeadlineSeconds to the Pod spec
Remove the completions field
Set backoffLimit: 0
objective.explanation: A Job's Pod template must use restartPolicy Never or OnFailure. Always is not allowed because Job Pods are meant to run to completion. backoffLimit, completions and deadlines do not affect this validation rule.

objective.question: A Pod in namespace 'web' must call a Service named 'db' in namespace 'prod' on port 5432. Which hostname works from inside the Pod?
options: db
db.prod.svc.cluster.local
prod.db.svc.cluster.local
db.svc.prod.cluster.local
objective.explanation: The Service DNS format is <service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local, so the answer is db.prod.svc.cluster.local. The short name 'db' only resolves inside the same namespace, and the other options put the parts in the wrong order.

objective.question: A liveness probe has only httpGet and initialDelaySeconds: 5 set. Everything else uses the defaults. The application hangs after it has been running for a while. Roughly how long after the hang does the kubelet restart the container?
options: About 10 seconds (one failed check)
It never restarts; liveness only removes the Pod from Service endpoints
About 1 second (the first timeout)
About 30 seconds (3 failed checks, 10 seconds apart)
objective.explanation: The defaults are periodSeconds 10, timeoutSeconds 1 and failureThreshold 3. The kubelet restarts the container after three failures in a row, about 30 seconds. Removing a Pod from endpoints is what a readiness probe does, not a liveness probe.

objective.question: A Pod has two containers. Both set CPU and memory requests equal to their CPU and memory limits. Which QoS class does Kubernetes assign?
options: Burstable
Critical
Guaranteed
BestEffort
objective.explanation: A Pod is Guaranteed when every container has CPU and memory limits and the requests equal those limits. Burstable means some requests or limits are set but the Pod does not meet the Guaranteed rule. BestEffort means none are set. There is no 'Critical' QoS class.

objective.question: In namespace 'app' you apply a NetworkPolicy with podSelector: {}, policyTypes: [Ingress], and no ingress rules. The cluster's CNI enforces NetworkPolicy. What is the effect?
options: Ingress to every Pod in 'app' is denied unless another policy allows it
Both ingress and egress are denied for all Pods in 'app'
Only traffic from other namespaces is blocked
All ingress traffic is allowed, because no rules means no restriction
objective.explanation: An empty podSelector selects every Pod in the namespace. Listing Ingress with no rules allows nothing, so this is a default-deny for ingress. Policies are additive, so other policies can still allow traffic. Egress is not affected because only Ingress is listed in policyTypes.

objective.question: In the exam you need a Deployment YAML file for nginx with 3 replicas that you can then edit to add probes. Which command is fastest and correct?
options: kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx --replicas=3 --dry-run=server > web.yaml
kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx --replicas=3 --dry-run=client -o yaml > web.yaml
kubectl apply deployment web --image=nginx --replicas=3 -o yaml
kubectl run web --image=nginx --replicas=3 -o yaml > web.yaml
objective.explanation: kubectl create deployment with --dry-run=client -o yaml prints the manifest without creating anything, and you redirect it to a file. kubectl run creates a Pod and no longer supports --replicas. The server dry-run option has no -o yaml, so it prints nothing useful. kubectl apply does not take these generator flags.

objective.question: Deployment 'api' is on revision 4 and the latest release is broken. You must return to the image used in revision 2. Which command does this?
options: kubectl rollout undo deployment/api
kubectl rollout restart deployment/api --revision=2
kubectl rollout history deployment/api --revision=2 --apply
kubectl rollout undo deployment/api --to-revision=2
objective.explanation: rollout undo with --to-revision=N rolls back to that exact revision. A plain undo goes only to the previous revision, which is 3. restart only recreates Pods with the current template, and history only shows revisions.

objective.question: On a fresh kind cluster you create a valid Ingress for host app.local that points to a working ClusterIP Service. kubectl get ingress shows no ADDRESS, and requests never reach the app. What is the most likely reason?
options: No ingress controller is installed in the cluster
Ingress resources need a NetworkPolicy to be activated
The Service must be type LoadBalancer
Ingress only works with NodePort Services
objective.explanation: An Ingress resource is only a set of rules. An ingress controller must be running to put those rules into effect, and kind does not install one by default. Ingress backends can be ClusterIP Services, and NetworkPolicy does not activate Ingress.

objective.question: A NetworkPolicy in namespace 'app' selects the backend Pods and has the ingress rule below. Which traffic does this rule allow?

code.code:
ingress:
- from:
  - namespaceSelector:
      matchLabels:
        team: ops
    podSelector:
      matchLabels:
        role: monitor

options: Only Pods labelled role=monitor in namespace 'app'; the namespaceSelector is ignored
Nothing. The manifest is invalid because one 'from' entry cannot hold two selectors
All Pods in namespaces labelled team=ops, plus Pods labelled role=monitor in any namespace
Only Pods labelled role=monitor that run in namespaces labelled team=ops
objective.explanation: When namespaceSelector and podSelector sit in the same list element, they are combined with AND. If they were two separate elements, each starting with '-', they would be combined with OR, which is the behaviour described in option two. The manifest is valid, and the namespaceSelector is not ignored.

objective.question: A Deployment reads ConfigMap 'app-cfg' in two ways. It uses envFrom for environment variables, and it also mounts the whole ConfigMap as a volume at /etc/app (no subPath). You run kubectl edit configmap app-cfg and change a value. What do the running Pods see?
options: The mounted files update after the kubelet sync delay, but the environment variables keep the old value until the Pods are recreated
Neither changes until the Pods are recreated, because ConfigMaps are read only at Pod start
The Deployment automatically starts a rolling update because its ConfigMap changed
Both the environment variables and the mounted files update within seconds
objective.explanation: Environment variables are set once, when the container starts. A ConfigMap volume mounted without subPath is refreshed by the kubelet eventually, usually within about a minute. Kubernetes does not trigger a rollout when a ConfigMap changes, so you need kubectl rollout restart or a checksum annotation on the Pod template.

objective.question: Users get connection timeouts to Service 'web'. The Pods are Running and Ready. What is the cause?

code.code:
# kubectl get endpoints web
# NAME   ENDPOINTS   AGE
# web    <none>      10m
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  selector:
    app: web
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 8080
---
# Deployment pod template labels:
#   labels:
#     app: web-app

options: The Service selector app=web does not match the Pod label app=web-app, so no endpoints are created
kube-proxy must be restarted after a Service is created
ClusterIP Services need type: NodePort before they can route to Pods
targetPort 8080 does not match port 80, so the Service drops the traffic
objective.explanation: An empty ENDPOINTS list means the selector matches no Ready Pods. Here the selector is app=web but the Pods are labelled app=web-app. Setting port and targetPort to different values is normal and is not the problem. Neither the Service type nor a kube-proxy restart is involved.

objective.question: A CronJob has schedule '*/5 * * * *' and concurrencyPolicy: Forbid. Each Job run takes about 12 minutes. What happens?
options: The running Job is killed every 5 minutes and replaced by a new one
The CronJob controller marks the CronJob as failed after the first overlap
Schedules that fall due while a Job is still running are skipped. The next Job starts at the first schedule time after the current Job finishes
A new Job starts every 5 minutes, so up to three Jobs run at the same time
objective.explanation: Forbid skips a new run when the previous Job has not finished. Allow, which is the default, would let runs overlap. Replace would cancel the running Job and start a new one. No policy marks the CronJob as failed.

objective.question: A legacy app needs up to 4 minutes to start. The container has the probes below. What happens when a Pod starts?

code.code:
startupProbe:
  httpGet: {path: /healthz, port: 8080}
  periodSeconds: 10
  failureThreshold: 30
livenessProbe:
  httpGet: {path: /healthz, port: 8080}
  periodSeconds: 10
  failureThreshold: 3

options: The startup probe and the liveness probe run in parallel from the start, so the container restarts after about 30 seconds
The Pod is rejected because startupProbe and livenessProbe cannot use the same endpoint
The startup probe allows up to about 300 seconds. Liveness checks begin only after the startup probe succeeds, so the app starts normally
The liveness probe restarts the container after about 30 seconds because the app is not up yet
objective.explanation: While a startup probe is configured and has not yet succeeded, liveness and readiness probes are disabled. Here 30 × 10 s gives the app about 300 seconds, which covers the 4-minute start. Using the same endpoint for both probes is allowed.

objective.question: Namespace 'team-a' has the ResourceQuota below and no LimitRange. A developer runs kubectl run nginx --image=nginx -n team-a without any resource settings. What is the result?

code.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: compute
  namespace: team-a
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "2"
    requests.memory: 4Gi
    limits.memory: 8Gi

options: The Pod is created, and Kubernetes copies default requests from the quota
The Pod stays Pending until the scheduler finds free quota
The API server rejects the Pod as forbidden because it must specify the quota-tracked requests and limits
The Pod is created with BestEffort QoS and does not count against the quota
objective.explanation: When a ResourceQuota tracks compute resources, every new Pod in that namespace must set those resources. Otherwise admission rejects the Pod. A LimitRange with default values would fill in the missing values. The quota itself never supplies defaults, and rejection happens at admission, not at scheduling.

objective.question: A new Pod stays in Pending. kubectl describe pod shows the event below. What is the most likely cause and fix?

code.code:
Warning  FailedScheduling  default-scheduler  0/3 nodes are available: 3 Insufficient memory.

# Pod spec excerpt
resources:
  requests:
    memory: 8Gi
  limits:
    memory: 8Gi

options: The memory request is larger than what any node can still allocate. Lower the request or add node capacity.
The container was OOMKilled during startup. Raise the memory limit.
A ResourceQuota in the namespace is exhausted. Raise the quota.
The memory limit is too high. The kubelet refuses to start containers whose limit exceeds free memory, so lower the limit only.
objective.explanation: The scheduler places Pods by their requests against each node's allocatable capacity, and here no node has 8Gi free. Limits do not affect scheduling, and a quota violation rejects the Pod at creation rather than leaving it Pending. OOMKilled needs a running container, which never existed.

objective.question: Applying this Secret fails with an 'illegal base64 data' error. Which change fixes it with the least effort?

code.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: db
type: Opaque
data:
  password: S3cret!

options: Change type to kubernetes.io/basic-auth
Change kind to ConfigMap, because Secrets cannot hold special characters
Rename data to stringData and keep the plain value
Put the value in quotes: password: "S3cret!"
objective.explanation: Every value under data must be base64-encoded. stringData accepts plain text, and the API server encodes it for you. Quoting does not make the value valid base64, and the Secret type or a ConfigMap does not fix the encoding problem.

objective.question: Exam task: 'Use context k8s-c2. In namespace orders, create ConfigMap app-cfg with MODE=prod and a Deployment web (image nginx) that loads it with envFrom. Confirm it is rolled out.' Which order of steps is correct?

code.code:
A. kubectl config use-context k8s-c2
B. kubectl create configmap app-cfg --from-literal=MODE=prod -n orders
C. kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx -n orders --dry-run=client -o yaml > web.yaml
D. Edit web.yaml and add envFrom: - configMapRef: name: app-cfg
E. kubectl apply -f web.yaml
F. kubectl rollout status deployment/web -n orders

options: B, A, C, D, E, F
A, C, E, D, B, F
C, D, E, A, B, F
A, B, C, D, E, F
objective.explanation: Switch context first, or every later command may run against the wrong cluster. Create the ConfigMap before the Pods that need it, generate and edit the YAML before you apply it, then verify. The other orders either touch the wrong cluster or apply the YAML before the envFrom edit.

objective.question: A Pod shows ImagePullBackOff. The event says: 'pull access denied for registry.example.com/team/api, repository does not exist or may require authorization'. The image and tag are correct. What fixes it?
options: Create a generic Secret with the registry password and load it into the container with envFrom
Create a docker-registry Secret in the Pod's namespace and reference it under spec.imagePullSecrets
Increase the Pod's restart backoff so the registry has time to respond
Set imagePullPolicy: Always so the kubelet retries with fresh credentials
objective.explanation: Private registries need credentials that the kubelet uses at pull time. Those come from imagePullSecrets, either on the Pod or on its ServiceAccount, in the same namespace. Environment variables are only visible inside a container that has already started, and pull policy or backoff settings do not add credentials.

objective.question: Deployment 'api' was created from YAML. Its Pod template labels are app.kubernetes.io/name: api and tier: backend, and the containers listen on 8080. Which command creates a ClusterIP Service on port 80 that actually gets endpoints?
options: kubectl expose deployment api --port=80 --target-port=8080
kubectl create service nodeport api --tcp=80:8080
kubectl expose deployment api --port=8080 --target-port=80
kubectl create service clusterip api --tcp=80:8080
objective.explanation: kubectl expose copies the Deployment's selector, so the Service matches the Pods. kubectl create service always sets the selector app=<name>, here app=api, which matches no Pods, so the Service has no endpoints. Option C reverses the Service port and the container port.

objective.question: kubectl apply rejects this Deployment. What is wrong?

code.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: frontend
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web
        image: nginx:1.27

options: The container name must match the Deployment name label
spec.selector does not match the Pod template labels. The template must carry app: web.
matchLabels is not allowed in apps/v1. Use matchExpressions instead.
replicas must be at least 3 for a RollingUpdate Deployment
objective.explanation: The API server checks that the selector matches the template labels and rejects the object with 'selector does not match template labels'. Remember that a Deployment's selector is immutable after creation, so fix it before the first apply. The other options describe rules that do not exist.

objective.question: CronJob 'backup' runs at 02:00. You must check right now that the job works, without changing the CronJob. Which command do you use?
options: kubectl create cronjob backup --now
kubectl patch cronjob backup -p '{"spec":{"schedule":"* * * * *"}}'
kubectl run backup-test --from=cronjob/backup
kubectl create job backup-test --from=cronjob/backup
objective.explanation: kubectl create job --from=cronjob/<name> starts a one-off Job from the CronJob's jobTemplate immediately. kubectl run has no --from flag and there is no --now flag. Patching the schedule changes the CronJob, which the task forbids.

objective.question: Pod 'web' has been in status Init:0/1 for minutes. Its init container is named wait-db. Which command shows why it is stuck?
options: kubectl logs web --previous
kubectl describe deployment web
kubectl logs web -c wait-db
kubectl logs web
objective.explanation: An init container's logs must be requested by name with -c. Without -c, kubectl targets the main container, which has not started yet (PodInitializing). --previous is for a restarted container, and describing the Deployment will not show the init container's output.

objective.question: A Job has restartPolicy: Never and backoffLimit: 3. The container always exits with code 1. How many Pods are created before the Job is marked Failed?
options: Unlimited, until you delete the Job
objective.explanation: backoffLimit counts retries. The first attempt plus 3 retries gives 4 failed Pods, then the Job gets condition Failed with reason BackoffLimitExceeded. With restartPolicy Never each retry is a new Pod, started after an increasing delay. 6 is the default backoffLimit, which is not used here.

objective.question: A Pod is stuck in CreateContainerConfigError. The Secret 'db' exists in the same namespace and holds a single key named 'password'. What is the cause?

code.code:
env:
- name: DB_PASS
  valueFrom:
    secretKeyRef:
      name: db
      key: passwd

options: The readiness probe fails before the container starts
The container is OOMKilled while it reads the Secret
The Pod references key 'passwd', which does not exist in Secret 'db'
The image cannot be pulled from the registry
objective.explanation: The kubelet cannot build the container's environment because the referenced key is missing, so it reports CreateContainerConfigError. Pull failures show ErrImagePull or ImagePullBackOff. A failing readiness probe leaves a Pod Running but not Ready, and OOMKilled needs a running container.

objective.question: In namespace shop, a NetworkPolicy lets only Pods labelled app=frontend reach Service 'api'. You want to prove the policy works the way a frontend Pod experiences it. Which command is the best test?
options: kubectl run tmp --rm -it --restart=Never --image=busybox -n shop -- wget -qO- -T 2 http://api
kubectl port-forward svc/api -n shop 8080:80, then curl localhost:8080
kubectl run tmp --rm -it --restart=Never --image=busybox --labels=app=frontend -- wget -qO- -T 2 http://api
kubectl run tmp --rm -it --restart=Never --image=busybox -n shop --labels=app=frontend -- wget -qO- -T 2 http://api
objective.explanation: The test Pod must be in the same namespace and carry app=frontend so the policy treats it like a frontend. Without the label the request should be blocked. Option C runs in the default namespace, where the short name 'api' does not resolve. Port-forward goes through the API server and kubelet, so it does not test the in-cluster path that the NetworkPolicy controls.

subjective.question: Explain the difference between liveness, readiness and startup probes. When would you use each one?
subjective.answer: A liveness probe asks whether the container is still healthy. If it fails failureThreshold times in a row, the kubelet restarts the container. I use it to recover from deadlocks or hangs. A readiness probe asks whether the container can serve traffic right now. If it fails, the Pod is removed from Service endpoints but not restarted. I use it while caches warm up or when a dependency is down, and it also controls when a rolling update can move forward. A startup probe protects slow-starting apps. Liveness and readiness checks are held back until the startup probe succeeds, so a slow boot does not trigger restarts. The defaults are periodSeconds 10, timeoutSeconds 1, failureThreshold 3 and successThreshold 1. A common mistake is making liveness check external dependencies. If the database goes down, every Pod then restarts in a loop.
keyPoints: Liveness failure restarts the container
Readiness failure removes the Pod from endpoints without a restart and gates rollouts
Startup probe holds back the other probes for slow starts
Know the defaults: period 10s, timeout 1s, failureThreshold 3
Do not make liveness depend on external services

subjective.question: What are resource requests and limits? What happens when a container goes over its CPU limit versus its memory limit? How do they decide the QoS class?
subjective.answer: A request is what the scheduler reserves for the container. A Pod is placed only on a node with enough unreserved capacity to meet its requests. A limit is the most the container may use at runtime. CPU can be compressed, so a container over its CPU limit is throttled and slows down but keeps running. Memory cannot be compressed, so a container over its memory limit is killed and shows OOMKilled with exit code 137. The QoS class comes from these settings. Guaranteed means every container has CPU and memory limits equal to its requests. Burstable means some requests or limits are set but the Pod does not meet the Guaranteed rule. BestEffort means none are set. When a node runs short of memory, the kubelet usually evicts BestEffort Pods first, then Burstable Pods that use more than their requests. Guaranteed Pods are evicted last. In production I always set memory requests and limits.
keyPoints: Requests drive scheduling; limits cap runtime usage
CPU over limit means throttling
Memory over limit means OOMKilled, exit code 137
Guaranteed, Burstable and BestEffort rules
QoS affects eviction order under memory pressure

subjective.question: Compare ConfigMaps and Secrets. Are Kubernetes Secrets secure by default? How do you give either one to a Pod?
subjective.answer: Both store key-value configuration outside the image. ConfigMaps hold non-sensitive data. Secrets hold passwords, tokens and keys. By default, Secret values are only base64-encoded, which is encoding, not encryption. Anyone who can read the Secret object can decode it. To make Secrets safer you enable encryption at rest in etcd, restrict get and list on Secrets with RBAC, and often use an external secret manager. You can give either one to a Pod in three ways. Use env with valueFrom (configMapKeyRef or secretKeyRef) for single keys. Use envFrom to load all keys. Or mount it as a volume, where each key becomes a file. Volume mounts are updated after a short delay when the object changes. Environment variables are not, so the Pod must restart to pick up changes. For the exam, I create them with kubectl create configmap or kubectl create secret generic, using --from-literal or --from-file.
keyPoints: ConfigMap for non-sensitive data, Secret for sensitive data
Secrets are base64-encoded, not encrypted, by default
Encryption at rest, RBAC and external secret managers
Three ways in: env valueFrom, envFrom, volume
Volumes update after a delay; env vars need a Pod restart

subjective.question: Describe the ClusterIP, NodePort and LoadBalancer Service types. A Service is not routing traffic. How do you debug it?
subjective.answer: ClusterIP is the default. It gives a stable virtual IP that is reachable only inside the cluster. NodePort also opens the same port on every node, from the default range 30000–32767. LoadBalancer builds on NodePort and asks the cloud provider for an external load balancer. Every Service uses a label selector to find Pods, and the matching ready Pods become its endpoints. To debug, I first run kubectl get endpoints or endpointslices for the Service. If the list is empty, either the selector does not match the Pod labels (I compare with kubectl get pods --show-labels) or the Pods are not passing readiness. Next, I check that targetPort matches the port the container actually listens on. Then I test from inside the cluster with a temporary Pod, for example kubectl run tmp --image=busybox --restart=Never -it --rm -- wget -qO- svc.ns:port. Finally, I check whether a NetworkPolicy is blocking the traffic.
keyPoints: ClusterIP is internal; NodePort uses 30000–32767; LoadBalancer is external via the cloud
Selector to labels to endpoints
Empty endpoints mean a label mismatch or unready Pods
Check that targetPort matches the container port
Test with a temporary Pod and check NetworkPolicies

subjective.question: What is the relationship between a Pod, a ReplicaSet and a Deployment? Why do we normally create Deployments rather than ReplicaSets?
subjective.answer: A Pod is the smallest unit you can deploy. It is one or more containers that share a network namespace and volumes. A bare Pod is not recreated if its node fails. A ReplicaSet keeps a set number of Pods matching a label selector running, and replaces any that die. A Deployment manages ReplicaSets. When you change the Pod template, for example the image, the Deployment creates a new ReplicaSet. It then scales the new one up and the old one down according to its strategy. It keeps the old ReplicaSets so you can roll back. Managing ReplicaSets directly would mean doing rolling updates and rollbacks by hand. So we use Deployments for stateless apps and use rollout status, history and undo. In the exam, kubectl create deployment gives you all of this, while kubectl run with --restart=Never gives you only a bare Pod.
keyPoints: A Pod is the basic unit and does not self-heal on its own
A ReplicaSet keeps the replica count using a selector
A Deployment creates a new ReplicaSet for each template change
Old ReplicaSets make rollback possible
Deployments give rollout status, history and undo

subjective.question: Explain how Jobs and CronJobs work. Cover completions, parallelism, backoffLimit and the CronJob settings you would tune in production.
subjective.answer: A Job runs Pods until a set number of them finish successfully. completions is how many successful runs are needed. parallelism is how many Pods can run at once. backoffLimit, which defaults to 6, is how many retries are allowed before the Job is marked failed. activeDeadlineSeconds caps the total run time. The Pod template must use restartPolicy Never or OnFailure. A CronJob creates Jobs on a cron schedule, such as '*/5 * * * *'. In production I set concurrencyPolicy. Allow is the default. Forbid skips a new run if the previous one is still running. Replace cancels the old run and starts the new one. I also set successfulJobsHistoryLimit and failedJobsHistoryLimit so old Jobs do not pile up, and startingDeadlineSeconds for runs that were missed. A ttlSecondsAfterFinished on the Job cleans up finished Jobs. To build one fast: kubectl create cronjob name --image=busybox --schedule='*/5 * * * *' -- cmd.
keyPoints: completions, parallelism, backoffLimit (default 6)
restartPolicy must be Never or OnFailure
CronJob concurrencyPolicy: Allow, Forbid, Replace
History limits and startingDeadlineSeconds
Imperative kubectl create job and create cronjob

subjective.question: Write out, in words, a NetworkPolicy that allows only Pods labelled app=frontend to reach Pods labelled app=backend on TCP 8080. What pitfalls should you watch for?
subjective.answer: I would create a NetworkPolicy in the backend namespace. Its podSelector uses matchLabels app=backend, and policyTypes is [Ingress]. It has one ingress rule. The from section has a podSelector with app=frontend, and ports has protocol TCP, port 8080. Once the backend Pods are selected by any Ingress policy, all other ingress to them is denied. Pitfalls to watch for. First, NetworkPolicy works only if the CNI enforces it. Some CNIs silently ignore policies. Second, a podSelector inside from matches only the policy's own namespace. For a frontend in another namespace, put namespaceSelector and podSelector in the same from entry, which means AND. Two separate list entries mean OR, which is a common YAML mistake. Third, policies only add allowed traffic. You cannot deny with one policy what another allows. Fourth, if you add an egress default-deny, remember to allow DNS on port 53, UDP and TCP, or name lookups break.
keyPoints: podSelector selects the target backend; from selects the frontend; port 8080
Being selected by a policy means default-deny for that direction
The CNI must enforce NetworkPolicy
namespaceSelector plus podSelector in one entry is AND; separate entries are OR
Allow DNS egress when using egress default-deny

subjective.question: The CKAD is a two-hour hands-on exam. How do you use kubectl efficiently to finish all the tasks in time?
subjective.answer: First, speed comes from not hand-writing YAML. I set export do='--dry-run=client -o yaml' and use the k alias for kubectl. Then I generate skeletons, for example k create deploy web --image=nginx $do > web.yaml, k run, k create job, cronjob, configmap and secret, and k expose to create Services. I edit only the parts I need, such as probes or resources. kubectl explain pod.spec.containers.livenessProbe --recursive shows field names faster than searching. The official Kubernetes docs are allowed, so I bookmark the pages for NetworkPolicy, Ingress, probes and PersistentVolumeClaims. In every task I first run the given kubectl config use-context command and note the namespace, because working in the wrong cluster gives zero marks. I use kubectl set image, kubectl scale and kubectl label for quick changes. I skip any task worth a low share of the marks that is taking too long, flag it and come back. The pass mark is 66%, so steady progress beats perfection.
keyPoints: Aliases and a $do dry-run variable
Generate YAML imperatively, then edit
kubectl explain and allowed docs bookmarks
Always switch context and namespace for each task
Time management: flag and skip, 66% pass mark

subjective.question: Walk through deploying your own container image to a local kind cluster with probes, resource limits and an Ingress. What are the kind-specific gotchas?
subjective.answer: First, I build the image and load it into kind with kind load docker-image myapp:1.0, because the cluster nodes cannot see my local Docker images. I set imagePullPolicy IfNotPresent. Using the :latest tag defaults to Always, which causes ErrImagePull. For Ingress, I create the cluster with a config that sets extraPortMappings for ports 80 and 443. Some controller guides also need an ingress-ready node label. Then I install an ingress controller, because kind ships without one. Next I generate a Deployment with kubectl create deployment and dry-run, and add readiness and liveness httpGet probes on a health endpoint. I also add CPU and memory requests and limits. I expose it with a ClusterIP Service and write an Ingress with ingressClassName, a host and a Prefix path. I map the host to 127.0.0.1 in /etc/hosts and test with curl. If it fails, I check the endpoints, probe events in kubectl describe, and the controller logs.
keyPoints: kind load docker-image; avoid the :latest pull policy trap
extraPortMappings in the kind cluster config
Install an ingress controller; set ingressClassName
Probes plus requests and limits in the Deployment
Debug via endpoints, describe events and controller logs

subjective.question: A rolling update to a new image starts, but the new Pods crash and the rollout stalls. Explain what Kubernetes does, how you detect it, how you recover, and when you would choose Recreate instead.
subjective.answer: With RollingUpdate (maxSurge 25% and maxUnavailable 25% by default), Kubernetes creates new Pods and removes old ones only as new Pods become Ready. If the new Pods crash or fail readiness, the rollout stops progressing. Old Pods stay within the maxUnavailable budget, so users still see the old version. This is why good readiness probes matter. Without them, broken Pods count as available. I detect the problem with kubectl rollout status deployment/x, which waits and reports the failure, and with kubectl get rs, where the new ReplicaSet is not becoming ready. kubectl describe and logs --previous show the cause. After progressDeadlineSeconds the Deployment condition reports ProgressDeadlineExceeded. To recover, I run kubectl rollout undo, or add --to-revision=N, and check kubectl rollout history. Then I fix the image and roll forward. I choose Recreate when two versions must never run together, for example with incompatible schema changes or a single-writer volume. The cost is downtime, because all old Pods are killed first.
keyPoints: The rollout waits on readiness; old Pods keep serving
Detect with rollout status, get rs, describe and logs --previous
progressDeadlineSeconds and ProgressDeadlineExceeded
Recover with rollout undo or --to-revision
Recreate avoids mixed versions but causes downtime

subjective.question: You apply this egress NetworkPolicy to the frontend Pods. After that, the frontend can no longer reach http://backend:8080, even though the backend Pods are allowed. Explain why and fix it.

code.code:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: frontend-egress
  namespace: shop
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: {app: frontend}
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  egress:
  - to:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels: {app: backend}
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 8080

subjective.answer: Once a Pod is selected by an Egress policy, all outbound traffic that is not explicitly allowed is denied. That includes DNS. The frontend first needs to resolve 'backend' through CoreDNS, which runs in kube-system on UDP and TCP port 53. The policy only allows TCP 8080 to backend Pods, so the lookup fails, and from the app's side it looks as if the backend is down. The fix is a second egress rule that allows port 53 on UDP and TCP to the DNS Pods. You can select them with a namespaceSelector on the label kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system, combined with a podSelector k8s-app: kube-dns. To confirm the cause, run kubectl exec into a frontend Pod and try nslookup backend. Then try curl to the backend Pod IP directly. If the IP works and the name fails, DNS is the problem.
keyPoints: An Egress policyType denies all outbound traffic that is not listed, including DNS
Name resolution needs UDP and TCP 53 to CoreDNS in kube-system
Add an egress rule that uses a namespaceSelector plus a podSelector for the kube-dns Pods
Test the Pod IP and the Service name separately to isolate DNS from routing

subjective.question: Review this probe configuration. The /health endpoint returns 500 whenever the database is unreachable. What happens during a 2-minute database outage, and how would you redesign it?

code.code:
readinessProbe:
  httpGet: {path: /health, port: 8080}
  periodSeconds: 5
livenessProbe:
  httpGet: {path: /health, port: 8080}
  periodSeconds: 5
  failureThreshold: 3

subjective.answer: Within about 15 seconds of the outage, the liveness probe fails three times and the kubelet restarts every replica. The containers restart over and over while the database is down, which adds load and creates noise. CrashLoopBackOff delays can also slow recovery after the database returns. Restarting the app does not fix a database outage, so this liveness check is wrong. Liveness should answer one question: is this process itself stuck? It should use a cheap /livez endpoint with no external checks. Readiness can include dependency checks, for example a /readyz that tests the database. Then, during the outage, Pods are only removed from Service endpoints and are not killed. Callers get fast failures, and Pods return to the endpoints automatically when the database recovers. If the app starts slowly, add a startup probe, and set sensible timeoutSeconds values.
keyPoints: Using a dependency check in liveness causes restart cascades across all replicas
Liveness checks the process only; readiness can check dependencies
Failing readiness removes Pods from endpoints without restarting them
Use separate endpoints, and a startup probe for slow-starting apps

subjective.question: Explain what this Ingress does for each request path listed in the comment. Then explain why pathType matters.

code.code:
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  rules:
  - host: shop.local
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /api
        pathType: Prefix
        backend: {service: {name: api, port: {number: 80}}}
      - path: /
        pathType: Exact
        backend: {service: {name: web, port: {number: 80}}}
# requests: /api, /api/v1/items, /apiv2, /, /about

subjective.answer: The rule applies only when the Host header is shop.local. /api and /api/v1/items go to the api Service. Prefix matching works on whole path elements split by '/', and both of these paths start with the element 'api'. /apiv2 does not match the Prefix rule, because 'apiv2' is a different element from 'api'. It also does not match the Exact '/' rule, so it falls to the controller's default backend, which usually returns 404. Only the exact path '/' goes to web. /about also gets a 404, because Exact '/' does not match it. To send everything else to the web Service, change that path to Prefix '/'. When several Prefix rules match, the longest one wins. pathType matters because Exact, Prefix and ImplementationSpecific behave differently. ImplementationSpecific leaves the matching to the controller. In the exam, read the task carefully and set the pathType it asks for.
keyPoints: The host rule filters on the Host header
Prefix matches whole path elements, so /apiv2 does not match /api
Exact '/' matches only '/'; unmatched paths go to the default backend
Longest matching prefix wins; ImplementationSpecific depends on the controller

subjective.question: A team changes a ConfigMap that their Deployment reads through env vars. The app keeps using old values for hours. Explain why, and give two ways to roll out config changes reliably.
subjective.answer: Environment variables from a ConfigMap are read once, when the container is created. Kubernetes does not watch the ConfigMap for changes, and it does not restart Pods when it is edited. So the old values stay until each Pod is recreated for some other reason. The first fix is a manual or CI step: kubectl rollout restart deployment/app. This changes a restartedAt annotation on the Pod template and triggers a normal rolling update, with probes and maxUnavailable still respected. The second fix is to tie the config to the Pod template. You can add a checksum of the ConfigMap as a Pod annotation, which Helm does, or use versioned, immutable ConfigMaps such as app-cfg-v2 and update the reference. A changed template always rolls out, and it can be rolled back with kubectl rollout undo. Mounting the ConfigMap as a volume without subPath does update the files, but only if the app reloads them.
keyPoints: Env vars are set at container start and never refresh
Editing a ConfigMap does not trigger a rollout
kubectl rollout restart starts a controlled rolling update
Checksum annotations or versioned immutable ConfigMaps make config changes traceable and easy to roll back

subjective.question: A company shares one cluster among several dev teams. One team's Pods keep taking all the node memory, and other teams' Pods get evicted. Which namespace-level Kubernetes objects would you use, and how do they work together?
subjective.answer: I would give each team its own namespace with two objects. The first is a ResourceQuota. It caps the total the namespace can use, for example requests.cpu, requests.memory, limits.memory, and object counts such as pods. Once a quota tracks compute resources, any Pod that does not set those resources is rejected at admission. The second is a LimitRange, which fixes that problem. It injects default requests and limits into containers that do not set them, and it can also enforce a minimum and maximum per container. With both in place, every container gets a memory limit. A runaway container is then OOMKilled inside its own limit instead of putting pressure on the whole node. Requests also give the scheduler correct numbers. For important workloads, I would set requests equal to limits to get Guaranteed QoS, which makes those Pods the last to be evicted. I would verify the setup with kubectl describe quota and kubectl describe limitrange.
keyPoints: ResourceQuota caps the total per namespace and forces Pods to declare resources
LimitRange adds default and min/max values per container
Memory limits keep OOM kills inside the container instead of causing node pressure
QoS class affects eviction order; Guaranteed Pods are evicted last

subjective.question: You must send about 10% of traffic for Service 'shop' to a new image version, using only core Kubernetes objects. Describe the setup, including the kubectl commands you would use.
subjective.answer: I would run two Deployments behind one Service. Deployment shop-stable has 9 replicas with labels app=shop, track=stable. Deployment shop-canary has 1 replica with the new image and labels app=shop, track=canary. The Service selects only app=shop, so it sends traffic to all 10 Pods. kube-proxy spreads connections roughly evenly across the endpoints, which gives about 10% to the canary. This split is approximate and works per connection, not per request. To build it quickly, run kubectl create deployment shop-canary --image=shop:2 --replicas=1 --dry-run=client -o yaml, add the labels, and apply the file. Check the endpoints with kubectl get endpoints shop and kubectl get pods -l app=shop --show-labels. If the canary looks healthy, update the stable Deployment with kubectl set image and scale the canary to zero. If it misbehaves, run kubectl scale deployment shop-canary --replicas=0. For precise weights, you would need ingress controller canary annotations or a service mesh.
keyPoints: Two Deployments share a common label; each also has its own track label
The Service selects only the shared label
The traffic split follows the replica ratio and is approximate, per connection
Promote with kubectl set image; abort by scaling the canary to zero

subjective.question: Case study: in namespace shop, deploy an 'orders' API with 3 replicas. It reads LOG_LEVEL from config and DB_PASSWORD from a Secret. It must receive traffic only when /ready returns 200, be limited to 500m CPU and 256Mi memory, be reachable at http://shop.local/orders, and accept traffic only from the ingress controller's namespace. List the objects you would create, in order, and the key field in each.
subjective.answer: Switch to the given context first, and create namespace shop if it does not exist. Then create ConfigMap orders-cfg with LOG_LEVEL and Secret orders-db with DB_PASSWORD using kubectl create --from-literal. Next, generate the Deployment with --dry-run=client -o yaml. Add envFrom for the ConfigMap, a secretKeyRef for DB_PASSWORD, a readinessProbe with httpGet on /ready, and requests and limits of 500m CPU and 256Mi memory. Add a startupProbe only if the app boots slowly. After that, create a ClusterIP Service with kubectl expose deployment orders --port=80 --target-port=8080. Then add an Ingress with the correct ingressClassName, host shop.local, path /orders with pathType Prefix, and backend orders on port 80. Finally, add a NetworkPolicy that selects app=orders, with policyTypes Ingress and a from rule using namespaceSelector kubernetes.io/metadata.name=ingress-nginx (or whatever the controller's namespace is) on port 8080. Verify with kubectl get endpoints and a curl that sends the Host header.
keyPoints: Create the ConfigMap and Secret before the Deployment that references them
The readinessProbe controls whether a Pod receives traffic, and resources set the limits
Use expose so the Service selector matches, and set an Ingress with ingressClassName, host and a Prefix path
Write the NetworkPolicy with a namespaceSelector on the automatic kubernetes.io/metadata.name label
Verify with endpoints and a curl that sends the Host header

subjective.question: A Pod is in CrashLoopBackOff. Describe a systematic way to find the cause, and what common exit codes and events tell you.
subjective.answer: Start with kubectl describe pod. Look at Last State, the exit code and the Events. Exit code 137 with reason OOMKilled means the memory limit was hit. 137 without OOMKilled usually means a SIGKILL, often after a failing liveness probe, which the Events show as 'Liveness probe failed' followed by a restart. Exit code 1 is an application error. 127 usually means the command or binary was not found, which points to wrong command or args. Next, run kubectl logs <pod> --previous to read the output of the crashed attempt, because the current container may have no logs yet. Then check the inputs: wrong command or args, a missing env var or config file, a ConfigMap mounted at the wrong path, or a dependency that is down. If the logs are empty, temporarily override the command with sleep 3600 in a copy of the Pod. Exec in and run the entrypoint by hand. Fix the manifest, apply it, and watch with kubectl get pod -w.
keyPoints: Use describe to read Last State, the exit code and Events
Use logs --previous to see the crashed container's output
Know the exit codes: 137 means OOM or SIGKILL, 1 is an app error, 127 means command not found
Check whether the liveness probe caused the restarts
Debug by overriding the command to sleep and exec-ing into the container

subjective.question: Spot the mistakes in this Deployment excerpt. For each one, say what happens when you apply it or at runtime.

code.code:
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: myrepo/api:latest
        ports:
        - name: web
          containerPort: 8080
        resources:
          requests: {cpu: 500m, memory: 256Mi}
          limits:   {cpu: 250m, memory: 512m}
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet: {path: /ready, port: http}

subjective.answer: There are four problems. First, the CPU request of 500m is higher than the CPU limit of 250m. The API server rejects this because a request must be less than or equal to its limit. Second, memory '512m' means 512 millibytes, about half a byte, not 512 MiB. It also sits below the 256Mi request, so it is rejected too. The author meant 512Mi. Third, the readinessProbe uses the named port 'http', but the container declares its port as 'web'. The kubelet cannot resolve the port, so the probe keeps failing, the Pod never becomes Ready and the Service has no endpoints. Use port: web or 8080. Fourth, the :latest tag makes the default imagePullPolicy Always. You cannot tell which build is running, and rollbacks are unreliable. Pin a version tag or a digest. After these fixes, set the CPU and memory requests at or below the limits.
keyPoints: A request higher than its limit fails validation
The m suffix on memory means millibytes; use Mi or Gi
A probe port name must match a declared container port name
