Avoid :latest; pin a tag or digest for repeatable rollouts

subjective.question: Your app needs a database schema migration before each new version runs. Compare running the migration in an init container with running it in a Kubernetes Job. Which is better here, and why?
subjective.answer: An init container runs once per Pod, before the app container starts. With 3 replicas, 3 migrations run at the same time during every rollout. They also run again whenever a Pod is rescheduled or restarted on a new node. That causes lock contention and race conditions, and a slow migration also slows the whole rollout and can trip readiness deadlines. A Job runs the migration once, has its own backoffLimit and activeDeadlineSeconds, keeps its logs in one place, and your pipeline can wait for it with kubectl wait --for=condition=complete before it updates the Deployment. So a Job is better for migrations. Write migrations to be idempotent and backward compatible, so old Pods keep working while the new schema is applied. Init containers are still the right tool for per-Pod work, such as waiting for a dependency to come up or rendering a config file into a shared emptyDir volume.
keyPoints: An init container runs per replica and on every restart, so migrations can run concurrently
A Job runs once and has its own retry and deadline controls
A pipeline can gate the rollout with kubectl wait on the Job
Migrations should be idempotent and backward compatible
Init containers suit per-Pod setup, such as waiting for a dependency

subjective.question: A team wants to expose 12 HTTP services from one cluster. Compare a LoadBalancer Service per app, an Ingress, and Gateway API. Which would you choose today, and what does CKAD expect you to know?
subjective.answer: A LoadBalancer Service per app is simple, but each one gets its own cloud load balancer and IP. With 12 services that costs more, and TLS and routing end up spread over 12 places. Ingress puts L7 HTTP routing behind a single entry point. Host and path rules send traffic to ClusterIP Services, and TLS is set in one place. It only works if a controller is installed and ingressClassName matches it, and anything beyond basic routing usually needs controller-specific annotations. Gateway API is the newer successor. It splits the roles: the platform team owns the GatewayClass and Gateway, and app teams own their HTTPRoutes. Header matching and traffic splitting are part of the API itself, not annotations. The community ingress-nginx controller has been announced for retirement, so for a new platform I would choose Gateway API with a supported implementation. For CKAD, you must still write Ingress resources quickly: the rules, pathType, backend service name and port, ingressClassName, and TLS secrets.
keyPoints: A LoadBalancer per app means more cost, more IPs and scattered TLS
Ingress gives one L7 entry point but needs a controller and a matching ingressClassName
Gateway API offers role separation and built-in traffic features
ingress-nginx is announced for retirement; Gateway API is the long-term successor
CKAD still tests the Ingress resource

subjective.question: Deployment 'api' reads a database password from Secret 'db' as an env var. You must rotate the password with no downtime. Put the steps in order and explain why the order matters.
subjective.answer: First, add the new password on the database side and keep the old one valid, so old and new Pods can both connect during the change. Second, create a new Secret, for example db-v2, with the new password. Editing 'db' in place does not change env vars in running Pods and gives you nothing clean to roll back to. Third, update the Deployment to reference db-v2. This changes the Pod template, so a rolling update starts. A working readinessProbe and maxUnavailable: 0 keep enough capacity serving. Fourth, watch kubectl rollout status and check the logs and endpoints of the new Pods. If something fails, kubectl rollout undo returns to the old Secret reference. Fifth, once every Pod uses db-v2, revoke the old password in the database. Sixth, delete the old Secret. If you revoke the old password before the rollout finishes, old Pods lose database access. If you edit the Secret in place, you must also run kubectl rollout restart, and you lose the easy rollback.
keyPoints: Allow the old and new credentials together before you change anything
A versioned Secret name gives a template change and a clean rollback
Env vars never refresh, so the change needs a rollout
Readiness probes and maxUnavailable: 0 keep the service up
Revoke the old credential only after the rollout is verified

subjective.question: Service api-svc exposes port 8080. With the Ingress below, curl http://localhost/api/orders on your kind cluster returns 404 from nginx. Find every problem.

code.code:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: shop
  namespace: shop
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  rules:
  - host: shop.local
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /api
        pathType: Exact
        backend:
          service:
            name: api-svc
            port:
              number: 80

subjective.answer: The 404 comes from the controller itself, so the controller is running and the request reaches it. Routing is the problem. First, the host does not match. Curling localhost sends Host: localhost, but the rule only matches shop.local. Use curl -H 'Host: shop.local' http://localhost/api/orders, or add shop.local to /etc/hosts. Second, pathType: Exact matches only /api, not /api/orders. Change it to Prefix, which matches /api and every path under it on segment boundaries. Third, the backend port is 80, but api-svc listens on 8080. After you fix the host and path, requests would still fail with an error such as 503 because the backend port does not exist on the Service. Set port number 8080. Also confirm that api-svc is in namespace shop, because an Ingress can only point to Services in its own namespace, and that the Service has endpoints. Then use kubectl describe ingress to check that the backends resolve.
keyPoints: A 404 from nginx means the request reached the controller but no rule matched
The Host header must match the rule host
Exact matches only /api; Prefix also covers sub-paths
The backend port must match a port on the Service
The Ingress and its backend Service must be in the same namespace

subjective.question: A CronJob was supposed to run at 02:00 last night but did not. How do you troubleshoot it? List the likely causes.
subjective.answer: Start with kubectl get cronjob backup. Check LAST SCHEDULE and the SUSPEND column, then run kubectl describe cronjob to read its events. Next, run kubectl get jobs to see whether a Job was created and failed, or was never created. Common causes: First, suspend: true was left set. Second, a time zone mismatch. The schedule is read in the controller manager's time zone, often UTC, unless spec.timeZone is set, for example Asia/Kolkata. 02:00 UTC is 07:30 IST. Third, concurrencyPolicy: Forbid while an earlier Job is still running or hung, so the new run is skipped. Fourth, startingDeadlineSeconds is too small, so a run that was delayed by controller downtime is skipped. Fifth, a Job was created, but its Pods failed with image, config or quota errors, or hit backoffLimit. Sixth, a schedule typo, such as swapping the minute and hour fields. Check failed Pods with kubectl logs, and set successfulJobsHistoryLimit and failedJobsHistoryLimit so there is history to inspect.
keyPoints: Check LAST SCHEDULE, SUSPEND and the CronJob's events
Without spec.timeZone, the schedule follows the controller's zone, often UTC
concurrencyPolicy Forbid with a stuck earlier Job skips new runs
startingDeadlineSeconds can cause missed runs
Separate 'Job never created' from 'Job created but failed'

subjective.question: This policy is meant to let Prometheus in namespace monitoring scrape the api Pods on port 9090. After you apply it, Prometheus still cannot scrape, and the frontend can no longer call the api. Explain both failures and fix them.

code.code:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-monitoring
  namespace: app
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: {app: api}
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
  - from:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels: {name: monitoring}
    ports:
    - port: 9090

subjective.answer: Failure one: the namespaceSelector matches the label name=monitoring, but namespaces do not get that label unless someone adds it. Kubernetes automatically adds kubernetes.io/metadata.name=<namespace> instead. The selector matches nothing, so Prometheus is blocked. Change it to matchLabels: {kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring}, or label the namespace yourself. Failure two: once any Ingress policy selects app=api, those Pods are isolated for ingress, and only traffic allowed by some policy gets in. Frontend traffic on 8080 was never allowed, so it is now dropped. Add a second ingress rule, or a separate policy, that allows from podSelector app=frontend on port 8080. Policies add up, so the second rule only adds permission. Verify both paths with a labelled busybox test Pod and kubectl describe networkpolicy. Also make sure 9090 is the container's real metrics port, because NetworkPolicy ports refer to Pod ports, not Service ports.
keyPoints: Namespaces carry kubernetes.io/metadata.name automatically, not a 'name' label
Selecting a Pod in any Ingress policy blocks all ingress that is not allowed
Policies add up; add an explicit rule for the frontend
NetworkPolicy ports are Pod/container ports
Test with Pods that carry the right labels

subjective.question: An API's p99 latency spikes during traffic peaks. There are no restarts and no OOMKills, and memory looks normal. The container has requests cpu 200m and limits cpu 300m. What is the likely cause, how do you confirm it, and what would you change?
subjective.answer: The likely cause is CPU throttling. The CPU limit is enforced through the Linux CFS quota, so when the container uses its 300m share within a scheduling period, it is paused until the next period. Nothing is killed, which is why you see no restarts, only slow responses. Memory limits behave differently, because exceeding them triggers an OOMKill. To confirm, run kubectl top pod during a peak and see usage pinned near 300m. If Prometheus is available, compare container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total with container_cpu_cfs_periods_total from cAdvisor; a high ratio confirms throttling. Fixes: set the CPU request to the real steady usage so the scheduler reserves enough. Raise the CPU limit, or remove it for latency-sensitive services where your platform policy allows that, while keeping requests so scheduling stays fair. Scale out with more replicas or an HPA based on CPU. Load-test after the change and watch the throttling ratio and p99.
keyPoints: A CPU limit throttles the container through the CFS quota; it never kills it
Exceeding a memory limit causes an OOMKill, which explains the different symptom
Confirm with kubectl top and the cAdvisor throttling metrics
Right-size requests, then raise or remove CPU limits, or scale out

subjective.question: During a timed practice set, a learner ran these commands in order. The task said: 'In namespace shop, create Deployment web (nginx:1.25, 3 replicas), update it to nginx:1.27, create Secret db with password p@ss$word, and expose web on port 80.' Spot each mistake and give the corrected command.

code.code:
kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx:1.25 --replicas=3 -n shop
kubectl set image deployment/web web=nginx:1.27 -n shop
kubectl create secret generic db --from-literal=password=p@ss$word -n shop
kubectl run web2 --image=nginx --replicas=2 -n shop
kubectl expose deployment web --port=80

subjective.answer: Line 1 is correct. Line 2 fails with 'unable to find container named web'. kubectl create deployment names the container after the image, so it is called nginx. Use kubectl set image deployment/web nginx=nginx:1.27 -n shop. Line 3 runs without an error, but the shell expands $word to an empty string, so the stored password is 'p@ss'. Use single quotes: --from-literal=password='p@ss$word'. Line 4 was not part of the task, and it fails anyway because kubectl run no longer accepts --replicas; it only creates Pods. Use kubectl create deployment if you need a Deployment. Line 5 leaves out -n shop, so kubectl looks for web in the default namespace and reports NotFound. Use kubectl expose deployment web --port=80 -n shop. A quick habit prevents most of these: set the namespace for the context with kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=shop, and check container names with kubectl get deploy web -o wide.
keyPoints: create deployment names the container after the image
Single-quote literals that contain $ to stop shell expansion
kubectl run creates only Pods and has no --replicas flag
A missing -n sends the command to the default namespace
Set the context namespace once to avoid repeated mistakes

steps.overview: This step covers the administrator side of Kubernetes: how the control plane fits together, how to install and upgrade a cluster with kubeadm, how to back up and restore etcd, and how to secure access and storage. Troubleshooting carries the largest weight in the CKA (about 30%), and cluster architecture, installation and configuration carries about 25%. The exam is hands-on in live clusters, so you must work fast from the terminal and the official docs.
objectives: Explain the role of kube-apiserver, etcd, kube-scheduler, kube-controller-manager, kubelet and kube-proxy, and locate each on a kubeadm node.
Install a cluster with kubeadm and upgrade it one minor version at a time, control plane first, then workers.
Take an etcd snapshot with etcdctl and restore it with etcdutl, then repoint the etcd static pod to the restored data directory.
Configure RBAC, service accounts, PersistentVolumes, PersistentVolumeClaims and StorageClasses, and verify them with kubectl auth can-i and kubectl get.
Diagnose NotReady nodes, broken networking and failing pods using kubectl, systemctl, journalctl and crictl.

concepts.explanation: kube-apiserver is the only component that talks to etcd. Every other component and kubectl talk to the API server on port 6443. kube-scheduler picks a node for each pending pod. kube-controller-manager runs the reconcile loops for objects such as Deployments, ReplicaSets and Nodes. On kubeadm clusters, all of these run as static pods.

The kubelet reads static pod manifests directly from a folder on the node, not from the API server. On kubeadm clusters this folder is /etc/kubernetes/manifests, set by staticPodPath in /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml. If you edit or move a file there, the kubelet recreates or removes that pod. This is how you fix a broken API server or etcd manifest.

etcd is the key-value store that holds all cluster state. It listens for clients on 2379 and for peers on 2380. On kubeadm clusters its certificates are in /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd and its data is in /var/lib/etcd. Losing etcd without a backup means losing the cluster's state.

The kubelet is a systemd service on every node. It registers the node, runs pods through the container runtime (CRI, for example containerd) and reports status. kube-proxy runs as a DaemonSet and programs iptables or IPVS rules so that Service IPs reach pod endpoints. If the kubelet is down, the node becomes NotReady. If kube-proxy is broken, Services stop routing traffic.

You upgrade one minor version at a time, for example 1.33 to 1.34, never 1.32 to 1.34. On the first control plane node, upgrade the kubeadm package, then run 'kubeadm upgrade plan' and 'kubeadm upgrade apply vX.Y.Z'. Next, drain the node, upgrade kubelet and kubectl, run 'systemctl daemon-reload', restart the kubelet and uncordon. Other control plane nodes and the workers use 'kubeadm upgrade node' instead of apply.

'etcdctl snapshot save' needs the endpoint, the CA cert, a client cert and a key. 'etcdutl snapshot restore --data-dir <new-dir>' writes a fresh data directory. On recent etcd versions this restore command lives in etcdutl, and the old etcdctl restore is deprecated. After restoring, change the etcd-data hostPath in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml to point at the new directory, then wait for etcd and the API server to come back.

A Role grants verbs on resources inside one namespace. A ClusterRole is cluster-wide, or can be reused across namespaces. A RoleBinding attaches a Role or a ClusterRole to subjects within one namespace. A ClusterRoleBinding grants access across the whole cluster. Check what a subject can do with 'kubectl auth can-i <verb> <resource> --as=system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<sa> -n <ns>'.

Service accounts are identities for pods. Each namespace gets a 'default' service account. Since v1.24, long-lived token Secrets are no longer created automatically. Pods get short-lived projected tokens instead, and 'kubectl create token <sa>' issues one on demand. You set the account on a pod with spec.serviceAccountName, and you turn off token mounting with automountServiceAccountToken: false.

A PersistentVolume (PV) is a piece of storage. A PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) is a request for storage, and it binds to a PV with matching capacity, access mode and storageClassName. A StorageClass provisions PVs dynamically through a provisioner. Its reclaimPolicy (Delete or Retain) and volumeBindingMode (Immediate or WaitForFirstConsumer) control what happens on release and when the PV binds.

For workloads, use kubectl describe, kubectl logs (with --previous for crashed containers) and kubectl get events --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp. For nodes, use systemctl status kubelet, journalctl -u kubelet, and crictl ps -a and crictl logs, which work even when the API server is down. For networking, check Service selectors against pod labels, kubectl get endpoints or endpointslices, CoreDNS pods, NetworkPolicies and the CNI pods.

keyFacts: CKA: performance-based, 2 hours, pass mark 66%, one free retake. You may use kubernetes.io/docs and the Kubernetes blog during the exam.
Domain weights: Troubleshooting 30%, Cluster Architecture/Installation/Configuration 25%, Services & Networking 20%, Workloads & Scheduling 15%, Storage 10%.
Ports: API server 6443, etcd 2379 (clients) and 2380 (peers), kubelet 10250, controller-manager 10257, scheduler 10259, NodePort range 30000–32767.

Key paths: /etc/kubernetes/manifests (static pods), /etc/kubernetes/pki (certs), /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf (admin kubeconfig), /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml (kubelet config), /var/lib/etcd (etcd data).
kubeadm leaf certificates are valid for 1 year and the CA for 10 years. Check them with 'kubeadm certs check-expiration' and renew with 'kubeadm certs renew all'.
Upgrade order: kubeadm first, then control plane (apply), then kubelet/kubectl on that node, then each worker (drain, kubeadm upgrade node, kubelet, uncordon). Go one minor version at a time.
The kubelet may be at most three minor versions older than the kube-apiserver, and never newer than it.
PV access modes: ReadWriteOnce (RWO), ReadOnlyMany (ROX), ReadWriteMany (RWX), ReadWriteOncePod (RWOP). Reclaim policies: Retain and Delete (Recycle is deprecated).
Always run 'kubectl config use-context <name>' (or the context command the exam gives you) at the start of every task. Each task can target a different cluster.

example.caption: etcd backup and restore on a kubeadm control plane node (run as root)
example.code:
# 1. Read endpoint and cert paths from the etcd static pod
grep -E 'listen-client-urls|cert-file|key-file|trusted-ca-file' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml

# 2. Take a snapshot
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl \
  --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  snapshot save /opt/etcd-backup.db

# 3. Verify the snapshot
etcdutl snapshot status /opt/etcd-backup.db -w table

# 4. Restore into a NEW data directory (do not overwrite the live one)
etcdutl snapshot restore /opt/etcd-backup.db --data-dir /var/lib/etcd-restore

# 5. Point the etcd static pod at the restored data
sed -i 's#path: /var/lib/etcd$#path: /var/lib/etcd-restore#' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml

# 6. Wait for etcd and kube-apiserver to restart, then check
watch crictl ps
kubectl get pods -A

pitfalls: Forgetting to switch kubectl context at the start of a task. Your work lands in the wrong cluster and scores zero.
Restoring etcd into the live /var/lib/etcd directory, or forgetting to update the hostPath in etcd.yaml. etcd keeps serving the old data, or never starts.
Skipping 'systemctl daemon-reload' and 'systemctl restart kubelet' after upgrading the kubelet package. The node keeps reporting the old version.
Trying to skip minor versions in a kubeadm upgrade, or upgrading workers before the control plane.
Binding a ClusterRole with a ClusterRoleBinding when the task asks for one namespace only. Use a RoleBinding to keep the access namespace-scoped.
A PVC stuck in Pending because of a storageClassName, access mode or size mismatch with the PV. Always compare 'kubectl describe pvc' output with the PV spec.

workflow.title: Hands-on lab: build, back up, break and recover

steps.label: Prepare nodes and runtime
steps.detail: On every VM, disable swap, load the overlay and br_netfilter modules, set the sysctls, then install containerd plus kubeadm, kubelet and kubectl from pkgs.k8s.io.

steps.label: Initialise the control plane
steps.detail: Run 'kubeadm init --pod-network-cidr=<cidr>', copy admin.conf to ~/.kube/config, then install a CNI such as Calico or Flannel.

steps.label: Join the worker nodes
steps.detail: Run the printed 'kubeadm join' command on each worker, or regenerate it with 'kubeadm token create --print-join-command', and confirm all nodes are Ready.

steps.label: Snapshot etcd
steps.detail: Create some test Deployments, take an etcdctl snapshot with the etcd certs, and verify it with 'etcdutl snapshot status'.

steps.label: Break a worker node
steps.detail: Stop the kubelet, or corrupt /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml, and watch the node turn NotReady.

steps.label: Diagnose and recover
steps.detail: Use systemctl status kubelet and journalctl -u kubelet to find the cause, fix it, restart the kubelet and confirm the node is Ready.

steps.label: Restore etcd from snapshot
steps.detail: Delete the test Deployments, restore the snapshot into a new data directory, update etcd.yaml, and confirm the Deployments come back.

project.title: kubeadm-etcd-recovery-lab
project.summary: A two-node kubeadm lab (cp1 control plane, worker1 worker) that you build, back up with etcd snapshots, restore, and break and repair on the kubelet side, plus an RBAC and storage workload to test permissions and PV/PVC binding. node-prep.sh and kubeadm-config.yaml build the cluster, the etcd scripts cover backup and restore, break-fix-node.sh covers node troubleshooting, rbac-storage.yaml covers RBAC and storage, and README.md ties the steps together, including the upgrade.
project.run:
sudo ./scripts/node-prep.sh control-plane   # on cp1
sudo ./scripts/node-prep.sh worker          # on worker1
sudo kubeadm init --config kubeadm-config.yaml --upload-certs   # on cp1
mkdir -p $HOME/.kube && sudo cp /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf $HOME/.kube/config && sudo chown $(id -u):$(id -g) $HOME/.kube/config
kubectl apply -f https://github.com/flannel-io/flannel/releases/latest/download/kube-flannel.yml
sudo kubeadm token create --print-join-command   # run the printed command on worker1 with sudo
kubectl apply -f manifests/rbac-storage.yaml
sudo ./scripts/etcd-backup.sh
sudo ./scripts/etcd-restore.sh /var/backups/etcd/<snapshot>.db
./scripts/break-fix-node.sh break worker1 && ./scripts/break-fix-node.sh diagnose worker1 && ./scripts/break-fix-node.sh fix worker1

files.code:
# kubeadm-etcd-recovery-lab (Step 6: CKA)

Two Ubuntu 22.04/24.04 VMs: `cp1` (control plane) and `worker1`.
Each needs 2 vCPU and 2 GB RAM or more. Hostnames must match the node names.

## 1. Build the cluster
1. On both nodes, run `scripts/node-prep.sh` (`control-plane` on cp1, `worker` on worker1).
2. On cp1, edit `kubeadm-config.yaml`: set `advertiseAddress` to cp1's IP.
3. Run `kubeadm init --config kubeadm-config.yaml`, then install Flannel. Flannel uses 10.244.0.0/16.
4. Join worker1 with the command from `kubeadm token create --print-join-command`.
5. Check: `kubectl get nodes` shows both nodes Ready.
   Also run `kubectl get pods -n kube-system` to see the static pods named `*-cp1`.

## 2. Back up and restore etcd (the checkpoint)
1. Create test data: `kubectl create configmap before-backup --from-literal=k=v`.
2. Back up: `sudo scripts/etcd-backup.sh`.
3. Create more data: `kubectl create configmap after-backup --from-literal=k=v`.
4. Restore: `sudo scripts/etcd-restore.sh /var/backups/etcd/<file>.db`.
5. Check the result. `before-backup` exists and `after-backup` is gone.

**Exam variant:** restore with `--data-dir /var/lib/etcd-restore`.
Then change the etcd volume `hostPath.path` in `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml` to that directory.
The kubelet sees the changed manifest and recreates the etcd static pod.

## 3. Break a node and recover it
`scripts/break-fix-node.sh break|diagnose|fix worker1`

The script stops the kubelet on worker1, then you diagnose it the CKA way:
- `kubectl describe node`
- `systemctl status kubelet`
- `journalctl -u kubelet`

After that, the script repairs the kubelet.

## 4. RBAC and storage
Apply `manifests/rbac-storage.yaml`. On worker1, run `sudo mkdir -p /mnt/data` first.
Then test the service account's permissions:
```
kubectl auth can-i list pods -n app-team --as=system:serviceaccount:app-team:app-sa   # yes
kubectl auth can-i delete pods -n app-team --as=system:serviceaccount:app-team:app-sa # no
```
Check storage with `kubectl get pv,pvc -n app-team`. The PVC stays Pending until the pod is scheduled, because the StorageClass uses WaitForFirstConsumer.

## 5. Upgrade one minor version (control plane first)
1. Change `K8S_MINOR` in the repo URL to the next minor version, then run `apt-get update`.
2. Upgrade kubeadm on cp1: `apt-mark unhold kubeadm && apt-get install -y kubeadm='1.34.*' && apt-mark hold kubeadm`.
3. Review and apply: `kubeadm upgrade plan`, then `kubeadm upgrade apply v1.34.x`.
4. Drain cp1: `kubectl drain cp1 --ignore-daemonsets`.
5. Upgrade kubelet and kubectl on cp1, then run `systemctl daemon-reload && systemctl restart kubelet`.
6. Bring it back: `kubectl uncordon cp1`.
7. Upgrade worker1 the same way, but use `kubeadm upgrade node` instead of `upgrade apply`.

# kubeadm init --config kubeadm-config.yaml  (v1beta4 is the config API for kubeadm 1.31+)
apiVersion: kubeadm.k8s.io/v1beta4
kind: InitConfiguration
localAPIEndpoint:
  advertiseAddress: 192.168.56.10      # cp1 IP - change to yours
  bindPort: 6443                       # kube-apiserver port
nodeRegistration:
  name: cp1                            # must match the hostname
  criSocket: unix:///run/containerd/containerd.sock
---
apiVersion: kubeadm.k8s.io/v1beta4
kind: ClusterConfiguration
kubernetesVersion: v1.33.0             # match the kubeadm package you installed
clusterName: lab
controlPlaneEndpoint: "192.168.56.10:6443"
networking:
  podSubnet: 10.244.0.0/16             # Flannel default CIDR
  serviceSubnet: 10.96.0.0/12
etcd:
  local:
    dataDir: /var/lib/etcd             # restore script swaps this directory
---
apiVersion: kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: KubeletConfiguration
cgroupDriver: systemd                  # must match containerd SystemdCgroup = true
staticPodPath: /etc/kubernetes/manifests   # control plane runs as static pods from here

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Prepare a node for kubeadm. Usage: sudo ./node-prep.sh control-plane|worker
set -euo pipefail
ROLE=${1:?usage: node-prep.sh control-plane|worker}
K8S_MINOR=v1.33          # pkgs.k8s.io has one repo per minor version
ETCD_VER=v3.5.21         # etcdctl/etcdutl for backups (control plane only)

# kubelet requires swap off by default
swapoff -a
sed -i '/ swap / s/^/#/' /etc/fstab

# Kernel modules and sysctls needed for pod networking
printf 'overlay\nbr_netfilter\n' > /etc/modules-load.d/k8s.conf
modprobe overlay && modprobe br_netfilter
cat > /etc/sysctl.d/k8s.conf <<EOF
net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables = 1
net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-ip6tables = 1
net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1
EOF
sysctl --system

# Container runtime: containerd with the systemd cgroup driver
apt-get update
apt-get install -y containerd apt-transport-https ca-certificates curl gpg
mkdir -p /etc/containerd
containerd config default > /etc/containerd/config.toml
sed -i 's/SystemdCgroup = false/SystemdCgroup = true/' /etc/containerd/config.toml
systemctl restart containerd && systemctl enable containerd

# kubeadm, kubelet, kubectl from the community repo
mkdir -p /etc/apt/keyrings
curl -fsSL https://pkgs.k8s.io/core:/stable:/${K8S_MINOR}/deb/Release.key | gpg --dearmor -o /etc/apt/keyrings/kubernetes-apt-keyring.gpg
echo "deb [signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/kubernetes-apt-keyring.gpg] https://pkgs.k8s.io/core:/stable:/${K8S_MINOR}/deb/ /" > /etc/apt/sources.list.d/kubernetes.list
apt-get update
apt-get install -y kubelet kubeadm kubectl
apt-mark hold kubelet kubeadm kubectl   # stop accidental upgrades
systemctl enable --now kubelet

# crictl talks to containerd (used in troubleshooting and the restore script)
echo 'runtime-endpoint: unix:///run/containerd/containerd.sock' > /etc/crictl.yaml

if [[ "$ROLE" == "control-plane" ]]; then
  curl -fsSL -o /tmp/etcd.tgz https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/releases/download/${ETCD_VER}/etcd-${ETCD_VER}-linux-amd64.tar.gz
  tar -xzf /tmp/etcd.tgz -C /tmp
  install /tmp/etcd-${ETCD_VER}-linux-amd64/etcdctl /tmp/etcd-${ETCD_VER}-linux-amd64/etcdutl /usr/local/bin/
  etcdctl version
fi
echo "Node prepared as $ROLE"

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Take an etcd snapshot on cp1. Run as root: sudo ./etcd-backup.sh
set -euo pipefail
BACKUP_DIR=/var/backups/etcd
PKI=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd          # certs created by kubeadm
SNAPSHOT="$BACKUP_DIR/snap-$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S).db"
mkdir -p "$BACKUP_DIR"

# Read these values in an exam from /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml:
#   --listen-client-urls, --trusted-ca-file, --cert-file, --key-file
export ETCDCTL_API=3                  # default in etcd 3.4+, kept for clarity
etcdctl \
  --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert="$PKI/ca.crt" \
  --cert="$PKI/server.crt" \
  --key="$PKI/server.key" \
  snapshot save "$SNAPSHOT"

# Verify the file (hash, revision, total keys)
etcdutl snapshot status "$SNAPSHOT" -w table

# Keep the 7 most recent snapshots
ls -1t "$BACKUP_DIR"/snap-*.db | tail -n +8 | xargs -r rm -f
echo "Saved $SNAPSHOT"

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Restore etcd from a snapshot on a single control-plane node (cp1).
# Usage: sudo ./etcd-restore.sh /var/backups/etcd/snap-YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS.db
set -euo pipefail
SNAPSHOT=${1:?usage: etcd-restore.sh <snapshot.db>}
NODE_NAME=$(hostname)                      # etcd member name = node name (cp1)
CP_IP=${CP_IP:-$(hostname -I | awk '{print $1}')}
RESTORE_DIR=/var/lib/etcd-restore
MANIFESTS=/etc/kubernetes/manifests
PARKED=/etc/kubernetes/manifests-parked

etcdutl snapshot status "$SNAPSHOT" -w table   # fail early on a bad file

# 1. Stop the static pods. The kubelet removes them when their manifests disappear.
mkdir -p "$PARKED"
mv "$MANIFESTS"/*.yaml "$PARKED"/
echo "Waiting for etcd and kube-apiserver to stop..."
while crictl ps | grep -qE 'etcd|kube-apiserver'; do sleep 2; done

# 2. Restore into a NEW data dir (etcdutl replaces the deprecated 'etcdctl snapshot restore')
rm -rf "$RESTORE_DIR"
etcdutl snapshot restore "$SNAPSHOT" \
  --data-dir "$RESTORE_DIR" \
  --name "$NODE_NAME" \
  --initial-cluster "$NODE_NAME=https://$CP_IP:2380" \
  --initial-advertise-peer-urls "https://$CP_IP:2380"

# 3. Swap directories so etcd.yaml (hostPath /var/lib/etcd) needs no edit
mv /var/lib/etcd "/var/lib/etcd.old.$(date +%s)"
mv "$RESTORE_DIR" /var/lib/etcd

# 4. Bring the control plane back
mv "$PARKED"/*.yaml "$MANIFESTS"/
systemctl restart kubelet
echo "Waiting for the API server..."
until kubectl --kubeconfig /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf get --raw /readyz >/dev/null 2>&1; do sleep 3; done

kubectl --kubeconfig /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf get nodes
kubectl --kubeconfig /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf get configmaps   # expect before-backup, not after-backup

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Break, diagnose and repair a worker node from cp1 over SSH.
# Usage: ./break-fix-node.sh break|diagnose|fix worker1
set -euo pipefail
ACTION=${1:?usage: break-fix-node.sh break|diagnose|fix <node>}
NODE=${2:?node name, e.g. worker1}

case "$ACTION" in
  break)
    # Simulate the most common CKA node fault: the kubelet is stopped and disabled
    ssh "$NODE" 'sudo systemctl stop kubelet && sudo systemctl disable kubelet'
    echo "Kubelet stopped. The node turns NotReady after about 40s (node-monitor-grace-period)."
    ;;
  diagnose)
    kubectl get nodes -o wide                                   # STATUS NotReady
    kubectl describe node "$NODE" | sed -n '/Conditions:/,/Addresses:/p'   # 'Kubelet stopped posting node status'
    ssh "$NODE" 'systemctl status kubelet --no-pager || true'   # inactive (dead) / disabled
    ssh "$NODE" 'sudo journalctl -u kubelet -n 20 --no-pager'   # last kubelet logs
    ssh "$NODE" 'sudo crictl ps | head'                         # runtime still up?
    ssh "$NODE" 'systemctl is-active containerd'
    ;;
  fix)
    # Enable at boot AND start now. Forgetting 'enable' fails after a reboot.
    ssh "$NODE" 'sudo systemctl daemon-reload && sudo systemctl enable --now kubelet'
    kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready "node/$NODE" --timeout=120s
    kubectl get nodes
    ;;
  *) echo "unknown action: $ACTION"; exit 1 ;;
esac

# RBAC + storage demo. On worker1 first: sudo mkdir -p /mnt/data
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata: { name: app-team }
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata: { name: app-sa, namespace: app-team }
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role                              # namespaced; ClusterRole would be cluster-wide
metadata: { name: pod-reader, namespace: app-team }
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]                       # "" = core API group
  resources: ["pods", "persistentvolumeclaims"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]       # read only: delete is denied
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata: { name: app-sa-pod-reader, namespace: app-team }
subjects:
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: app-sa
  namespace: app-team
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: pod-reader
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
---
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata: { name: local-storage }
provisioner: kubernetes.io/no-provisioner   # static PVs only, no dynamic provisioning
volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer     # bind when the pod is scheduled
reclaimPolicy: Retain
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata: { name: local-pv-1 }
spec:
  capacity: { storage: 1Gi }
  accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
  storageClassName: local-storage
  persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain
  local: { path: /mnt/data }
  nodeAffinity:                         # required for local volumes
    required:
      nodeSelectorTerms:
      - matchExpressions:
        - { key: kubernetes.io/hostname, operator: In, values: ["worker1"] }
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata: { name: data-pvc, namespace: app-team }
spec:
  storageClassName: local-storage       # must match the PV's class
  accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
  resources: { requests: { storage: 1Gi } }
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: { name: web, namespace: app-team }
spec:
  serviceAccountName: app-sa            # pod gets app-sa's token and permissions
  containers:
  - name: nginx
    image: nginx:1.27
    ports: [{ containerPort: 80 }]
    volumeMounts: [{ name: data, mountPath: /usr/share/nginx/html }]
  volumes:
  - name: data
    persistentVolumeClaim: { claimName: data-pvc }

revision.examFocus: This step maps to the CKA domains Cluster Architecture, Installation & Configuration (25%), Troubleshooting (30%) and Storage (10%). Together they are about two-thirds of the marks. The exam gives you live clusters and scores the end state, not your commands. So the real skill is doing etcd restores, kubeadm upgrades, RBAC, PVCs and broken-node fixes quickly and correctly, using kubernetes.io/docs only to copy syntax.

compare.difference: The binding decides the scope, not the role. A RoleBinding grants the ClusterRole's permissions only inside the RoleBinding's namespace. A ClusterRoleBinding grants them in every namespace and on cluster-scoped resources.
compare.chooseA: Pick this when the task says 'in namespace X only' but wants to reuse a ClusterRole such as view or edit, or an existing custom ClusterRole.
compare.chooseB: Pick this when the task needs access to nodes, PVs, namespaces or other cluster-scoped resources, or says 'across all namespaces'.

compare.difference: Cordon only marks the node unschedulable, and existing pods keep running. Drain cordons the node and also evicts its pods.
compare.chooseA: Pick cordon when the task says 'stop new pods landing on node X' but leave current workloads alone.
compare.chooseB: Pick drain (usually with --ignore-daemonsets) before upgrading or doing maintenance on a node, then uncordon afterwards.

compare.b: crictl ps -a / crictl logs / journalctl -u kubelet
compare.difference: kubectl needs a working API server. crictl and journalctl work on the node itself, even when the API server or kubelet is down.
compare.chooseA: Use kubectl when the API server answers and you are debugging an ordinary pod, Service or PVC.
compare.chooseB: Use these after SSH to the node when kubectl times out with 'connection refused' on 6443, or when a node is NotReady.

compare.difference: The kubelet runs a static pod directly from a file on one node, with no scheduler or controller involved. A DaemonSet is an API object that the controller places on every matching node.
compare.chooseA: Pick a static pod when the task says 'run this pod on node X so that the kubelet manages it', or when you are fixing control-plane components.
compare.chooseB: Pick a DaemonSet when the task wants one pod per node across the cluster, including nodes added later.

compare.difference: With Retain, the PV and its data stay after the PVC is deleted, and the PV goes to Released. You must clean it up by hand before reuse. With Delete, the backing storage is removed along with the PV.
compare.chooseA: Pick Retain when the task says data must survive deletion of the claim.
compare.chooseB: Pick Delete for dynamically provisioned, disposable storage. It is the usual default for a StorageClass.

cues.cue: API server not responding / connection refused on port 6443
cues.pick: SSH to the control-plane node, then run crictl ps -a and check /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
cues.why: A typo in a static pod manifest (wrong flag, path or port) stops the container, and only node-level tools can show you why.

cues.cue: Node shows NotReady
cues.pick: systemctl status kubelet, then journalctl -u kubelet, then fix /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml or the systemd drop-in, then restart kubelet
cues.why: Most exam NotReady faults are a stopped or disabled kubelet, a bad config path or a wrong CA file, not a network failure.

cues.cue: Pod stuck in Pending
cues.pick: kubectl describe pod and read the Events
cues.why: Events name the cause directly: insufficient CPU or memory, an untolerated taint, a nodeSelector or affinity mismatch, or an unbound PVC.

cues.cue: Service exists but returns nothing
cues.pick: kubectl get endpoints (or endpointslices) and compare the Service selector with the pod labels and targetPort
cues.why: An empty endpoints list almost always means a selector or label mismatch, or a port that does not match the container port.

cues.cue: Check whether service account X can do Y
cues.pick: kubectl auth can-i <verb> <resource> -n <ns> --as=system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<sa>
cues.why: This proves your RBAC works before you move on, and the grader checks the same permission.

cues.cue: Upgrade the cluster to the next version
cues.pick: kubeadm upgrade plan, then apply on the first control-plane node, kubeadm upgrade node on the others, then drain, upgrade and uncordon each worker
cues.why: apply is used once on the first control-plane node. Every other node uses 'kubeadm upgrade node'.

cues.cue: Save an etcd snapshot to a given path
cues.pick: etcdctl snapshot save with --endpoints https://127.0.0.1:2379 and the --cacert, --cert and --key files from /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd
cues.why: A live snapshot needs TLS client auth. Copy the exact file paths from the flags in etcd.yaml instead of guessing them.

cues.cue: PVC is Pending and no StorageClass is mentioned
cues.pick: Make the PVC match the PV: same storageClassName (including empty ""), a compatible access mode, and a requested size no larger than the PV
cues.why: Static binding fails silently on any mismatch, and a default StorageClass can hijack a PVC that leaves storageClassName unset.

scenario.situation: You are on cluster k8s-c2. A snapshot exists at /opt/backup/etcd-snap.db. The task says: restore etcd from this snapshot so that the cluster returns to its earlier state, and make sure the API server comes back. etcd runs as a kubeadm static pod on controlplane-1 with data in /var/lib/etcd. What is the correct sequence?
reasoning: First switch context to k8s-c2 and SSH to controlplane-1. Restore is a node-level file operation, so kubectl alone cannot do it.
Reject restoring into /var/lib/etcd. That directory holds the live data, and the restore needs an empty or new directory. Choose a new path such as /var/lib/etcd-restore.

Run 'etcdutl snapshot restore /opt/backup/etcd-snap.db --data-dir /var/lib/etcd-restore'. On older etcd, 'etcdctl snapshot restore' still works but is deprecated. No TLS flags are needed because no running server is involved.

Edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml and change the hostPath of the etcd-data volume to /var/lib/etcd-restore. Changing only --data-dir is wrong, because the path inside the container stays the same.
The kubelet recreates the etcd pod. Wait for it with crictl ps, and if the API server looks stuck, restart the kubelet. Then confirm with kubectl get pods -A that the earlier objects have reappeared.
scenario.answer: Restore the snapshot to a new data directory with etcdutl (or etcdctl on older versions). Then point the etcd-data hostPath in etcd.yaml to that directory and let the kubelet recreate etcd. This avoids overwriting live data and is the only change the static pod needs.

memoryAids: Upgrade order 'A-P-K-W': Admin tool (kubeadm), Plane (upgrade apply), Kubelet + kubectl on that node, Workers one by one (drain, upgrade node, kubelet, uncordon).
etcd restore 'New Dir, New Path': restore to a NEW directory, then change the hostPath in etcd.yaml. If you forget either one, etcd serves old data or never starts.
PVC Pending check 'C-A-S': Class name, Access mode, Size. Compare all three between describe pvc and the PV.
cheatSheet: Start every task with the given context command, and re-read which node you must SSH to.
etcd TLS flags: copy the cert paths from the command section of /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml. Do not type them from memory.
Verify a snapshot with 'etcdutl snapshot status <file>' before you report the task as done.
Editing a static pod manifest is enough. The kubelet watches the directory and recreates the pod. Do not use kubectl apply on these files.
Find staticPodPath in /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml if a task uses a non-default manifest directory.
pkgs.k8s.io repos are per minor version. Point the apt repo at the new minor before installing the new kubeadm, and unhold or hold the packages around the install.
After the kubelet package upgrade, run daemon-reload and restart kubelet, then confirm the new version with kubectl get nodes.
Imperative RBAC is fastest: kubectl create role, rolebinding or clusterrole with --verb, --resource, --serviceaccount=ns:name.
A pod uses a service account through spec.serviceAccountName. You cannot change it on a running pod, so recreate the pod or edit its Deployment.
A PV is cluster-scoped and a PVC is namespaced. Create the PVC in the namespace the task names.
Expired certs show up as an API server that will not start or x509 errors. Run kubeadm certs renew, then restart the control-plane static pods.
Use kubectl explain and the -o yaml --dry-run=client output to build manifests instead of writing YAML from scratch.
selfCheck: I can take and restore an etcd snapshot, including editing the etcd.yaml hostPath, in under 10 minutes without notes.
I can upgrade a kubeadm control-plane node and one worker by one minor version, and explain why each step comes in that order.
I can bring a NotReady node back to Ready using only systemctl, journalctl and the kubelet config files.
I can fix a broken kube-apiserver static pod by reading crictl output and correcting the manifest.
I can create a namespace-scoped permission for a service account and prove it with kubectl auth can-i --as.
I can find why a PVC is Pending and fix it so that it binds to the intended PV.

objective.question: A worker node's kubelet cannot reach etcd directly, but the kube-apiserver on the control plane can. Which port does kube-apiserver use to reach etcd as a client?
objective.explanation: etcd serves client traffic, including kube-apiserver, on 2379. Port 2380 is for etcd peer traffic between members, 6443 is the API server and 10250 is the kubelet API.

objective.question: On a kubeadm cluster, kube-scheduler is crashing because of a wrong flag. Its pod shows in kube-system as kube-scheduler-controlplane. What is the correct way to fix it?
options: kubectl delete pod kube-scheduler-controlplane -n kube-system so the Deployment recreates it
Edit the kube-scheduler ConfigMap in kube-system and restart the kubelet
Edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml on the control plane node; the kubelet recreates the pod
kubectl edit pod kube-scheduler-controlplane -n kube-system and change the flag
objective.explanation: kube-scheduler is a static pod, and the API object is only a read-only mirror pod. The kubelet watches /etc/kubernetes/manifests and recreates the pod when the file changes. No Deployment manages it, and editing the mirror pod does not fix the real pod.

objective.question: You are upgrading a kubeadm cluster by one minor version. What is the correct order on the first control plane node?
options: Upgrade the kubeadm package, run kubeadm upgrade plan and kubeadm upgrade apply, then drain the node, upgrade kubelet and kubectl, restart kubelet, and uncordon
Upgrade all workers first, then the control plane
Run kubeadm upgrade node, then upgrade the kubeadm package, then kubelet
Upgrade kubelet and kubectl, then kubeadm, then run kubeadm upgrade apply
objective.explanation: kubeadm is upgraded first so it can upgrade the control plane components. Then you upgrade the kubelet and kubectl on that node. 'kubeadm upgrade node' is for additional control plane nodes and workers, and the control plane must never be older than the kubelets.

objective.question: Your kube-apiserver runs v1.33. Which kubelet version is NOT supported under the Kubernetes version skew policy?
objective.explanation: A kubelet may be up to three minor versions older than kube-apiserver (1.30–1.33 here), but it must never be newer. That rules out v1.34.

objective.question: Task: save an etcd snapshot to /opt/etcd-backup.db on a kubeadm control plane. Which command is correct?
options: etcdctl snapshot save /opt/etcd-backup.db --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key
etcdctl snapshot save /opt/etcd-backup.db --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.crt
kubectl etcd backup --file=/opt/etcd-backup.db
etcdctl snapshot save /opt/etcd-backup.db --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2380
objective.explanation: etcd needs TLS on the client port 2379, with the etcd CA and a client certificate and key from /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd. Port 2380 is for peers, kubectl has no etcd backup command, and the cluster CA at /etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.crt is not the etcd CA.

objective.question: The service account 'monitor' in namespace 'ops' must list pods in ALL namespaces. You created a ClusterRole 'pod-reader' with get and list on pods. What else is required?
options: A ClusterRoleBinding that binds ClusterRole pod-reader to subject ServiceAccount ops:monitor
A Role in each namespace bound with a ClusterRoleBinding
Nothing; a ClusterRole applies automatically to all service accounts
A RoleBinding in namespace ops that references ClusterRole pod-reader
objective.explanation: A ClusterRoleBinding grants a ClusterRole's permissions cluster-wide. A RoleBinding that references a ClusterRole only grants access inside the RoleBinding's namespace, and a ClusterRoleBinding cannot reference a Role.

objective.question: You create a PVC that uses a StorageClass with volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer. No pod uses the PVC yet, and it shows Pending. What does this mean?
options: This is expected; the volume is provisioned and bound only when a pod using the PVC is scheduled
The PVC's access mode is invalid
A static PV with Retain policy is needed first
The provisioner has failed and the StorageClass must be recreated
objective.explanation: WaitForFirstConsumer delays binding and provisioning until a pod that uses the PVC is scheduled. This lets the volume be created in the right zone or topology for that pod. Pending is normal in this state and is not an error.

objective.question: A database pod needs a volume that only one single pod in the whole cluster can mount read-write at any time. Which access mode guarantees this?
options: ReadOnlyMany
ReadWriteOncePod
ReadWriteMany
ReadWriteOnce
objective.explanation: ReadWriteOncePod limits read-write access to a single pod. ReadWriteOnce limits access to a single node, so several pods on that node can still share the volume. RWX and ROX allow many consumers.

objective.question: A worker node shows NotReady. SSH works. What is the most effective first check?
options: systemctl status kubelet and journalctl -u kubelet on the node
Restart kube-apiserver on the control plane
Check the NodePort range in kube-proxy
kubectl delete node and rejoin it immediately
objective.explanation: A NotReady node usually means the kubelet is stopped, misconfigured or cannot reach the runtime or API server. The kubelet's service status and logs show the cause quickly. Deleting the node or restarting the API server does not diagnose anything.

objective.question: kubectl reports x509 'certificate has expired' errors on a kubeadm cluster that was installed 13 months ago and never upgraded. What is the correct fix?
options: Run kubeadm certs check-expiration, then kubeadm certs renew all, then restart the control plane static pods and refresh your admin kubeconfig
Run kubeadm reset and reinstall the cluster
Delete /etc/kubernetes/pki and restart the kubelet
Regenerate the cluster CA, because the CA is valid for only 1 year
objective.explanation: kubeadm leaf certificates last 1 year; the CA lasts 10 years, so the CA is still valid. After 'kubeadm certs renew all' you must restart the control plane components, and you should copy the renewed admin.conf to ~/.kube/config. Resetting the cluster or deleting the PKI directory destroys it.

objective.question: A developer applies this manifest. What access does user 'priya' get?

code.code:
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: priya-edit
  namespace: dev
subjects:
- kind: User
  name: priya
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
roleRef:
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: edit
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io

options: The permissions of the 'edit' ClusterRole, but only inside namespace 'dev'
The 'edit' permissions in 'dev' plus read access to cluster-scoped resources such as nodes
Nothing, because a RoleBinding cannot reference a ClusterRole
The permissions of the 'edit' ClusterRole in every namespace of the cluster
objective.explanation: A RoleBinding can reference a ClusterRole. The permissions then apply only in the RoleBinding's namespace. Cluster-wide access needs a ClusterRoleBinding, and namespaced bindings never grant access to cluster-scoped resources like nodes.

objective.question: On a kubeadm control plane you ran 'etcdutl snapshot restore /opt/etcd-backup.db --data-dir /var/lib/etcd-restore'. The command succeeded, but the cluster still shows the old state. What is the missing step?
options: Restart the kube-apiserver with 'systemctl restart kube-apiserver'
Run 'kubectl apply -f /var/lib/etcd-restore' to replay the objects
Edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml so the etcd-data hostPath volume points to /var/lib/etcd-restore, then wait for kubelet to recreate the etcd pod
Run 'kubeadm init phase etcd local' to load the new data
objective.explanation: A restore writes a new data directory. etcd keeps using the old one until its static pod manifest's hostPath points to the new path. kubelet watches the manifest and restarts etcd. kube-apiserver is a static pod, not a systemd unit, and kubectl cannot read etcd data files.

objective.question: You run 'kubectl drain node01' before maintenance. It fails with errors about DaemonSet-managed pods and pods using emptyDir volumes. Which command completes the drain correctly?
options: kubectl drain node01 --grace-period=0 --skip-daemonsets
kubectl delete node node01 then kubectl drain node01
kubectl cordon node01 --force
kubectl drain node01 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
objective.explanation: --ignore-daemonsets skips DaemonSet pods, which would be recreated on the node anyway. --delete-emptydir-data accepts that the emptyDir data will be lost. Cordon only marks the node unschedulable, '--skip-daemonsets' is not a real flag, and deleting the node first is not a drain.

objective.question: A new pod stays Pending. 'kubectl describe pod' shows this event. What is the most likely fix?

code.code:
Warning  FailedScheduling  default-scheduler
0/3 nodes are available: 1 node(s) had untolerated taint
{node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane: }, 2 node(s) didn't match
Pod's node affinity/selector. preemption: 0/3 nodes are available:
3 Preemption is not helpful for scheduling.

options: Correct the pod's nodeSelector, or add the matching label to a worker node
Restart kube-scheduler because it has a stale node cache
Increase the pod's priorityClass so preemption can evict other pods
Remove the control-plane taint so the pod can run on the control plane
objective.explanation: The two workers were rejected only because of the nodeSelector or affinity mismatch, so fixing the label or selector is the right fix. Removing the control-plane taint is a poor workaround, and the event says preemption does not help. Nothing points to a scheduler fault.

objective.question: You edit a bound PVC to increase its storage from 5Gi to 10Gi. The API rejects the change, saying only dynamically provisioned PVCs can be resized and the StorageClass must support resize. The PVC was dynamically provisioned. What do you change?
options: Set allowVolumeExpansion: true on the PVC's StorageClass, then edit the PVC request again
Delete the PV so it is recreated at 10Gi
Change the PVC accessModes to ReadWriteMany
Set reclaimPolicy: Retain on the StorageClass
objective.explanation: Expansion is allowed only when the StorageClass has allowVolumeExpansion: true, and the CSI driver must support it. Reclaim policy and access modes do not affect resizing. Deleting the PV risks losing data.

objective.question: You need to confirm that service account 'builder' in namespace 'ci' can create deployments in namespace 'app'. Which command checks this correctly?
options: kubectl get rolebinding -n app --as=serviceaccount:ci:builder
kubectl auth whoami -n app --serviceaccount=ci/builder
kubectl auth can-i create deployments -n ci --as=builder
kubectl auth can-i create deployments -n app --as=system:serviceaccount:ci:builder
objective.explanation: To impersonate a service account, use the username format system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<name>, and pass the namespace being tested with -n. Option B checks the wrong namespace and uses a plain user name. The other two options do not test the permission.

objective.question: After restoring an etcd snapshot to /var/lib/etcd-restore, you edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml as shown. etcd starts, but the cluster looks empty, with no Deployments or Services. What is the mistake?

code.code:
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - etcd
    - --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd-restore
    # other flags unchanged
    volumeMounts:
    - mountPath: /var/lib/etcd
      name: etcd-data
  volumes:
  - hostPath:
      path: /var/lib/etcd
      type: DirectoryOrCreate
    name: etcd-data

options: The kubelet must be restarted, because static pod manifests are only read at boot

Only --data-dir was changed. The hostPath still mounts the old /var/lib/etcd, so /var/lib/etcd-restore inside the container is a new empty directory. Point the hostPath at /var/lib/etcd-restore and keep --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd
The volumeMounts mountPath must match the hostPath type DirectoryOrCreate
The snapshot must be restored with --skip-hash-check before etcd can read it
objective.explanation: The restored data is on the host, so the hostPath must point to it. Changing only --data-dir makes etcd write a fresh, empty data directory inside the container's own filesystem. The kubelet watches the manifests directory and needs no restart, and there is no need to skip the hash check.

objective.question: The control plane is already on the new minor version. Which order is correct for upgrading worker node01?
options: Drain node01 from the control plane, upgrade the kubeadm package on node01, run 'kubeadm upgrade node', upgrade kubelet and kubectl, run 'systemctl daemon-reload' and 'systemctl restart kubelet', then uncordon
Drain node01, upgrade kubelet and kubectl, restart the kubelet, then run 'kubeadm upgrade node' and uncordon
Upgrade the kubeadm package, run 'kubeadm upgrade node', uncordon, then drain and upgrade the kubelet
Upgrade kubelet and kubectl, run kubeadm upgrade apply, drain, uncordon
objective.explanation: Workers use 'kubeadm upgrade node', not 'upgrade apply'. The kubelet is upgraded after kubeadm has updated the node's kubelet configuration, and the node is drained first and uncordoned last. The other orders skip the drain, use the wrong subcommand, or upgrade the kubelet too early.

objective.question: A service account bound to this Role still gets Forbidden when it runs 'kubectl create deployment' in its namespace. What is the cause?

code.code:
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: deployer
  namespace: app
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["deployments"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "create", "update"]

options: The verbs list must include 'patch' before 'create' is allowed
resources must be written in the singular form, 'deployment'
A Role cannot grant access to Deployments. Only a ClusterRole can
Deployments belong to the 'apps' API group. The empty string means the core group, so apiGroups must be ["apps"]
objective.explanation: RBAC matches on API group and resource together. Deployments are served under apps/v1, so a rule for the core group ("") never matches them. A Role can grant access to namespaced resources such as Deployments, and resource names are plural.

objective.question: An admin created a static PV with no storageClassName. The PVC below also omits storageClassName. The cluster has a default StorageClass 'standard'. The PVC ends up Bound to a new dynamically provisioned volume instead of the manual PV. Why, and what is the fix?

code.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: data
spec:
  accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 5Gi

options: PVs without a storageClassName cannot be bound at all. Add storageClassName: standard to the PV
ReadWriteOnce always triggers dynamic provisioning. Use ReadWriteMany
The DefaultStorageClass admission plugin set storageClassName to 'standard' on the PVC, so it can only match class 'standard'. Set storageClassName: "" in the PVC to bind to the class-less PV
The PV is too large, so the controller provisioned a smaller one. Reduce the PV size to 5Gi
objective.explanation: A PVC with no storageClassName gets the default class added by admission. It then only matches PVs of that class, so the class-less PV is never chosen. An explicit empty string opts the PVC out of the default class. A PV larger than the request can still bind, and access modes do not trigger provisioning.

objective.question: In the CKA exam, each task begins with a line such as 'kubectl config use-context k8s-c2'. What should you do first?
options: Run it only if the task mentions a namespace
Run it once at the start of the exam
Run the given context command before anything else in that task
Ignore it, because all tasks share the same cluster
objective.explanation: Tasks can target different clusters. Work done in the wrong context scores zero, so you switch context at the start of every task, not just once.

objective.question: A freshly joined worker stays NotReady. 'journalctl -u kubelet' shows the line below. What is the fix?

code.code: E... run.go: "command failed" err="failed to run Kubelet: running with swap on is not supported, please disable swap or set --fail-swap-on flag to false"

options: Run 'swapoff -a', comment out the swap entry in /etc/fstab so it stays off after a reboot, then restart the kubelet
Delete the node object with kubectl and let it re-register
Run 'kubeadm reset' on the control plane
Reinstall containerd and rejoin the node
objective.explanation: By default the kubelet refuses to start while swap is on. Turning swap off now and removing it from fstab fixes the cause and keeps it fixed after a reboot. The container runtime and the node object are not the problem.

objective.question: You run 'kubectl delete pod kube-scheduler-controlplane -n kube-system'. What happens?
options: The scheduler is gone until you rerun 'kubeadm init phase control-plane scheduler'
The kube-system ReplicaSet recreates it on any available node
The API server refuses the delete, because control plane pods are protected
The kubelet recreates it almost at once, because it is the mirror of a static pod defined in /etc/kubernetes/manifests. To stop it you must move the manifest out of that directory
objective.explanation: Static pods are managed by the kubelet from manifest files. The API object is only a mirror, so deleting it changes nothing that lasts. No ReplicaSet owns these pods, and the API server does not block the delete.

objective.question: Client pods get 'connection refused' from Service 'web'. 'kubectl get endpoints web' lists pod IPs on port 80. The container runs an app listening on 8080. What is the cause?

code.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  selector:
    app: web
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 80

options: The Service needs type NodePort to be reached from inside the cluster
targetPort is 80, but the container listens on 8080. Set targetPort: 8080
kube-proxy is not running on the nodes
The selector does not match any pods
objective.explanation: Endpoints exist, so the selector matches. Traffic is forwarded to pod port 80, where nothing listens, and that gives 'connection refused'. A ClusterIP Service is reachable inside the cluster, and the Service rules are clearly being programmed.

objective.question: Straight after 'kubeadm init', 'kubectl get nodes' shows the control plane NotReady and the CoreDNS pods stay Pending. What is the most likely reason?
options: The kubeconfig file in ~/.kube/config is wrong
The kube-proxy DaemonSet failed to deploy
No pod network (CNI) add-on is installed yet
etcd has not finished starting
objective.explanation: The kubelet reports NotReady until a CNI plugin is configured, and CoreDNS waits for pod networking. A wrong kubeconfig would stop kubectl working at all, and the cluster is answering. A failed etcd would also take down the API.

objective.question: You create a Deployment. 'kubectl get deploy' shows it, but no ReplicaSet and no pods are ever created, and there are no events. Existing pods keep running. Which component is most likely down?
options: kube-proxy
kube-controller-manager
kubelet on the worker nodes
kube-scheduler
objective.explanation: The Deployment controller inside kube-controller-manager creates the ReplicaSets and pods. If the scheduler were down, pods would exist but stay Pending without a node. kube-proxy and the kubelet do not create API objects.

objective.question: You need to join a new worker to a kubeadm cluster installed two days ago. The join command printed at install time fails with an authentication error. What do you run on the control plane?
options: kubeadm init phase upload-certs
kubeadm certs renew all
kubectl certificate approve node02
kubeadm token create --print-join-command
objective.explanation: Bootstrap tokens created by kubeadm init expire after 24 hours by default. The command creates a new token and prints a complete join command. Renewing certificates or uploading certificates does not fix an expired token.

subjective.question: Explain what each control plane and node component does when you run 'kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx'.
subjective.answer: kubectl sends the request to kube-apiserver on port 6443. The API server authenticates and authorises the request, runs admission, and stores the Deployment in etcd. kube-controller-manager watches the API server. Its Deployment controller creates a ReplicaSet, and the ReplicaSet controller creates Pod objects. kube-scheduler sees pods with no nodeName, filters and scores the nodes, and binds each pod to a node. The kubelet on that node watches for pods bound to it. It asks the container runtime (for example containerd) through CRI to pull the image and start the containers. It then reports status back to the API server. kube-proxy runs on every node and programs iptables, IPVS or nftables rules so that Services reach the pods. Only the API server talks to etcd directly; every other component goes through the API server.
keyPoints: API server is the only component that talks to etcd
Controller-manager reconciles Deployment to ReplicaSet to Pods
Scheduler binds pods to nodes
Kubelet runs containers through the CRI runtime
kube-proxy programs Service routing on each node

subjective.question: Walk through backing up and restoring etcd on a kubeadm control plane, from memory.
subjective.answer: First, I get the endpoint and certificate paths from /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml. To back up, I run: etcdctl --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key snapshot save /opt/backup.db. I verify it with 'etcdutl snapshot status /opt/backup.db'. To restore, I run 'etcdutl snapshot restore /opt/backup.db --data-dir /var/lib/etcd-restore'. Older tools use 'etcdctl snapshot restore', which still works but is deprecated. Restore is an offline operation, so it does not need TLS flags. Next, I edit etcd.yaml and change the etcd-data hostPath volume to /var/lib/etcd-restore. If --data-dir in the command is also changed, it must stay consistent with the volume mount. The kubelet then recreates the etcd static pod. I wait for etcd and the API server to come back and check them with crictl ps. Finally, I confirm with kubectl get pods -A that the old state has returned.
keyPoints: Save uses port 2379 with cacert, cert and key from /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd
Restore goes into a new data directory
Update the hostPath in the etcd static pod manifest
Verify the snapshot and the cluster afterwards
Know etcdutl versus the deprecated etcdctl restore

subjective.question: Describe the full kubeadm upgrade process for a cluster with one control plane and two workers.
subjective.answer: I upgrade one minor version at a time, for example 1.32 to 1.33. First, I update the package repository to the target minor version. On the control plane, I upgrade the kubeadm package and run 'kubeadm upgrade plan' to see the available versions. Then I run 'kubeadm upgrade apply v1.33.x'. This upgrades the static pod components and also renews the certificates. Next, I drain the control plane node with --ignore-daemonsets and upgrade the kubelet and kubectl packages. Then I run systemctl daemon-reload, restart the kubelet, and uncordon the node. For each worker, I upgrade kubeadm on the worker, drain it from the control plane, and run 'kubeadm upgrade node' on the worker. Then I upgrade the kubelet and kubectl, restart the kubelet, and uncordon. I finish with kubectl get nodes to confirm the versions. The control plane goes first because a kubelet must never be newer than the API server.
keyPoints: One minor version at a time
Upgrade kubeadm first, then upgrade apply on the first control plane
Workers use kubeadm upgrade node
Drain, upgrade kubelet/kubectl, restart kubelet, uncordon
Skew policy: kubelet never newer than the API server

subjective.question: What are static pods, and how do they differ from DaemonSet pods?
subjective.answer: A static pod is managed directly by the kubelet on one node, not by the API server. The kubelet watches a directory, which is /etc/kubernetes/manifests on kubeadm clusters. The path is set by staticPodPath in /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml. The kubelet runs any pod manifest it finds in that directory. It also creates a read-only mirror pod in the API so you can see the static pod, with the node name added to the pod name. To change or remove a static pod, you edit or move the file; deleting the mirror pod does nothing. kubeadm runs the API server, controller-manager, scheduler and etcd this way because they must start before an API server exists. DaemonSet pods are created by a controller through the API server, are scheduled onto every matching node, and are managed with kubectl. In the exam, you find the static pod path by reading the kubelet config.
keyPoints: Managed by the kubelet from a directory, not by the API server
staticPodPath is in the kubelet config
Mirror pods are read-only
Used to run the control plane before the API server exists
DaemonSets are API-driven controllers

subjective.question: Design least-privilege RBAC for a CI service account that deploys only to namespace 'app', and show how you would verify it.
subjective.answer: Create the service account: kubectl create sa ci -n app. Create a namespaced Role, for example: kubectl create role deployer -n app --verb=get,list,watch,create,update,patch --resource=deployments,services,configmaps. Add pods with only get and list if CI needs to read rollout status. Bind the Role: kubectl create rolebinding ci-deployer -n app --role=deployer --serviceaccount=app:ci. I avoid ClusterRoles and wildcards, and I do not grant access to secrets unless it is required. To verify, I impersonate the account: kubectl auth can-i create deployments -n app --as=system:serviceaccount:app:ci should return yes. Checking the same verb with -n default should return no. kubectl auth can-i --list --as=... shows everything the account can do. A Role plus a RoleBinding keeps the permissions inside the namespace.
keyPoints: Role and RoleBinding for namespace scope
Explicit verbs and resources, no wildcards
Subject format serviceaccount ns:name
Verify with kubectl auth can-i --as
Test both allowed and denied cases

subjective.question: How have service account tokens changed in recent Kubernetes versions, and how does a pod get its token?
subjective.answer: Every namespace has a 'default' service account, and pods use it unless spec.serviceAccountName says otherwise. Since Kubernetes 1.24, creating a service account no longer creates a long-lived token Secret automatically. Pods instead receive short-lived, audience-bound tokens through the TokenRequest API. The kubelet mounts the token as a projected volume at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount and rotates it before it expires. For a manual token, I run 'kubectl create token <sa> -n <ns>', optionally with --duration. If a legacy non-expiring token is truly needed, you create a Secret of type kubernetes.io/service-account-token with the service-account annotation, but this is discouraged. To stop a pod mounting a token, set automountServiceAccountToken: false on the pod or the service account. Permissions still come only from RBAC bindings to the service account.
keyPoints: Default SA is used if none is specified
No automatic Secret tokens since 1.24
Projected, time-bound tokens from the TokenRequest API
kubectl create token for manual tokens
automountServiceAccountToken: false to disable mounting

subjective.question: Explain how PV, PVC and StorageClass work together, including reclaim policies.
subjective.answer: A PersistentVolume is a piece of storage in the cluster. A PersistentVolumeClaim is a user's request for storage, with a size, access mode and optional storageClassName. In static provisioning, an admin creates PVs, and Kubernetes binds a PVC to a matching PV by class, size and access mode. In dynamic provisioning, the PVC names a StorageClass, and that class's provisioner, usually a CSI driver, creates the PV automatically. A StorageClass can be marked as the default, can set volumeBindingMode (Immediate or WaitForFirstConsumer), and can set allowVolumeExpansion to allow resizing PVCs. The reclaim policy decides what happens after the PVC is deleted. With Delete, the PV and the backing storage are removed; this is the usual default for dynamic volumes. With Retain, the PV moves to Released, the data stays, and an admin must clean it up or clear claimRef before it can be reused. Recycle is deprecated. Pods mount the PVC, not the PV.
keyPoints: PV is the supply, PVC is the request
StorageClass enables dynamic provisioning through a provisioner
Binding matches class, size and access mode
Retain leaves the PV Released; Delete removes storage
WaitForFirstConsumer and allowVolumeExpansion

subjective.question: In your lab you broke a worker node. How do you diagnose and recover a node that is NotReady?
subjective.answer: From the control plane, I run kubectl get nodes and kubectl describe node <name>. The Conditions section and recent events often show 'Kubelet stopped posting node status'. I then SSH to the node. I check systemctl status kubelet and read journalctl -u kubelet -f. Common causes are a stopped or disabled kubelet, a wrong path or typo in /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml or in the systemd drop-in, a bad kubeconfig or expired client certificate, a stopped containerd, swap still on, or a missing CNI. I fix the cause, for example by correcting the config or running 'systemctl enable --now containerd kubelet'. Then I run systemctl daemon-reload and restart kubelet. crictl ps confirms that containers are running. Back on the control plane, I wait for Ready and uncordon the node if I drained it. I always run systemctl enable as well so the fix survives a reboot.
keyPoints: describe node for conditions
systemctl status and journalctl -u kubelet
Check the kubelet config, the runtime and certificates
daemon-reload, restart and enable
Confirm Ready and uncordon

subjective.question: A Service returns no response from client pods. How do you troubleshoot it step by step?
subjective.answer: I work from the client to the backend. First, kubectl get svc,endpointslices (or kubectl get endpoints) for the service. If there are no endpoints, the selector does not match the pod labels, or the pods are not Ready. I compare with kubectl get pods --show-labels and check the readiness probes. Next, I check that targetPort matches the containerPort the app really listens on. Then I test from a debug pod, for example busybox or netshoot: curl the pod IP directly, then the ClusterIP, then the DNS name svc.ns.svc.cluster.local. If DNS fails, I check the CoreDNS pods and logs in kube-system and the pod's /etc/resolv.conf. If the pod IP works but the ClusterIP does not, I check the kube-proxy pods and logs. If even pod-to-pod traffic fails, I suspect the CNI or a NetworkPolicy that blocks traffic. For a NodePort service, I confirm the port is in 30000–32767 and reachable on the node IP.
keyPoints: Endpoints empty means a selector or readiness problem
targetPort must match the container port
Test pod IP, then ClusterIP, then DNS
CoreDNS and kube-proxy checks
NetworkPolicy or CNI if pod-to-pod traffic fails

subjective.question: What is your strategy for the CKA exam itself?
subjective.answer: The CKA is performance-based, lasts 2 hours, needs 66% to pass, and includes one free retake. The domain weights guide my practice: Troubleshooting 30%, Cluster Architecture, Installation and Configuration 25%, Services and Networking 20%, Workloads and Scheduling 15%, and Storage 10%. At the start of every task, I run the context command the task gives me, because each task can target a different cluster. Working on the wrong cluster scores zero even when the commands are correct. I use imperative commands with --dry-run=client -o yaml to generate manifests quickly, and I keep the kubectl alias k. kubernetes.io/docs and the Kubernetes blog are allowed, so I know where to find the etcd, kubeadm upgrade and RBAC pages. I skip long tasks first and come back to them, because questions have different weights. After each task, I verify the result with get, describe or auth can-i. If I SSH to a node, I make sure to return to the base terminal.
keyPoints: Format: 2 hours, 66% to pass, one free retake
Domain weights, with Troubleshooting the largest at 30%
Switch context at the start of every task
Imperative commands and the allowed docs
Flag long tasks and verify every answer

subjective.question: A pod is in CrashLoopBackOff after a new deployment. Explain how you find the cause and fix it.
subjective.answer: First I run 'kubectl describe pod' and look at Last State, the exit code and the events. Exit code 137 with reason OOMKilled means the memory limit is too low. Exit code 1 usually means an application error. Next I run 'kubectl logs <pod> --previous', because the current container may have just restarted and have no logs yet. Common causes are a wrong command or args, a missing ConfigMap or Secret key, a bad environment variable, or a liveness probe that kills the container too early. I compare the pod spec with the last working revision using 'kubectl rollout history'. I fix the cause in the Deployment, not in the pod, because the ReplicaSet will recreate pods from the template. If the release is badly broken, I run 'kubectl rollout undo' to restore service first and debug afterwards.
keyPoints: kubectl describe pod: exit code, reason and events
kubectl logs --previous for the crashed container
Check OOMKilled, probes, config and command errors
Fix the Deployment template; use rollout undo if needed

subjective.question: After editing /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml, every kubectl command returns 'connection refused'. How do you troubleshoot without the API server?
