subjective.answer: kubectl needs the API server, so I work directly on the control plane node. First I check whether kubelet sees the manifest. 'crictl ps -a | grep kube-apiserver' shows whether the container is crash-looping or was never created. If it exists, I run 'crictl logs <container-id>' to see the error, for example an unknown flag or a wrong certificate path. If no container exists, the YAML itself is probably invalid. I check 'journalctl -u kubelet' for parse errors, and pod logs under /var/log/pods may also help. I fix the manifest, ideally by comparing it with a backup copy I saved outside the manifests directory. I never keep backups inside that directory, because kubelet would try to run them too. Then I wait for kubelet to recreate the pod and confirm with 'kubectl get nodes'.
keyPoints: Use crictl ps -a and crictl logs on the node
journalctl -u kubelet shows manifest parse errors
Check for typos in flags, paths and YAML indentation
Keep backups outside /etc/kubernetes/manifests

subjective.question: Compare kube-proxy modes and explain how you would check which mode a kubeadm cluster uses.
subjective.answer: kube-proxy programs each node so that traffic to Service virtual IPs reaches backend pods. In iptables mode it writes NAT rules. These are simple and reliable, but rule updates and matching slow down with thousands of Services. IPVS mode uses the kernel's IPVS load balancer with hash tables, so it scales better and offers several balancing algorithms. The nftables mode is the modern successor to iptables mode, with better performance; it became generally available in recent releases, while iptables remains the default on Linux. On kubeadm, the mode is set in the kube-proxy ConfigMap in kube-system, so I run 'kubectl -n kube-system get cm kube-proxy -o yaml' and check the 'mode' field. An empty value means the default. I can confirm in the kube-proxy pod logs, or by inspecting KUBE-SERVICES chains with iptables-save. Some CNIs, such as Cilium, can replace kube-proxy completely.
keyPoints: kube-proxy maps Service IPs to pod endpoints
iptables vs IPVS vs nftables trade-offs
Mode is set in the kube-proxy ConfigMap
Verify with logs or iptables-save; some CNIs replace kube-proxy

subjective.question: A developer bound to this Role can list pods, but 'kubectl logs' and 'kubectl exec' fail with Forbidden. Explain why and fix it.

code.code:
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: dev-pods
  namespace: app
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["pods"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]

subjective.answer: Logs and exec are subresources. RBAC treats them separately from the pods resource. 'kubectl logs' needs get on 'pods/log'. 'kubectl exec' needs create on 'pods/exec', because exec opens a new streaming session. The kubectl client also does a get on the pod first, which this Role already allows. The fix is to add a rule with apiGroups [""], resources ["pods/log"] and verbs ["get"]. If exec is really required, add another rule for resources ["pods/exec"] with verbs ["create"]. I would grant exec carefully, because it gives shell access to containers and their mounted secrets. Then I verify with 'kubectl auth can-i get pods/log -n app --as=<user>' and 'kubectl auth can-i create pods/exec -n app --as=<user>'. This follows least privilege: grant only the subresources the developer actually needs.
keyPoints: logs and exec are subresources: pods/log, pods/exec
pods/log needs get; pods/exec needs create
exec is powerful, so grant it sparingly
Verify with kubectl auth can-i on the subresource

subjective.question: A team deleted a PVC by mistake. The PV had reclaimPolicy Retain and now shows Released. How do you bring the data back into use by a new PVC?
subjective.answer: With Retain, Kubernetes keeps the PV and its data, but marks it Released. It still holds a claimRef to the deleted PVC, so no new claim can bind to it. First I back up or snapshot the underlying disk if I can. Then I edit the PV and remove spec.claimRef, or patch it with 'kubectl patch pv <name> --type=json -p [{"op":"remove","path":"/spec/claimRef"}]'. The PV becomes Available. Next I create a new PVC with a matching storageClassName, an access mode the PV offers and a request no larger than the PV's capacity. To make sure it binds to this exact PV, I set spec.volumeName in the PVC. Once the PVC shows Bound, I redeploy the workload. In production, I would also set Retain on critical StorageClasses so this recovery stays possible.
keyPoints: Retain keeps the data; the PV becomes Released
The stale claimRef blocks rebinding
Remove claimRef to make the PV Available
Use volumeName with a matching class, access mode and size

subjective.question: Pods can reach other pods by IP but cannot resolve Service names like 'web.app.svc.cluster.local'. How do you troubleshoot cluster DNS?
subjective.answer: First I reproduce the problem from a test pod: 'kubectl run dns-test --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 -- nslookup kubernetes.default'. Then I check /etc/resolv.conf inside the pod. The nameserver should be the kube-dns Service IP, and the search domains should include svc.cluster.local. If not, the kubelet clusterDNS setting is wrong. Next I check CoreDNS with 'kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l k8s-app=kube-dns'. I also confirm that the kube-dns Service has endpoints. If the pods are crashing, their logs often show a Corefile error or a forward loop. I then review the coredns ConfigMap. If CoreDNS is healthy but queries time out, the problem is probably the path to it. I check kube-proxy and the CNI on the client's node, and any NetworkPolicy that blocks UDP or TCP port 53 egress. After the fix, I restart CoreDNS if needed and test again.
keyPoints: Test with nslookup from a busybox pod
Check the pod's resolv.conf and kubelet clusterDNS
Check CoreDNS pods, logs, Corefile and Service endpoints
Check kube-proxy, the CNI and NetworkPolicy for port 53

subjective.question: Case study: in a new namespace 'payments', the app must run as service account 'payment-api'. It may read only the Secret 'db-creds' and may list ConfigMaps. It needs a 20Gi ReadWriteOnce volume from StorageClass 'fast'. Describe how you build and verify this.
subjective.answer: First I create the namespace and the service account: 'kubectl create ns payments' and 'kubectl create sa payment-api -n payments'. Next I create a Role with two rules. The first gives 'get' on secrets with resourceNames: [db-creds]. The second gives 'get' and 'list' on configmaps. I grant only 'get' on the Secret, because 'list' and 'watch' cannot be usefully limited by name and would expose every Secret. A RoleBinding in 'payments' binds the Role to the service account, so access stays inside the namespace. Then I create a PVC with storageClassName: fast, accessModes ReadWriteOnce and a 20Gi request. The pod spec sets serviceAccountName: payment-api and mounts the PVC. To verify, I run 'kubectl auth can-i get secret/db-creds --as=system:serviceaccount:payments:payment-api -n payments', expecting yes. The same check for another Secret, and 'list secrets', must say no. Finally I confirm the PVC shows Bound.
keyPoints: Role and RoleBinding, not cluster-wide objects
resourceNames with 'get' only, because 'list' cannot be limited by name
PVC with the correct storageClassName, access mode and size
Pod sets serviceAccountName
Check both allowed and denied actions with auth can-i --as

subjective.question: You restored an etcd snapshot and edited etcd.yaml. Now the etcd pod never comes up, and kubectl gives 'connection refused'. How do you find the cause?
subjective.answer: Without the API server I work on the control plane node itself. I run 'crictl ps -a | grep etcd' to see whether the container exists and is exiting, then 'crictl logs <id>' to read the error. If no container exists, the manifest probably fails to parse, so I check 'journalctl -u kubelet' for YAML or validation errors. The common causes are these. The hostPath points to a directory that does not exist, or that holds the restore only in a nested subdirectory. --data-dir and the volume mount disagree. The restore was done into the live /var/lib/etcd while the old member data was still there. An indentation mistake was made while editing. I also check that the restored directory contains a 'member' folder. If needed, I keep a copy of the original manifest outside the manifests directory so I can compare. Once etcd runs, the API server reconnects, and I confirm with 'kubectl get pods -A'.
keyPoints: Use crictl ps -a and crictl logs when the API is down
journalctl -u kubelet shows manifest parse errors
Check the hostPath, the data-dir and the mount match
The restored directory must contain the member folder
Keep a backup of the manifest outside /etc/kubernetes/manifests

subjective.question: Compare 'kubectl cordon', 'kubectl drain' and 'kubectl delete node'. Which would you use for kernel patching, and which for removing a node for good?
subjective.answer: Cordon only marks the node unschedulable. Running pods stay where they are, and new pods are not placed there. Drain cordons the node and then evicts its pods using the Eviction API, so PodDisruptionBudgets are respected. You usually need --ignore-daemonsets, and --delete-emptydir-data if pods use emptyDir. Delete node removes the Node object from the API. If the kubelet is still running and configured to register, the node can come back. Deleting the object does not clean up the machine. For kernel patching I drain, patch and reboot, check the node is Ready, and then uncordon. Cordon alone is enough when I just want to stop new work landing on a suspicious node while I investigate. To retire a node, I drain it, delete the node object, and on the machine run 'kubeadm reset' and clean up the CNI and iptables state.
keyPoints: Cordon blocks new scheduling only
Drain evicts pods and respects PodDisruptionBudgets
Delete node removes only the API object
Patching: drain, then uncordon
Retire: drain, delete node, kubeadm reset

subjective.question: Put in order the steps to add a new worker node to an existing kubeadm cluster, and say why each step matters.
subjective.answer: First, prepare the OS. Turn swap off permanently, load the overlay and br_netfilter modules, and set net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables and net.ipv4.ip_forward to 1. Without these, pod networking breaks. Second, install a container runtime such as containerd and set its cgroup driver to systemd, to match the kubelet. A mismatch causes unstable nodes. Third, add the pkgs.k8s.io repository for the cluster's minor version. Install kubeadm, kubelet and kubectl at matching versions and run 'apt-mark hold' so they are not upgraded by accident. Fourth, on the control plane, run 'kubeadm token create --print-join-command', because the original token may have expired. Fifth, run that join command on the new node as root. Finally, run 'kubectl get nodes' and wait for Ready. If it stays NotReady, check that the CNI DaemonSet pod started on the new node and read the kubelet logs.
keyPoints: Swap off, kernel modules and sysctls first
Container runtime with a matching systemd cgroup driver
Matching package versions, then hold them
Create a fresh join command
Verify Ready and check the CNI pod on the node

subjective.question: A colleague wrote this script to upgrade the cluster from v1.33 to v1.34. Spot the mistakes.

code.code:
# run on worker node01; control plane not upgraded yet
apt-get update
apt-get install -y kubelet=1.34.1-1.1 kubeadm=1.34.1-1.1
kubeadm upgrade apply v1.34.1
# done

subjective.answer: There are several mistakes. First, the order is wrong. The control plane must be upgraded first, and a kubelet newer than the API server is not supported. Second, 'kubeadm upgrade apply' is for the first control plane node only. Workers use 'kubeadm upgrade node'. Third, the node is never drained, so workloads are disrupted with no safe eviction. Fourth, the kubelet is upgraded together with kubeadm. The correct sequence upgrades kubeadm, runs the kubeadm step, and then upgrades the kubelet. Fifth, there is no 'systemctl daemon-reload' and 'systemctl restart kubelet', so the node keeps reporting the old version. Sixth, if the packages were held, the install fails without 'apt-mark unhold' first, and they should be held again afterwards. The pkgs.k8s.io repository must also be switched to the v1.34 channel. The fixed flow is: upgrade the control plane, then on the worker drain, upgrade kubeadm, run kubeadm upgrade node, upgrade kubelet and kubectl, reload and restart, and uncordon.
keyPoints: Control plane before workers
Workers use 'upgrade node', not 'upgrade apply'
Drain before and uncordon after
Run daemon-reload and restart the kubelet
Unhold and re-hold packages, and switch the repo to the new minor version

subjective.question: User 'arjun' should read pods in namespace 'dev' using the Role 'app-reader' that already exists in namespace 'app'. This binding was applied without errors, but arjun gets Forbidden. What is wrong, and how do you fix it?

code.code:
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: dev-read
  namespace: dev
subjects:
- kind: User
  name: arjun
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: app-reader
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io

subjective.answer: roleRef has no namespace field. A Role referenced by a RoleBinding is always looked up in the RoleBinding's own namespace, here 'dev'. There is no 'app-reader' Role in 'dev', so the binding points at nothing. RBAC allows a binding to a missing role, so it is created without error but grants nothing. Roles cannot be shared across namespaces. There are two fixes. I can create the same Role in 'dev'. Or, better if many namespaces need it, I can turn the rules into a ClusterRole and reference it with kind: ClusterRole in a RoleBinding in 'dev'. That still limits access to 'dev'. roleRef is immutable, so I delete and recreate the binding rather than edit it. I verify with 'kubectl auth can-i list pods -n dev --as arjun'.
keyPoints: roleRef resolves a Role in the binding's own namespace
A binding to a missing role is accepted but grants nothing
Copy the Role, or use a ClusterRole with a RoleBinding
roleRef is immutable, so delete and recreate
Verify with auth can-i --as

subjective.question: After a rolling update, new pods of a single-replica database Deployment stay in ContainerCreating with a 'Multi-Attach error for volume' event. What is the cause, and what are your options?
subjective.answer: The volume is ReadWriteOnce block storage, which can attach to only one node at a time. The rolling update started the new pod on a different node while the old pod still held the volume, so the attach failed. On an ungraceful node failure the old attachment can also linger until it times out. First I confirm with 'kubectl describe pod' and 'kubectl get volumeattachments'. For a single-writer database, the right fix is strategy type: Recreate, so the old pod stops before the new one starts. Using a StatefulSet is even better, because it gives stable identity and handles one pod per volume. If the old node is dead, I make sure that pod is really gone, by force-deleting it only after confirming the node is down, so the attachment is released. I would not change the access mode to ReadWriteMany for a database unless the storage and the application actually support shared writers.
keyPoints: RWO block volumes attach to one node at a time
A rolling update overlaps the old and new pods
Use the Recreate strategy or a StatefulSet
Check VolumeAttachment objects
Force-delete only after confirming the node is down

subjective.question: For a three-node on-premises cluster with fast local NVMe disks, which is better for a database: local PersistentVolumes or a dynamic StorageClass backed by network storage? Explain the trade-offs.
subjective.answer: Local PVs give the best latency and throughput, because the disk is on the node. The cost is that the data is tied to that node. If the node dies, the pod cannot move without the data, so the database itself must replicate, as Postgres replicas or Cassandra do. Local PVs are created statically with a nodeAffinity. They should use a StorageClass with provisioner kubernetes.io/no-provisioner and volumeBindingMode WaitForFirstConsumer, so the scheduler picks a node that has the disk before binding. Network storage through a CSI driver with dynamic provisioning is easier to run. PVCs are created on demand, can often be expanded and snapshotted, and the pod can be rescheduled to another node. The downside is extra network latency and dependence on the storage system. My choice: use local PVs for databases that replicate themselves and need speed, and use dynamic network storage when the application relies on Kubernetes to move it and keep the data.
keyPoints: Local PV: fast but tied to one node
Use nodeAffinity, no-provisioner and WaitForFirstConsumer
Dynamic CSI storage: portable, resizable, easier to operate
Base the choice on whether the application replicates itself

subjective.question: All nodes are Ready. Pods on node02 can reach pods on node02, but they cannot reach pods on node01 or node03. How do you troubleshoot this?
subjective.answer: Same-node traffic works, so the problem is in the cross-node overlay or routing, and probably on node02. First, I run 'kubectl get pods -n kube-system -o wide' and look at the CNI pod on node02, such as calico-node, cilium or flannel. If it is crashing or not ready, I read its logs. Second, I confirm that the node's pod CIDR does not overlap with the node network or another node's range. Third, I check the host firewall and any cloud security group. The CNI's tunnel or BGP ports must be open between nodes, for example VXLAN on UDP or BGP on TCP 179, depending on the plugin. Fourth, on node02 I check that IP forwarding is on and that br_netfilter is loaded, because a rebuilt node often misses these. Finally, I test pod-to-pod by IP from a debug pod, and capture packets on the tunnel interface with tcpdump if needed. Restarting the CNI pod after fixing the config usually restores the routes.
keyPoints: Same-node success points at the overlay or routing
Check the CNI pod on the affected node first
Check firewall rules for the CNI's tunnel or BGP ports
Check ip_forward, br_netfilter and CIDR overlaps
Test pod IP to pod IP, and use tcpdump if needed

subjective.question: A Deployment shows 0/3 READY, and 'kubectl get pods -l app=web' returns nothing. The ReplicaSet exists. How do you find the cause?
subjective.answer: A ReplicaSet that exists without pods means pod creation is being rejected, or its controller is not acting on it. I start with 'kubectl describe rs <name>' and read the events, because the reason is usually written there. A common case is 'exceeded quota'. A ResourceQuota in the namespace blocks new pods, or demands requests and limits that the pod spec lacks. 'kubectl describe quota' and 'kubectl describe limitrange' confirm this. Another case is an admission rejection, such as Pod Security Admission blocking a privileged container, or a webhook denying the pod. A third case is a service account named in the pod spec that does not exist. If the ReplicaSet has no events at all, I check kube-controller-manager in kube-system. I compare this with pods that exist but are Pending, which is a scheduling problem and is debugged with 'kubectl describe pod' instead.
keyPoints: kubectl describe rs holds the rejection events
ResourceQuota and LimitRange are frequent causes
Admission or Pod Security rejections, and a missing ServiceAccount
No events at all points to the controller-manager
No pods (creation problem) differs from Pending pods (scheduling problem)

subjective.question: A teammate suggests backing up etcd by copying /var/lib/etcd with rsync every night instead of using 'etcdctl snapshot save'. Which is better, and why?
subjective.answer: etcdctl snapshot save is better. It takes a consistent point-in-time snapshot through the etcd API while etcd keeps serving. It also needs the endpoint and TLS certificates, which proves the backup came from a healthy member. With 'etcdutl snapshot status' you can check its hash, revision and size, and the file restores cleanly with 'etcdutl snapshot restore'. Copying the live data directory while etcd writes to it can capture a half-written database and WAL that do not match, and you only find out at restore time. It also copies the member identity and cluster ID, which causes trouble when restoring to a new or multi-member cluster. A file-level copy is safe only when etcd is stopped. That means downtime, and it is still awkward to restore. In practice I schedule snapshot save with a timestamped filename, copy the file off the node, protect it because it contains Secrets, and test a restore regularly.
keyPoints: A snapshot is consistent and taken online
A live file copy can be corrupt or inconsistent
Verify snapshots with 'etcdutl snapshot status'
Store backups off the node and protect them, since they contain Secrets
Test restores regularly

steps.overview: This step teaches you to define cloud infrastructure as versioned code with Terraform, from providers and resources through to remote state, modules and drift handling. These topics are the core of the HashiCorp Terraform Associate exam. They also appear in the IaC sections of DOP-C02 and AZ-400, and in almost every DevOps interview.
objectives: Write Terraform configurations using providers, resources, variables, outputs and data sources.
Configure a remote backend with state locking and explain why shared state matters.
Build and call reusable modules, and separate environments using workspaces or directories.
Run the init, plan, apply and destroy lifecycle, and interpret plan output and exit codes.
Import existing resources and detect, then fix, configuration drift.

concepts.explanation: A provider is a plugin that translates HCL into API calls for a platform such as AWS, Azure, Kubernetes or GitHub. You declare it in a required_providers block with a source like hashicorp/aws and a version constraint. terraform init downloads it and records the exact version and hashes in .terraform.lock.hcl. You should commit this lock file to Git.

A resource block creates and manages an object, and Terraform owns its full lifecycle. A data block only reads an existing object, such as an AMI or an existing VPC, and never changes it. You reference them as aws_vpc.main.id and data.aws_ami.ubuntu.id.

Input variables parameterise a module and can carry a type, a default, validation rules and sensitive = true. Locals are named expressions used only inside a module, to avoid repetition. Outputs expose values to the caller or the CLI. In a root module, outputs can also be read from another configuration through terraform_remote_state.

State maps your configuration to real-world object IDs. It also stores metadata and dependencies. By default it lives locally in terraform.tfstate. State can contain secrets in plain text, even for values marked sensitive. Protect it with access control and encryption, and never commit it to Git.

A backend decides where state is stored, for example S3, azurerm, gcs or HCP Terraform. Remote backends let a team share one source of truth. Locking stops two applies from corrupting state at the same time. If a crash leaves a stale lock, you can clear it with terraform force-unlock LOCK_ID, but use this only with care.

Any directory of .tf files is a module. The directory where you run Terraform is the root module. You call child modules with a module block and a source, which can be a local path, a Git URL or a registry address with a version. Good modules take inputs, expose outputs and hide internal details. Run terraform init again after you add or change a module source.

CLI workspaces give separate state files for the same configuration. Every configuration starts with a workspace named default. Inside the code, terraform.workspace returns the current workspace name. For strongly isolated prod and dev environments, many teams prefer separate directories or separate backends per environment, because workspaces share the same code and the same backend credentials.

Drift happens when real infrastructure no longer matches state, for example after a manual console change. terraform plan -refresh-only shows drift without proposing changes to infrastructure. An import block (Terraform 1.5 and later) or terraform import brings existing objects under management. A moved block lets you rename or refactor resources without destroying them.

keyFacts: Core workflow: write, then terraform init, then plan, then apply. terraform destroy is an alias for terraform apply -destroy.

Variable precedence, from lowest to highest: default value, TF_VAR_name environment variables, terraform.tfvars, terraform.tfvars.json, *.auto.tfvars (in lexical order), then -var and -var-file on the command line. The last value set wins.
terraform plan -detailed-exitcode returns 0 for no changes, 1 for an error and 2 when changes are present. This is useful in CI drift checks.
Version constraint ~> 5.0 allows any 5.x release but not 6.0. Pin providers in required_providers, and pin Terraform itself with required_version.
S3 backend: from Terraform 1.10, use_lockfile = true gives native S3 locking. DynamoDB-based locking is deprecated.
terraform taint is deprecated. Use terraform apply -replace=ADDRESS to force one resource to be recreated.
terraform fmt formats code and terraform validate checks syntax and internal consistency. Neither command contacts the real infrastructure APIs.
count creates instances indexed by number. for_each creates instances keyed by map or set keys. Prefer for_each when removing one item should not shift the others.
Backend blocks cannot use variables. Use partial configuration with terraform init -backend-config=FILE. Changing the backend requires terraform init -migrate-state.
terraform state list, state show, state mv and state rm inspect or edit state. A removed block (1.7 and later) stops managing a resource without destroying it.

example.caption: Root module: remote state in S3 with native locking, calling network, container service and database modules

pitfalls: Committing terraform.tfstate or .tfvars files that hold secrets to Git. Add both to .gitignore, and keep .terraform.lock.hcl in Git.
Believing sensitive = true encrypts a value. It only hides the value in CLI output. The value is still plain text in state.
Using count over a list and then removing a middle item. The indexes shift and Terraform destroys and recreates resources. Use for_each with stable keys instead.
Fixing drift by hand in the console. Instead, change the code, or accept the real-world change using -refresh-only and then update the code to match.
Exam trap: terraform init is needed again after adding a provider, adding a module or changing the backend. plan never changes real infrastructure.

Hardcoding values that change between environments, such as instance sizes or names. The checkpoint's clean destroy also fails if a database has deletion protection enabled or skip_final_snapshot = false.

workflow.title: Hands-on: modular stack with remote state, from build to clean destroy

steps.label: Bootstrap state bucket
steps.detail: Create a versioned, encrypted S3 bucket once, outside this stack, to hold remote state.

steps.label: Write reusable modules
steps.detail: Build network, ecs-service and rds modules, each with typed variables and clear outputs.

steps.label: Wire root and backend
steps.detail: Call the modules from the root, pass outputs between them, and configure the S3 backend with use_lockfile.

steps.label: Init, format, validate
steps.detail: Run terraform init, then terraform fmt -recursive, then terraform validate before planning.

steps.label: Plan and apply
steps.detail: Save a plan with terraform plan -out=tfplan, review it, then run terraform apply tfplan.

steps.label: Verify zero drift
steps.detail: Run terraform plan -detailed-exitcode and confirm exit code 0, which means no changes.

steps.label: Destroy in one command
steps.detail: Run terraform destroy and confirm that every resource in the state is removed.

project.title: terraform-ecs-rds-stack
project.summary: A Terraform project that builds a VPC, an ECS Fargate service running nginx and a PostgreSQL RDS database on AWS, using three reusable local modules, S3 remote state with native lockfile locking, and workspaces for dev/prod. versions.tf shows the provider and remote backend, main.tf shows variables, locals, a data source, module calls, a moved block, an import example and outputs, and the three module files show resources wired together through module inputs and outputs.
project.run:
aws s3api create-bucket --bucket mc-tfstate-CHANGE-ME --region ap-south-1 --create-bucket-configuration LocationConstraint=ap-south-1
aws s3api put-bucket-versioning --bucket mc-tfstate-CHANGE-ME --versioning-configuration Status=Enabled
terraform init
terraform workspace new dev
terraform fmt -check -recursive && terraform validate
terraform plan -out=tfplan
terraform apply tfplan
terraform plan -detailed-exitcode
terraform destroy -auto-approve

files.code:
# terraform-ecs-rds-stack

Week 10 hands-on: network + container service + database, built from reusable modules with remote state.

## Layout
- `versions.tf` - Terraform/provider versions, S3 backend, AWS provider.
- `main.tf` - root module: variables, locals, data source, module calls, moved/import, outputs.
- `modules/network` - VPC, public subnets (app), private subnets (database).
- `modules/app` - ECS Fargate cluster, task definition, service, security group.
- `modules/db` - RDS PostgreSQL in private subnets, reachable only from the app.

## Before you start
1. Terraform 1.10 or later (needed for `use_lockfile`). AWS CLI logged in.
2. Create a versioned S3 bucket for state. Put its name in `versions.tf`.
   Backend blocks cannot read variables; you can also pass `-backend-config="bucket=..."` to `terraform init`.

## Environments
- `terraform workspace new dev` / `terraform workspace new prod`.
- Each workspace has its own state file under `env:/<workspace>/` in the bucket.
- `local.env` picks CIDR and DB size from `var.env_settings`.

## Checkpoint
- After `terraform apply`, run `terraform plan -detailed-exitcode`.
  Exit code 0 = no changes. Exit code 2 = drift or config change.
- Tear down everything: `terraform destroy -auto-approve`.
  (`skip_final_snapshot = true` lets RDS delete in one command.)

## Try drift
Change a tag on the VPC in the AWS console, then run `terraform plan`.
Terraform shows the difference; `apply` puts it back. Use `terraform plan -refresh-only` to only inspect drift.

## Exam notes
- State holds real IDs and can hold secrets: keep it remote, encrypted, locked.
- `moved` renames an address without destroying the object.
- `import` blocks bring existing objects under management; `-generate-config-out` can write the HCL.

revision.examFocus: This step maps to almost every objective of the current Terraform Associate exam: IaC concepts, the core workflow, providers, state and backends, modules, variables and outputs, and drift. The exam uses short multiple-choice and true/false items that test which command, block or file fits a situation. The same ideas appear in AWS DOP-C02 (SDLC automation and configuration management/IaC) and in AZ-400 (infrastructure as code in pipelines), where you must pick safe state handling, environment separation and drift detection in CI.

compare.difference: count addresses instances by position (resource[0]), so removing a middle item shifts every later index. for_each addresses instances by stable key (resource["web"]), so only the removed key is affected.
compare.chooseA: Pick count for N identical copies or an on/off toggle such as count = var.enabled ? 1 : 0.
compare.chooseB: Pick for_each when each instance has its own identity, such as subnets per AZ or users by name, and items may be added or removed later.

compare.difference: A resource is created, updated and destroyed by Terraform and lives in state as managed. A data source only reads something that already exists, such as an AMI, a VPC built by another team or a secret, and Terraform never changes it.
compare.chooseA: Pick resource when Terraform must own the lifecycle of the object.
compare.chooseB: Pick data when the question says 'look up', 'existing', 'managed by another team' or 'latest image'.

compare.b: Separate directories or root modules with separate backends
compare.difference: Workspaces share one configuration and one backend, with a separate state per workspace. Separate directories give separate code, credentials and backends, which gives stronger isolation.
compare.chooseA: Pick workspaces for short-lived or near-identical copies, such as feature-branch test stacks, using terraform.workspace in names.
compare.chooseB: Pick separate directories or backends when environments such as prod and dev need different accounts, access controls or real isolation.

compare.difference: Import brings an object Terraform does not yet manage into state. -refresh-only updates state for objects already managed, so it records drift without changing infrastructure.
compare.chooseA: Pick import when a resource was created by hand or by another tool and must now be managed by Terraform.
compare.chooseB: Pick -refresh-only when a managed resource was changed outside Terraform and you want to accept that change into state.

compare.b: removed block or terraform state rm
compare.difference: moved renames or relocates an address, for example into a module or from count to for_each, and keeps the same real object. removed and state rm make Terraform forget the object, while the real object keeps running.
compare.chooseA: Pick moved when refactoring code and the plan would otherwise show destroy and create.
compare.chooseB: Pick removed (declarative, reviewable in a PR) or state rm (imperative) when the resource should stop being managed by this configuration.

cues.cue: resource was changed manually in the console; detect it in CI
cues.pick: terraform plan -detailed-exitcode in a scheduled pipeline (exit code 2 means drift)
cues.why: It fails the job only when real infrastructure differs from code, and it never changes anything.

cues.cue: two engineers ran apply at the same time and state got corrupted
cues.pick: Remote backend with state locking (S3 with use_lockfile = true, or HCP Terraform)
cues.why: Locking lets only one write operation hold the state at a time.

cues.cue: rename or move a resource into a module without downtime
cues.pick: moved block
cues.why: It maps the old address to the new one, so the plan shows a move instead of destroy and create.

cues.cue: use an existing VPC or the latest AMI
cues.pick: data source
cues.why: Data sources read existing objects without taking ownership of them.

cues.cue: value must not appear in plan output
cues.pick: sensitive = true on the variable or output, plus an encrypted backend with restricted access for the state
cues.why: sensitive only masks CLI output; protecting the stored value needs backend encryption and IAM.

cues.cue: recreate one broken instance only
cues.pick: terraform apply -replace=ADDRESS
cues.why: It is the supported replacement for the deprecated taint command and is scoped to one address.

cues.cue: same module, different sizes per environment
cues.pick: Input variables with a per-environment .tfvars file passed using -var-file
cues.why: Command-line var files have the highest precedence and keep the code identical across environments.

cues.cue: check code in a pre-commit hook without cloud credentials
cues.pick: terraform fmt -check and terraform validate
cues.why: Neither contacts provider APIs. validate still needs init, but init -backend=false is enough.

scenario.situation: Your team manages three application servers with aws_instance.app using count over a list of names. You are now moving them into a reusable module and switching to for_each keyed by name. A test plan shows all three instances will be destroyed and recreated, and production cannot accept downtime. What is the best way to complete the refactor?
reasoning: The goal is to change addresses in code, not the real servers, so any option that destroys and recreates is wrong.
terraform apply -replace and -refresh-only do not help. The first forces recreation, and the second only syncs attributes, not addresses.
terraform state rm followed by import would work but is manual, error-prone and not reviewable. It is a fallback, not the best answer.
moved blocks such as from = aws_instance.app[0] and to = module.app.aws_instance.this["web1"] declare each address change in code and go through normal plan review.
Run plan and confirm it shows only moves with 0 to add and 0 to destroy, then apply.
scenario.answer: Add a moved block for each instance, mapping the old count index to the new module for_each key, and confirm plan shows no create or destroy before applying. This is declarative, reviewable and keeps the real servers untouched.

memoryAids: Workflow 'I-P-A-D': Init (download providers, modules and backend), Plan (preview, safe), Apply (change), Destroy (apply -destroy). Run init again after any change to providers, modules or backend.
Variable precedence 'D-E-F-A-C' (Default, Env TF_VAR, Files tfvars, Auto tfvars, Command line): the closer the value is to your keyboard, the stronger it wins.
State fixes by intent: Rename = moved, Forget = removed, Adopt = import, Accept drift = refresh-only, Rebuild = -replace.
cheatSheet: plan is always safe. It reads real infrastructure but never changes it. Only apply or destroy change things.
Data sources are read during plan. A resource is created only during apply.
Remote backend = shared state + locking + encryption at rest. Local state suits a single learner only.
Backend blocks cannot use variables. Use -backend-config for values, and init -migrate-state to move existing state.
Registry modules should be pinned with the version argument. Local path modules have no version argument.
Outputs in a child module are the only way the parent can read its values: module.NAME.OUTPUT.
terraform.workspace returns the current workspace name. The default workspace is always called 'default' and cannot be deleted.
HCP Terraform workspaces are not the same as CLI workspaces. Each one has its own variables, runs and state.
lifecycle options: prevent_destroy blocks destroy, create_before_destroy avoids gaps, and ignore_changes tolerates expected drift such as autoscaling counts.
Import block plus terraform plan -generate-config-out=FILE drafts HCL for imported resources. Review it before apply.
Commit .terraform.lock.hcl. Ignore .terraform/, *.tfstate* and secret .tfvars files.
For a one-command destroy, turn deletion protection off and set skip_final_snapshot = true (or provide a final snapshot name) on databases before running destroy.
selfCheck: I can explain, without notes, which commands need terraform init again, and why plan never changes real infrastructure.
I can choose between count and for_each, and convert one to the other using moved blocks without recreating resources.
I can set up an S3 remote backend with native locking using partial configuration, and migrate local state into it.
I can pick the right tool for import, moved, removed, -refresh-only and -replace from a one-line scenario.
I can build network, container service and database modules, apply them, get a plan with no changes, and destroy everything in one command.
I can wire terraform plan -detailed-exitcode into a CI job that flags drift on exit code 2.

objective.question: A team sets a variable 'instance_type' in four places: a default of t3.micro in variables.tf, TF_VAR_instance_type=t3.small in the shell, terraform.tfvars with t3.medium, and prod.auto.tfvars with t3.large. They run 'terraform apply' with no -var or -var-file flags. Which value is used?
options: t3.small
t3.large
t3.medium
t3.micro
objective.explanation: *.auto.tfvars files load after terraform.tfvars, which loads after environment variables, which override the default, so t3.large wins. Only -var or -var-file on the command line would override it.

objective.question: A nightly CI job runs 'terraform plan -detailed-exitcode' against production to detect drift. The job exits with code 2. What does this mean?
options: The plan succeeded and changes are present
The state is locked by another run
The plan succeeded with no changes
The plan failed because of a syntax or provider error
objective.explanation: With -detailed-exitcode, 0 means no changes, 1 means an error and 2 means a successful plan with changes present. A locked state shows up as an error (exit code 1), not as code 2.

objective.question: In required_providers, the AWS provider is pinned with version = "~> 5.0". Which releases does this constraint allow?
options: Any 5.x release, but not 6.0
Exactly version 5.0.0
Any release 5.0 or higher, including 6.x
Only 5.0.x patch releases
objective.explanation: The pessimistic operator ~> allows only the rightmost given component to increase. ~> 5.0 allows 5.1, 5.90 and so on, but not 6.0; ~> 5.0.0 would restrict it to 5.0.x patches.

objective.question: An EC2 instance managed by Terraform is in a bad state and must be destroyed and recreated on the next apply. Its configuration is unchanged. What is the recommended approach?
options: terraform apply -replace=aws_instance.web
terraform state rm aws_instance.web, then terraform apply
terraform refresh, then terraform apply
terraform taint aws_instance.web, then terraform apply
objective.explanation: terraform taint is deprecated, and -replace shows the replacement in the plan for review. state rm only makes Terraform forget the resource, so the old instance keeps running while a duplicate is created.

objective.question: You create three subnets from the list ["a", "b", "c"] using count. Later you remove "a" from the list. What happens on the next plan, and what would avoid it?
options: Terraform errors because count lists cannot shrink; use depends_on to fix it
Nothing changes until terraform import is run; use a moved block to avoid it
Subnets at index 0 and 1 are changed or replaced and index 2 is destroyed; using for_each over a set avoids this
Only subnet a is destroyed; count already tracks items by value
objective.explanation: count keys instances by number, so removing the first item shifts every later item to a new index. for_each keys instances by map or set keys, so removing "a" destroys only that instance.

objective.question: An engineer writes bucket = var.state_bucket inside a backend "s3" block so that each environment can use a different bucket. 'terraform init' fails. What is the correct fix?
options: Set TF_VAR_state_bucket before running init
Wrap the backend block in a module and pass the bucket as an input
Remove the bucket argument and supply it with terraform init -backend-config=FILE (partial configuration)
Use a local value instead of a variable in the backend block
objective.explanation: Backend blocks cannot use variables or locals because the backend is set up before any variables are evaluated. Partial configuration through -backend-config is the supported way to vary backend settings.

objective.question: A team on Terraform 1.10 or later stores state in Amazon S3. They want state locking with the fewest extra resources and no deprecated features. What should they configure?
options: use_lockfile = true in the S3 backend block
S3 Object Lock in compliance mode on the bucket
Nothing, because S3 versioning provides locking automatically
A DynamoDB table set through the dynamodb_table argument
objective.explanation: From Terraform 1.10, use_lockfile = true gives native S3 locking with a lock file in the bucket, and DynamoDB-based locking is deprecated. Bucket versioning and Object Lock protect object history, but they do not provide Terraform state locking.

objective.question: A pull-request pipeline must check that Terraform code is formatted and internally consistent. The runner has no cloud credentials. Which pair of commands fits this requirement?
options: terraform refresh and terraform validate
terraform fmt -check and terraform plan -refresh=false
terraform fmt -check and terraform validate
terraform plan and terraform show
objective.explanation: terraform fmt and terraform validate do not contact real infrastructure APIs, so they run safely without credentials. validate does need providers installed first, for example with terraform init -backend=false. plan and refresh need provider credentials, and refresh also needs access to state.

objective.question: The networking team manages a shared VPC in its own Terraform project. Your project must place a database in that VPC without taking ownership of it. What should you use?
options: terraform import of the VPC into your state
A moved block pointing to the VPC
A data "aws_vpc" block that looks up the VPC by tag or ID
A resource "aws_vpc" block with the same CIDR
objective.explanation: A data source reads an existing object without managing it. Importing the VPC or declaring it as a resource would make two projects manage the same VPC, and Terraform could change or destroy it.

objective.question: You rename resource aws_db_instance.main to aws_db_instance.primary during a refactor into a module. You want the existing database kept, not destroyed and recreated. What is the cleanest declarative way to do this?
options: Run terraform apply -replace=aws_db_instance.main
Add lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true } and apply
Add a removed block for aws_db_instance.main
Add a moved block with from = aws_db_instance.main and to = module.db.aws_db_instance.primary
objective.explanation: A moved block records the address change in code, so the plan shows a move and no destroy. A removed block stops managing the resource, -replace forces recreation, and prevent_destroy only makes the plan fail without updating the address.

objective.question: Your root module deploys most resources in ap-south-1. A child module must create an ACM certificate in us-east-1 for CloudFront. Given the provider blocks below, how should the module block pass the correct provider?
options: provider = aws.use1
alias = "use1"
region = "us-east-1"
providers = { aws = aws.use1 }
objective.explanation: A module block uses the providers map to give the child module an aliased provider configuration. The singular provider meta-argument works on resource and data blocks, not on module blocks. alias and region are not module meta-arguments, so they would only work if the module declared matching input variables.

objective.question: An Auto Scaling group is managed by Terraform. Scaling policies change its desired capacity during the day, so every terraform plan proposes resetting desired_capacity to 2. The team wants Terraform to set the initial value and then leave it alone. What should they add to the aws_autoscaling_group resource?
options: lifecycle { ignore_changes = [desired_capacity] }
depends_on = [aws_autoscaling_policy.scale_out]
lifecycle { create_before_destroy = true }
lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }
objective.explanation: ignore_changes tells Terraform to use the argument when it creates the resource, but to ignore later differences between the configuration and the real value. prevent_destroy only blocks deletion. create_before_destroy changes the order of replacement. depends_on changes ordering and does not suppress the diff.

objective.question: Two engineers and a CI runner get different AWS provider patch versions from the same constraint, version = "~> 5.40". Which statement about the .terraform.lock.hcl file is correct?
options: It records the selected provider versions and their checksums. Commit it to version control, and use terraform init -upgrade to move to newer versions within the constraint.
It is created only by remote backends and has no effect with local state.
It records the module versions downloaded from the registry, so it should be in .gitignore.
It holds the state lock and must be deleted if a run crashes.
objective.explanation: The dependency lock file pins the exact provider versions and hashes that terraform init selected. Committing it gives every machine the same versions, and init -upgrade updates it deliberately. It is not the state lock, it does not track module versions, and it works with any backend.

objective.question: A module exposes the database password as shown. Which statement is true?
options: The value is hidden as (sensitive value) in plan and apply output, but it is still stored in plain text in state and can be read with terraform output -raw db_password.
Terraform will refuse to apply because outputs cannot reference random_password.
The value is never written to state, so it cannot be read by other configurations.
The value is encrypted inside the state file by Terraform itself.
objective.explanation: sensitive = true only redacts the value in CLI output. State still holds it in plain text, so you must protect the backend with encryption and access control. Terraform does not encrypt state itself, and random_password results can be output.

objective.question: Someone resized an RDS instance in the console, and the team has decided to keep the new size. Before they edit the code, they want to review the real-world changes and record them in state, without changing any infrastructure. What should they run?
options: terraform apply -replace=aws_db_instance.main
terraform state rm aws_db_instance.main
terraform plan -refresh=false
terraform apply -refresh-only
objective.explanation: apply -refresh-only shows the drift and, after you approve it, updates state to match reality without changing any infrastructure. You then update the code so later plans are clean. plan -refresh=false skips drift detection. -replace would rebuild the database. state rm would stop Terraform from managing the database.

objective.question: You run terraform destroy for the checkpoint and get the error below. What is the correct way to destroy the whole stack?

code.code:
Error: Instance cannot be destroyed

  on modules/db/main.tf line 1:
   1: resource "aws_db_instance" "this" {

Resource module.db.aws_db_instance.this has lifecycle.prevent_destroy
set, but the plan calls for this resource to be destroyed.

options: Remove prevent_destroy (or set it to false) in the module code, then run terraform destroy.
Set deletion_protection = false on the instance; this overrides prevent_destroy.
Run terraform state rm module.db.aws_db_instance.this and then run destroy again.
Run terraform destroy -force.
objective.explanation: prevent_destroy is read from the configuration and cannot be overridden by a CLI flag, so you must change the code and then destroy. state rm would leave a running, unmanaged database. deletion_protection is a separate RDS API setting and does not affect Terraform's lifecycle check.

objective.question: The first apply of this configuration in a new account fails with an 'Invalid for_each argument' error saying the set includes values that cannot be determined until apply. What is the cause and the best fix?
options: The splat [*] does not work on resources. Replace it with values(aws_subnet.private) and keep toset().
Terraform cannot order the two resources. Add depends_on = [aws_subnet.private] to the association.
for_each only accepts maps, never sets. Wrap the expression in tomap() instead of toset().
The subnet IDs are unknown at plan time, so they cannot be for_each keys. Use for_each = aws_subnet.private and set subnet_id = each.value.id.
objective.explanation: for_each keys must be known during plan. Subnet IDs only exist after apply. Iterating over the subnet resource itself reuses its static keys (the AZ names), and the IDs can be unknown values. depends_on does not make values known. for_each accepts sets of strings, so tomap() is not the issue.

objective.question: terraform init fails on this module block. What is the correct fix?
options: Remove the version argument and pin the Git tag in the source: source = "git::https://github.com/acme/tf-ecs-service.git?ref=v1.4.0".
Add the module to required_providers with the same version.
Change version to a constraint such as "~> 1.4", because exact versions are not allowed.
Run terraform init -upgrade so Terraform can resolve the version from Git tags.
objective.explanation: The version argument only works for modules from a module registry. For Git sources, you pin a tag, branch or commit with ?ref=. -upgrade and constraint syntax do not help, and required_providers is only for providers.

objective.question: var.db_password is declared with sensitive = true. terraform plan fails on this output with 'Output refers to sensitive values'. A consumer module needs this value. What is the right fix?
options: Add sensitive = true to the output block.
Nothing in the code. Run terraform apply -auto-approve, which skips this check.
Move the string into a local, because locals remove the sensitive marking.
Wrap the value in nonsensitive() so the output works like any other output.
objective.explanation: Terraform makes you mark an output as sensitive when its value comes from a sensitive value. The value can then still be passed to other modules, but it is hidden in CLI output. nonsensitive() would print the password. Locals keep the sensitive marking, and no apply flag skips this check.

objective.question: You want to bring a manually created S3 bucket under Terraform using config-driven import (Terraform 1.5 or later). Which order of steps is correct?
options: Write an import block with to and id → run terraform plan -generate-config-out=generated.tf → review and tidy the generated code → run plan again until it shows only the import and no changes → terraform apply.
Run terraform plan -generate-config-out=generated.tf with no import block → terraform apply → add an import block to record the ID.
Write the full resource block by hand → run terraform import → add an import block → terraform apply.
Run terraform apply → write an import block → run terraform plan -generate-config-out=generated.tf → review the generated code.
objective.explanation: The import block tells Terraform which address and real ID to link. -generate-config-out writes draft configuration for that block. You clean the draft until the plan shows only the import and no changes, and then apply. Config generation needs an import block, and the import only reaches state during apply.

objective.question: The backend is configured as shown. An engineer runs terraform workspace new staging and then terraform apply. Where is the staging state stored?
options: s3://acme-tf-state/staging/app/terraform.tfstate
In a local terraform.tfstate.d/staging folder, because workspaces are always local
s3://acme-tf-state/env:/staging/app/terraform.tfstate
s3://acme-tf-state/app/terraform.tfstate, shared with the default workspace
objective.explanation: The S3 backend stores state for non-default workspaces under workspace_key_prefix, which defaults to env:. The path is therefore env:/<workspace>/<key>. Only the default workspace uses the key on its own. terraform.tfstate.d is used only by the local backend.

objective.question: terraform plan fails with 'Module is incompatible with count, for_each, and depends_on'. What is the cause?
options: The child module has its own provider block. Remove it, define an aliased us-east-1 provider in the root, and pass it with providers = { aws = aws.use1 }.
var.domains must be a map, because modules only accept maps in for_each.
The module needs a required_providers block with configuration_aliases before it can use any region.
ACM certificates cannot be created with for_each. Use count instead.
objective.explanation: A module that contains its own provider configuration is treated as a legacy module. It cannot be used with count, for_each or depends_on. Provider configuration belongs in the root module and is passed down. Sets of strings are valid for_each values, and count would fail the same way.

objective.question: A nightly drift job runs the command below. Someone opened port 22 on a security group in the console, yet the job keeps exiting with code 0. Why?

code.code: terraform plan -refresh=false -detailed-exitcode -input=false

options: -refresh=false makes Terraform compare the code with the stored state only. It never reads the real infrastructure, so it cannot see drift.
-input=false suppresses the diff, so the exit code is always 0.
Security group rules added in the console can never be detected by Terraform.
-detailed-exitcode returns 0 for drift and 2 only for configuration changes.
objective.explanation: Drift detection depends on the refresh step, which reads the real resources. With -refresh=false, the plan only compares configuration with state, which still matches. Exit code 2 means changes are present, whatever their source. -input=false only disables interactive prompts.

objective.question: What is wrong with this resource block?
options: Nothing. count limits how many for_each items are created.
each.key is not available in for_each over a set. Use each.index.
ECR repositories do not support meta-arguments.
count and for_each cannot both be set in one block. Keep for_each and remove count.
objective.explanation: A resource can use count or for_each, but not both. Terraform returns an invalid combination error. With a set, each.key and each.value are both the element, and each.index does not exist.

objective.question: In a brand-new account, terraform plan fails with 'no matching EC2 VPC found' on this configuration. What is the cause and the fix?
options: The data source has no dependency on aws_vpc.main, so it is read during plan, before the VPC exists. Reference aws_vpc.main.id directly and remove the data source.
Terraform reads all data sources after creating resources. The error comes from a missing IAM permission.
Data sources cannot filter on tags. Use the id argument instead.
The AWS provider caches VPC lookups. Run terraform init -upgrade.
objective.explanation: Terraform reads a data source during plan when all its arguments are known. Nothing links this data source to the VPC, so the lookup runs while no VPC exists. A resource that is managed in the same configuration should be referenced directly. Data sources are for objects owned elsewhere.

objective.question: Security requires that the RDS master password never appears in Terraform state or variables, and that it can be rotated without a code change. Which approach meets both requirements?
options: Put it in prod.tfvars and encrypt the state bucket with SSE-KMS.
Pass it through TF_VAR_db_password from the CI secret store.
Set manage_master_user_password = true on aws_db_instance, so RDS creates the password in AWS Secrets Manager and manages it there.
Generate it with random_password and mark the output sensitive = true.
objective.explanation: With manage_master_user_password, RDS generates and stores the password in Secrets Manager and can rotate it, so Terraform never handles the value. random_password and TF_VAR values still end up in state as plain text. Encrypting the bucket protects the state at rest, but the secret is still in state and in a tfvars file.

objective.question: A pull request job runs terraform plan -out=tfplan and stores the plan file as an artifact. Two days after merge, the deploy job runs terraform apply tfplan and fails with 'Saved plan is stale'. What is the most likely cause and the correct response?
options: Another apply changed the state after the plan was created. Run a fresh plan, review it, and apply the new plan.
The provider lock file changed. Delete .terraform.lock.hcl and apply again.
The artifact was corrupted. Run terraform apply -refresh-only tfplan.
Plan files expire after 24 hours. Raise the expiry with -lock-timeout.
objective.explanation: A saved plan is tied to the state it was built from. If any apply changes that state, Terraform refuses to apply the old plan, which is a safety feature. Plans have no time-based expiry, -lock-timeout only controls waiting for a lock, and deleting the lock file removes your provider pins.

subjective.question: Walk through the core Terraform workflow. What does each step do, and why is terraform init needed?
subjective.answer: The workflow is write, init, plan, apply. First I write configuration in HCL, which declares providers, resources, data sources, variables and outputs. terraform init prepares the working directory. It downloads the providers that match my required_providers constraints, records their exact versions and checksums in .terraform.lock.hcl, installs modules and configures the backend where state is stored. Without init, Terraform has no providers and cannot reach state. terraform plan refreshes state against real infrastructure, compares it with the configuration and shows what it will create, change or destroy. I can save the plan with -out and review it. terraform apply carries out that plan. terraform destroy is an alias for terraform apply -destroy, which removes everything in the state. In CI, I run init, fmt -check, validate and plan on pull requests. Apply runs only after review.
keyPoints: Order: write, init, plan, apply
init installs providers and modules, configures the backend and writes the lock file
plan compares configuration with refreshed state and real infrastructure
destroy is an alias for apply -destroy

subjective.question: What is Terraform state, why should a team use a remote backend, and what problem does locking solve?
subjective.answer: State is Terraform's record that maps each resource address in the code to a real object ID, along with its attributes and dependencies. Terraform uses it to work out what to change. With local state, each engineer has a different copy, the file can be lost, and secrets sit on laptops. A remote backend such as S3, azurerm, GCS or HCP Terraform keeps one shared copy. It is usually encrypted and versioned, and access is controlled. Locking stops two runs from writing to the same state at the same time, which could corrupt it or cause conflicting changes. On S3 with Terraform 1.10 and later, I set use_lockfile = true for native locking, because DynamoDB locking is deprecated. If a crashed run leaves a stale lock, I use terraform force-unlock with the lock ID, but only after I confirm that no run is active.
keyPoints: State maps resource addresses to real object IDs and attributes
A remote backend gives one shared, durable, access-controlled copy
Locking prevents concurrent writes and state corruption
S3 native locking uses use_lockfile; DynamoDB locking is deprecated
force-unlock is used only for stale locks

subjective.question: For this week's task, how would you design reusable modules for a network, a container service and a database?
subjective.answer: I create three child modules: network, service and database. A root module per environment calls them. The network module takes inputs such as the CIDR block and availability zones. It outputs the VPC ID, the private and public subnet IDs, and perhaps a security group ID. The database module takes the VPC ID, the subnet IDs, the instance size and a secret reference. It outputs the endpoint and port, and I mark anything sensitive with sensitive = true. The service module takes the subnets, the container image, the desired count and the database endpoint, and it outputs the service URL. The root module wires outputs into inputs, so module.network.private_subnet_ids feeds the other two modules. Each module declares its own required_providers but no provider configuration. I pin module versions, for example with a Git ref or a registry version. Variables get types, descriptions and validation blocks. I use for_each for repeated items such as subnets, so removing one subnet does not shift the others.
keyPoints: Separate network, service and database modules, called by a root module per environment
Outputs of one module are wired into the inputs of another
Typed, validated variables; sensitive outputs marked
Pin module versions; child modules keep no provider configuration
for_each for stable repeated resources

subjective.question: Compare CLI workspaces with separate directories (or separate state files) for managing dev, staging and prod. Which would you choose and why?
subjective.answer: CLI workspaces let one configuration and one backend hold several state files. I switch between them with terraform workspace select, and the code can read terraform.workspace to change names or sizes. This works well for short-lived or near-identical copies, such as feature environments. Its weakness is that every environment shares the same code, backend and credentials. It is also easy to apply to prod while the wrong workspace is selected, and the code can fill up with workspace conditionals. For long-lived environments, I prefer a separate root directory per environment. Each one calls the same versioned modules and has its own tfvars, its own backend configuration (often passed with -backend-config) and its own credentials. Prod can then use an older module version than dev, access can be separated, and the risk of applying to the wrong environment is lower. Note that HCP Terraform workspaces are a different concept from CLI workspaces.
keyPoints: CLI workspaces give separate state with shared code and backend
terraform.workspace can parameterise names and sizes
Risks: the wrong workspace selected and shared credentials
Separate directories allow per-environment backends, credentials and module versions
HCP Terraform workspaces differ from CLI workspaces

subjective.question: What is drift, and how would you detect and handle it automatically in a pipeline?
subjective.answer: Drift is when real infrastructure no longer matches the state and configuration. A common cause is someone changing a security group in the console. During plan, Terraform refreshes state and shows the difference. To detect drift automatically, I schedule a CI job that runs terraform init and then terraform plan -detailed-exitcode -lock=false with read-only credentials. Exit code 0 means no drift, 2 means changes are present, and 1 means an error. On code 2, the job alerts the team and attaches the plan output. There are two ways to handle it. If the manual change was wrong, I run apply to restore the code's version. If the change was right, I update the code so it matches reality. I can also use terraform plan -refresh-only, followed by apply -refresh-only, to accept attribute changes into state without changing the infrastructure. In the long term, I reduce drift by limiting console write access and sending all changes through pull requests.
keyPoints: Drift means reality differs from code or state
Scheduled plan with -detailed-exitcode; code 2 means changes present
Either revert by applying, or update the code to accept the change
-refresh-only updates state without changing infrastructure
Prevent drift by restricting manual changes

subjective.question: How do you bring an existing, manually created resource under Terraform management?
subjective.answer: There are two ways. The older way is the terraform import command, for example terraform import aws_s3_bucket.logs my-logs-bucket. It writes the object into state, but I must write the matching resource block myself first. The modern way, from Terraform 1.5, is a declarative import block in the configuration, with 'to' set to the resource address and 'id' set to the real object ID. Import blocks are reviewed in pull requests and show up in the plan. I can also run terraform plan -generate-config-out=generated.tf, which drafts the resource block for me. In both cases, I then run plan and adjust the code until plan shows no changes. That proves the code matches reality. I never import the same object into two states, because two projects would then manage it. After a successful apply, the import block can stay or be removed, because it has no further effect.
keyPoints: terraform import CLI writes to state; you write the resource block yourself
import block (1.5 and later) is declarative and reviewable in plan
-generate-config-out drafts the configuration
Iterate until plan shows no changes
Never import one object into two states

subjective.question: Explain moved, removed, terraform state mv and terraform state rm. When would you use each?
subjective.answer: All four change how state maps to code without touching the real infrastructure. A moved block, from Terraform 1.1, declares that an address has changed. An example is renaming a resource or moving it into a module. It is reviewed in code and applied through plan, so it is safe for every teammate and every environment. terraform state mv does the same thing imperatively from the command line. It is useful for one-off fixes, but it leaves no record in code and you must repeat it in each environment. A removed block, from 1.7, tells Terraform to stop managing a resource. With lifecycle destroy = false, the real object stays. A typical use is handing a resource to another project. terraform state rm is the imperative equivalent. I prefer the declarative blocks in team repositories. I run terraform state list and state show first, to confirm the exact addresses.
keyPoints: moved renames an address declaratively; state mv does it imperatively
removed (1.7 and later) stops managing a resource without destroying it; state rm is imperative
Declarative blocks are reviewable and repeatable across environments
Inspect addresses first with state list and state show

subjective.question: How do you handle secrets such as a database password in Terraform?
subjective.answer: First, I never hard-code secrets in .tf or committed tfvars files. I pass them at run time through TF_VAR_ environment variables injected by CI, or I read them from a secrets manager with a data source. Even better, I let the service generate and store the password itself, for example the managed master-password option on RDS, so Terraform never handles it. I mark variables and outputs as sensitive = true. That hides them in plan and apply output only. They are still stored in plain text in state. So the state backend must be encrypted, versioned and tightly access-controlled, and state files must never go into Git. Newer Terraform versions also offer ephemeral values and write-only arguments, which keep some values out of state entirely. I use them where the provider supports them.
keyPoints: No secrets in code or committed tfvars
Inject through CI environment variables or a secrets manager; prefer service-managed secrets
sensitive = true only hides output; values are still in state
Encrypt and restrict the state backend; never commit state
Ephemeral values and write-only arguments avoid storing some values in state

subjective.question: The checkpoint requires that terraform plan shows no changes right after a clean apply. If it shows changes, what are the likely causes and fixes?
subjective.answer: A non-empty plan straight after an apply is called a perpetual diff. Common causes are these. First, the provider normalises a value: JSON policies with a different key order or whitespace, uppercase versus lowercase, or a default the API fills in. The fix is to write the normalised form, for example with jsonencode, or to use the provider's recommended pattern. Second, a value is computed at apply time, such as timestamp() or uuid(), and it changes on every run. I remove it or use a stable resource instead. Third, another system changes the resource, such as an autoscaler changing desired_count. I add lifecycle ignore_changes for that attribute. Fourth, two resources manage the same setting, for example inline rules alongside separate rule resources. I keep only one. I also check that no for_each or count key depends on unknown values. A clean plan proves the code is idempotent. Then terraform destroy removes the whole stack in one command.
keyPoints: A perpetual diff is a non-empty plan after apply
Provider normalisation: JSON order, case, API defaults
Volatile functions like timestamp() and uuid()
External changes: use ignore_changes deliberately
Overlapping resource definitions; prove idempotency before destroy

subjective.question: How do you pin Terraform and provider versions, and how do you move existing local state to an S3 backend?
subjective.answer: In the terraform block, I set required_version, for example ">= 1.10, < 2.0", to pin Terraform itself. I set required_providers with a source and a constraint, such as hashicorp/aws with "~> 5.0". That constraint allows any 5.x release but not 6.0. terraform init writes the exact versions and checksums to .terraform.lock.hcl. I commit that file, so CI and teammates get identical providers. I upgrade deliberately with terraform init -upgrade. To migrate state, I first create the bucket with versioning and encryption turned on. Then I add a backend "s3" block with use_lockfile = true. Because backend blocks cannot use variables, I supply the environment-specific values through terraform init -backend-config=prod.s3.tfbackend. Next, I run terraform init -migrate-state and confirm the copy. Finally, I check with terraform state list and a plan that shows no changes, and only then delete the local state file.
keyPoints: required_version pins Terraform; required_providers pins providers
~> 5.0 allows 5.x but not 6.0
Commit .terraform.lock.hcl; upgrade with init -upgrade
Partial backend configuration with -backend-config
init -migrate-state, then verify with state list and a plan that shows no changes

subjective.question: A CI job was killed partway through terraform apply. Every run since then fails with 'Error acquiring the state lock'. How do you recover safely?

code.code:
Error: Error acquiring the state lock
Lock Info:
  ID:        3f2a9c1e-...
  Path:      tf-state-prod/network/terraform.tfstate
  Operation: OperationTypeApply
  Who:       runner@ci-42
  Created:   2026-02-10 09:14:03 UTC

subjective.answer: First, confirm that no apply is still running. Check the CI system for job ci-42 and make sure the process is really gone. Unlocking while an apply is live can corrupt state. Once you are sure it is dead, run terraform force-unlock with the lock ID from the error, from the same directory and backend configuration. Next, check whether the interrupted apply created resources that never reached state. Run terraform plan and read it carefully. If it wants to create something that already exists, use an import block or terraform import instead of creating a duplicate. If state looks damaged, restore an earlier version from S3 versioning. To prevent a repeat, give CI jobs a graceful shutdown so Terraform can release the lock. Also use a concurrency group so only one apply runs per state.
keyPoints: Verify the holding process is really gone before unlocking
Use terraform force-unlock with the exact lock ID
Run plan afterwards to find partially created or orphaned resources
Use bucket versioning to restore damaged state
Prevent recurrence with pipeline concurrency control and graceful cancellation

subjective.question: Explain what this dynamic block produces. When is a dynamic block appropriate, and when is it overkill?
subjective.answer: The dynamic block creates one nested ingress block for each entry in the map. Here it produces two rules: one for port 80 described as 'http' and one for port 443 described as 'https'. Inside content, the iterator is named after the block, so ingress.key is the map key and ingress.value is the port. A dynamic block fits when the number of nested blocks comes from input, for example a module that accepts a list of rules from callers. It is overkill when the set is fixed and small. Writing out the blocks is easier to read, and HashiCorp advises against overusing dynamic blocks. For security groups specifically, separate aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule resources with for_each are often better. Each rule then becomes its own resource in state, which is easier to change, import or remove one at a time.
keyPoints: Generates one nested block per element of for_each
Iterator is named after the block: ingress.key and ingress.value
Suited to modules whose callers supply a variable number of nested blocks
Avoid for fixed, small sets because readability suffers
Separate rule resources with for_each give per-rule state addresses

subjective.question: How does Terraform decide the order in which it creates resources? When do you actually need depends_on?
subjective.answer: Terraform builds a dependency graph from references. If a subnet uses aws_vpc.main.id, Terraform knows the VPC must exist first. It creates independent resources in parallel, with a default parallelism of 10, and destroys them in reverse order. Most of the time these implicit dependencies are enough, and they are better because the dependency is visible in the data flow. You need depends_on only when a dependency exists but no attribute is referenced. One example is an EC2 instance whose startup script calls S3 and needs an IAM role policy to be attached first. Another is a module that must wait for another module's side effects. Use it sparingly. depends_on on a data source or module can delay reads until apply time. That makes plans show more 'known after apply' values and can cause unexpected diffs. Where you can, pass a real attribute instead.
keyPoints: The graph is built from attribute references (implicit dependencies)
Independent resources run in parallel; destroy happens in reverse order
depends_on is for hidden dependencies with no reference, such as IAM propagation
depends_on on data sources or modules defers reads and adds unknown values
Prefer passing real attributes over explicit depends_on

subjective.question: Your container service module is consumed by three teams. How would you version and publish it so a breaking change does not break their production stacks?
subjective.answer: I would keep the module in its own Git repository or publish it to a private registry, such as HCP Terraform's private registry, and release it with semantic version tags. Consumers pin a version. With a registry source they write version = "~> 2.1". With a Git source they use ?ref=v2.1.0, because Git sources do not support the version argument. Local paths like ./modules suit a single repository but give no versioning across teams. Breaking changes, such as a renamed variable or a changed resource address, get a major version bump and release notes. Inside the module I add moved blocks so internal refactors do not destroy resources when users upgrade. Each release is tested with an examples directory and the terraform test framework or a CI apply-and-destroy. Teams then upgrade on their own schedule, running plan in dev before prod, and run terraform init -upgrade to fetch the new version.
keyPoints: Separate repository or private registry with semantic version tags
Registry sources use the version argument; Git sources use ?ref=
Major version bump plus release notes for breaking changes
moved blocks inside the module to avoid destroy and recreate on upgrade
Test releases in CI; consumers upgrade per environment with init -upgrade

subjective.question: What does this configuration enforce, and at which point in the workflow does each check run?
subjective.answer: The validation block restricts environment to dev, staging or prod. Terraform checks it while it evaluates input variables, during plan or apply.
