Another option is to include a content hash in the ConfigMap name, which is what Kustomize's configMapGenerator does. I would not depend on manual kubectl rollout restart, because it is not recorded in Git and breaks the GitOps model.
keyPoints: Rollouts trigger only on pod template changes
envFrom values are read at container start
Add a checksum/config annotation using sha256sum
Alternative: hashed ConfigMap names
Avoid manual rollout restarts in GitOps

subjective.question: A CI job was killed in the middle of helm upgrade. Now every new upgrade fails with 'another operation (install/upgrade/rollback) is in progress'. How do you diagnose and recover safely?

code.code:
$ helm upgrade --install web ./web -n prod -f values-prod.yaml
Error: UPGRADE FAILED: another operation (install/upgrade/rollback) is in progress

subjective.answer: Helm keeps the release state in Secrets in the release namespace. The killed job left the latest revision with the status pending-upgrade, and Helm refuses to start a new operation. First I run helm history web -n prod to confirm that the last revision is pending-upgrade, and I make sure no other pipeline is really running. Then I check that the workloads match the last good revision. The usual recovery is helm rollback web <last-deployed-revision> -n prod. This creates a new revision with status deployed and clears the lock. After that, the normal upgrade works. Deleting the pending release Secret is a last resort and must be done carefully. To prevent a repeat, I run upgrades with --wait and a timeout, plus the auto-rollback-on-failure flag, and I stop parallel deploys to one release with CI concurrency controls. In a GitOps setup, letting Argo CD render the chart avoids this problem.
keyPoints: Release state is stored in namespace Secrets
Interrupted upgrade leaves pending-upgrade status
Check helm history and confirm no other job is running
Recover with helm rollback to the last deployed revision
Prevent with wait/timeout, auto-rollback and CI concurrency limits

subjective.question: Your Ansible playbook is a single 600-line file used by three teams. Explain how you would refactor it into roles. What goes in defaults versus vars, and why does it matter?
subjective.answer: I would split the playbook by responsibility into roles such as common, nginx and app. Each role follows the standard layout: tasks/main.yml, handlers/main.yml, templates/, files/, defaults/main.yml, vars/main.yml and meta/main.yml for dependencies. The top-level site.yml becomes short. It maps host groups to roles, and each team reuses the roles with its own inventory. The defaults versus vars choice matters for precedence. Role defaults have the lowest precedence of all, so they are the safe, overridable settings, such as nginx_port: 80. Teams override them in group_vars or host_vars. Role vars have high precedence and beat inventory variables, so I keep only internal constants there, such as OS package names. Putting tunables in vars is a common mistake, because inventory overrides then silently fail. I would version the roles, share them through a Git repo or a collection, and test each one with Molecule, including an idempotency check.
keyPoints: Standard role directory layout
site.yml maps groups to roles
defaults have the lowest precedence and are user-tunable
vars have high precedence and are for internal constants
Version, share and test roles with Molecule

subjective.question: You must patch and restart a service on 40 web servers behind a load balancer with Ansible, without an outage. If a bad change breaks hosts, the rollout must stop early. How would you write the play?

code.code:
- hosts: webservers
  become: true
  serial: "25%"
  max_fail_percentage: 10
  tasks:
    - name: Update app package
      ansible.builtin.package:
        name: myapp
        state: latest
      notify: restart myapp
  handlers:
    - name: restart myapp
      ansible.builtin.service:
        name: myapp
        state: restarted

subjective.answer: By default, Ansible runs each task across all hosts at once, so restarting 40 servers together causes an outage. serial makes it a rolling update. With 25%, Ansible runs the whole play on 10 hosts, finishes them, and then moves to the next batch. Handlers run at the end of each batch, so only a quarter of the servers restart at one time. max_fail_percentage: 10 stops the play when more than 10% of hosts in a batch fail, so a bad release does not spread. I would improve the play in three ways. Use pre_tasks to drain each host from the load balancer, with delegate_to on the LB or a cloud module. Add a post_task with ansible.builtin.uri to check a health endpoint before putting the host back. Pin the package version rather than using latest, so runs stay repeatable and idempotent. I would start with serial: 1 as a canary batch, for example serial: [1, "25%"].
keyPoints: serial gives rolling batches
Handlers flush per batch
max_fail_percentage stops a bad rollout
Drain from the LB and health-check with pre/post tasks
Pin versions and use a canary batch

subjective.question: Case study: A bank wants GitOps for 12 microservices across dev, staging and prod. Its requirements are: every prod change needs two approvals and an audit trail; no engineer has write access to prod clusters; secrets never appear in Git; any release can be undone in minutes. Design the solution.
subjective.answer: I would use one GitOps config repo with envs/dev, envs/staging and envs/prod folders, each holding Helm values that pin image tags or digests. Argo CD runs in or near each cluster and pulls from Git, so CI never holds cluster credentials. Branch protection plus CODEOWNERS on envs/prod enforces two approvals. Git history and PR records then give the audit trail of who changed what, and when. Engineers get read-only RBAC in Kubernetes and in Argo CD projects. Prod sync rights belong only to the Argo CD service account. For secrets, I would use External Secrets Operator with Vault or a cloud secret manager, so Git holds only references. Rollback is a git revert of the promotion commit, which Argo CD syncs within minutes. selfHeal is on, so manual drift is reverted. Argo CD notifications go to the change-management channel.
keyPoints: Pull-based Argo CD, so CI and humans need no prod write access
Branch protection and CODEOWNERS give approvals and the audit trail
Pinned image tags or digests in per-environment values folders
External Secrets or Vault; only references live in Git
Rollback by git revert, with selfHeal against drift

subjective.question: An Argo CD Application shows Synced but has been Progressing for 20 minutes. It never reaches Healthy. How do you find the cause? Name the usual suspects.
subjective.answer: Synced means the cluster matches Git. Progressing means some resource has not passed its health check. I would open the resource tree in Argo CD, or run argocd app get, to see which resource is not Healthy. For a Deployment, I check whether the rollout is stuck. Common causes are failing readiness probes, ImagePullBackOff from a wrong tag or missing pull secret, CrashLoopBackOff, or pods stuck Pending for lack of CPU, memory or a PVC. Pod events and logs show which one it is. A frequent non-pod cause is an Ingress or a LoadBalancer Service. Argo CD treats it as Progressing until status.loadBalancer is populated, so a missing ingress controller or cloud load balancer leaves it there forever. A PVC waiting for a StorageClass behaves the same way. I fix the cause in Git, not by hand, and let Argo CD sync again.
keyPoints: Synced and Healthy are separate; find the specific unhealthy resource
Check rollout, probes, image pulls, scheduling and pod events
Ingress or LoadBalancer stays Progressing without load balancer status
Fix in Git rather than patching the cluster

subjective.question: Spot the mistakes in this production values file, which is committed to the GitOps repo. Explain each one and give the fix.

code.code:
replicaCount: 1
image:
  repository: myorg/payments
  tag: latest
  pullPolicy: IfNotPresent
db:
  host: prod-db.internal
  password: S3cr3tP@ss
resources: {}
livenessProbe: {}
readinessProbe: {}

subjective.answer: First, tag: latest is mutable. Git does not change when a new image is pushed, so nothing syncs, and you cannot roll back to a known build. Also, with IfNotPresent, nodes keep whatever image they cached, so different pods may run different code. Pin a version tag or a digest. Second, the database password is plain text in Git, and it stays in history even after you delete it. Move it to External Secrets, SOPS or Sealed Secrets, and rotate it now, because it has leaked. Third, replicaCount: 1 in prod gives no high availability and causes downtime during node drains. Use at least two replicas, or an HPA, plus a PodDisruptionBudget. Fourth, empty resources means no requests or limits, so scheduling is unreliable and the pod can be evicted early. Fifth, empty probes mean broken pods still get traffic and rollouts cannot detect failure.
keyPoints: Mutable latest tag breaks sync and rollback; pin a tag or digest
Plain-text password must move to a secret manager and be rotated
A single replica is not production-ready
Missing resources and probes hurt scheduling and safe rollouts

subjective.question: Which tool is better for each job: Ansible, or Helm with Argo CD? Use these jobs: hardening 200 VM hosts, deploying a web app on Kubernetes, and installing an agent on bare-metal nodes before they join a cluster. Explain your reasoning.
subjective.answer: Ansible is best for host-level configuration. It connects over SSH, uses idempotent modules for packages, files, users and services, and works on machines that have no Kubernetes. So hardening 200 VMs, and preparing bare-metal nodes with packages, kernel settings, a container runtime and an agent before they join a cluster, are Ansible jobs. Keep the playbooks in Git and run them from CI or AWX. Deploying a web app on Kubernetes fits Helm with Argo CD. Helm templates the manifests per environment, and Argo CD keeps reconciling the cluster to Git all the time, with drift detection and self-heal. Ansible only acts when someone runs it, and it has no continuous drift correction. Using Ansible to apply Kubernetes manifests is possible, but it is effectively push-based CI. Using Argo CD for VM settings is impossible. Many teams use both: Ansible builds the platform, and GitOps runs the workloads on it.
keyPoints: Ansible: SSH-based, idempotent host configuration, runs on demand
Helm with Argo CD: Kubernetes workloads with continuous reconciliation
Node preparation before cluster join is an Ansible job
The tools complement each other, not compete

subjective.question: A production app was installed by hand with helm install web ./web -n shop. You must move it under Argo CD without downtime or recreating resources. Put the steps in order and explain the risks.
subjective.answer: 1. Commit the chart and the exact values in use to Git. Get them with helm get values web -n shop, so the rendered output matches. 2. Create an Argo CD Application with the same destination namespace and helm.releaseName: web. Then the templated names and the app.kubernetes.io/instance labels match the live objects. Leave automated sync and prune off at first. 3. Check the diff in Argo CD. It should show no changes, or only labels and annotations. Fix the values until the diff is clean. 4. Run a manual sync. Argo CD adopts the existing objects and applies them in place, so nothing is recreated. 5. Remove Helm's ownership by deleting the sh.helm.release.v1.web.* secrets. Never run helm uninstall, because it deletes the workload. 6. Turn on automated sync, selfHeal and then prune. The main risks are immutable field changes, such as selectors, which force a recreate, and early pruning of objects that are missing from Git.
keyPoints: Commit identical values and keep the same release name
Manual sync with no prune until the diff is clean
Delete the Helm release secrets; never run helm uninstall
Enable automation in stages; watch immutable fields

subjective.question: A PR changing image.tag to 1.8.0 in envs/prod/values.yaml was merged. Argo CD shows Synced on the last commit, but prod pods still run 1.7.2. List the likely causes in the order you would check them.

code.code:
spec:
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/acme/gitops.git
    targetRevision: release-1.7
    path: charts/web
    helm:
      valueFiles:
        - values.yaml
        - values-prod.yaml

subjective.answer: First, compare the Application source with the PR. Here targetRevision is release-1.7, but the PR was merged to main, so Argo CD is tracking a branch the PR never touched. Second, the paths do not match. The PR edited envs/prod/values.yaml, but the Application reads charts/web/values-prod.yaml, so the edited file is never used. Third, check precedence. A helm.parameters or valuesObject entry in the Application would override image.tag, even after fixing the paths. Fourth, run helm template locally with the same files and confirm that the rendered image is 1.8.0. The chart might ignore .Values.image.tag, for example by using .Chart.AppVersion. Finally, confirm that the Application points at the correct cluster and namespace. The fix is to align targetRevision and the valueFiles path with where promotions are really committed.
keyPoints: Synced only means the cluster matches the source Argo CD tracks
targetRevision points at the wrong branch
valueFiles path differs from the file the PR edited
Parameter overrides and chart templating can hide value changes

subjective.question: Find the problems in this Ansible play and rewrite the key parts.

code.code:
- hosts: webservers
  tasks:
    - name: Install nginx
      shell: apt-get install -y nginx
    - name: Copy config
      copy:
        src: nginx.conf
        dest: /etc/nginx/nginx.conf
      notify: reload nginx
  handlers:
    - name: restart nginx
      service:
        name: nginx
        state: restarted

subjective.answer: There are four problems. First, there is no become: true. Installing packages and writing to /etc need root, so the tasks fail with permission errors. Second, shell: apt-get is not idempotent in reporting. It shows changed on every run and skips package-manager logic. Use ansible.builtin.apt with name: nginx, state: present and update_cache: true. Third, the notify name 'reload nginx' does not match the handler 'restart nginx'. Ansible errors because no handler has that name, so the service would never be refreshed. Use matching names, and prefer state: reloaded for config changes, because it avoids dropping connections. Fourth, the config is copied without validation. Add validate: 'nginx -t -c %s' so a broken file is never put in place. Use fully qualified module names, such as ansible.builtin.copy, for clarity. After the fix, a second run should report changed=0.
keyPoints: Missing become for privileged tasks
Replace shell apt-get with the apt module
notify and handler names must match exactly
Validate config before writing; prefer reloaded; prove with a second run

subjective.question: For promotion across dev, staging and prod, compare Helm values files per environment with Kustomize overlays per environment. When is each better, and can you combine them?
subjective.answer: Helm values files suit apps you package and share, or apps where environments differ in parameters: replicas, image tag, resources, hostnames. The chart owns the templates, each environment has a small values file, and promotion is a one-line tag change. The downside is that anything not exposed as a value needs a chart change, and templates become hard to read. Kustomize overlays suit plain manifests you own. A base holds the real YAML, and overlays patch only what differs, with no templating language. They make it easy to change any field, but they get messy when many parameters vary. Both Argo CD and Flux support both. You can combine them: render a third-party Helm chart, then patch it with Kustomize, for example to add labels or sidecars the chart does not expose. Kustomize can inflate a Helm chart, and Flux can apply post-renderers on a HelmRelease. Choose based on who owns the templates.
keyPoints: Helm: parameterised, reusable charts; promotion via values
Kustomize: template-free base plus patches, any field
Both are supported by Argo CD and Flux
They can be combined via Helm inflation or post-rendering

subjective.question: Compare two ways to update the image tag in Git after CI builds: (a) the CI pipeline opens a PR or commit to the GitOps repo, or (b) an image automation controller such as Flux Image Automation or Argo CD Image Updater. Which would you choose for prod, and why?
subjective.answer: With (a), CI builds and pushes the image, then commits the new tag, usually through a PR, to the environment's values file. It is explicit and reviewable, and it fits approval gates. CI needs only Git write access to the config repo, not cluster access. With (b), a controller watches the registry. When a new tag matches a policy, such as semver within 1.x, it writes the tag back to Git or updates the Application. This gives less pipeline code and fast feedback, and it is good for dev, where every build should deploy. For prod, I prefer (a) with a PR. Production needs a deliberate, approved promotion of a tag already tested in staging, not automatic pickup of whatever the registry contains. A common pattern is (b) for dev, and PR-based promotion for staging and prod. In both cases, the result must be a pinned tag or digest recorded in Git.
keyPoints: CI commit or PR: explicit, reviewable, needs only repo access
Image automation: registry-driven, policy-based, low effort
Automation suits dev; prod needs approved promotion
Git must always record the pinned version

subjective.question: A playbook works against dev but fails on prod hosts. Some hosts show UNREACHABLE, and others show 'Missing sudo password'. Walk through how you diagnose and fix it.

code.code:
ansible-playbook -i inventories/prod/hosts.ini site.yml
# web3 | UNREACHABLE! => ssh: connect to host ... timed out
# web5 | FAILED! => Missing sudo password

subjective.answer: These are two separate problems. For UNREACHABLE, first confirm what Ansible actually resolves. Run ansible-inventory -i inventories/prod --host web3 to check ansible_host, ansible_user, ansible_port and the ssh key variables. Prod often uses different group_vars, a bastion or a different user. Then test with ansible web3 -i inventories/prod -m ping -vvv and look at the SSH command it builds. The cause is usually a firewall, a missing jump-host ProxyCommand or a wrong IP. For 'Missing sudo password', the connection works, but the remote user needs a password for sudo, while dev had NOPASSWD. Either configure a sudoers rule for the automation account, or supply the become password safely: use --ask-become-pass interactively, or ansible_become_password stored in Ansible Vault. Never put it in plain text. Finally, run with --check --diff --limit on one host before the full run.
keyPoints: UNREACHABLE is a connection problem; sudo errors are a privilege problem
Use ansible-inventory --host to see resolved variables
ansible -m ping -vvv to debug SSH, bastion or firewall
Become password via sudoers policy or Ansible Vault, never plain text

subjective.question: CKA/CKAD scenario: install the chart bitnami/nginx as release web in namespace web-ns with 3 replicas. Then upgrade it to 4 replicas. Then roll back to the first revision. Give the commands in order and point out the mistakes candidates usually make.

code.code:
helm repo add bitnami https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
helm repo update
helm install web bitnami/nginx -n web-ns --create-namespace --set replicaCount=3
helm upgrade web bitnami/nginx -n web-ns --reuse-values --set replicaCount=4
helm history web -n web-ns
helm rollback web 1 -n web-ns
kubectl get deploy -n web-ns

subjective.answer: The order is: add and update the repo, install, upgrade, check the history, roll back, then verify. The release name comes before the chart: helm install web bitnami/nginx. Every command needs -n web-ns. Helm releases are namespaced, so if you forget -n on upgrade, history or rollback, you get 'release not found' or, worse, a second release in default. Use --create-namespace if the namespace does not exist. On upgrade, either pass all your values again or use --reuse-values, otherwise values from earlier --set flags are reset to chart defaults. helm rollback needs the release name and a revision number, and it creates a new revision (here, 3) rather than deleting history. Confirm the result with helm history and kubectl get deploy. Check the chart's value key with helm show values, because not every chart uses replicaCount.
keyPoints: Syntax is helm install RELEASE CHART
-n on every command; --create-namespace when needed
Upgrade resets --set values unless you pass them again or use --reuse-values
Rollback needs release name and revision, and adds a new revision

steps.overview: This step teaches you how to see inside a running system and run it reliably. You will instrument a service with OpenTelemetry and Prometheus client libraries, query it with PromQL, build Grafana dashboards, and turn SLOs into alerts that page people only for real user pain. This is the core of the Prometheus Certified Associate (PCA) exam, and it also appears in the monitoring domains of DOP-C02 and AZ-400 and in SRE interviews.
objectives: Instrument a service with request-rate, error and duration (RED) metrics using a Prometheus client or OpenTelemetry SDK
Write PromQL queries using rate(), sum by(), histogram_quantile() and recording rules
Define SLIs and SLOs, calculate an error budget, and write a multi-window burn-rate alert
Build a Grafana dashboard that shows golden signals and SLO status for one service
Run an incident from page to blameless postmortem using a runbook linked from the alert

concepts.explanation: Metrics are cheap numeric time series used for dashboards and alerts. Logs are timestamped event records used for detail and debugging. Traces follow one request across services as a tree of spans with a shared trace ID. Alert on metrics, then use traces and logs to find the cause.

OTel is a CNCF vendor-neutral standard of APIs, SDKs and the OTLP protocol for metrics, logs and traces. The OTel Collector receives, processes (batch, filter, add attributes) and exports telemetry to backends such as Prometheus, Jaeger, Grafana Tempo or Amazon CloudWatch. Auto-instrumentation covers common frameworks; manual instrumentation adds business spans and attributes.

Prometheus scrapes HTTP /metrics endpoints on a schedule and stores samples in its local time-series database. Targets are found via static_configs or service discovery such as kubernetes_sd_configs, and relabel_configs filter and rewrite labels before scraping. The Pushgateway exists only for short-lived batch jobs, not for normal services.

A counter only goes up (it resets to zero on restart), for example http_requests_total. A gauge goes up and down, for example memory in use. A histogram exposes _bucket{le=...}, _sum and _count series and can be aggregated across instances. A summary computes quantiles on the client and cannot be aggregated across instances correctly.

rate() gives the per-second average increase of a counter over a range and handles counter resets; irate() uses only the last two samples and suits fast-moving graphs, not alerts. Aggregate with sum by (label) or without (label). histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(x_bucket[5m]))) gives p95 latency. Always apply rate() first, then sum(); never rate() a sum.

Recording rules precompute expensive queries into new series named level:metric:operations, for example job:http_requests:rate5m. Alerting rules fire when an expression returns results; the for clause keeps an alert pending until the condition holds that long. Prometheus sends firing alerts to Alertmanager, which handles grouping, inhibition, silences and routing to receivers such as PagerDuty, Slack or email.

concepts.term: SLI, SLO, SLA and error budget
concepts.explanation: An SLI is a measured ratio of good events to valid events, such as successful requests divided by all requests. An SLO is the target for that SLI over a window, such as 99.9% over 30 days. An SLA is a contract with penalties and is usually looser than the SLO. The error budget is 1 minus the SLO; while budget remains you ship, and when it is spent you prioritise reliability work.

Burn rate is how fast you consume the error budget compared with the allowed pace; burn rate 1 uses exactly the whole budget over the SLO window. The Google SRE Workbook recommends multi-window, multi-burn-rate alerts, for example page when the 1h and 5m burn rates are both above 14.4. The short window lets the alert clear quickly once the problem stops.

RED (Rate, Errors, Duration) suits request-driven services. USE (Utilization, Saturation, Errors) suits resources such as CPU, disk and queues. Google's four golden signals are latency, traffic, errors and saturation. Page on user-facing symptoms and leave causes such as high CPU for dashboards or tickets.

Use clear roles: an incident commander coordinates, an operations lead fixes, and a communications lead updates stakeholders. Mitigate first (rollback, failover, feature flag) and find root cause later. A blameless postmortem records timeline, impact, contributing factors and owned action items, and it focuses on system and process gaps, not on individuals.

keyFacts: Prometheus defaults: server port 9090, Alertmanager 9093, node_exporter 9100; global scrape_interval and evaluation_interval both default to 1m.
Every scrape adds the up series per target: 1 means the scrape succeeded, 0 means it failed. Use up == 0 to alert on dead targets.
Choose a rate() range of at least 4x the scrape interval so each window holds enough samples.
Counter names end in _total; units go in the name using base units, such as _seconds and _bytes, never milliseconds.
Every unique label combination is a new time series. Never put user IDs, emails or raw URLs in labels, because high cardinality breaks Prometheus.
Error budget for 99.9% over 30 days is 0.1% of 43,200 minutes, about 43.2 minutes. For 99.99% it is about 4.3 minutes.
SRE Workbook page thresholds: burn rate 14.4 over 1h (with a 5m short window) uses 2% of a 30-day budget; burn rate 6 over 6h (with a 30m short window) uses 5%.
OTLP default ports: 4317 for gRPC and 4318 for HTTP.
Alertmanager group_by, group_wait, group_interval and repeat_interval control noise. Inhibition mutes lower alerts when a higher alert fires, and silences mute alerts for a set time.
Rules for paging: page only for urgent, user-visible, actionable symptoms, and attach a runbook_url annotation to every alert.

example.caption: SLO burn-rate alert for a 99.9% availability SLO, with recording rules and a runbook link (rules file loaded by Prometheus)
example.code:
groups:
  - name: checkout-slo
    rules:
      - record: job:http_requests:error_ratio_rate5m
        expr: |
          sum by (job) (rate(http_requests_total{code=~"5.."}[5m]))
          / sum by (job) (rate(http_requests_total[5m]))
      - record: job:http_requests:error_ratio_rate1h
        expr: |
          sum by (job) (rate(http_requests_total{code=~"5.."}[1h]))
          / sum by (job) (rate(http_requests_total[1h]))
      - alert: CheckoutErrorBudgetFastBurn
        expr: |
          job:http_requests:error_ratio_rate1h{job="checkout"} > (14.4 * 0.001)
          and
          job:http_requests:error_ratio_rate5m{job="checkout"} > (14.4 * 0.001)
        for: 2m
        labels:
          severity: page
          team: payments
        annotations:
          summary: "Checkout users are seeing errors; 2% of the 30-day error budget is burning per hour"
          description: "Error ratio over 1h is {{ $value | humanizePercentage }} (SLO 99.9%)."
          runbook_url: "https://runbooks.example.com/checkout/high-error-rate"
          dashboard: "https://grafana.example.com/d/checkout-slo"
# Load test to fire it: hey -z 10m -c 50 http://checkout/pay?fail=0.05
# Latency p95: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])))

pitfalls: Using rate() on a gauge, or sum() before rate(). rate() is only for counters and must run on raw series before aggregation, or counter resets give wrong results.
Averaging quantiles from summaries across pods. Averaged percentiles are mathematically wrong, so use histograms with histogram_quantile() over sum by (le).
Paging on causes such as CPU over 80% or a single pod restart. These create noise. Page on SLO burn and user-facing symptoms, and send the rest to tickets.
Setting the SLO at 100% or copying the SLA value. A 100% target leaves no error budget, and an SLO equal to the SLA gives no warning before a breach.
Exam trap: the for clause delays firing (pending state), while Alertmanager group_wait delays sending the notification. They are different settings in different components.
Adding high-cardinality labels such as user_id or full request path. Series count explodes, memory grows, and queries slow down.

workflow.title: From instrumented service to a trusted SLO page

steps.label: Instrument RED metrics
steps.detail: Add a http_requests_total counter with method and code labels and a http_request_duration_seconds histogram via a Prometheus client or the OTel SDK.

steps.label: Expose and scrape
steps.detail: Serve /metrics, add a scrape job or ServiceMonitor, and confirm the target shows up == 1 on the Prometheus Targets page.

steps.label: Define SLI and SLO
steps.detail: Write the SLI as non-5xx requests divided by all requests, set a 99.9% 30-day SLO, and agree it with the service owner.

steps.label: Write recording and alert rules
steps.detail: Precompute error ratios for 5m and 1h, add a 14.4x multi-window burn-rate alert, and validate the file with promtool check rules.

steps.label: Route and document
steps.detail: Configure Alertmanager routes by severity and team, and write the runbook that the alert's runbook_url points to.

steps.label: Fire with a load test
steps.detail: Inject errors under load with a tool such as hey or k6, then watch the alert go pending, fire and resolve in Grafana and Alertmanager.

steps.label: Review and postmortem
steps.detail: Run a blameless review of the drill, tune thresholds that caused noise, and track action items to closure.

project.title: orders-slo
project.summary: A small Python orders API exposes RED metrics (request rate, errors, duration) that Prometheus scrapes. Recording rules turn them into SLI ratios, multi-window burn-rate alerts guard a 99.5% availability SLO, Alertmanager pages only for fast burns, and a k6 load test with injected errors fires the page. main.py holds the instrumented service, prometheus.yml the scrape config, rules.yml the SLI and SLO alert rules, alertmanager.yml the noise-free routing, loadtest.js the traffic, and README.md the runbook the alert links to.
project.run:
docker compose up -d
curl -s localhost:8080/api/orders && curl -s localhost:8080/metrics | grep http_requests_total
ERROR_RATE=0.2 docker compose up -d app
docker compose --profile load run --rm k6
open http://localhost:9090/alerts and http://localhost:9093 (page fires after about 2-4 minutes)
docker compose down

files.code:
services:
  app:
    image: python:3.12-slim
    working_dir: /app
    volumes: ["./app:/app"]
    command: sh -c "pip install --no-cache-dir 'flask>=3' 'prometheus-client>=0.20' && python main.py"
    environment:
      ERROR_RATE: ${ERROR_RATE:-0.01}   # override with ERROR_RATE=0.2 to burn the budget
      PORT: "8080"
    ports: ["8080:8080"]

  prometheus:
    image: prom/prometheus:v3.1.0
    command:
      - --config.file=/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml
      - --web.enable-lifecycle          # allows POST /-/reload after editing rules
    volumes:
      - ./prometheus/prometheus.yml:/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml:ro
      - ./prometheus/rules.yml:/etc/prometheus/rules.yml:ro
    ports: ["9090:9090"]
    depends_on: [app, alertmanager]

  alertmanager:
    image: prom/alertmanager:v0.27.0
    command: ["--config.file=/etc/alertmanager/alertmanager.yml"]
    volumes:
      - ./alertmanager/alertmanager.yml:/etc/alertmanager/alertmanager.yml:ro
    ports: ["9093:9093"]

  grafana:
    image: grafana/grafana:11.4.0
    environment:
      GF_AUTH_ANONYMOUS_ENABLED: "true"   # local demo only
      GF_AUTH_ANONYMOUS_ORG_ROLE: Admin
    ports: ["3000:3000"]                  # add data source http://prometheus:9090

  k6:
    image: grafana/k6:latest
    profiles: ["load"]                    # only runs when asked
    command: run /scripts/loadtest.js
    environment:
      BASE_URL: http://app:8080
    volumes: ["./loadtest.js:/scripts/loadtest.js:ro"]
    depends_on: [app]

global:
  scrape_interval: 15s       # how often Prometheus pulls /metrics
  evaluation_interval: 15s   # how often recording and alerting rules run

rule_files:
  - /etc/prometheus/rules.yml

alerting:
  alertmanagers:
    - static_configs:
        - targets: ["alertmanager:9093"]

scrape_configs:
  - job_name: orders-api      # becomes the job label used in every rule
    metrics_path: /metrics
    static_configs:
      - targets: ["app:8080"]
        labels:
          service: orders-api

  - job_name: prometheus      # Prometheus scrapes itself too
    static_configs:
      - targets: ["localhost:9090"]

# SLO: 99.5% of /api/orders requests succeed over 30 days. Error budget = 0.5%.
groups:
  - name: orders-api-sli
    rules:  # Recording rules: precompute the SLI error ratio per window.
      - record: job:slo_errors_per_request:ratio_rate5m
        expr: sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="orders-api",route="/api/orders",code=~"5.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="orders-api",route="/api/orders"}[5m]))
      - record: job:slo_errors_per_request:ratio_rate30m
        expr: sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="orders-api",route="/api/orders",code=~"5.."}[30m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="orders-api",route="/api/orders"}[30m]))
      - record: job:slo_errors_per_request:ratio_rate1h
        expr: sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="orders-api",route="/api/orders",code=~"5.."}[1h])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="orders-api",route="/api/orders"}[1h]))
      - record: job:slo_errors_per_request:ratio_rate6h
        expr: sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="orders-api",route="/api/orders",code=~"5.."}[6h])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="orders-api",route="/api/orders"}[6h]))
      - record: job:http_request_duration_seconds:p99_5m   # for the Grafana duration panel
        expr: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="orders-api"}[5m])))

  - name: orders-api-slo-alerts
    rules:
      # Fast burn: 14.4x budget rate (2% of 30-day budget in 1h). Short window confirms it is still happening.
      - alert: OrdersAPIHighErrorBudgetBurn
        expr: |
          job:slo_errors_per_request:ratio_rate1h > (14.4 * 0.005)
          and
          job:slo_errors_per_request:ratio_rate5m > (14.4 * 0.005)
        for: 2m
        labels:
          severity: page
        annotations:
          summary: "Orders API is failing requests: error budget burning 14x too fast"
          description: "{{ $value | humanizePercentage }} of /api/orders requests return 5xx (SLO 99.5%)."
          runbook_url: "https://github.com/your-org/orders-slo/blob/main/README.md#runbook-ordersapihigherrorbudgetburn"

      # Slow burn: 6x over 6h. Real problem but not urgent, so it opens a ticket, not a page.
      - alert: OrdersAPIErrorBudgetBurnSlow
        expr: |
          job:slo_errors_per_request:ratio_rate6h > (6 * 0.005)
          and
          job:slo_errors_per_request:ratio_rate30m > (6 * 0.005)
        for: 15m
        labels:
          severity: ticket
        annotations:
          summary: "Orders API error budget is draining steadily"
          description: "6h error ratio is {{ $value | humanizePercentage }}; budget will run out early."
          runbook_url: "https://github.com/your-org/orders-slo/blob/main/README.md#runbook-ordersapihigherrorbudgetburn"

# Route by severity so only fast SLO burns wake someone up.
route:
  receiver: ticket                 # default: never page by accident
  group_by: [alertname, service]   # one notification per problem, not per series
  group_wait: 30s
  group_interval: 5m
  repeat_interval: 4h
  routes:
    - matchers: ['severity="page"']
      receiver: oncall-page
      repeat_interval: 1h
    - matchers: ['severity="ticket"']
      receiver: ticket

# If the page is firing, silence the matching slow-burn ticket (no duplicate noise).
inhibit_rules:
  - source_matchers: ['severity="page"']
    target_matchers: ['severity="ticket"']
    equal: [alertname, service]

receivers:
  # Empty receivers are valid: alerts show in the UI at :9093 for this demo.
  # In real work add pagerduty_configs / slack_configs / webhook_configs here.
  - name: oncall-page
  - name: ticket

# orders-slo

RED metrics + SLO burn-rate alerting for a tiny orders API.

- Rate: `sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="orders-api"}[5m]))`
- Errors: `job:slo_errors_per_request:ratio_rate5m`
- Duration: `job:http_request_duration_seconds:p99_5m`

SLO: 99.5% of `/api/orders` requests succeed over 30 days (error budget 0.5%).
Fast burn (14.4x, 1h AND 5m) pages. Slow burn (6x, 6h AND 30m) opens a ticket.
CPU spikes or a single 500 page nobody: we alert on user-facing symptoms only.

## Try it
1. `docker compose up -d`, then check targets at http://localhost:9090/targets.
2. `ERROR_RATE=0.2 docker compose up -d app` to inject 20% failures.
3. `docker compose --profile load run --rm k6`.
4. Watch the alert go Pending then Firing at :9090/alerts; see it routed at :9093.
5. Validate rules: `docker compose exec prometheus promtool check rules /etc/prometheus/rules.yml`.

## Runbook: OrdersAPIHighErrorBudgetBurn
**Symptom:** users get 5xx from /api/orders; budget gone in about 2 days at this rate.
1. Acknowledge the page; open an incident channel; name an incident commander.
2. Check the Errors and Duration panels: did it start with a deploy? Roll back first.
3. Check dependencies (database) logs and traces for the failing requests.
4. Mitigate, confirm the 5m ratio drops below 0.072, then resolve.
5. Write a blameless postmortem within 5 working days: timeline, impact, budget used, actions.

revision.examFocus: This step maps most directly to the Prometheus Certified Associate (PCA). Its domains cover observability concepts, Prometheus fundamentals, PromQL (the heaviest weighted), instrumentation and exporters, and alerting and dashboarding. The same ideas appear in the monitoring, logging and incident-response domains of AWS DOP-C02, in the instrumentation-strategy domain of AZ-400, and in cluster troubleshooting on the CKA. Multiple-choice exams test whether you can pick the correct PromQL expression, metric type or Alertmanager setting, and whether you page on symptoms rather than causes.

compare.difference: A counter only goes up and resets to zero on restart. A gauge can go up or down. Only counters should be wrapped in rate(), increase() or irate().
compare.chooseA: Pick a counter for things that accumulate, such as requests served, errors or bytes sent (names end in _total).
compare.chooseB: Pick a gauge for current values such as memory in use, queue depth, temperature or in-flight requests, and use avg_over_time() or deriv() on them.

compare.difference: A histogram exposes _bucket series with an le label, so quantiles are calculated on the server and can be aggregated across instances. A summary calculates quantiles inside each client, and those quantiles cannot be combined.
compare.chooseA: Pick a histogram when you need a fleet-wide p95/p99 or an SLO on latency, using histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(x_bucket[5m]))).
compare.chooseB: Pick a summary only for a single instance when you need an exact client-side quantile and will never aggregate it.

compare.difference: The for clause keeps an alert in the pending state until its condition has held for that long. group_wait is how long Alertmanager buffers a new alert group before it sends the first notification.
compare.chooseA: Choose for when the question is about ignoring short spikes before an alert becomes firing.
compare.chooseB: Choose group_wait when the question is about batching related alerts into one notification after they have already fired.

compare.difference: Inhibition is a rule-based, automatic mute that applies while a source alert is firing. A silence is a manual, time-boxed mute that you create through matchers in the Alertmanager UI or with amtool.
compare.chooseA: Choose inhibition for cases like 'if the cluster or datacenter-down alert fires, suppress the per-service alerts'.
compare.chooseB: Choose a silence for planned maintenance or a known issue with a fixed end time.

compare.difference: A recording rule precomputes an expression and saves the result as a new series. An alerting rule evaluates an expression and sends alerts to Alertmanager when it returns results.
compare.chooseA: Choose a recording rule when dashboards or SLO maths repeat an expensive query, named level:metric:operations, for example job:http_requests:rate5m.
compare.chooseB: Choose an alerting rule when someone must be notified, and add labels such as severity plus annotations such as summary and runbook_url.

cues.cue: error ratio / percentage of failed requests
cues.pick: sum(rate(errors_total[5m])) / sum(rate(requests_total[5m]))
cues.why: Take the rate of each counter first, then aggregate, then divide, so the result is a ratio between 0 and 1.

cues.cue: short-lived or batch job that finishes before a scrape
cues.pick: Pushgateway
cues.why: Prometheus pulls metrics, so a job that exits before the next scrape must push its final metrics to a gateway that Prometheus can scrape.

cues.cue: alert when a metric disappears or was never reported
cues.pick: absent(metric) or absent_over_time()
cues.why: A comparison such as x == 0 returns nothing when the series does not exist, so only absent() can catch a missing series.

cues.cue: page quickly on a fast burn but avoid false alarms
cues.pick: Multiwindow, multi-burn-rate alert (long window AND short window both above the threshold)
cues.why: The long window proves the burn is significant, and the short window makes the alert clear soon after the problem stops.

cues.cue: long-term storage or a global view across many Prometheus servers
cues.pick: remote_write to Thanos, Cortex or Mimir (or federation for aggregated series)
cues.why: Local Prometheus storage is designed for one node and limited retention, not for durable multi-cluster history.

cues.cue: lowest noise for on-call / alert fatigue
cues.pick: Page on SLO burn rate and user-facing symptoms; route cause-based alerts to tickets; use group_by and inhibition
cues.why: A page should only go out for urgent, actionable, user-visible symptoms.

cues.cue: vendor-neutral instrumentation for metrics, logs and traces
cues.pick: OpenTelemetry SDK plus OpenTelemetry Collector exporting OTLP
cues.why: You instrument once and can then change backends in the Collector without touching application code.

cues.cue: exam asks for the total count over a period, not per second
cues.pick: increase(x_total[1h])
cues.why: increase() equals rate() multiplied by the range in seconds, and it handles counter resets the same way.

scenario.situation: Your checkout API has a 99.9% availability SLO over 30 days. It exposes http_requests_total with a code label, and Prometheus scrapes it every 15s. On-call engineers complain that they are paged at night when CPU passes 80%, but they missed a real 40-minute outage in which 3% of requests failed. You must redesign alerting so real user impact pages fast and noise stops. What should you do?
reasoning: Remove options that keep the cause-based CPU page, or that only raise its threshold. CPU is a cause, not a user symptom, so it belongs in a ticket or on a dashboard.
Remove options that alert with a for clause on a raw error count. Counts grow with traffic and do not relate to the error budget.
Remove options that use irate() or a 30s rate window. With a 15s scrape, a window under 4x the interval is too noisy and irate() is meant for graphs, not alerts.
Burn rate = error ratio / (1 - 0.999). An error ratio of 3% gives a burn rate of 30, which is well above 14.4, so a 1h/5m multiwindow rule would have paged within minutes.
Keep the option that pages on burn rate 14.4 over 1h AND 5m, sends a ticket at burn rate 6 over 6h AND 30m (or lower), adds runbook_url, and moves CPU alerts to a ticket route.
scenario.answer: Replace the CPU page with multiwindow burn-rate alerts on the error ratio from sum(rate(http_requests_total{code=~"5.."}[w])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total[w])). Page at 14.4x (1h and 5m), ticket at slower burns, and attach a runbook_url, because this pages only for user-visible budget loss and catches the outage.

memoryAids: RED for services (Rate, Errors, Duration), USE for resources (Utilisation, Saturation, Errors), and the four golden signals are Latency, Traffic, Errors, Saturation. Ask: is it a request or a machine?
'Rate before sum, le stays in': apply rate() to raw counters first, then sum by (le) before histogram_quantile().
'For waits to fire, group waits to send': the for clause lives in Prometheus, group_wait lives in Alertmanager.
cheatSheet: Burn rate = observed error ratio / (1 - SLO). A burn rate of 1 uses exactly the whole budget over the SLO window.
Order of operations: rate() on the raw counter, then sum by (labels), then divide or apply histogram_quantile().
histogram_quantile() needs the le label kept in the aggregation. Dropping le gives no result or a wrong one.
Use rate() for alerts and recording rules. Use irate() only for fast-moving graphs, because it uses just the last two samples.
absent() catches missing series. up == 0 catches a scrape that failed.
Recording rule naming is level:metric:operations. Alert labels carry severity for routing, and annotations carry summary, description and runbook_url.
An Alertmanager route tree matches on labels. group_by merges alerts, and repeat_interval controls how often a still-firing alert is re-sent.
Summary quantiles cannot be aggregated. Histograms can, at the cost of one series per bucket.
The SLO must be stricter than the SLA, so you get warning and room to act. Internal SLOs are never 100%.
A Collector pipeline is receivers, then processors, then exporters. Use the batch and memory_limiter processors in production.
Postmortems are blameless. Record a timeline, impact, root and contributing causes, and action items with owners, and focus on system fixes rather than people.
Exporters turn third-party systems into /metrics: node_exporter for hosts, blackbox_exporter for probing endpoints, kube-state-metrics for Kubernetes object state.
selfCheck: I can write PromQL from memory for the error ratio, p99 latency from a histogram, and requests per second by service.
I can calculate the error budget and burn rate for any SLO and window, and explain why 14.4x over 1h pages.
I can choose between a counter, gauge, histogram and summary for a given metric, and name it with the correct base unit and suffix.
I can explain the difference between for, group_wait, group_interval, repeat_interval, inhibition and silences, and say which component owns each.
I can decide whether a signal should page, open a ticket, or only appear on a dashboard, and attach a runbook to every alert.
I can describe how OpenTelemetry SDKs, the Collector and OTLP send traces, metrics and logs to separate backends.

objective.question: Your service has a 99.9% availability SLO measured over a 30-day window. Roughly how much full downtime does the error budget allow in that window?
options: About 7.2 hours
About 14.4 minutes
About 43.2 minutes
About 4.3 minutes
objective.explanation: 30 days is 43,200 minutes, and 0.1% of that is about 43.2 minutes. About 4.3 minutes is the budget for 99.99%. The other values do not match 0.1% of 30 days.

objective.question: Prometheus scrapes your service every 15 seconds. A teammate writes rate(http_requests_total[15s]) on a dashboard and sees gaps and jumpy values. What is the smallest range that follows the usual guidance?
objective.explanation: The range should be at least 4x the scrape interval, so 4 x 15s = 1m. Each window then holds enough samples for rate() to work reliably. Ranges of 30s or less often contain only one or two samples, or none.

objective.question: Request latency is recorded in a histogram named http_request_duration_seconds. Which query correctly returns the 95th percentile latency across all instances over the last 5 minutes?
options: quantile(0.95, rate(http_request_duration_seconds_sum[5m]))
avg_over_time(http_request_duration_seconds_count[5m]) * 0.95
histogram_quantile(0.95, http_request_duration_seconds_bucket)
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])))
objective.explanation: histogram_quantile needs the per-second rate of the cumulative buckets, aggregated while keeping the le label. Without rate() the query uses lifetime totals. The _sum and _count series have no bucket information, so they cannot give a percentile.

objective.question: You are adding labels to http_requests_total. Which label set is safe for Prometheus at scale?
options: method, status_code, route (for example /orders/{id})
method, session_id, client_ip
method, email, raw request URL
method, status_code, user_id
objective.explanation: Every unique label combination creates a new time series. Method, status code and a templated route all have a small, bounded set of values. User IDs, emails, raw URLs, session IDs and client IPs are unbounded and cause a cardinality explosion.

objective.question: Per the SRE Workbook, you page when the burn rate is above 14.4 over 1 hour, confirmed by a 5-minute short window. If this condition holds for the full hour, how much of a 30-day error budget has been consumed?
objective.explanation: A burn rate of 1 uses the whole budget in 30 days (720 hours). 14.4 x 1h / 720h = 0.02, which is 2%. 5% is the threshold for a burn rate of 6 over 6 hours.

objective.question: Which metric name follows Prometheus naming conventions for a counter of handled HTTP requests and a histogram of their duration?
options: http_requests_count and http_request_latency_milliseconds
HttpRequestsTotal and http_request_duration
http_requests_total and http_request_duration_seconds
http_requests and http_request_duration_ms
objective.explanation: Counter names end in _total, and units go in the name in base units such as _seconds, never milliseconds. The other options use non-base units, leave out the unit, or break the snake_case style.

objective.question: When a whole cluster goes down, on-call receives one critical ClusterDown page plus dozens of warning pages for individual services in that cluster. Which Alertmanager feature should you configure so the warnings are muted only while the critical alert is firing?
options: An inhibition rule
A longer repeat_interval
group_by: ['alertname']
A silence
objective.explanation: Inhibition mutes lower-severity alerts that match labels such as cluster while a higher-severity alert is firing, and it lifts automatically. A silence mutes alerts for a fixed time that someone sets by hand. repeat_interval and group_by only change how often and how notifications are bundled.

objective.question: Your application uses the OpenTelemetry SDK and exports OTLP over HTTP to a local OpenTelemetry Collector that uses default settings. Which port should the exporter target?
objective.explanation: The OTLP defaults are 4317 for gRPC and 4318 for HTTP. Port 9090 is the Prometheus server and 9093 is Alertmanager.

objective.question: You want an alert that fires when Prometheus can no longer scrape any node_exporter target. Which expression is the standard approach?
options: up{job="node"} == 0
rate(up{job="node"}[5m]) < 1
node_exporter_build_info == 0
absent(node_cpu_seconds_total) == 1
objective.explanation: Prometheus adds an up series for every target on every scrape. The value is 1 when the scrape succeeds and 0 when it fails, so up == 0 detects each dead target. rate() on a gauge like up makes no sense, and the other expressions do not reliably report scrape failure for each target.

objective.question: A nightly batch job runs for 20 seconds and then exits. Its metrics never appear in Prometheus, even though the job is listed in scrape_configs. What is the most appropriate fix?
options: Have the job push its final metrics to a Pushgateway, which Prometheus then scrapes
Increase evaluation_interval to 24h
Add the job's metrics as labels on the up series
Lower the global scrape_interval to 1s
objective.explanation: Prometheus uses a pull model, so a short-lived job can exit before it is scraped. The Pushgateway is the supported pattern for service-level batch jobs. A very short scrape interval is wasteful and still unreliable, and evaluation_interval controls rule evaluation, not scraping.

objective.question: A dashboard panel uses the query below. Every time a pod restarts, the panel shows a huge false spike in request rate. What is the cause and the fix?

code.code: rate(sum by (job) (http_requests_total)[5m:30s])

options: The subquery resolution of 30s is too coarse. Changing it to [5m:1s] removes the spike.
rate() cannot be applied to a subquery, so Prometheus falls back to irate() and returns the spike.
Pod restarts create stale series. Wrapping the query in avg_over_time() smooths the spike away.
Summing first hides each pod's counter reset. The summed series drops, rate() treats the drop as a reset and adds a large false increase. Use sum by (job) (rate(http_requests_total[5m])) instead.
objective.explanation: rate() handles counter resets per series, so you must rate each raw counter first and then aggregate. Sum-then-rate turns one pod's reset into a drop in the total, and rate() reads that as a huge increase. Subquery resolution and smoothing do not fix the order of operations, and rate() does accept subqueries.

objective.question: An alerting rule has 'for: 10m' and the rule group is evaluated every 1 minute. The expression is true for 7 consecutive evaluations, false for one evaluation, then true again. What does Prometheus do?
options: The alert fires immediately on the false evaluation, because 'for' only debounces the resolve.
The alert stays pending forever until someone silences it in Alertmanager.
The alert returns to inactive on the false evaluation. The pending timer restarts, and it fires only after the expression is true continuously for another 10 minutes.
The alert fires after 3 more minutes, because the 7 minutes already spent in pending are kept.
objective.explanation: 'for' requires the expression to be true at every evaluation for the full duration. One false result resets a pending alert to inactive. keep_firing_for exists, but it applies only to alerts that are already firing, not to pending ones.

objective.question: A service exposes latency as a Prometheus Summary with a pre-computed 0.95 quantile on each of 20 pods. The team graphs avg(http_request_duration_seconds{quantile="0.95"}) as the service-wide p95. What is the problem, and what should they do?
options: Summary quantiles cannot be meaningfully aggregated across instances. They should switch to a histogram and run histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(..._bucket[5m]))).
They should add a quantile="0.95" recording rule. Recording rules make summary quantiles aggregatable.
They should use max() instead of avg(). The maximum per-pod p95 equals the true service-wide p95.
Nothing is wrong. Averaging per-pod p95 values gives the exact service-wide p95.
objective.explanation: Summary quantiles are computed on the client, per instance, so averaging them or taking their max is statistically meaningless. Histogram buckets are counters that can be summed across instances before the quantile is estimated. Recording rules do not change this.

objective.question: A company wants to keep every trace that contains an error or takes longer than 2 seconds, and only 10% of all other traces. Which approach meets this requirement?
options: Use the tail_sampling processor in the OpenTelemetry Collector with status_code, latency and probabilistic policies. Route all spans of a trace to the same Collector instance.
Enable exemplars in Prometheus so that only error traces are stored.
Use the batch processor in the Collector with a larger batch size so that fewer traces are exported.
Configure a TraceIdRatioBased sampler at 0.1 in each application's OpenTelemetry SDK.
objective.explanation: Whether a trace had an error or was slow is known only after the trace completes, so the decision needs tail sampling. The Collector's tail_sampling processor does this, and it needs all spans of a trace in one instance, for example by using a load-balancing exporter tier. Head sampling in the SDK decides at the start of the trace, and neither exemplars nor batching do sampling.

objective.question: You want a warning alert that fires when a filesystem on a node will run out of space within the next 4 hours, based on its recent trend. Which expression is the standard approach?
options: increase(node_filesystem_avail_bytes[4h]) < 0
predict_linear(node_filesystem_avail_bytes{fstype!="tmpfs"}[6h], 4 * 3600) < 0
node_filesystem_avail_bytes / node_filesystem_size_bytes < 0.1
rate(node_filesystem_avail_bytes[6h]) < 0
objective.explanation: node_filesystem_avail_bytes is a gauge. predict_linear() fits a linear regression over the range and extrapolates it 4 hours ahead. rate() and increase() are meant for counters and misread a gauge's falls as resets. A static 10% threshold ignores how fast the disk is filling.

objective.question: Within 10 seconds, 40 HighErrorRate alerts start firing, all with cluster="prod-a" and each with a different pod label. Two minutes later, a 41st HighErrorRate alert fires for another pod in prod-a. With the route below, what does the on-call receiver get?

code.code:
route:
  receiver: oncall
  group_by: ['alertname', 'cluster']
  group_wait: 30s
  group_interval: 5m
  repeat_interval: 4h

options: One notification about 30 seconds after the first alert, containing all 40 alerts. The 41st alert arrives in an updated notification for the same group, about 5 minutes after that first notification.
No notification for 5 minutes, because group_interval delays the first notification of every new group.
One notification containing the first 40 alerts, then nothing new for 4 hours, because repeat_interval blocks the 41st alert.
41 separate notifications, one per pod, each sent as soon as the alert fires.
objective.explanation: Alerts sharing alertname and cluster form one group. group_wait holds the first notification for 30 seconds to batch the group. Changes to an existing group, such as a new alert, are sent after group_interval. repeat_interval only controls re-sending an unchanged group.

subjective.question: Explain the difference between metrics, logs and traces. Give an example of when you would reach for each one during an incident.
subjective.answer: Metrics are numeric time series, such as request rate, error ratio or latency percentiles. They are cheap to store and fast to query, so they drive dashboards and alerts. They tell me that something is wrong. Logs are timestamped records of discrete events, such as a stack trace or an 'order 123 failed payment validation' message. They tell me what happened inside one component. Traces follow a single request across services as a tree of spans with timings. They show where the time or the failure occurred in a distributed call path. In an incident, a burn-rate alert from metrics wakes me up. I then open a trace exemplar for a slow or failed request to see which downstream service is at fault. Finally, I read that service's logs, filtered by trace ID, to find the exact error. Correlating all three through shared trace IDs and labels is what makes a system observable.
keyPoints: Metrics: aggregated numbers, cheap, used for alerting and trends
Logs: detailed events, used for root-cause detail
Traces: request path across services, used to find where latency or errors occur
Correlate the three using trace IDs and consistent labels

subjective.question: What is OpenTelemetry, and what role does the OpenTelemetry Collector play in a production setup?
subjective.answer: OpenTelemetry is a CNCF project that provides vendor-neutral APIs, SDKs and a wire protocol, OTLP, for generating traces, metrics and logs. I instrument my code once, either automatically or manually, and I can change backends without touching the code. The Collector is a separate process that receives telemetry, processes it and exports it. A Collector pipeline has receivers (such as OTLP on 4317 for gRPC and 4318 for HTTP), processors (batching, memory limiting, attribute redaction, tail sampling) and exporters (Prometheus, Jaeger, a vendor backend). Apps usually send to a local agent Collector, often run as a DaemonSet or sidecar. That agent forwards to a gateway Collector. This decouples apps from backends, centralises sampling and PII scrubbing, and lets you add retries and batching. It also means that an outage in the backend does not directly slow down the application.
keyPoints: Vendor-neutral standard for traces, metrics and logs; OTLP protocol
Collector pipeline: receivers, processors, exporters
Default OTLP ports 4317 (gRPC) and 4318 (HTTP)
Agent and gateway patterns; central sampling, redaction and batching

subjective.question: Define SLI, SLO, SLA and error budget, and show how they relate using a 99.9% example.
subjective.answer: An SLI is a measured indicator of user experience. It is usually a ratio of good events to valid events, for example successful requests divided by total requests, or requests served under 300 ms divided by total requests. An SLO is the target for that SLI over a window, for example 99.9% of requests succeed over 30 days. An SLA is a contract with customers that carries consequences such as refunds. It should be looser than the internal SLO so the team gets a warning before breaching it. The error budget is 1 minus the SLO: here 0.1%. Over 30 days, or 43,200 minutes, that is about 43.2 minutes of full outage, or the equivalent fraction of failed requests. The budget is a decision tool. While budget remains, the team ships features and takes risks. When it is exhausted, the team slows releases and focuses on reliability work.
keyPoints: SLI = good events / valid events, measured from the user's perspective
SLO = internal target over a window; SLA = external contract, looser than the SLO
Error budget = 1 - SLO; 99.9% over 30 days is about 43.2 minutes
Budget policy governs release speed versus reliability work

subjective.question: Why is a simple 'error rate > 1% for 5 minutes' alert a poor SLO alert, and how does multi-window, multi-burn-rate alerting fix it?
subjective.answer: A static threshold has poor precision and poor recall at the same time. A short spike pages someone even though it hardly touches the budget. A slow leak just under 1% can quietly use up the whole month's budget without ever firing. Burn rate measures how fast you are spending the budget compared with the allowed pace. A burn rate of 1 spends exactly the budget over 30 days. The SRE Workbook recommends paging when the burn rate is above 14.4 over 1 hour, which is 2% of the budget, or above 6 over 6 hours, which is 5%. Slower burns, such as 1 over 3 days, become tickets. Each long window is paired with a short window, such as 5 minutes for 1 hour or 30 minutes for 6 hours. The short window confirms the problem is still happening, so the alert also resets quickly after recovery. The result is fast detection of serious incidents, no paging for blips, and alerts tied directly to user impact.
keyPoints: Static thresholds both over-page on spikes and miss slow burns
Burn rate = actual error rate / (1 - SLO)
14.4 over 1h (2%) and 6 over 6h (5%) page; slow burns become tickets
Short window (5m or 30m) confirms the issue is ongoing and speeds reset

subjective.question: Describe, or write, a Prometheus alerting rule for a fast-burn SLO alert on a 99.9% availability SLO. What labels and annotations must it carry?
subjective.answer: In a rule group I would write an alert named HighErrorBudgetBurn. Its expr compares two error ratios with the threshold 14.4 * 0.001. The 1-hour ratio is sum(rate(http_requests_total{code=~"5.."}[1h])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total[1h])), and it must be above the threshold. The same ratio over [5m] must also be above it, joined with 'and'. In practice I would precompute these ratios with recording rules. I would set a short 'for', such as 2m, to absorb scrape jitter. Labels: severity: page, plus service and team for routing in Alertmanager. Annotations: a summary that names the symptom, such as 'Checkout is burning error budget 14x faster than allowed'. A description with the current value using {{ $value }}. A runbook_url that links to the steps for diagnosis and mitigation. The symptom wording matters because on-call should know the user impact before opening anything else. I would test the rule with promtool and then fire it with a load test that injects errors.
keyPoints: Long window AND short window, both above 14.4 x (1 - SLO)
Use recording rules for the error-ratio series
severity, service and team labels for Alertmanager routing
Symptom-based summary and a mandatory runbook_url annotation; validate with promtool and a load test

subjective.question: Compare the RED method, the USE method and Google's four golden signals. Which would you apply to a REST API and which to a database host?
subjective.answer: RED stands for Rate, Errors and Duration. It is request-centric and suits services: how many requests per second, how many fail, and how long they take. USE stands for Utilisation, Saturation and Errors. It is resource-centric and comes from Brendan Gregg. It suits CPUs, disks, memory and network: how busy the resource is, how much work is queued, and what error counts it shows. The four golden signals are latency, traffic, errors and saturation. They are essentially RED plus saturation. For a REST API I would build RED dashboards and base SLO alerts on errors and duration, because those are what users feel. For a database host I would use USE, for example CPU utilisation, disk I/O wait and queue length (saturation), and connection errors, using node_exporter on port 9100. USE metrics usually become dashboards and tickets, not pages, unless saturation is about to cause user-visible failure.
keyPoints: RED = Rate, Errors, Duration for request-driven services
USE = Utilisation, Saturation, Errors for resources
Golden signals = latency, traffic, errors, saturation
Page on user-facing RED symptoms; use USE mostly for diagnosis

subjective.question: What is a cardinality explosion in Prometheus, how would you detect one, and how would you fix it?
subjective.answer: Each unique combination of metric name and label values is a separate time series. If a label holds unbounded values, such as user IDs, emails, raw URLs with IDs in them, or request IDs, the series count grows without limit. Memory use on Prometheus rises, queries slow down, and the server can run out of memory. To detect it, I check prometheus_tsdb_head_series for sudden growth and use the TSDB status page in the Prometheus UI, which lists the metrics and labels with the most series. A query such as topk(10, count by (__name__)({__name__=~".+"})) also helps. To fix it, I change the instrumentation to use bounded labels, such as a templated route like /users/{id} instead of the raw path. In the meantime I can drop or relabel the bad label with metric_relabel_configs, and set sample limits on scrape jobs. Per-user detail belongs in logs or trace attributes, not metric labels.
keyPoints: Every label combination is a new series; unbounded labels explode the count
Detect via prometheus_tsdb_head_series, the TSDB status page and topk count queries
Fix instrumentation with templated routes and bounded values
Short-term: metric_relabel_configs to drop labels, sample_limit; move per-request detail to logs and traces

subjective.question: What are recording rules, and why are they useful for SLO dashboards and alerts?
subjective.answer: Recording rules let Prometheus evaluate an expression on a schedule, set by evaluation_interval, which defaults to 1m. The result is stored as a new time series. The convention is to name it level:metric:operations, for example job:http_requests:rate5m or service:sli_error_ratio:rate1h. For SLOs, a burn-rate alert needs the same error ratio over several windows: 5m, 30m, 1h, 6h and longer. Computing those over raw, high-volume counters on every dashboard refresh and every alert evaluation is expensive and slow. Recording rules compute each ratio once, so alert expressions stay short and readable, dashboards load fast, and every consumer uses an identical definition of the SLI. They also reduce the risk of copy-paste mistakes between alerts and panels. I would keep recording and alerting rules in version control, test them with promtool test rules, and deploy them through CI or GitOps along with the service.
keyPoints: Precompute expressions into new series on each evaluation interval
Naming convention level:metric:operations
Make multi-window SLO ratios cheap, consistent and reusable
Version-control and test with promtool; deploy through CI or GitOps

subjective.question: Walk through how you would run an incident and then write a blameless postmortem for it.
subjective.answer: When a page fires, I acknowledge it and assess the user impact. If the incident is serious, I declare it and assign roles. The incident commander coordinates and makes decisions. An operations lead works hands-on on the fix. A communications lead updates stakeholders and the status page. A scribe keeps a timeline. The first priority is mitigation, not root cause: roll back, fail over, scale up or disable a feature flag. I keep updates regular in a single incident channel. After resolution, I write a blameless postmortem within a few days. It includes a summary, the impact in users and minutes, how much error budget was consumed, a detailed timeline, how the incident was detected, the root cause and contributing factors, what went well and what did not, and action items with owners and due dates. Blameless means we examine systems and processes, not individuals. People acted reasonably with the information they had, which encourages honest reporting and real fixes.
keyPoints: Clear roles: incident commander, operations, communications, scribe
Mitigate first; find root cause later
Postmortem: impact, timeline, detection, root cause, contributing factors, action items with owners
Blameless culture focuses on systems and processes, not people

subjective.question: Your team complains about noisy on-call. How would you reduce noise with alert design and Alertmanager, and how would you prove your new SLO alert works?
subjective.answer: First, I audit the alerts. Each page must be urgent, user-visible and actionable, and it must have a runbook_url. Cause-based pages, such as high CPU on one pod, become tickets or dashboard panels. Symptom-based burn-rate alerts replace them. In Alertmanager, group_by on labels such as alertname, service and cluster bundles related alerts into one notification. group_wait sets how long to wait before the first notification of a group. group_interval sets how often updates to that group are sent. repeat_interval stops the same alert from being re-sent too often. Inhibition rules mute warnings while a related critical alert fires. Silences cover planned maintenance. Routing sends severity: page to the pager and everything else to chat or tickets. To prove the SLO alert works, I run a load test, for example with k6, against the service while injecting errors. I then confirm that the burn-rate alert fires, that it names the symptom and links the runbook, and that it resolves once the errors stop.
keyPoints: Page only for urgent, user-visible, actionable symptoms with a runbook_url
group_by, group_wait, group_interval and repeat_interval control notification volume
Inhibition for dependent alerts, silences for maintenance, severity-based routing
Validate with a load test plus fault injection: the alert fires, names the symptom and resolves

subjective.question: After you deploy a new service to Kubernetes, its target shows as DOWN on the Prometheus Targets page with the error shown below. How would you troubleshoot this step by step?

code.code:
Endpoint: http://10.42.3.17:8080/metrics
State: DOWN
Error: Get "http://10.42.3.17:8080/metrics": context deadline exceeded

subjective.answer: Context deadline exceeded means Prometheus reached for the endpoint but got no response within scrape_timeout. So the target was discovered and only the scrape itself failed. First, I check that the pod is Running and Ready, and that the app really listens on 8080 and serves /metrics. I run kubectl port-forward and curl the endpoint. If the metrics are on a different port or path, I fix the Service port name, the ServiceMonitor or the scrape annotations. Next, I test the network from the Prometheus pod with curl or wget to the pod IP. A NetworkPolicy that blocks the monitoring namespace is a common cause. If the endpoint answers but slowly, the /metrics handler may be expensive or the response huge because of high cardinality. I measure the response size and time, then fix the labels or raise scrape_timeout carefully. Finally, I confirm that up{job="..."} returns 1 and that scrape_duration_seconds stays well under the timeout.
keyPoints: Read the error: discovery worked, but the scrape timed out
Verify the pod, port and path with port-forward and curl
Check NetworkPolicies between the Prometheus and app namespaces
Check for slow or huge /metrics responses using scrape_duration_seconds
Confirm the fix using up == 1

subjective.question: Halfway through the month, your service has used its entire 30-day error budget. The product team wants to ship a large new feature this week. How do you handle this, and what should an error budget policy say?
subjective.answer: An exhausted budget means users have already had more unreliability than we agreed was acceptable. So the default answer is to slow down risky change, not to keep shipping as normal. A written error budget policy, agreed in advance by product, engineering and SRE leadership, makes this a rule rather than an argument. Typically, it freezes non-critical feature releases until the budget recovers over the rolling window. Security fixes and reliability fixes are still allowed. It also shifts engineering effort to the top causes from recent postmortems and names who can grant exceptions. For this feature, I would share the budget burn data, the incidents that caused it and the fixes in progress. If the business still needs the launch, an exec can approve an exception. We would then reduce the risk with a feature flag, a canary rollout and a tested rollback. The key idea is that the SLO, not opinion, decides how fast we ship.
keyPoints: An exhausted budget means reliability work takes priority over features
A pre-agreed, written error budget policy removes negotiation during the crisis
The policy usually freezes non-critical releases but allows security and reliability fixes
Exceptions need a named approver
Lower the risk of any release with feature flags, canaries and rollback

subjective.question: Service A calls service B directly over HTTP, and also publishes messages to Kafka that service C consumes. In your tracing backend, the A-to-B calls appear in one trace, but service C's spans always start new, separate traces. Why does this happen, and how do you fix it?
subjective.answer: Traces join across services through context propagation. The caller injects the trace context, usually as the W3C traceparent header, and the callee extracts it and creates child spans. For HTTP, OpenTelemetry's instrumentation libraries do this automatically, which is why A to B works. For Kafka, the context must travel inside the message headers. If the producer does not inject it, or the consumer does not extract it, C starts a new root span. To fix it, I use the OpenTelemetry Kafka instrumentation for both client libraries, or I call the propagator API manually. That means inject into the record headers when producing and extract when consuming. I also check that both sides use the same propagators, for example tracecontext and baggage. For asynchronous or batch consumers, span links are often more accurate than parent-child relationships. Finally, I check that no proxy or broker configuration strips the headers.
keyPoints: Traces join only through context propagation (W3C traceparent)
HTTP instrumentation propagates context automatically; messaging often needs explicit inject and extract in message headers
Both sides must use the same propagators
Use span links for async and batch consumers
Check that intermediaries do not strip the headers

subjective.question: Your latency SLO says 99% of requests to the checkout service complete in under 300 ms. The histogram has a bucket at le="0.3". Write the PromQL SLI and explain the design choices.

code.code:
sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="checkout",le="0.3"}[5m]))
/
sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count{job="checkout"}[5m]))

subjective.answer: This is a ratio SLI: good events divided by valid events. Histogram buckets are cumulative, so the le="0.3" bucket already counts every request that finished in 300 ms or less. Dividing it by _count gives the fraction of fast requests. The SLO is met when this ratio is at least 0.99. The error rate for burn-rate alerts is 1 minus the ratio. This is exact, unlike histogram_quantile(), which interpolates within buckets. For that reason, the SLO threshold must match a real bucket boundary, which is something you decide when you instrument the service. I would rate each series first and then sum, so that counter resets are handled correctly. I might also exclude health checks, or count only certain status codes, so that 'valid' means real user requests. Finally, I would save the ratio as recording rules over several windows, such as 5m, 30m, 1h and 6h. That keeps burn-rate alerts and dashboards cheap to evaluate.
keyPoints: Ratio SLI: requests under the threshold divided by total requests
Buckets are cumulative, so le="0.3" counts all requests of 300 ms or less
The threshold must be an exact bucket boundary; this is more exact than histogram_quantile
Rate first, then sum; filter out non-user traffic
Precompute several windows with recording rules for burn-rate alerts

subjective.question: You are asked to build a Grafana dashboard for a team's REST service, and the org already has hundreds of unmaintained dashboards. How would you design this one so on-call engineers actually use it?
subjective.answer: I would design it around the questions on-call asks first: are users hurting, and since when? The top row shows the SLO status: the current SLI, the error budget remaining and the burn rate.
