project.title: hello-pipeline
project.summary: A tiny Python web service that goes from git commit to a production Kubernetes cluster: GitHub Actions builds, smoke-tests and pushes the image, then commits the new image tag so Argo CD (GitOps) deploys it, and a script reports the DORA metrics. app/main.py and Dockerfile are the code, .github/workflows/pipeline.yml is CI/CD, k8s/ and argocd/ are the GitOps deployment, scripts/dora.py measures delivery performance, and README.md is the portfolio write-up with diagram, metrics and exam plan.
project.run:
docker build -t hello-pipeline --build-arg APP_VERSION=local .
docker run --rm -p 8080:8080 hello-pipeline
curl -fsS localhost:8080/healthz
kubectl apply -f argocd/application.yaml
git push origin main
GITHUB_REPOSITORY=your-org/hello-pipeline GITHUB_TOKEN=<token> python3 scripts/dora.py

files.code:
"""hello-pipeline: a minimal HTTP service with health and version endpoints.
Standard library only, so the image stays small and there is nothing to install.
"""
import json
import os
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, ThreadingHTTPServer

PORT = int(os.environ.get("PORT", "8080"))          # same port as Dockerfile and k8s Service
APP_VERSION = os.environ.get("APP_VERSION", "dev")  # set to the git SHA at build time


class Handler(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def _send(self, status, body):
        data = json.dumps(body).encode()
        self.send_response(status)
        self.send_header("Content-Type", "application/json")
        self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(data)))
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(data)

    def do_GET(self):
        if self.path == "/healthz":
            # Used by the CI smoke test and the Kubernetes probes
            self._send(200, {"status": "ok"})
        elif self.path == "/":
            # The version lets you prove which commit is running in production
            self._send(200, {"app": "hello-pipeline", "version": APP_VERSION})
        else:
            self._send(404, {"error": "not found"})

    def log_message(self, fmt, *args):
        # One line per request to stdout, picked up by kubectl logs
        print(f"{self.address_string()} {fmt % args}", flush=True)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(f"hello-pipeline {APP_VERSION} listening on :{PORT}", flush=True)
    ThreadingHTTPServer(("0.0.0.0", PORT), Handler).serve_forever()

# Small, non-root image for hello-pipeline
FROM python:3.12-slim

# The pipeline passes the git SHA so the running app reports its own version
ARG APP_VERSION=dev
ENV APP_VERSION=${APP_VERSION} \
    PORT=8080 \
    PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1

WORKDIR /app
COPY app/main.py .

# Run as an unprivileged user (matches runAsNonRoot in k8s/deployment.yaml)
USER 65534:65534

EXPOSE 8080
CMD ["python", "main.py"]

# Commit -> build -> smoke test -> push -> GitOps deploy
name: pipeline

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    paths-ignore: ['k8s/**', 'README.md']   # the deploy commit must not re-trigger the build
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: write    # deploy job commits the new image tag
  packages: write    # push to GitHub Container Registry

jobs:
  build-test-push:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Set lowercase image name   # GHCR needs lowercase
        run: echo "IMAGE=ghcr.io/${GITHUB_REPOSITORY,,}" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"
      - name: Build image tagged with the commit SHA
        run: docker build -t "$IMAGE:$GITHUB_SHA" --build-arg APP_VERSION="$GITHUB_SHA" .
      - name: Smoke test the container
        run: |
          docker run -d --name app -p 8080:8080 "$IMAGE:$GITHUB_SHA"
          for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do curl -fsS localhost:8080/healthz && exit 0; sleep 2; done
          docker logs app; exit 1
      - uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
      - name: Push image
        run: docker push "$IMAGE:$GITHUB_SHA"

  deploy:
    needs: build-test-push
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production          # add required reviewers here for a manual gate
    concurrency: production          # one deploy at a time
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Bump image tag in the GitOps manifest
        run: |
          IMAGE="ghcr.io/${GITHUB_REPOSITORY,,}"
          sed -i "s|image: ghcr.io/.*|image: $IMAGE:$GITHUB_SHA|" k8s/deployment.yaml
          grep 'image:' k8s/deployment.yaml
      - name: Commit and push (Argo CD syncs this to the cluster)
        run: |
          git config user.name "github-actions[bot]"
          git config user.email "41898282+github-actions[bot]@users.noreply.github.com"
          git commit -am "deploy: hello-pipeline $GITHUB_SHA"
          git push

# Desired production state. Argo CD applies whatever is in this folder.
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: hello-pipeline
  labels:
    app: hello-pipeline
spec:
  replicas: 2
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxUnavailable: 0        # never drop below 2 ready pods during a deploy
      maxSurge: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: hello-pipeline
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: hello-pipeline
    spec:
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true
      containers:
        - name: app
          image: ghcr.io/your-org/hello-pipeline:latest   # replaced by the pipeline with the commit SHA
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          env:
            - name: PORT
              value: "8080"
          readinessProbe:      # a bad build never receives traffic
            httpGet:
              path: /healthz
              port: 8080
            periodSeconds: 5
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /healthz
              port: 8080
            periodSeconds: 10
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 50m
              memory: 32Mi
            limits:
              memory: 128Mi
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: hello-pipeline
spec:
  selector:
    app: hello-pipeline
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080

# Apply once: kubectl apply -f argocd/application.yaml
# Argo CD then pulls k8s/ from main and keeps the cluster in sync.
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: hello-pipeline
  namespace: argocd              # namespace where Argo CD is installed
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/your-org/hello-pipeline.git   # your public repo
    targetRevision: main
    path: k8s                    # only the manifests, not this file
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: hello
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true                # delete resources removed from git
      selfHeal: true             # undo manual kubectl changes (drift)
    syncOptions:
      - CreateNamespace=true

"""Estimate DORA metrics from the last 30 days of pipeline runs on main.
Usage: GITHUB_REPOSITORY=owner/repo GITHUB_TOKEN=... python3 scripts/dora.py
A successful run = one production deploy (Argo CD syncs within minutes).
"""
import json
import os
import urllib.request
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone

REPO = os.environ["GITHUB_REPOSITORY"]
TOKEN = os.environ.get("GITHUB_TOKEN", "")
URL = (f"https://api.github.com/repos/{REPO}/actions/workflows/pipeline.yml/runs"
       "?branch=main&status=completed&per_page=100")


def ts(s):
    return datetime.fromisoformat(s.replace("Z", "+00:00"))


req = urllib.request.Request(URL, headers={"Accept": "application/vnd.github+json"})
if TOKEN:
    req.add_header("Authorization", f"Bearer {TOKEN}")
runs = json.load(urllib.request.urlopen(req))["workflow_runs"]

since = datetime.now(timezone.utc) - timedelta(days=30)
runs = sorted((r for r in runs if ts(r["created_at"]) >= since), key=lambda r: r["created_at"])
ok = [r for r in runs if r["conclusion"] == "success"]
failed = [r for r in runs if r["conclusion"] == "failure"]

# Lead time for changes: commit timestamp -> pipeline finished
lead = [(ts(r["updated_at"]) - ts(r["head_commit"]["timestamp"])).total_seconds() / 60 for r in ok]

# Time to restore: first failure -> next success (proxy for failed deployment recovery)
restore, broken_at = [], None
for r in runs:
    if r["conclusion"] == "failure" and broken_at is None:
        broken_at = ts(r["updated_at"])
    elif r["conclusion"] == "success" and broken_at is not None:
        restore.append((ts(r["updated_at"]) - broken_at).total_seconds() / 60)
        broken_at = None

print(f"Runs in last 30 days       : {len(runs)}")
print(f"Deployment frequency       : {len(ok) / 30 * 7:.1f} per week")
if lead:
    print(f"Median lead time (minutes) : {sorted(lead)[len(lead) // 2]:.1f}")
if runs:
    print(f"Change failure rate (proxy): {len(failed) / len(runs):.0%}")
if restore:
    print(f"Mean time to restore (min) : {sum(restore) / len(restore):.1f}")

# hello-pipeline: commit to production

Every push to `main` is built, smoke-tested, pushed to GHCR and deployed to Kubernetes by Argo CD. No manual `kubectl` in the path.

## Architecture
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  Dev[git push main] --> GA[GitHub Actions: build + smoke test]
  GA --> GHCR[(ghcr.io image:SHA)]
  GA -->|commit new tag| Repo[k8s/deployment.yaml]
  Repo --> Argo[Argo CD auto-sync]
  Argo --> K8s[Deployment x2 + Service]
  GHCR --> K8s
```

## Setup
1. Replace `your-org` in `k8s/deployment.yaml` and `argocd/application.yaml`.
2. Make the GHCR package public (or add an imagePullSecret).
3. Install Argo CD, then `kubectl apply -f argocd/application.yaml`.
4. Push a change. Check `curl <service>/` returns the new commit SHA.

## DORA metrics this pipeline improves
| Metric | How | Measure |
|---|---|---|
| Deployment frequency | Every merge to main deploys | `scripts/dora.py` |
| Lead time for changes | No manual steps, minutes not days | commit -> run finished |
| Change failure rate | Smoke test + readiness probe block bad builds | failed runs / runs |
| Time to restore | `git revert` -> Argo CD rolls back | failure -> next success |

## Exam plan (Week 14)
1. Terraform Associate first (multiple choice, online proctored). Book it now.
2. Then CKAD or CKA (performance-based, live cluster, 2 hours, 66% pass). Use both included simulator sessions under timed conditions.
3. Then a cloud DevOps exam: AWS DOP-C02 or Microsoft AZ-400.

## Exam-day readiness
- Run the proctoring system check days before; valid government photo ID.
- Clear desk, closed room, one screen, stable internet.
- Kubernetes exams: set `alias k=kubectl`, switch context for every task, use `--dry-run=client -o yaml`, skip hard tasks and return.

revision.examFocus: This step covers exam strategy, not a single exam domain: choosing the order of Terraform Associate, CKAD/CKA and a cloud DevOps exam, and surviving exam-day conditions. It also covers the portfolio evidence that interviewers check: a commit-to-production pipeline and DORA metrics you can actually measure. The Kubernetes exams test speed and accuracy on live clusters. The multiple-choice exams test scenario judgement under a clock. Interviews test whether your DORA numbers are real.

compare.difference: CKAD focuses on building and running workloads (Pods, Deployments, ConfigMaps, probes, Jobs, Services). CKA adds cluster operations such as kubeadm upgrades, etcd backup and restore, node troubleshooting, RBAC and networking.
compare.chooseA: Pick CKAD first if your daily work is shipping apps to Kubernetes and you want the faster win.
compare.chooseB: Pick CKA first if you run or fix clusters, or if the job role says platform or SRE.

compare.difference: The simulator is deliberately harder and longer than the real exam. It is a training tool, not a score predictor.
compare.chooseA: Use it a week or more before the exam to find weak areas and practise the exam interface.
compare.chooseB: Trust your readiness for the real exam if you finish most simulator tasks and can explain each solution, even if your simulator score looks low.

compare.difference: DOP-C02 is a standalone professional exam. The AZ-400 Expert title is awarded only if you also hold AZ-104 or AZ-204.
compare.chooseA: Choose DOP-C02 if your target employers run on AWS and you can commit to a long, scenario-heavy paper.
compare.chooseB: Choose AZ-400 if your target employers use Azure or Azure DevOps and you already hold, or plan to take, AZ-104 or AZ-204.

compare.a: Deployment frequency / lead time for changes
compare.b: Change failure rate / time to restore
compare.difference: The first pair measures throughput (how fast change flows). The second pair measures stability (how often change breaks things and how quickly you recover).
compare.chooseA: Quote these when your pipeline adds automation that removes waiting, such as automated tests, auto-deploy on merge or smaller batches.
compare.chooseB: Quote these when your pipeline adds safety, such as canary or blue-green releases, automated rollback, health checks and alerts.

compare.difference: Both are short multiple-choice exams. Terraform Associate is the cheaper, more widely requested baseline, and its IaC skills feed directly into later cloud exams.
compare.chooseA: Default to Terraform Associate as the first exam on this path.
compare.chooseB: Go with GitHub Actions first only if your current job is already built on Actions and you can pass it quickly.

cues.cue: Which exam should a beginner book first to build momentum?
cues.pick: Terraform Associate
cues.why: It is short, cheap and multiple choice, so a quick pass keeps motivation up for the harder hands-on exams.

cues.cue: Task says 'set the context to …' or names a cluster
cues.pick: Run kubectl config use-context <name> before any other command
cues.why: Grading checks the named cluster only, so correct work done on another cluster scores nothing.

cues.cue: Running out of time in the CKA/CKAD simulator
cues.pick: Imperative commands plus --dry-run=client -o yaml, then edit the YAML
cues.why: Generating manifests is far faster than typing them, and you can skip hard tasks and return later.

cues.cue: How did you measure lead time?
cues.pick: Time from commit (or merge) timestamp to production deploy timestamp, taken from CI/CD logs
cues.why: A number with a stated source and method is defensible in an interview; a guess is not.

cues.cue: A cloud key was committed to the repo history
cues.pick: Revoke and rotate the key first, then rewrite history (for example with git filter-repo) and add secret scanning
cues.why: Once pushed, a secret must be treated as leaked, so cleaning history alone is not enough.

cues.cue: Pipeline adds automated rollback and canary releases
cues.pick: Change failure rate and time to restore
cues.why: These safety features reduce the impact of bad changes and speed recovery, which are the stability metrics.

cues.cue: Online proctored exam with a work laptop, VPN or second monitor
cues.pick: Use a personal machine, disconnect extra monitors and run the vendor system check days before
cues.why: Blocked ports, corporate security agents or extra screens commonly stop or cancel the session.

cues.cue: CKA/CKAD: 'Can I look this up?'
cues.pick: Official Kubernetes documentation only, inside the exam browser
cues.why: Other sites are not allowed, so practise finding YAML examples in kubernetes.io/docs quickly.

scenario.situation: Priya has six weeks before job interviews. She knows Terraform from work, has used Kubernetes for three months, and has never sat a hands-on exam. She plans to book DOP-C02 first because it is the most respected, and then do Terraform Associate and CKAD. Which plan gives her the best chance of earning certificates before interviews?
reasoning: DOP-C02 first is a known trap. It is long and costly, and an early fail drains time and confidence.
She already uses Terraform, so Terraform Associate is a quick, low-risk first pass that gets a certificate on her CV within the first one or two weeks.
CKAD fits her app-focused Kubernetes experience. She should practise timed tasks, use both Killer.sh sessions, and keep the free retake as a safety net.
A cloud professional exam comes last, once IaC and Kubernetes skills are solid, because its scenarios assume both.
scenario.answer: Book Terraform Associate first, then CKAD with timed simulator practice, then the cloud DevOps exam. This order gives early wins and builds the skills each later exam assumes.

memoryAids: Exam order 'T-K-C': Terraform, then Kubernetes, then Cloud. Climb from easy to hard.
DORA 'Two Fast, Two Safe': Frequency and Lead time are fast; Failure rate and Restore time are safe.
Every Kubernetes task: 'Context, Copy, Check'. Switch context, copy names exactly from the task, then check the result with kubectl get or describe.
cheatSheet: Book the first exam now; a fixed date drives study better than open-ended prep.
CKA/CKAD: set alias k=kubectl and a dry-run variable at the start, and use kubectl explain for field names.
Skip any Kubernetes task taking more than about 7–8 minutes, flag it, and come back later.
Copy resource names and namespaces from the task text; typos score zero.
Killer.sh gives two sessions with a limited access window each. Do the first early and the second a few days before the exam.
A low simulator score is normal because it is harder than the real exam. Review every solution afterwards.
Run the proctoring system check days before, on the same machine, network and room you will use.
Keep a clear desk, valid ID, one monitor and no VPN; close every other app.
The repo README needs an architecture diagram of commit → build → test → scan → deploy → monitor.
Every DORA claim needs a before value, an after value and a data source.
Before making the repo public, scan the full history for secrets; no keys, .tfstate or kubeconfig files.
Newer DORA reports call time to restore 'failed deployment recovery time'. Know both names for interviews.
selfCheck: I can justify my exam order and name the date I have booked for the first exam.
I can finish a Killer.sh session within the time limit, switching context correctly on every task.
I can pass the proctoring system check on the exact setup I will use on exam day.
I can walk an interviewer through my pipeline diagram from commit to production in under two minutes.
I can state each DORA metric my pipeline improves, with before and after values and how I measured them.
I can show that my public repository history contains no secrets, state files or kubeconfig.

objective.question: You are starting the certification part of the DevOps path. You already use Terraform at work and are learning Kubernetes. Which exam order matches the recommended sequence?
options: DOP-C02 first, then CKA, then Terraform Associate
AZ-400 first, because it needs no other Microsoft certification
CKA and CKAD on the same day, then Terraform Associate
Terraform Associate, then CKAD or CKA, then a cloud DevOps exam such as DOP-C02 or AZ-400
objective.explanation: The sensible order starts with the shorter multiple-choice Terraform Associate, moves to the hands-on Kubernetes exams, and ends with the broad professional cloud DevOps exam. DOP-C02 is the hardest of these and fits best at the end. AZ-400 needs AZ-104 or AZ-204 to earn the Expert title.

objective.question: A CKA task begins with: 'Set the configuration context: kubectl config use-context k8s-prod'. You are still in the context from the previous task. You create the Deployment correctly and move on. What is the most likely result?
options: No marks, because the work was done in the wrong cluster and the grader checks the named context
The exam software switches the context for you, so there is no impact
Partial marks, because the grader checks every context
Full marks, because the Deployment manifest is correct
objective.explanation: Each task is graded against the cluster named in its context. If you skip the use-context command, your work ends up in the wrong cluster and earns nothing. The exam does not switch the context for you.

objective.question: During the CKAD exam you forget the exact field layout of a NetworkPolicy. Which resource may you use?
options: Stack Overflow in a second browser tab
The official Kubernetes documentation in the exam browser
A printed cheat sheet kept on your desk
A personal GitHub gist of your practice YAML
objective.explanation: CKA and CKAD allow the official Kubernetes documentation inside the exam browser. Other websites, personal notes and printed material are not allowed.

objective.question: A learner scores 55% in a Killer.sh simulator session three days before the CKA. What is the best interpretation?
options: The simulator is harder than the real exam, so they should review the missed tasks, work on speed, and use the remaining session
The simulator uses a different pass mark, so the score means nothing
They should cancel the exam, because simulator scores match real scores exactly
They will certainly fail because the pass mark is 66%
objective.explanation: Killer.sh is designed to be harder than the real exam, so a lower score there does not predict failure. Its real value is the solution walkthrough and the time-pressure practice. Treat it as a diagnostic tool, not a forecast.

objective.question: Your team wants a DORA dashboard that shows whether releases are stable. Which two metrics belong to the stability group?
options: Change failure rate and time to restore service
Deployment frequency and time to restore service
Lead time for changes and change failure rate
Deployment frequency and lead time for changes
objective.explanation: Change failure rate and time to restore measure stability. Deployment frequency and lead time for changes measure speed (throughput).

objective.question: An Azure engineer passes AZ-400 but holds no other Microsoft certification. What is true about the Microsoft Certified: DevOps Engineer Expert title?
options: It also needs AZ-104 (Administrator) or AZ-204 (Developer)
It needs both AZ-104 and AZ-204
It also needs AZ-900 Fundamentals
It is awarded immediately on passing AZ-400
objective.explanation: The Expert title requires AZ-400 plus one prerequisite, either AZ-104 or AZ-204. AZ-900 is not a prerequisite, and you do not need both associate exams.

objective.question: You are planning your pace for AWS DOP-C02, which has 75 questions in 180 minutes. Which plan is the most realistic?
options: Answer every question in order and never flag
About 5 minutes per question so each scenario gets full attention
About 2 minutes per question on the first pass, flag long scenarios, then use the remaining time for flagged items
About 1 minute per question, leaving 105 minutes for review
objective.explanation: 180 minutes for 75 questions is about 2.4 minutes each. A first pass at about 2 minutes per question leaves roughly 30 minutes for flagged questions. Five minutes per question would need 375 minutes, which is far over the limit.

objective.question: Your pipeline adds a canary stage. If error rate or latency breaches a threshold, Argo Rollouts automatically aborts and returns traffic to the stable version within minutes. Which DORA metric does this mainly improve?
options: Time to restore service
Code review throughput
Lead time for changes
Deployment frequency
objective.explanation: Automatic abort and rollback cut the time from a failed change to a healthy service, which is time to restore. It can also reduce how many failures reach all users. It does not directly change how often you deploy or how long a commit takes to reach production, and code review throughput is not a DORA metric.

objective.question: You are taking an online proctored exam, such as Terraform Associate, from home. Which preparation step is most likely to stop the exam being delayed or revoked?
options: Run the provider's system check beforehand, clear the desk, close other applications, and have valid ID ready
Join an hour late, since online exams have flexible start times
Keep your phone face up on the desk in case the proctor calls
Keep a second monitor on so you can read the clock
objective.explanation: Online proctoring needs a passing system check, a clean workspace, no other applications running and a valid ID. Extra monitors and a phone in reach usually break the rules. Check-in windows are strict, so joining late is risky.

objective.question: A candidate fails the CKAD on the first attempt with 61%. What is true?
options: The registration includes one free retake within the eligibility period
They must wait one year before trying again
They passed, because the pass mark is 60%
They must pay the full fee again to retake
objective.explanation: CKA and CKAD registrations include one free retake, and the pass mark is 66%. A score of 61% is a fail, but the candidate can use the included retake without paying again.

objective.question: You are practising speed techniques for the CKA. What does the last command below do?

code.code:
alias k=kubectl
export do="--dry-run=client -o yaml"
k create deployment web --image=nginx:1.27 --replicas=3 $do > web.yaml

options: It writes a Deployment manifest with 3 replicas to web.yaml without creating anything in the cluster
It creates the Deployment with 0 replicas first and saves the manifest so you can scale it later
It validates the Deployment on the API server and fails if the image does not exist
It creates the Deployment in the cluster and also saves a copy of its YAML to web.yaml
objective.explanation: With --dry-run=client, kubectl builds the object locally and prints it as YAML, so nothing is sent to the cluster and the output goes to web.yaml for editing. Server-side validation needs --dry-run=server, and no image check happens in either mode.

objective.question: Your portfolio README reports DORA lead time for changes. A single change has the timestamps below. What is its lead time for changes?

code.code:
commit pushed:            09:00
PR merged to main:        11:30
CI pipeline finished:     11:50
running in production:    14:10

options: 2 hours 40 minutes
2 hours 50 minutes
5 hours 10 minutes
20 minutes
objective.explanation: DORA defines lead time for changes as the time from code committed to code successfully running in production, so the answer is 09:00 to 14:10. The other options measure only part of the path, such as CI duration or merge-to-production time.

objective.question: In your portfolio repository, the GitHub environment named 'production' has required reviewers configured. What happens when this workflow runs after staging succeeds?

code.code:
jobs:
  deploy-prod:
    needs: deploy-staging
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: ./deploy.sh prod

options: The workflow fails because environment jobs must be in a separate workflow file
The job skips checkout and runs only when someone triggers it with workflow_dispatch
The job waits for a required reviewer to approve it, and the production environment secrets are only available after approval
The job runs at once, and reviewers are notified after the deploy finishes
objective.explanation: When a job references an environment that has protection rules, the job pauses until a required reviewer approves it. The environment's secrets are not exposed to the job before approval. No separate file or manual trigger is needed.

objective.question: Last month your pipeline made 50 production deployments. 4 were rolled back, 2 needed a hotfix, and 1 more failed in staging and never reached production. What is the change failure rate?
objective.explanation: Change failure rate is the share of production deployments that cause a failure needing remediation, such as a rollback or hotfix. That is 6 out of 50, or 12%. The staging failure never reached production, so it does not count.

objective.question: A CKA task says: 'Solve this question on instance: ssh cka-cp2'. You edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml in the terminal you are already in, and the command succeeds. What is the most likely outcome?
options: The exam terminal automatically forwards file edits to the host named in the task
You changed a file on the wrong machine, so the task's cluster is unchanged and the task scores nothing
The kubelet on cka-cp2 detects the edit over the network and restarts the API server
The change is applied, because all exam hosts share the same /etc/kubernetes directory
objective.explanation: Static Pod manifests are read only by the kubelet on that node, so you must SSH to the named host, usually with sudo, before editing. Each host has its own filesystem. Remember to exit back to the base terminal before starting the next task.

objective.question: Before you publish your pipeline repository, you find that terraform.tfstate was committed months ago. It contains a database password in plain text. Which action fully fixes the problem?
options: Rotate the leaked credentials, purge the file from Git history, move state to a remote backend with locking, and ignore *.tfstate
Make the repository private until the hiring process is over
Mark the password variable as sensitive = true so it is masked in the state file
Delete terraform.tfstate in a new commit and add it to .gitignore
objective.explanation: A new commit leaves the secret in Git history, so you must treat the secret as compromised, rotate it, and rewrite the history. sensitive = true only hides values in CLI output; they are still stored in plain text in state. A remote backend with locking and a .gitignore entry stop it happening again, and making the repository private does not undo the earlier exposure.

subjective.question: Explain the order in which you would take Terraform Associate, CKA or CKAD, and a cloud DevOps exam, and why.
subjective.answer: I would start with Terraform Associate. It is a one-hour, multiple-choice, online proctored exam costing about USD 70. It is a low-risk first certificate, and infrastructure as code underpins everything else I build. Next I would take CKAD or CKA. Both are two-hour, performance-based exams in a live cluster with a 66% pass mark. They need many hours of hands-on practice, so I schedule them once my Kubernetes work is routine. I would pick CKAD if I mostly ship applications and CKA if I run clusters. Last comes a cloud DevOps exam: AWS DOP-C02 (75 questions, 180 minutes, USD 300, pass 750/1000) or AZ-400, which needs AZ-104 or AZ-204 for the Expert title. These professional exams test end-to-end design, so they gain the most from the earlier skills. The order builds confidence and spreads the cost.
keyPoints: Terraform Associate first: short, multiple choice, low cost
CKAD or CKA next: hands-on, needs practice in a live cluster
Cloud DevOps exam last: broadest and most expensive
Choose CKAD or CKA based on your role
Note that AZ-400 needs AZ-104 or AZ-204

subjective.question: How does preparing for a performance-based exam like CKA differ from preparing for a multiple-choice exam?
subjective.answer: A multiple-choice exam rewards recognition. You can study concepts and eliminate wrong options. A performance-based exam gives you a terminal and live clusters, and you must complete the tasks yourself. So I train for speed and accuracy at the command line. I use imperative commands such as kubectl create and kubectl run with --dry-run=client -o yaml to generate manifests and then edit them. I set an alias like k=kubectl and get fast with vim and YAML indentation. I practise finding pages in the official Kubernetes docs quickly, because that is the only reference allowed. I also make it a habit to switch context at the start of every task, and to verify my result with kubectl get or describe. For multiple choice I would use question banks. For CKA I repeat timed labs until the common tasks feel automatic.
keyPoints: Multiple choice tests recognition; performance-based tests doing
Use imperative commands and --dry-run=client -o yaml for speed
Navigate the official docs quickly, the only allowed reference
Switch context first and verify every task
Practise with timed labs, not just reading

subjective.question: Your CKA registration includes Killer.sh simulator sessions. How would you use them to get the most value?
subjective.answer: I would not use the first session too early. I would book it once I have covered the syllabus, about one to two weeks before the exam. I sit it under real conditions: two hours, no notes, only the Kubernetes docs. I expect a lower score than in the real exam, because the simulator is deliberately harder. Afterwards, the environment stays available for a while, so I redo every task I missed or did slowly, and I read the provided solutions to learn faster commands. I note my weak areas, for example etcd backup or troubleshooting a broken kubelet, and drill them. I save the second session for a few days before the exam. I use it to confirm my pace and my habits, such as switching context, skipping and flagging heavy tasks, and checking my work. The score matters less than the gaps it reveals.
keyPoints: Use the sessions after covering the syllabus, not on day one
Sit them under real exam conditions
The simulator is harder, so do not panic about the score
Redo missed tasks and study the solutions
Use the second session to confirm pace and habits

subjective.question: Walk me through your end-to-end pipeline repository from commit to production.
subjective.answer: A developer opens a pull request on GitHub. GitHub Actions runs lint, unit tests and a security scan, then builds a container image tagged with the commit SHA and pushes it to the registry. After the merge, a job updates the image tag in a separate GitOps config repository. Argo CD watches that repository and syncs the change, first to staging and then to production. Production uses a canary rollout, and Prometheus metrics act as the gate: if error rate or latency breaches a threshold, the rollout is aborted. Terraform manages the cluster and the cloud resources, with plan on every pull request and apply only after approval. Grafana dashboards and alerts give observability. The README has an architecture diagram, setup steps, and the DORA metrics before and after automation. Anyone can clone it and follow a commit all the way to production.
keyPoints: PR checks: lint, tests, scan, then build an image tagged with the commit SHA
GitOps: update the config repo, Argo CD syncs the environments
Progressive delivery with metric-based rollback
Terraform for infrastructure, with plan on PR and gated apply
README with a diagram and DORA metrics

subjective.question: What are the DORA four key metrics, and how would you measure each from your own pipeline?
subjective.answer: DORA groups four metrics into speed and stability. Deployment frequency is how often you deploy to production. I count successful production syncs or deploy workflow runs per day or week. Lead time for changes is the time from commit to running in production. I subtract the commit timestamp from the production deploy timestamp, using the commit SHA in the image tag to link them. Change failure rate is the share of deployments that cause a failure needing a rollback, hotfix or incident. I tag rollbacks and incidents against deployments and divide by total deployments. Time to restore service is how long it takes to recover from a failure. I measure from the alert firing to the service being healthy again. The first two show speed and the last two show stability. Elite teams improve both together rather than trading one for the other.
keyPoints: Deployment frequency: production deploys per period
Lead time: time from commit to running in production
Change failure rate: failed deploys divided by total deploys
Time to restore: time from failure to recovery
Speed and stability should improve together

subjective.question: What should the architecture diagram in your portfolio repository show, and what mistakes would you avoid?
subjective.answer: The diagram should tell the commit-to-production story at a glance. I would show the developer and the Git repository, the CI system and its stages, the container registry, the GitOps config repository, Argo CD, the staging and production clusters, and the Terraform-managed cloud resources. I would also show the observability stack: Prometheus, Grafana and alerting. Arrows should show the direction of flow and label key events, such as 'PR opened', 'image pushed' and 'sync'. I would mark the trust boundaries and where secrets come from, for example OIDC to the cloud instead of long-lived keys. Mistakes to avoid: cramming in every component until it is unreadable, using unlabelled icons, letting the diagram drift from the real code, and skipping the rollback path. I keep the diagram as code, for example in Mermaid, so it is versioned with the repository.
keyPoints: Show the full flow from commit to production
Include CI, registry, GitOps, clusters, Terraform and observability
Label the arrows; show the secrets and trust boundaries
Show the rollback path
Keep it readable and versioned, for example as Mermaid

subjective.question: Describe your exam-day readiness checklist for an online proctored exam.
subjective.answer: A day or two before, I run the provider's system check on the exact laptop and network I will use. I close VPNs and background applications. I confirm that my government ID matches my registration name exactly. On the day, I use a quiet room with a clear desk and a single monitor, and my phone stays out of reach. I join the check-in early, because check-in includes room scans and ID checks. I keep a wired connection or a stable Wi-Fi backup and charge the laptop. During the exam I follow the proctor's instructions, avoid reading questions aloud and stay in camera view. For CKA and CKAD, I also prepare my opening routine in my head: set the alias, check the context in every task, and plan which tasks to skip and return to. Good logistics protect the score my preparation earned.
keyPoints: Run the system check on the same machine and network
ID must match the registration name
Clear desk, single monitor, no phone in reach
Join check-in early and keep the network stable
Have a mental routine for the hands-on exam

subjective.question: How would you manage your time in a two-hour CKA or CKAD exam with a 66% pass mark?
subjective.answer: The tasks carry different weights and vary in difficulty, so I do not work strictly in order. On each task I read the question fully, switch to the named context, and judge the effort. If a task looks long, or I get stuck after a few minutes, I flag it and move on. I collect the quick wins first, because 66% does not need perfection. I generate YAML with imperative commands instead of writing it from scratch, and I copy names directly from the question to avoid typos. After each task I verify it with kubectl get, describe or a quick test, because unverified work is a common way to lose marks. I keep the final part of the exam for flagged tasks, and I attempt partial solutions, since partially completed work can still earn some credit. Calm, steady progress beats perfectionism.
keyPoints: Tasks are weighted; do not get stuck on one
Flag hard tasks and collect quick wins first
Switch context and copy names exactly
Verify every task
Save time at the end for flagged and partial work

subjective.question: An interviewer asks: 'Your README claims your pipeline improved change failure rate. How do you know?' How do you answer honestly?
subjective.answer: I would explain the method, not just the number. First, I defined a failure: a production deployment that needed a rollback, hotfix or incident. Then I set a baseline by running the old manual process for a fixed number of deployments and recording the failures. After I added automated tests, image scanning and a canary with metric-based abort, I recorded the same data for a similar number of deployments. Rollbacks are tagged in Argo CD history and incidents are linked to commit SHAs, so the numbers can be checked. I would also state the limits. It is a personal project with low traffic and small sample sizes, so the trend matters more than the exact percentage. I also track the other three metrics, to show that stability did not improve simply because I deployed less often.
keyPoints: Define what counts as a failure first
Set a baseline, then compare after the change
Make the data traceable through tags and commit SHAs
State the limits: sample size, traffic
Check the other DORA metrics to avoid gaming one

subjective.question: A hiring manager says: 'Certificates are easy to collect. What proves you can actually do the work?' How do you respond using your portfolio?
subjective.answer: I agree that a certificate alone is not proof. That is why I pair one with a working repository. CKA is performance-based, so passing it already shows I can fix and configure a live cluster under time pressure. My repository shows the rest. Terraform builds the infrastructure. GitHub Actions tests, scans and builds images. Argo CD deploys through GitOps, and a canary with Prometheus-based rollback protects production. The commit history shows how I fixed real failures, and the README has an architecture diagram and DORA metrics before and after automation. I would invite them to pick any commit and I would trace it to production live. I can also explain the trade-offs I made, such as using GitOps instead of push-based deploys, or OIDC instead of static cloud keys. The certificate shows the baseline; the repository shows judgement.
keyPoints: A performance-based certificate shows hands-on skill
The repository shows code going from commit to production
Commit history shows real problem-solving
Offer a live walkthrough of one commit
Explain the design trade-offs

subjective.question: You are reviewing this workflow before showcasing it in your portfolio. What would you change to make it a safe, credible commit-to-production pipeline?

code.code:
on: push
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: docker build -t myorg/app:latest .
      - run: docker push myorg/app:latest
        env:
          AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID: ${{ secrets.AWS_KEY }}
          AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY: ${{ secrets.AWS_SECRET }}
      - run: kubectl set image deploy/app app=myorg/app:latest

subjective.answer: There are four problems. First, it deploys on every push to any branch with no tests, lint or image scan, so nothing stops a bad change. I would trigger production only from main, after a test job, using needs. Second, the latest tag is mutable. Rollbacks and audits become guesswork, and Kubernetes may not even roll out because the image reference has not changed. I would tag images with the commit SHA. Third, it uses long-lived AWS keys. I would use OIDC with id-token: write and a scoped IAM role. Fourth, it pushes directly to production with no staging step and no approval. I would deploy to staging, run smoke tests, and then gate production with a protected environment. Better still, I would update the image tag in a GitOps config repository and let Argo CD sync it. I would also set minimal permissions and pin action versions.
keyPoints: No test, scan or branch filter before deploying
Mutable latest tag breaks rollback and traceability; use the commit SHA
Replace static cloud keys with OIDC federation
Add staging, a protected production environment, or a GitOps handoff

subjective.question: Explain what this Argo CD Application does in your portfolio pipeline, and why CI does not run kubectl apply against production.

code.code:
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: shop-prod
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/me/shop-config
    targetRevision: main
    path: overlays/prod
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: shop
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true
      selfHeal: true

subjective.answer: This Application tells Argo CD to watch the overlays/prod path on the main branch of the shop-config repository and keep the shop namespace matching it. With automated sync, every merged change is applied without anyone running a command. prune: true deletes resources that were removed from Git. selfHeal: true reverts manual drift, for example if someone edits a Deployment with kubectl. In my pipeline, CI builds and tests the app, pushes an image tagged with the commit SHA, and then opens a pull request that bumps the tag in shop-config. CI never holds production cluster credentials. The cluster pulls changes instead of CI pushing them. Git becomes the audit log, and rollback is a git revert. This separation reduces the blast radius if the CI system is compromised, and it makes the state of production reviewable.
keyPoints: Argo CD syncs the cluster to a Git path and branch
prune removes deleted resources; selfHeal reverts drift
CI updates the image tag in the config repository instead of deploying
Pull model keeps cluster credentials out of CI; rollback is a git revert

subjective.question: During a CKAD practice session, a task's Pod is in CrashLoopBackOff and you have about six minutes left for it. Describe your troubleshooting sequence.
subjective.answer: First I confirm the context and namespace given in the task, because the wrong namespace wastes the most time. Then I run kubectl get pod with -o wide and kubectl describe pod, and I look at Events, Last State, the exit code and the probes. Next I run kubectl logs, and kubectl logs --previous, because the current container may have just restarted. The common causes are a wrong command or args, a missing ConfigMap or Secret key, a bad environment variable, a liveness probe that is too aggressive, or an OOMKilled container with exit code 137. A Pod's container spec cannot be edited in place. So I run kubectl get pod -o yaml to a file, fix the file, and replace it with kubectl replace --force. For a Deployment, I edit it directly. Finally I verify that the Pod is Running and Ready. If I am still stuck after the time box, I flag the task and move on.
keyPoints: Check the context and namespace first
Use describe for events, exit codes and probes; use logs --previous
Know the common causes: command, config references, probes, OOMKilled
Pods are mostly immutable: export, edit, replace --force; time-box and flag

subjective.question: Your dashboard shows a high deployment frequency, but lead time for changes is about four days. What could explain this, and how would you investigate and improve it?
subjective.answer: High frequency with long lead time usually means changes queue up before deployment, even though the deploy step itself is fast. Small config or automated commits may be inflating the frequency, while feature work sits in long-lived branches or waits days for review. I would break lead time into stages using timestamps: first commit to PR opened, PR opened to approved, merged to deployed. That shows where the time goes. Often review wait is the biggest share, followed by manual approval gates or a slow staging soak. The fixes follow from the data. Use smaller PRs and trunk-based development with feature flags. Set review SLAs or use pairing. Replace manual gates with automated checks, such as tests, policy and canary analysis. I would also check how frequency is counted, so that bot commits and rollbacks do not hide the real picture.
keyPoints: Fast deploys do not mean fast flow; work waits upstream
Break lead time into stages to find the bottleneck
Common causes: review wait, long-lived branches, manual gates
Fixes: small batches, trunk-based development, automated gates, honest counting

subjective.question: How would you structure the Terraform in your portfolio repository for dev, staging and production, and how would you show Terraform changes safely in pull requests?
subjective.answer: I would put reusable modules, such as network, cluster and registry, in a modules directory. Each environment gets a thin root configuration with its own variables and its own remote state, for example separate keys in an S3 backend with state locking, or separate HCP Terraform workspaces. I prefer separate root configurations over CLI workspaces for production, because the state, credentials and blast radius are fully isolated, and the differences are visible in code. On a pull request, CI runs terraform fmt -check, validate, tflint and a security scan. It then runs terraform plan and posts the plan summary as a PR comment, using read-only credentials through OIDC. Apply runs only after merge, from the saved plan, behind an environment approval for production. Provider versions are pinned and the lock file is committed. This shows a reviewer that infrastructure changes go through the same controls as application code.
keyPoints: Reusable modules plus a thin root configuration per environment
Separate remote state with locking per environment
Plan on the PR with read-only OIDC credentials; apply after merge with approval
fmt, validate, lint and scan checks; pinned providers and committed lock file

subjective.question: The CKA and CKAD run on a specific Kubernetes version stated by the Linux Foundation. How do you make your practice environment match the exam, and why does it matter?
subjective.answer: I check the current exam version on the official Linux Foundation and CNCF curriculum pages before I start. Then I build practice clusters on that minor version, using kubeadm on VMs for CKA, because the exam expects control-plane and upgrade work, and kind or minikube for quick CKAD drills. Version matters for several reasons. kubectl flags, API versions and default behaviour change across releases. Features graduate or get removed. The documentation you are allowed to use during the exam matches the exam version. If you practise on an old cluster, you may memorise deprecated fields, or miss newer topics that appear in the current curriculum. I also practise only with the allowed documentation sites, not blogs, and I finish with the Killer.sh sessions. Those run in an environment like the exam, so the version and the interface feel familiar on exam day.
keyPoints: Confirm the exam's Kubernetes version from the official curriculum
Practise with kubeadm for CKA and lightweight clusters for CKAD drills
API versions, flags and features change between releases
Use only the allowed docs, and finish with Killer.sh in an exam-like environment
